Methods

The research methods for this article consist of thirty-two in-depth key informant interviews, participant observation, and document analysis. In 2014 and 2015, I interviewed NGO representatives (six), Barangay officials (six), tribal leaders (three), leaders of palm oil cooperatives (five), palm oil laborers (ten), and various activists (two) involved in campaigns against extractive industries on Palawan. Most interviews were two to three hours long and the sample was purposeful, involving referrals by knowledgeable others. Most interviews were conducted in Tagalog in the case area of Biluan, southern Palawan, in the town proper and lowland, coastal sitios (villages). With the exception of major public figures, all respondent names and locations were given pseudonyms.

Introduction

I n Southeast Asia, the role and legitimacy of civil society has been challenged in the context of new environmental governance regimes overlapping with deepening commodity production in contested frontiers (Tsing 2003; Barney 2009; Li 2014). In an era of declining donor aid and deregulation (Malhotra 2000), nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) have negotiated new objectives in line with intensifying local aspirations that emerge at the intersection of commodity production and governance (S. Singh 2012). In these interstitial spaces, NGOs and their allies have reflected on the legitimacy of their advocacy and interventions in terms of how local farmers view the contrasting benefits being promised from shifting governance and commodity production regimes. In various countries, NGOs have mounted difficult campaigns as their advocacy for indigenous tenure and livelihood is complicated by politically and economically contested partnerships between indigenous leaders, their own people, and extractive industries (B € uscher and Davidov 2013)-political alliances that reconfigure as contrasting identities, values, and authority become entangled and realigned for strategic interests and outcomes (Horowitz 2012).

The political objectives of transnational NGO campaigns-and their motives in deploying assumptions and symbolic images of indigenous peoples for specific goals (Conklin and Graham 1995; de la Cade ~ na and Starn 2007)-are increasingly challenged in the context of intensifying agrarian change defined by associated land grabs, deforestation, commodity production, and the governmental politics that legitimize extractivism (McCarthy, Vel, and Suraya 2012; Gururani and Vandergeest 2014). At the governance and extraction nexus, NGOs now face difficult decisions about how to exercise campaigns with the sustained moral legitimacy from an earlier era (Bryant 2005), as local people weigh livelihood options between the oft-intangible benefits of governance and the seemingly tangible benefits of extractivism. The moral authority of NGOs 'doing good' is now subject to question as extractive industries forge new commodity spaces (Tsing 2003; Moore 2009).

data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF GEOGRAPHERS

data.Keywords Plus: MARRIAGE; GENDER; GEOGRAPHIES; MASCULINITIES; RELIGION; VIOLENCE; WORK; LEH
data.text: This article uses ethnographic research conducted in Bemni, a village in Uttarakhand, north India, to make a distinctive contribution to geographies of love. Building on fieldwork with young people between sixteen and thirty years old who work as mediators or advisors in Bemni in relation to premarital or extramarital affairs, I argue that practices and narratives of romantic love are strongly implicated in processes of social change. In the rural Uttarakhandi context, young people often use the idea of being specialists in love to bolster their own position and resolve conflict. I also provide a counterpoint to geographical youth research stressing the reactionary politics of marginalized young people. I show instead that in a region relatively unaffected by strong religious- or caste-based conflict, youth are able to ameliorate rather than exacerbate violent action, even while they reproduce aspects of caste, class, and gender inequality.

Bemni, Uttarakhand

Uttarakhand was established as a separate state in 2000. It contained approximately 10 million people in 2011. Uttarakhand ranks near the bottom of the table of states in India in terms of infant mortality, life expectancy, literacy, death rate, birth rate, percapita income, and electrification of villages. Poor governance, especially a poor record of policing, exacerbates problems of economic growth and human development.

Two thirds of the Uttarakhand population are upper caste (Brahmins and Kshatriyas, also called general castes [GCs]), with 17 percent scheduled caste (SC) in 2011 (Office of the Registrar General [ORG] 2011). There is close overlap between people's caste status and access to land, social contacts, and salaried work in Uttarakhand (see Dyson 2008, 2010). Strong gender norms are characteristic of rural Uttarakhand such that women are not expected to engage in paid work outside the household. In other cases they are permitted to do so but only in a narrow range of areas, such as teaching and work in government nurseries (Klenk 2010). In addition, cultural prescriptions surround the sexual activity of girls and young women. In rural areas in particular, people typically regard a girl or woman entering sexual relations prior to marriage or outside the conjugal relationship as having transgressed social mores (see Chowdhry 2004).

Youth in Bemni

Several young people said that they had become downhearted as a result of rising unemployment. At the same time, many reflected on their position in more positive terms. They said that they constituted a new generation in Bemni of youth ( yuwa or jawaani ). Until the 1980s, young people married in their midteens, moving directly from childhood ( bachpan ) to adulthood ( bare ). Rising education among men and later women, however, led to a delay in marriage. By 2012, the average age of young women at marriage was around twenty-three and for young men around twenty-seven (author's household census 2012). This shift created a new period of 'youth' that had not previously existed in the village. In Bemni, youth ( jawaani ) is commonly imagined as a period that lasts from puberty until marriage. For men, the notion of youth has extended still further. As many men and some young women continue education into their late twenties and even thirties, and after getting married, the category of youth has become partially detached from its former association with a premarital period.

Young people also maintained that a social revolution in India associated with improved communication, rising education, and increasing understanding of citizenship meant that youth are able to serve wider society. Introduction

I was walking though the village of Bemni in March 2012 when Rajendra Singh ran around a corner and almost knocked me off the path. Rajendra was in his late twenties and referred to himself as unemployed, although he was a small farmer and he earned money working on government projects in the village.

'No, no . . . , ' he said, 'There is a man who has been having an extramarital affair. I am going to help sort out the situation.' He stopped as I looked at him. 'What can I do?' Hethen went on. 'I have got to sort it out ( theek karna hai ).'

Negotiations surrounding 'affairs' was a topic that constantly emerged during my social research in the north Indian village of Bemni. In 2012 I would often be sitting outside the small room in which I stayed in the village and find myself being drawn into conversations about the infidelity of a married man in Bemni or the intimate relations that had developed between two college students (see also Parry 2001; Mody 2002; Smith 2011). I soon came to understand the importance of premarital elopements and marital affairs in social discussion and the particular significance that the concept of love (the English word) had developed in social reflection on these events. What also became increasingly evident was that a self-styled generation of young people between sixteen and thirty years old were important players in efforts to understand and resolve love and affairs, not through reactionary efforts to police marriage or romantic intimacy but at the more mundane level of seeking to resolve the issue at hand: 'sort it out' ( theek karna hai ) as Rajendra expressed the idea. By investigating the role that educated unemployed or underemployed youth in Bemni play in mediating and advising on disputes over affairs, I seek in this article to inform geographical scholarship on love and youth.

I contribute to research on love in geography by showing how practices and narratives of love are closely intertwined with processes of social reproduction and social change in a region of north India. I draw particular attention to the role of young people as interpreters of love and as agents of some degree of social transformation (cf. Smith 2009; Pratt 2012; Morrison, Johnston, and Longhurst 2013). The article also makes a more specific contribution to geographical research on marginalized youth. I argue that educated unand underemployed young people engage inventively and somewhat constructively with notions of love and intimacy, even in the face of social disappointment. My account of youth also serves as a specific counterpoint to studies that have focused on the violent and reactionary behavior of marginalized youth in South Asia with respect to notions of love and intimacy (Chowdhry 2007; Smith 2009, 2012).

Love

It is possible to discern two distinct but overlapping strands of work on love within contemporary human geography (see also Morrison, Johnston, and Longhurst 2013). The first strand examines how love, in the sense of a powerful feeling of attachment typically involving strong romantic affection, has been implicated in social and political processes in different sites and at various periods in history. Such work includes consideration of how political organizations shape hegemonic visions of love (Smith 2009, 2012), accounts of the affective process through which scholars might develop an 'ethics of care' (Lawson 2007), analysis of migrant women who maintain strong affective ties across national boundaries (Pratt 2012), and discussion of the social and political processes through which people develop various types of 'nonhuman' love-for pets (Nast 2006), objects (Geoghegan and Hess 2015), and landscapes (Wylie 2009), for example.

Youth

The article contributes to geographies of youth through highlighting the constructive everyday social action of young people in north India, even in the context of unemployment and underemployment. Young people have become agents of change in various parts of the contemporary Global South (Ansell 2016). This reflects a social revolution occurring across large parts of this region. First, in many parts of Latin America, Africa, and Asia since the early 2000s, the spread of new communication technologies has heightened young people's understanding of dynamics occurring outside their local areas. Mobile phone ownership has increased rapidly, and an increasing percentage of the population have access to the Internet (Doron and Jeffrey 2013). Second, a spread of education has provided people with basic literacy and numeracy skills and also in many cases instilled new aspirations, as evident in South Asia and subSaharan Africa. Third, there has been a spread of citizenship norms across the Global South, in particular, for example, through school textbooks and via the media, nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), and government pronouncements.

Opinions on Resource Development in Dagestan

To evaluate the potential impact of hydrocarbon development on the rural residents of Dagestan, in the summer of 2010 two of the article's coauthors conducted a survey ( N = 956) among residents living near Dagestan's Caspian Sea coast. The survey consisted of a structured questionnaire with twenty-three questions that queried respondents on the following subjects: demographic information such as age, gender, and educational level; baseline economic statistics such as employment status, socioeconomic condition, and migration preferences; opinions on the economic situation in Dagestan; and prospects for expanded oil and gas production (Eldarov et al. 2011). Broadly stated, the survey had two aims to (1) evaluate economic and environmental conditions in rural Dagestan; and (2) gauge residents' positions on nascent oil and gas development in Dagestan's coastal region.

The survey used convenience sampling at fourteen rural locations. This article considers public opinion in the republic of Dagestan on the expansion of hydrocarbon production in the Russian sector of the Caspian Sea. The article reports the findings of a survey ( N = 956) conducted in 2010 in fourteen rural locations in the republic. Overall, respondents uniformly oppose the proposed expansion of offshore oil and gas production in the Russian sector of the Caspian Sea, seeing little economic benefit from this development and expressing concern about the environmental consequences. These findings resonate with work in geography on resource peripheries and development alternatives available in these locations. Key Words: Caspian Sea, environment, oil and gas production, public opinion survey, Russia.

Oil and Gas Production in the Russian Sector of the Caspian Sea

The transition away from communism-an economic system associated with top-down planning, an overweighting toward the military and armaments in industrial production, and single-industry settlements-consolidated Russia's dependency on oil and natural gas exports (Kotkin 2001). The decline in world oil prices from their peaks during the 1970s weakened the USSR's economic position during the mid- and late 1980s and is commonly viewed as one of the contributing factors to the country's breakup. In post-Soviet Russia, the devaluation of the ruble in 1998spurred domestic production and consumption in the broader economy, although much of this growth was subsidized through rents from natural resource extraction. Gustafson (2012) argues that the state is now even more dependent on rents to fund its budget; Russia's current situation can be characterized as a dual economy, with its reliance on natural resources, while failing to diversify into other growth sectors (Bradshaw 2008). Some parts of the Russian Federation, including resource-rich areas in the country's north and east, have benefited disproportionately from the extraction and export of resources such as oil, gas, and timber.

data.Article Title: Waves of rural brides: Female marriage migration in China
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE ASSOCIATION OF AMERICAN GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: China; marriage; migration; women
data.Keywords Plus: PUERTO-RICAN WOMEN; POST-MAO CHINA; GENDER; INEQUALITY; MOBILITY; FAMILY; MARKET
data.text: Conventional views on marriage migration consider it primarily family-related and portray female marriage migrants as mostly passive, tied movers. Marriage as an economic strategy is seldom studied. We argue that a structural framework enables analysis of the complexities underlying female marriage migration, stressing institutional, economic, and sociocultural factors that impose constraints on and provide opportunities for women's mobility. A review of the historical and social roles of marriage in China shows that its transactional nature undermines women's status but offers disadvantaged women an opportunity to achieve social and economic mobility. Based on statistical analyses of a one-percent sample of China's 1990 Census, we show that peasant women in poor areas are constrained by their institutional positions, rural origins, and low education and status, shutting them out from cities and the urban labor market. Yet in the face of these constraints, many women, in exchange for economic opportunities and agricultural work, pursue migration by marrying into rural areas in more developed regions and by moving over long distances. These rural brides in well-defined migration streams are testimony to the roles of social and kinship networks and of brokers in the marriage market. Men who are socially and/or economically disadvantaged but locationally privileged are able to draw brides from afar. Despite the neoclassical overtone of the notion that marriage migration is an economic strategy, we argue that a structural approach is necessary for understanding the complexities underlying female migration and for explaining the recent phenomenon of long-distance female marriage migration in China.

Empirical Analysis

Recent census and population surveys in China have inquired as to the primary 'reason of migration.' Both the 1987 one-percent Sample Survey and the 1990 Census offered nine options for reasons of migration: 'job transfer,' 'job assignment,' 'industry/business,' 'seek help from friends/relatives,' 'retirement,' 'joining family,' 'marriage,' 'study/training,' and 'other.' 13 The empirical analysis in this paper mainly employs a one-percent village-level sample of the 1990 Census 14 (SSB 1994). It contains information about every individual in all households of the sampled village-level units (villages, towns, or urban neighborhoods in cities). The 1990 Census defines a migrant as an individual five years or older whose usual place of residence on July 1, 1985 was in a different city, town, or county than that on July 1, 1990. Although this definition underestimates the actual volume of migration by excluding multiple moves, return migrants, migrants younger than five years old, and moves within the same city, town, or county, the census remains by far the most comprehensive source of

migration data in China. W e will first describe the pattern of female migration, then analyze the characteristics of these migrants and their husbands, and, third, investigate the spatial features of this migration. Assessing the Determinants of Marriage Migration

Theaboveanalyses provide general support for the importance of institutional, economic, and sociocultural factors in shaping female marriage migration. They also give weight to the argument that women in disadvantaged positions are more likely to pursue marriage as a strategy to achieve migration and to improve their social and economicmobility. In what follows, we further exami ne the effects of the above factors on interprovincial female marriage migration, using a logistic regression analysis in an effort to assess the relative significance of the factors thus far investigated.

The dependent variable in our analysis takes the value of 1 for marriage migration and 0 for other types of migration. There are four sets of independent variables variously referencing individual- and provincial-level data (T able 4). Spatial Pattern of Interprovincial Female Marriage Migration

Given the evidence thus far presented, we would expect that interprovincial female marriage migration would exhibit distinct spatial patterns. Indeed, marriage was the most important reason for female outmigration in twelve provinces, 18 with the highest proportions in the southwestern and poorer provinces of Yunnan (72.7 percent), Guizhou (71.2 percent), Sichuan (48.6 percent) and Guangxi (42.0 percent). Although the volume of outmigration varied among these four provinces, together they accounted for more than half (50.5 percent) of the total interprovincial female marriage migrants, forming a spatial core of sending provinces. For fourteen provinces, 19 marriage was the most important reason for female inmigration. The eastern coastal provinces of Hebei (63.0 percent), Jiangsu (54.5 percent), Fujian (50.6 percent) and Zhejiang (47.2 percent), as well as Anhui (59.1 percent) in central China, had the highest proportions of female marriage inmigrants. Most of these receiving provinces are economically more developed (see Figure 1), which is a major factor of marriagemigration destination. The three centrally administered municipalities of Beijing (11.3 percent), Tianjin (10.5 percent) and Shanghai (5.1 percent), on the other hand, had the lowest proportions of female marriage inmigrants outside of Tibet. Introduction

R esearch on women's mobility has proliferated recently, as more attention is given to the role of gender in the migration process (Chant and Radcliffe 1992; Pedraza 1991; Ellis et al. 1996). The neoclassical perspective emphasizes the economic rationality of migrants, and argues that women as well as men move in response to regional differentials in economic opportunities (e.g., Thadani and T odaro 1979). While economic opportunities are indeed a primary factor in the migration of men and women, studies using the neoclassical perspective tend to overlook the institutional, historical, and sociocultural complexities of human movements (Chant and Radcliffe 1992). Often neglecting the role of gender, they consider female migrants a homogeneous group and ignore the complex realities and constraints faced by women as a whole and female migrants in particular. The structural approach, on the other hand, explains female migration in relation to historical transformations of regional and national economies, the gendered segmentation of the labor market, and sociocultural constraints (e.g., Bennholdt-Thompson 1984; Bourque and Key 1981; Caplan 1985;

Moser 1981; Roberts 1978; Sassen-Koob 1983). This approach emphasizes the role of gender in the spatial organization of production, and the relations between production and genderdifferentiated migrations (Radcliffe 1991). Focusi n g on migration decisionmaking, the household-strategies approach emphasizes migration as a means of human-resource allocation andrisk diversification, mediated by the gendered division of labor and power relations within the household (e.g., W ood 1981).

These theoretical approaches are testimony to the complex and multilayered nature of the processes that govern female migration. Despite the dominance of the neoclassical economic framework in migration research, recent studies of female migration and the role of gender in migration have emphasized the structural approach. The latter, scholars argue, facilitates the incorporation of historical and sociocultural perspectives into understanding the interlinkages between migration and gender in two ways: by examining the constraints and opportunities that influence the choices of prospective migrants, and by evaluating the role of individual agency in

Marriage and Female Migration

Marriage, one of the most important events in the life cycle, is also an institution that imposes economic and sociocultural constraints on both women and men. In most societies, women are s u b j e c t t o a more demanding set of gendered expectations and responsibilities associated with marriage, and with their roles as wives and mothers. One of these expectations is that women will move at marriage to live with their husbands. Another related expectation is that women will follow their spouses when they migrate, mostly to support the latter's career development. Studies based on developing countries often consider women as passive, tied movers within marriage, viewing migration as a result of, but not the motive for, marriage (Bonney and Love 1991; Fincher 1993; Houstoun et al. 1984; Oberai and Singh 1983; Rosenzweig and Stark 1989; Thadani and T odaro 1984; Watts 1983). Wives in developed countries, likewise, are under considerable pressure to orient their roles around their husbands' career concerns (Bonney and Love 1991).

Women, Marriage, and Migration in China

In China, marriage is a social institution that directly connotes pragmatic and economic values, such as continuation of the family line (W olf 1972), increase in family labor resources (Croll 1984), formation of networks (Ebrey 1991), provision of old-age security (Potter and Potter 1990), and transfer of economic resources (Croll 1984). Historically, the labor, fertility, and person of Chinese women have been considered a property exchangeable in transactions, most notably through marriages (Croll 1984). Under the patrilocal tradition, daughters would eventually move out and join the husband's family, adding to its labor resources. As ground feeders, crows need open space for foraging, but they also need trees for nesting and roosting. Conflicts between corvids and people centered on the former's damage to agriculture. DANIEL W. GADE

abstract. The American crow ( Corvus brachyrhynchos ) falls into a category of wild organisms, called 'synanthropes,' that have developed an affinity for, or dependency on, human interventions in the landscape. The distribution and numbers of crows in North America east of the Mississippi River have been largely tied to the anthropogenic fragmentation of the forest. As ground feeders, crows need open space for foraging, but they also need trees for nesting and roosting. Conflicts between corvids and people centered on the former's damage to agriculture. Both Native American peoples and Euro-American settlers sought to thwart corvine preference for maize through a series of ingenious measures. After  rural concern about corvine depredations greatly diminished. The appearance of large winter roosts in cities shifted the conflict with crows. Like humans, crows have undergone change, and their synanthropic character can be seen as fundamental to their biogeography. Keywords: crow, maize, North America, synanthropy.

Crow Distributions and Past Processes

The continent-wide presence of the American crow places it as one of the most ubiquitous native avian species today (Figure  ). The same cannot be said for the past. The vegetation shifts that corresponded with the advance and retreat of the Pleistocene ice sheet affected crow distribution and numbers. Closed forest cover did not favor its spread, although lightning fires, blowdowns, beaver activity, and forest blight created local or regional openings that crows could have occupied until the canopy regenerated. Acorns, wild fruits and seeds, insects, eggs, and birds nourished prehuman crow populations. With the arrival of Homo sapiens on the North American continent the crow, preadapted to environmental change, benefited from the considerable power of paleotechnic humans to transform the surface of the earth. The open habitats that Paleo-Indian (  ,  - b.c. ) hunters and gatherers with the use of fire facilitated hunting, but they also encouraged crows.

The Microscale: Crows in the Cornfield

Corvine affinity for maize made the cornfield the stage on which man and bird played out a morality tale of the yeoman versus the feathered trickster. Maize offers omnivorous crows what it offers humans: a concentrated dose of carbohydrates and some protein. From the perspective of foraging efficiency, maize filched from the field at certain times of the year provides higher-quality nutrients with less expenditure of calories than does food obtained by predation or scavenging. A stout, long-

ish bill that can sink  centimeters into the soil equips the crow to efficiently dig up kernels. A pouch behind its tongue allows for the efficient transport of kernels to feed its young and itself. Because the crow does not scratch up the ground with its feet like a gallinaceous bird, subtle clues must enable the crow to know just where to find buried kernels that have not yet germinated (Barrows  ,  - ). Ravages of crows in a maize patch peak about ten days after planting. By then the seeds have germinated and sent up a plumular leaf above the soil. The crow pulls the radicle from the ground, exposing the seed swelled with moisture, and snaps it off.

data.Article Title: Toward Postsecular Feminism: Intersectionality and the Religious Subjectivities of Women Migrant Workers in China
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: feminism; intersectionality; postsecularity; religious agency; women migrant workers
data.Keywords Plus: RURAL-URBAN MIGRATION; GENDER; AGENCY; POWER
data.text: This article investigates the subjectivities of Christian women migrant workers within the context of China's social transformation, characterized by the interactive advancement of global capitalism, rural-to-urban migration, and Christian fever. Despite the burgeoning literature on women migrant workers in global capitalism within geographical scholarship, there has been less focus on women migrants' religious subjectivity and agency. Drawing on empirical research on the intersectional experiences of women migrant workers, this article seeks to advance a postsecular feminism by bringing intersectionality into conversation with debates on postsecularity and gender inequalities. First, we examine the intersectional matrix of domination imposed through state power, Chinese patriarchal culture, and the gendered and class-based disciplinary labor regime under global capitalism, which serves as an ontological condition in which women migrants' religious subjectivities form and are shaped. Second, we use intersectionality to help understand the process of becoming and a relation of emergence, wherein multiple agential qualities of women migrants-manifesting as counterpatriarchal subjects or through docile, tolerant, self-sacrificial, and pious femininity-arise at the intersections of religion, class, gender, and family. We therefore argue that postsecular feminist critique needs to carefully consider the patterns and diverse effects of intersectionality where both domination and religious agency are engendered and interwoven.

The Study

This article is based on a project that examines the religious subjectivity of Christian rural migrant workers in Shenzhen, China. It deploys an intersectional analytical frame to explore how migrant workers ' religion, gender, age, and class subjectivities mutually shape one another. The field work was conducted between 2014 and 2018 in Shenzhen ' s nine Protestant churches (including state-sanctioned

churches and house or underground churches). We interviewed fifty-two Christian migrant workers (thirty-two males and twenty females) and eight leaders, pastors, and preachers. Although this article primarily draws on the experiences of twenty women migrant workers between the ages of eighteen and forty-six, it also considers the perspectives of male Christians and their non-Christian family members or workmates to provide a relational account of gender subjectivities. The churches that migrant workers attend can be classified as either state-sanctioned or house or underground churches, the latter of which operate without the recognition of the state. The epistemological style of the former is often labeled as evangelism, characterized by a more intellectual and text-centric understanding of Christianity. Although some evangelist churches also operate in an underground manner, the house churches in the city organized by rural Christians often embrace Pentecostal styles that are more emotional and practice-centric (Huang 2014). An Intersectional Approach to Postsecular Feminism

Despite the acknowledgment of various power structures that shape and condition the subjectivities of women migrants, relatively little research has focused on how religion interacts with migrants ' constitution of gender subjectivities, and in particular, how religious resources and ethics enable women migrants to negotiate these multiple inequalities. Migrants ' religious lives not only allow them to imagine alternative subjectivities beyond those normalized by material and discursive power relations, but also provide support and a sense of community that enables them to materially and emotionally settle in new socioeconomic environments (Silvey 2013). The extent to which women ' s subjectivity and agency can be conveyed through and supported by religious ethics and piety, however, is debatable (Mahmood 2005; Braidotti 2008; Vasilaki 2016; Cloke et al. 2019). Religion might open up new spaces for the restoration of spiritual and sacred sources of agency for migrant women and thus reconstruct their subaltern subjectivities, or reproduce the gender- or class-based hierarchies that can thwart their agency (Gao and Qian 2019). Therefore, attention to religious practices can enable a more nuanced understanding of women migrants ' gender subjectivities as malleable and culturally conditioned.

This transformation has not only produced a more flexible and intensive sexual and class exploitation of migrant women, but also opened up the possibility for the formation of new forms of female subjectivity (C. Y. Zhang 2014). Existing discourses in scholarship tend to link Chinese rural migrant women ' s subjectivity to the power of state socialism, global capitalism, and familial patriarchy, which collectively produce the institutionalized domination over rural women migrants (Pun 2005; Ong 2007; Jacka 2013; Gaetano 2015). This line of thought normally situates migrant women ' s subjectivity in a domination -resistance dichotomy, implying that women ' s agency solely or primarily relies on oppositional practices and the

production of countersubjectivities. For example, Pun (2005) described rural migrant women ' as a specifically Chinese subaltern, [which] embodies the dual process of domination and resistance and is marked by various forms of collaboration, transgression, and defiance that together come to make up its complex, dissident, and heterogeneous subjects ' (16). They therefore might overlook the variegation of women migrant workers ' subjectivities and agency, and largely neglect how religion might interact with women migrant workers ' subject formations.

Women Migrants Under Global Capitalism

The last two decades have witnessed the burgeoning of feminist studies of migration, with focuses on not only women ' s specific migration patterns, experiences, and subjectivities but also how gender interacts with the wider spatial politics of difference, mobility, and labor in an era of globalization (Willis and Brenda 2002; Silvey 2004, 2013; Gaetano and Brenda 2010). This line of scholarship has shifted from studying women migrants as a distinct research category to studying the gendering of migration, and in particular how gender as a system of practices or ideology permeates every aspect of migration experiences. Instead of viewing gender as a dichotomous variable that shapes patterns of migration, critical feminist migration researchers argue that gender is better understood as a constitutive element of migration, given that ' the structures that precipitate migration flows and shape the economic experiences of all migrants are [themselves] gendered ' (Nawyn 2010, 142).

data.Article Title: Circular migration and the spaces of cultural assertion
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE ASSOCIATION OF AMERICAN GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: consumption; India; migration; regional modernities; work
data.Keywords Plus: RURAL LABOR; CONSUMPTION; MODERNITY
data.text: Harnessing primary and secondary evidence from India, our essay conceptualizes the cultural dynamics of migration. In so doing, it demonstrates the incompleteness of standard marginalist and Marxist accounts of labor circulation. As a corrective, we examine the linkages between culture, politics, space, and labor mobility and offer a way to think about them by building on poststructural critiques of development and postcolonial theories of migrant subjectivity. The proverbial compression of space-time not only has made extralocal work more viable for members of proletarianized groups but, more importantly, has allowed them to transfer their experiences of new ways of being into local contexts through acts of consumption and labor deployment that can become elements of a Gramscian counterhegemonic praxis. We argue that the possibility of this sort of body politics compels not merely a critique of the modernization paradigm that has organized classical migration studies but, more profoundly, a reassessment of the way we understand modernity itself We advocate an approach that provincializes the Eurowest and foregrounds the existence of pluritopic regional modernities.

Field Sites and Fieldwork

In giving empirical substance to our theoretical arguments on migration and modernity, we focus on two categories of subordinated groups in rural India: tribals and dalits. 13 Wedraw evidence from secondary materials, as well as fieldwork conducted by the authors between 1993 and 2001 in the Kheda and Baroda districts of Gujarat, Tiruvannamalai District of Tamil Nadu, and Midnapore District of West Bengal (Figure 1).

Abriefnoteonthegenesisofthisarticleseemsnecessary. Our initial projects were independent evaluations of the distributive and political impacts of development programs in two different agrarian settings (Gidwani studied how the introduction of a large surface-irrigation scheme transformed agrarian social relations in central Gujarat, particularly the bargaining power and political consciousness of low caste workers; Sivaramakrishnan examined how the introduction of joint forest management (JFM) schemes in eastern West Bengal intersected with regional tribal politics, and whether JFM marked a devolution in state control or a new form of governmentality). Although the link between circular migration and changes in the cultural assertiveness of subordinated caste and tribal groups was not the explicit focus of our initial research programs, the parallels between these geographically dispersed research sites soon became evident to us. Recent studies of migration by geographers and anthropologists have sought to expose the ideological moorings of the social categories that organize developmentalist understandings of time and space within modernization theory, its colonial antecedents, and its post-Fordist cognates. Contrary to the behavioralism of marginalist theories of migration and the structuralism of Marxist theories, new migration scholars have sought to restore agency to migrants by showing, through biographical and ethnographic research, how migrants apprehend, negotiate, and transform the social structures that impinge on their lives (Halfacree and Boyle 1993; Lowe 1996; Stack 1996; Mills 1999; Lawson 2000; McHugh2000).Inshort, although structuration theories, building on Saussurean semiotics and Marxist dialectics, have been around for at least two decades (exemplars include Bourdieu 1977 and Giddens 1984) and have offered sophisticated insights on the spatiotemporal recursivity of structure and agency, their empirical deployment within population geography and migration research is relatively recent.

Introduction

*Department of Geography and Institute of Global Studies, University of Minnesota ** Department of Anthropology, University of Washington

T his essay examines the relationship between circular migration, identity politics, and livelihood strategies against the backdrop of agrarian change in India. We consider the cultural dimensions of labor deployment and mobility in order both to evaluate and to supplement the practical reason embodied in the livelihood strategies of migrants. 1 Although neither migration nor its understanding as a material and symbolic activity is new, we suggest that what is new and important in terms of agrarian social relations is the intensity and rate at which labor, goods, and meanings are now able to circulate through space. In many parts of India, the forces of modernity have saturated the countryside to such an extent that semiotic and spatial dualisms that identify the ''rural'' as the realm of production and tradition and the ''urban'' as the realm of consumption and modernity now seem anachronistic. 2 At the same time, it is quite evident that the erasure of boundaries and the multiplication of spatial linkages have not followed a uniform pattern. As Watts (1992, 6) observes, ''[G]lobality and locality are inextricably linked, but through complex mediations and configurations of 'traditional society'; the nonlocal processes driving capital mobility are always experienced, constituted, and mediated locally. . . [through] a working and reworking of modernity.''

This underscores the point that villagers and villages have become cosmopolitan in myriad ways. In the process, they have become acquainted with worlds of goods and significations that carry all the baggage that accompany modernformsofdesire. 3 Butremarkably, these same forms of desire, and the consumptions of modernity they entail, can occasionally contain emancipatory potential for groups subordinated by place-specific relations of hierarchy. We are referring here to ideologies of class, caste, ethnicity, and gender that slot agents into normalized roles or identities and qualify their agency by making these roles appear as given-that is, as historically and spatially invariant. The primary purpose of this essay is to discuss migration and identity politics in terms of the renegotiation of group identities at the level of caste and tribal differences. 4

ADiscontented Look at Standard Models of Migration

Shreshta (1988, 183) suggests that five types of modeling approaches have shaped migration studies since Ravenstein's influential 1885 article, ''The Laws of Migration,'' formally inaugurated the field. They include: economic/behavioral models premised on utility maximization by migrants seeking better economic opportunities elsewhere; ecodemographic ''push'' models that identify population pressure and diminishing returns to labor as the primary causes of migration; spatial attraction or gravity models that emphasize urban ''pull'' factors, compensating for the rising transaction costs imposed on migration decisions by distance; anthroposociological models that highlight the importance of group networks and modernizing influences on migration; and neoMarxist dependency models that view uneven development and the articulation of precapitalist with capitalist modes of production as the root cause of migration.

Recent studies of migration by geographers and anthropologists have sought to expose the ideological moorings of the social categories that organize developmentalist understandings of time and space within modernization theory, its colonial antecedents, and its post-Fordist cognates. Contrary to the behavioralism of marginalist theories of migration and the structuralism of Marxist theories, new migration scholars have sought to restore agency to migrants by showing, through biographical and ethnographic research, how migrants apprehend, negotiate, and transform the social structures that impinge on their lives (Halfacree and Boyle 1993; Lowe 1996; Stack 1996; Mills 1999; Lawson 2000; McHugh2000).Inshort, although structuration theories, building on Saussurean semiotics and Marxist dialectics, have been around for at least two decades (exemplars include Bourdieu 1977 and Giddens 1984) and have offered sophisticated insights on the spatiotemporal recursivity of structure and agency, their empirical deployment within population geography and migration research is relatively recent.

data.Article Title: Nature, Agriculture, and Black Space-Making in Serra dos Tapes, Brazil
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: Black geographies; marronage; nature; oral history; quilombos
data.Keywords Plus: GEOGRAPHY
data.text: In this work, I focus on how Quilombolas in southern Brazil create territorial conceptions and practices. Contemporary quilombos constitute complex forms of social organization composed of different collectivities and political subjectivities whose ancestors resisted colonial slavery by creating free communities in urban and rural spaces. In Serra dos Tapes, rural Black Quilombola communities have struggled with geographic dispossession, socioeconomic inequalities, and everyday racism. At the same time, they have created space-making practices, thinking of their territory as a lived space. Agriculture plays an essential role in this process, articulating knowledge, creativity, and a unique relationship to nature. Black people in Serra dos Tapes consider the cultivation and their relation to nature meaningful in the constitution of their identities, food security, and autonomy. Results of this study were gained through the life history method. Taking Quilombolas' practices, narratives, and trajectories seriously in their political and epistemological importance, this article aims to offer some insights to advance discussions concerning the entanglement of race, nature, and environment within geographical studies.

Serra Dos Tapes

Serra dos Tapes is a region in the state of Rio Grande do Sul, southern Brazil, which covers the mountainous areas of the municipalities of Pelotas, S ~ ao Lourenc ¸o do Sul, Morro Redondo, Canguc ¸u, Turuc ¸u, and Arroio do Padre (Salamoni et al. 2021). Currently, in this mountain range, there are agricultural colonies of German and Italian origin represented by family farmers -also known as Colonos -in varied socioeconomic situations (Salamoni and Waskievicz 2013). There are also many rural Black communities, some of them presently recognized by the Brazilian state as quilombo remnants (Pinheiro 2014).

Part of the history of this region -which has the city of Pelotas as its main urban center -dates back to Portuguese colonization throughout the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries and to colonial slavery employed in cattle raising and jerky meat ( charque ) production (Gutierrez 2001). The headquarters of colonial properties, and the main economic activities, were located in the lowlands, as the flat terrain facilitated the raising of cattle and the installation of jerky farms, or charqueadas (Salamoni and Waskievicz 2013). In the vicinity of the flatlands are the sierras -which officially belonged to Portuguese landowners but were not often explored by them -defined by the undulating relief and dense vegetation. Introduction

A fter the abolition of slavery in 1888, Black people in Brazil continued to carve out spaces of resistance through art, religion, agriculture, and political and intellectual mobilizations. Those practices have challenged the antiBlack racism that relates symbiotically to space production in the Brazilian context (Campos 2010; Bledsoe 2015). The current multiplicity and ubiquity of rural Black Quilombola communities in southern Brazil, a region popularly noted for German and Italian colonization, invites us to reflect on how agriculture and the relationship with nature can be meaningful in the construction and consolidation of Black spaces facing reality marked by systematic dispossessions and everyday racism.

Contemporary quilombos constitute complex forms of social organization composed of different collectivities and political subjectivities whose ancestors resisted colonial slavery by creating free communities in urban and rural spaces. 1 In Serra dos Tapes, these Black communities view agriculture as a means of connecting with their ancestors and as their primary form of social, economic, cultural, and territorial reproduction (Gois and Miguel 2019). In this article, I direct my attention to how Quilombolas in southern Brazil create territorial conceptions and practices. More specifically, I observe how agriculture - not only as a set of techniques but as an articulation of knowledge, practices, and creativity -assumes, in the quilombo, importance in the creation of spaces that oppose the logic of domination and exploitation of nature, as well as in the development of nonhegemonic territorialities (Sodr  e 2002; Escobar 2008). For this, I focus on the histories and narratives of Quilombolas in the Alto do Caix ~ ao community. Through the method of life histories (Riley and Harvey 2007; Scott 2019, 2020), I acknowledge the political and epistemological significance of the trajectories of people in Quilombo Alto do Caix ~ ao, as well as the narratives and interpretations they elaborate on in their personal and collective events and on the reality in which they live.

To advance the discussion, I rely on the reflections of intellectuals who contribute to the growth of Black geographies as a political, theoretical, and epistemological stance and as spatial practices, experiences, and expressions (B. Nascimento 1985, 2018, 2021; Sodr  e 2002; McKittrick 2006, 2013; Bledsoe 2015, 2017; Scott 2019, 2020 ). Scott (2020), for instance, helps me reflect on how personal and familial narratives navigating within Black communities can inform about space-making processes and their specificities within a particular social context. In Brazil, anti-Black discourses and practices inaugurated during slavery (Bledsoe 2015) persisted in the postabolition era under new forms (Oliveira et al. 2017; Fischer, Grinberg, and Mattos 2018), such as residential segregation in cities (Campos 2012), religious intolerance (Teixeira and Ratts 2012), and police violence and criminalization of Black spaces (Campos 2010). data.Article Title: Translocal Precarity: Labor and Social Reproduction in Cambodia
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: Cambodia; labor; migration; precarity; social reproduction
data.Keywords Plus: MIGRATION; POLITICS; AGE; VULNERABILITY; DISPOSSESSION; EMPLOYMENT; HOUSEHOLD; GEOGRAPHY; MIGRANTS; PLACE
data.text: Many people in the Global South have left behind rural homes in search of employment in urban and transnational labor markets often defined by precarious work. Employment is insecure, uncertain, and temporary, and for transnational migrants, there is the constant risk of deportation. Although geographers have studied such migrant precarity, there is an increasing interest in its translocal dimensions, particularly related to how precarious work travels home and affects left-behind family members. This scholarship, however, tends to assume that precarity arises primarily in the spaces of production. Drawing on twenty months of ethnographic fieldwork in rural Cambodia, we argue that precarity simultaneously emerges from the challenges of social reproduction faced by kin in rural communities. As such, we further develop the concept of translocal precarity to capture the fragility of social reproduction strategies that migrant households employ across space. Translocal precarity is the looming threat that family members' efforts to support one another might fall apart due to the instability of urban labor markets in tandem with a lack of sustaining infrastructures in rural areas. Our argument advances geographic scholarship on precarity by explaining how it is experienced across the translocal relations that connect the productive and reproductive labor of household members living in different locations.

Method

To analyze translocal precarity, we draw on findings from broader ethnographic projects conducted by each author. Between 2013 and 2017, we each carried out twenty months of research in a rural village of 283 households in southern Cambodia. The village is in a district of approximately 100,000 people, located three hours by express bus from the capital city of Phnom Penh. For one full year between 2016 and 2017, we lived together with a Cambodian family in a hamlet of twenty-nine households within the village. 1 We chose our study village because it had social and economic characteristics commonly found in rural Cambodia. Residents were Buddhist Khmer speakers and the majority of households engaged in both subsistence and commodity rice agriculture. A minority of others were local merchants, small business owners, and civil servants. Within our hamlet, 55 percent of households had at least one member working outside of the province. Within these translocal households, 81 percent of migrants worked in a different province and 19 percent worked abroad in Thailand or South Korea. 2

While living in the village, we carried out participant observation of daily activities and community events, such as religious ceremonies, weddings, and funerals. This method enabled us to study the processes, meanings, and place-making activities central to the transformation of Cambodia ' s rural economy and society (Herbert 2000). Introduction

Department of Geography, National University of Singapore, Singapore † Department of Sociology, National University of Singapore, Singapore

W esat with Makara under the shade of a mango tree one afternoon while living in her rural Cambodian village. Her two young sons played in the rice field behind us while Makara nursed her newborn. She did not have the money to buy fish for dinner. Instead, her sons had to make do with a papaya given to her by a neighbor. ' We never have enough money for good food, ' Makara told us, ' so my children are always getting sick. ' Her husband, Dy, was away working in the capital city ' s booming construction sector. His jobs were short-term and low-paid, however, and the money he sent home was always too little.

Kunthea, a secondary school student who lived nearby, was also concerned about remittances. Like all her classmates, Kunthea took five hours of private classes per day on top of attending public school to prepare for the national twelfth-grade completion exam. She normally relied on money from her older sisters working in Thailand and in Cambodia ' s garment industry to pay for these classes, but one of her sisters had recently been laid off and had sent nothing home that month. Missing her private classes made Kunthea anxious. ' If I don ' t do well on the exam, I won ' t get into university. Then I ' ll never get a good job, ' she explained. Kunthea ' s mother and sisters were counting on her to support them in the future, and she did not want to fail them.

In this article, we draw on ethnographic research with Makara, Kunthea, and their families to further develop the concept of translocal precarity. Geographers and others have recently studied how precarity travels home, from the site of work to rural households, thereby harming the lives of left-behind family members (Alipio 2019; Tappe and Nguyen 2019; Yea 2019; Silvey and Parre ~ nas 2020). Such analyses tend to locate the source of precarity at the site of production and in the conditions faced by the individual migrant worker. Jobs are often in the informal urban economy, where labor protections are minimal (Davis 2004). Other jobs are in the formal sector, but global competition, surplus populations, and union suppression make them insecure and short-term positions (Munck 2013; Bernards 2018). For those migrants who travel across national borders, citizenship regimes make work even more precarious due to the looming possibility of deportation (Strauss and McGrath 2017; Ye and Yeoh 2018).

On Precarity

Precarity is most commonly used to describe the loss of security and stability in work (Millar 2017; Strauss 2018). It is linked to a wide range of factors, including low pay, uncertain working hours, a lack of worker representation, and limited access to employment rights, social benefits, and other protections. Precarity is ' not the fact of consistent unemployment, but the looming threat, and perhaps frequent fact, of it ' (Banki 2013, 2). The rise of precarious work has been linked to the economic transformations wrought by a post-Fordist regime of accumulation (Standing 2011), characterized by flexible production, time -space compression, and financial deregulation (Harvey 1989). As global capitalist production became more mobile in the 1970s and 1980s, labor unions lost many of their gains against capital in the European -American core countries. As a result, the traditional capitalist proletariat fragmented into a multitude of groups, marked by

' anger, anomie, anxiety, and alienation ' (Standing 2011, 19).

Precarious Life ' s Work

Yet even this reconstructed understanding of precarity tends to prioritize the conditions of work over the ways in which precarity is experienced as a part of daily life. In contrast, there is a strand of literature that has focused on the precarity of life itself (Millar 2017). Inspired by the work of Butler (2004, 2009), this scholarship draws attention to the existential condition of precariousness as a shared condition of all life. According to Butler (2009), ' Precariousness implies living socially, that is, the fact that one ' s life is always in some sense in the hands of the other ' (14). Our bodies, as social phenomena, are never only our own (Butler 2004). Life is sustained by reciprocal relations of dependency on people ' we may know, barely know, or know not at all ' (Butler 2009, 14). Importantly, Butler (2009) distinguished precariousness from precarity. Whereas precariousness is an existential fact of living socially, precarity ' designates that politically induced condition in which certain populations suffer from failing social and economic networks of support ' (Butler 2009, 25).

data.Article Title: A LIFE-STAGE APPROACH FOR DECOMPOSING SPATIOTEMPORAL POPULATION CHANGES ALONG AN URBAN-RURAL GRADIENT: IMPLICATIONS FOR REGIONAL PLANNING
data.Author Keywords: population; birth cohort; life course; life stage; urban; suburban; rural; regional planning; spatial planning; Spain
data.text: The study of population changes across space and time of cohorts at different life stages is relevant for regional planning, but it is often not taken into account. We focus on a case study along the urban-rural gradient of continental Spain from 2002 to 2017 at a municipal scale. Making use of longitudinal data from the municipal registers, we studied changes in total population and three birth cohorts: the cohort joining the workforce, the cohort at a mature working age and the cohort reaching retirement during the study period. The results showed key spatiotemporal population variations. The absolute population increased in 36% of the municipalities, but at least one of the study cohorts showed an increase in 75% of the municipalities. While the cohort joining workforce tended to concentrate in urban and suburban areas, the retiring cohort tended to move to small suburban and rural municipalities. In the next decades the retirement of large birth cohorts in Spain will be a relevant issue for planning. This methodological approach allows us to understand life cycle residential movements across urban, suburban and rural areas and better enables spatial planning decisions. The method can be applied to other study areas at different spatial and temporal scales.

DATA

Demographic data was obtained from the Spanish Continuous Municipal Register of the Spanish Statistical Office (INE), which indicates each municipality's official population by age on January 1 st of each year. The INE is an official and reliable source, however the data is not always precise because in some cases migrants take time to register in their new place of residence and inform their previous local registry. Introduction

T he change in population volumes across space and time is a relevant variable in relation to spatial planning for housing, services, and transportation (Singleton and Spielman 2014 ; Lee et al. 2016 ; Barcus and Halfacree 2017 ). In the last decades, numerous areas in Western countries have shown a population decrease caused by negative natural population balance (more deaths than births) and a negative total net migration rate (taking into account both internal and international migrations) due to migrations of individuals to other areas in search of work opportunities after a decline in the labor market (MartinezFernandez et al. 2016 ; Salvati 2019 ; Sobotka and Fürnkranz-Prskawetz 2020 ). At the same time, other areas have seen their population increase significantly. Thus, demographic trends vary between different areas with opposite population trajectories (Martinez-Fernandez et al. 2016 ; Batunova and Gunko 2018 ; GrosBalthazard and Talandier 2020 ).

The change in total population is the most common indicator used to assess population changes in a territory at different spatial scales (Martinez-Fernandez et al. 2016 ; United Nations 2019 ). The change in total population in an area

within a specific period depends on the sum between the natural balance (births minus deaths) and the net migration rate throughout the study period (Dax and Fischer 2018 ; Salvati 2019 ; Segers et al. 2020 ). In the current context of globalization of the workforce, in aging societies with low fertility rates of Western countries, the net migration rate could be a significant factor when compared to the natural balance rate in total population dynamics (United Nations 2019 ). Total net migration rates across space and time will depend not only on internal migration flows, but also on international migration flows (Martinez-Fernandez et al. 2016 ; Salvati 2019 ; Sobotka and Fürnkranz-Prskawetz 2020 ) and on those policies regulating them (Ueffing et al. 2015 ). Nevertheless, the study of total population changes in different locations does not take into account certain spatiotemporal demographic changes useful for regional planning, such as specific typologies for housing and priority services for different birth cohorts with distinct size (Andrews et al. 2009 ; Gibler et al. 2009 ; Lee et al. 2016 ; Barcus and Halfacree 2017 ).

data.text: The use of rural areas by the urban population is an important organizing principle in the study of the rural hinterland of urban centers. One of the important land uses identified within the urban field is recreation. This paper focuses on cottage property ownership in one part of the urban field, the rural-recreational countryside. Using three case studies from Canada, it was found that cottage properties account for a large proportion of local residential property. Although most cottage properties are owned by urban residents, up to one-quarter are owned by local residents. Using a questionnaire survey, it was also found that cottage owners are more likely to be older, better educated, and have higher incomes than rural residents.

Study Areas

The three case studies examined in this paper are the Rideau Lakes area of Ontario, the Cultus Lake area of British Columbia, and the

Beaubassin coastline of New Brunswick. In each case, the study areas are located near the outer bounds of the urban field and contain a mix of rural, small-town, and recreational property areas. Each study area also features established cottage property areas together with a rural community whose livelihood remains grounded in agriculture. In seeking to develop a socioeconomic profile of cottagers, we selected these study areas to explore possible regional variations in cottage landscapes. This is an important issue as there has been, and continues to be, tremendous variation in the strength of regional Canadian economies. To present information for only one study area runs the risk of making general statements based on findings that may in fact represent unique or idiosyncratic aspects of that region or area. Given that there is little additional research with which to compare our findings, it was decided that a multiple case study approach was more appropriate.

There has been a longstanding gap in the geographic literature concerning definitions of cottaging activity and related issues of data

quality. Definitions of cottaging and cottagers, as a type of land use and as a class of residential occupancy respectively, have proved too malleable to operationalize in a consistent manner (Coppock 1977; Hart 1984; Jaakson 1986; Hinch 1990). Clearly, the residential landscape within cottaging areas is complex. In all three study areas described above, there are examples of permanent residents living year-round at cottage property along the lake and examples of farm property used only as summer retreats. Micro-level analysis of individual behavior suggests that there are also examples of property use that fall between these extremes (Geipel 1992; Halseth 1993b). In this sense, we must recognize that cottage property can be distinguished by patterns of location and patterns of use or occupancy. In each of our study areas, the small-lot cottage properties could be easily distinguished from surrounding agricultural or rural residential properties. In addition, property use in terms of seasonal or permanent occupancy could be readily ascertained from local government records. Introduction

e rural hinterland surrounding cities is a T complex geographic landscape where local land use changes are differentially combined with development pressures generated by the processes of urbanization (Bryant et al. 1982; Osborne 1988). The pattern of recreational land uses of the urban-based population is one of the organizing constructs of the urban field or city's countryside models of the rural hinterland surrounding cities (Friedmann and Miller 1965; Bryant et al. 1982). This paper is interested in one of the important and longstanding forms of recreational land use in the rural hinterlands of cities, that of cottage or secondhome property ownership. The goal is to fill a gap in what is currently a paucity of data identifying the cottage property-owning population. For a variety of reasons, there has been renewed interest in rural and small-town research in recent years (Leckie 1989, 1993; Davies and Yeates 1991; Flora and Christenson 1991; Mackenzie 1992; Gober et al.

Background

The summer cottage at the lake is an immediately recognizable element of the recreational countryside. Indeed, cottages are a relatively common element within Western society. Examples from France (Clout 1977), Great Britain (Coppock 1977; Rogers 1977), Czechoslovakia (Gardavsky 1977), Sweden (Geipel1992), and Australia (Robertson 1977) stand as testament that the phenomenon is widespread. However, academic research has made only tentative attempts at tying together the importance of cottaging in the rural countryside and the role of cottage communities within the local rural community (Ragatz 1970; Coppock 1977; Jordan 1980; Wilkinson and Murray 1991; Halseth 1993a).

data.Article Title: Conservation or Decarbonization? Small Hydropower and State Logics of Green Development in China
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF GEOGRAPHERS
data.Keywords Plus: SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT; INTEGRATED CONSERVATION; PLANTATION FORESTRY; RENEWABLE ENERGY; ECO-CITY; CARBON; ACCUMULATION; POLITICS; URBAN; TERRITORIALIZATION
data.text: Through an analysis of small hydropower (SHP) in China, I argue that logics of green development offer a framework for analyzing why, how, and to what intended effect the state pursues different green agendas over time and space. For decades, China's central and provincial governments framed SHP as a model of green development, but in 2016 they instituted SHP restrictions due to ecological impacts and electricity waste, a situation blamed on local officials haphazardly approving too many plants. This interpretation, however, ignores a major shift in state logic for promoting SHP, first for conservation-based development in rural areas and then for low-carbon development in urban areas. These logics-which I abbreviate as conservation and decarbonization-are based on different political-economic problems that green development is meant to solve for the state, different places targeted for intervention, and different distributions of benefits and costs. Using this framework, I argue that a shift to decarbonization in the mid-2000s incentivized cash-strapped local governments in rural western China to build as many SHP plants as possible to export electricity and build local industries, leading to a subsequent bust. I illustrate this trajectory using case studies of three prefectures in Yunnan province. This article thus enriches scholarship on state-nature relations by theorizing the role of the state in shaping dominant discourses and practices of green development across space and their uneven outcomes. Key Words: China, conservation, decarbonization, green development, renewable energy.

Introduction

L ong seen by China ' s leaders as developmentally backward and ecologically degraded, western China has undergone a dramatic economic and environmental transformation in the last two decades. Beginning with the Great Western Development Strategy in the early 2000s, to the current Belt and Road Initiative, the central government has sought to bring the western provinces up to the developmental standard of the industrialized east. This effort is spearheaded by state mining and energy investments (Tian 2004). It also entails subsidies for large-scale ecological restoration and forest protection initiatives to combat land degradation (Bennett 2008). A 2010 national policy to set aside ' ecological function zones '-many of them in western China (China State Council 2016) -highlights the tension between state economic and environmental concerns. Indeed, China ' s leaders see issues of political stability and gross domestic product (GDP) growth as predicated on an economically dynamic and ecologically sound western ' frontier ' (Yeh 2009).

Small hydropower (SHP) exemplifies the changes taking place in western China. In China, SHP is defined as < 50 MW installed capacity, compared with the definition of < 10MW in many other countries (United Nations Industrial Development Organization and International Center on Small Hydro Power 2016). The first SHP plant in China began operation in 1911, and by the 1970s SHP generated electricity for millions of rural households (Kong et al. 2015). As of the end of 2015, more than 47,000 plants were in operation, with a combined installed capacity of 74.3 GW, nearly a quarter of China ' s total installed hydropower capacity (EPS China Data 2018). China ' s central and provincial governments have promoted SHP as a model of green development since the late 1990s, based on the argument that SHP replaces peasant firewood collection with electricity use, thus protecting forests and improving productivity through rural electrification (Cui and Qu 2008). Since the mid-2000s, authorities have also framed SHP as a renewable energy that contributes to national carbon emissions reductions. Indeed, before it was overtaken by wind energy in 2015, SHP was China ' s most widespread renewable energy technology, and China ' s leaders still uphold SHP as a green example that other countries can learn from (Harlan 2017).

The State of and in Green Development

Since the 1987 release of the World Commission on Environment and Development Our Common Future report (World Commission on Environment and Development 1987) -also known as the Brundtland Report -the idea of green development has been widely adopted by governments, multilateral institutions, and the public (Adams 2009). 3 Although opinions vary as to how green development should be achieved -and whether major sociopolitical change is needed (Bina 2013; P. Ferguson 2015) -its most prominent metanarrative is that economic growth, environmental protection, and social equity can be realized simultaneously through market instruments, technological innovation, and some state regulation (Banerjee 2003). 4 Over time, though, the main focus of green development discourse and practice has shifted alongside changing political -economic contexts and the emergence (and recognition) of particular socioenvironmental problems and solutions that are emphasized over others, which in turn shape whether or not green development is perceived to succeed or fail.

Shifting Green Agendas

Arguably the first major global issue framed as a green development challenge was the perceived linkage between poverty and environmental degradation, primarily in the rural Global South. This concern has origins in neo-Malthusian beliefs about population-induced resource exhaustion (Meadows, Meadows, and Behrens 1972), bolstered by the more recent view that degradation and scarcity occur because the poor are ' unable or unwilling ' to protect the environment (see Duraiappah [1998] for a review). In this interpretation, poverty and degradation reinforce each other in a ' downward spiral ' (Dasgupta 1995) -a view clearly stated in the Brundtland Report (World Commission on Environment and Development 1987, 6) -and reversing the spiral requires policies and programs that simultaneously lift incomes and encourage sound resource use.

data.Article Title: Unintended Developments: Gender, Environment, and Collective Governance in a Mexican Ejido
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE ASSOCIATION OF AMERICAN GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: environment; gender; governance; Mexico; neoliberalism
data.Keywords Plus: PROPERTY; NEOLIBERALISM; PRIVATIZATION; REFORM; LIMITS; CONSERVATION; QUESTION; NATURES; POLICY; STATES
data.text: This article examines the unintended outcomes of a neoliberal program designed to privatize Mexico's communal lands. Although postrevolutionary agrarian law excluded women from official landholding and leadership positions, steps toward land privatization inadvertently increased women's access to land, government resources, and political power. Using ethnographic and survey data collected in a Veracruz ejido, I demonstrate how Mexico's agrarian counterreforms triggered novel subjectivities and practices. While men acted as self-imagined private property owners and decreased participation in traditional governance institutions, women became registered land managers and leaders for the first time in the ejido's history. These interlocking processes stopped the land-titling program in its tracks and reinvigorated collective governance. Even state actors charged with carrying out ejido privatization were implicated in the empowerment of rural women and failure to fully privatize land. This research contributes to nature-society debates by arguing neoliberalism does not always end economic self-determination and communal governance in agrarian contexts. Rather, I demonstrate the ways in which processual policy, subjectivity, authority formation, objects, and environmental narratives combine to produce new political trajectories with positive implications for rural women and the environment.

Study Site and Methods

This article is the result of fieldwork carried out in an ejido called La Grullita located in central Veracruz, on the eastern flanks of shield volcano Cofre de Perote, near Coatepec (Figure 1). The community has a population of approximately 1,529 inhabitants, 156 of whom are registered ejidatarios (INEGI 2005). Except the urban area and a scattering of pasture plots, shadegrown coffee dominates land use in polyculture fi ncas (coffee orchards). Ecologists have shown that central Veracruz coffee systems provide several environmental benefits, including water catchment, nutrient cycling, and carbon sequestration (e.g., Greenberg, Bichier, and Sterling 1997; Moguel and Toledo 1999; Manson, Contreras Hern´ andez, and L´ opez-Barrera 2008). Veracruz plantations also possess levels of biodiversity similar to less altered forests in the region and serve as habitat corridors for migratory bird populations.

Between June 2003 and November 2008 I conducted twenty months of fieldwork in Veracruz. I was introduced to La Grullita in June 2006 during predissertation fieldwork and the ejido was one of two case study communities selected for my doctoral research. It quickly became clear that PROCEDE, women leaders, and collective tree-planting efforts were important ongoing topics of discussion within the ejido. Introduction

O n a September morning in 2008, Adela 1 waited in the lobby of Registro Agrario Nacional (RAN) 2 in Xalapa, capital city of Mexico's Veracruz state. Adela took over all aspects of coffee production when her husband died in 1999. Nine years and many bureaucratic procedures later, she was finally reregistering a two-hectare plot from her deceased husband's name to her own. The individuals gathered that morning reflected Veracruz's diverse agrarian landscapes and included lowland sugarcane growers, a Totonac leader from a vanilla-producing community, and several coffee producers. The crowd also represented Mexico's long history of gendered agrarian policies: Of fifty-four people waiting to speak with officials, only three were women.

Adela's presence at RAN was an unforeseen outcome of constitutional amendments designed to privatize Mexico's communal landholding system, the ejido. Adela's ejido entered the privatization program in 1997. Following initial steps toward privatization, women gained access to land and leadership positions and helped reassert collective governance. In other words, a policy designed to privatize communal lands not only played out differently than technocrats intended; it helped produce new subjectivities and authorities, ultimately stopping the land-titling process in its tracks.

I do not advocate for top-down development interventions, but I am interested in the unintended outcomes of such impositions and how they might help create new spaces for political change. More often than not, nature-society scholarship focuses on the damaging outcomes of capitalist development for people and environments: new forms of dispossession, gendered and raced exclusions, increased environmental contamination, and so forth. As Heynen and colleagues (2007) put it, 'While neoliberal policies are of course varied and unpredictable in their outcomes . . . we believe it is still reasonable to anticipate that they are more likely to produce negative than positive outcomes' (289). Researchers have demonstrated neoliberalism is anything but an ideal type; instead, policies possess unpredictable and variegated implications in different socioecological contexts (Bakker 2010; see also Larner 2003; Radcliffe 2005; Fisher 2009). This research contributes to this body of scholarship by demonstrating how state-led efforts to privatize communal land helped undo historic exclusions of women from leadership and landholding positions.

Nature-Society Dynamics in the Neoliberal Era

In the last thirty years, neoliberal economic development-led by governments, lending institutions, and other powerful organizations-became aligned with fiscal restraint, free trade, and privatization. Worldwide, agrarian livelihoods were deeply implicated in these efforts as diverse people and agroecosystems were labeled 'inefficient' and 'unviable' in terms of their ability to compete in liberalized markets. Property rights became the focus of attempts to make natural resource management, and human subjects, 'modern,' 'efficient,' and 'competitive' through privatization and enclosure measures.

Agrarian Reform and Gender in Mexico (1917-1992)

Between 1917 and 1992, the Mexican government expropriated large landholdings throughout the nation, redistributing resources to small-scale farmers, pastoralists, and fisherfolk in the form of communally managed ejidos. 3 Ejidos are often a combination of solares (urban plots), parcelas (farm plots), and a preagreed percentage of tierras de uso com´ un (commonsland and resources). In the decades following the Mexican Revolution, 28,000 ejidos and agrarian communities were created, occupying more than half of Mexico's arable land surface (Instituto Nacional de Estad´ ıstica y Geograf´ ıa [INEGI] 1990). By 1992, when constitutional amendments brought an end to Mexican land reform, millions of ejido members (hereafter ejidatarios ) were registered in these communities.
