data.text: Despite advances in mapping technologies and spatial data capabilities, global mapping inequalities are not declining. Inequalities in the coverage, quality, and currency of mapping persist, with significant gaps in remote and rural parts of the Global South. These regions, representing some of the most economically and resource-disadvantaged societies in the world, need high-quality mapping to aid in the delivery of essential services, such as health care, in response to severe challenges such as poverty, conflict, and global climate change. Volunteered geographic information (VGI) has shown potential as a solution to mapping inequalities. Contributions have largely been made in urban areas or in response to acute emergencies (e.g., earthquakes or floods), however, leaving rural regions that suffer from chronic humanitarian crises undermapped. An alternative solution is needed that harnesses the power of volunteer mapping more effectively to address regions in most need. Machine learning holds promise. In this article we propose centaur VGI, a hybrid system that combines the spatial cognitive abilities of human volunteers with the speed and efficiency of a machine. We argue that centaur VGI can contribute to mitigating some of the political and technological factors that produce inequalities in VGI mapping coverage and do so in the context of a case study in Acholi, northern Uganda, an inadequately mapped region in which the authors have been working since 2017 to provide outreach health care services to victims of major limb loss during conflict.

Centaur VGI

The apparent tension between the desire of computer scientists to automatically detect features and the resistance of the OSM community to accept automated edits reveals a possible middle ground: a centaur VGI approach whereby the classification accuracy and common sense of manual human input can be combined with the speed of the machine to enable more efficient volunteer mapping, also delivering a system that is compatible with the ethos of OSM. This centaur VGI workflow is summarized as follows:

  1. Computer searches satellite imagery for previously unmapped feature.
  2. Computer proposes geometry for feature.
  3. a. Volunteer approves, edits, or rejects geometry.
  4. b. Computer incorporates edits and rejections into the training set to improve performance.
  5. Computer proposes classification for feature.
  6. a. Volunteer approves or edits classification.
  7. b. Computer incorporates edits into the training set to improve performance.
  8. Volunteer submits edits to OpenStreetMap.

This kind of centaur-based approach can integrate seamlessly into existing editors such as the OSM iD editor (OpenStreetMap 2019a) or JOSM (2019)

software. It removes the need for users to search for features by providing in-editor suggestions that can be accepted, modified, or rejected before submission to the OSM database. Edits and rejections are fed back to the training set to improve the performance of the classification algorithm. Such an approach permits the human volunteer to concentrate on the cl

Research Context: Mapping Acholi, Uganda

Although the arguments we present in this article are framed in the context of global topographic mapping, they have primarily been formulated in the context of the authors ' ongoing research and humanitarian activity in the Acholi subregion of northern Uganda (Figure 3). This area was the focal point of a brutal conflict arising from an insurgency by Joseph Kony ' s Lord ' s Resistance Army (LRA), which lasted for almost two decades, during which atrocities were committed on a regular basis, including the kidnapping and enslavement of young children, severe mutilation, and the internal displacement of 90 percent of the population (Vinci 2005). The period between 1986 and 2005 is generally accepted as the duration of the conflict (Lamwaka 2016), but its legacy, including injuries from landmines placed in villages and fields, continues to this day. Acts of mutilation by the LRA contributed to the prevalence of disabilities in the region and were intended to be highly visible and symbolic. Mutilation was used to control the population (Vinci 2005): Ears and lips, for example, were cut off as a signal to beware of informing on the LRA, whereas bicycle riders had their legs cut off to inhibit communication among the local population (Vinci 2005). Integrating VGI and Machine Learning

Although VGI provides an invaluable resource for many humanitarian applications, further consideration needs to be given to how it might address persistent inequalities in global mapping coverage. ML has been one of the most successful areas of computer science research in recent decades, with applications in a wide variety of fields (Gillies et al. 2016). Although it remains difficult for nonexperts to use (Gillies et al. 2016), the emergence of increasingly high-level ML platforms such as Google TensorFlow is rapidly lowering barriers to entry, resulting in the application of ML techniques to a wide variety of problems in almost all fields of research (Jordan and Mitchell 2015). From a mapping perspective, one of the clearest applications of ML techniques is feature recognition in remotely sensed imagery. A typical system is conceptually relatively straightforward:

  1. A training set of data is created in which features such as roads, footpaths, or buildings in imagery data are manually identified and labeled.
  2. The training set is used to train an algorithm, which learns how to recognize the labeled features using statistical analysis.
  3. The trained algorithm is then used to search for the same statistical patterns in new imagery and identify new features.

Introduction

MCGIS, Department of Geography, The University of Manchester † MCGIS, Humanitarian and Conflict Response Institute, The University of Manchester ‡ Faculty of Medicine, Gulu University #

I nequalities in the coverage, quality, and currency of mapping persist, with significant gaps in remote and rural parts of the Global South that suffer from ongoing chronic humanitarian crises. These areas in particular could benefit significantly were they able to implement national spatial data infrastructures (SDIs) in support of the UN 2030 Sustainable Development Goals. Scott and Rajabifard (2017), though, recognize that many developing nations currently ' continue to face problems of poor data quality, lack of timely data and a lack of interoperability between different sources of data ' (64). Mapping is rarely explicitly discussed in policy fora but is fundamental for SDIs. Nor do these areas attract the same level of attention from humanitarian mapping volunteers as those with more acute emergencies (e.g., a serious disease outbreak or a significant natural hazard leading to a disaster or humanitarian crisis).

It has been suggested that volunteered geographic information (VGI 1 ; Goodchild 2007) might offer a potential solution for these kinds of regions. There are significant concerns, however, from official sources regarding data quality, ownership, and knock-on impacts on professional employment in the mapping sector (Olteanu-Raimond et al. 2017), and there is no guarantee that a given feature will ever be mapped (Hagenauer and Helbich 2012). In addition, practical issues relating to volunteer motivation and the pragmatic combination of technologies have hindered widespread adoption of VGI for addressing mapping inequalities. Machine learning (ML) 2 has already been widely deployed to automate aspects of the mapping process, in particular in the field of extracting features from remotely sensed image data (Zhu et al. 2017). To date, however, advances in this area have focused on conceptual or technical challenges, instead of offering practical solutions

Global Inequalities in Mapping

Over the years, several attempts have been made to quantify variations in mapping at different scales, including analyses at an international level (e.g., Perkins 1987; Parry and Perkins 2000), regional level (e.g., B € ohme 1991), and more detailed and multimethod surveys of individual countries (e.g., Radcliffe 2009). Variations in map coverage across the world have received particular attention from technical and official reviews, and professional bodies have vested interests in charting progress in their fields. International comparative metrics have been produced documenting an apparently inexorable advance in mapping (see, e.g., Konecny, Breitkopf, and Radtke 2016). The International Cartographic Association and the United Nations Committee of Experts on Global Geospatial Information Management (UN-GGIM) have undertaken periodic surveys on global map coverage, based on self-reporting from each individual country (Konecny, Breitkopf, and Radtke 2016). These surveys suggest a gradual improvement and reduction in inequalities, with more of the globe covered at larger scales as scientific enterprise progresses.

Volunteered Geographical Information

Despite a growing body of research into VGI in the past decade, its definition remains somewhat nebulous, encompassing a wide variety of data types and modes of volunteering (Craglia, Ostermann, and Spinsanti 2012) and an even wider range of activities, practices, and motivations (Haklay 2013). A number of typologies of VGI have been developed, the most frequently cited of which focuses on the distinction between explicit or implicit volunteering and geographic information (Craglia, Ostermann, and Spinsanti 2012). Here, we refer only to VGI that can be considered as both explicitly volunteered and explicitly geographical, the archetypical example of which is the user-generated content of OpenStreetMap (OSM). OSM was originally intended as a response to the strict licensing associated with national mapping agencies such as the Ordnance Survey and the then-emergent Web mapping services (e.g., Google Maps) but has increasingly come to be used in humanitarian mapping over the past decade (Anderson, Sarkar, and Palen 2019).

Introduction

Beekeeping may be seen as aperfect model of responsible, sustainable agriculture. It can greatly benefit rural communities by providing additional food, medicine and income.

Economic marginalization, the frequent failure of past development interventions, and the need of local communities in rural Africa to secure economic survival have encouraged a focus on indigenous knowledge and self-reliance strategies (Burkey 1993; Binns 1995). The academic and policyattention increasinglybeing paid to these considerations represents a fundamental shift in development foci and a concerted response to the perceived negative effects of structural adjustment programs in rural Africa (Taylor and Mackenzie 1992). Where local self-reliance strategies exist and, in certain instances, where they are supported by external agencies, they often "constitute the only means of survival for local communities, providing an invaluable basis for reviving local self-reliance and restructuring regional development on more indigenous and self-reliant lines" (Gooneratne 1992, 3). These issues have particular relevance to indigenous beekeeping in the rural areas of the countries that make up the Southern African Development Community (Louw 1992) (Figure 1). Beekeeping, it can be argued, is an ecologically and technically appropriate form of income generation for communities in some of the most economically and environmentally poor areas of Africa. Its role in promoting economic self-reliance and the need to enhance this role were identified in the important Banjul Bee Declaration of 1991 (Bees for Development 1991).

Although beekeeping can only rarely become the sole source of income and livelihood for people in the Third World, its role as a source of supplementary earnings, food, and employment should not be underestimated. THE MOVE TO SELF-RELIANCE

Desperate economic realities in Africa both oblige and compel many communities to seek solutions to the circumstances in which they find themselves. According to the United Nations, "for almost goo million people, approximately one-sixth of mankind, the march of human progress has become a retreat. In many nations, development is being thrown into reverse. And after decades of steady economic advance, large areas of the world are being thrown back into poverty" (Gooneratne and Mbilinyi 1992, 22). This statement is particularly pertinent in Africa, where the effective collapse of government services, infrastructure, and social provision in many areas is coupled with hyperinflation, vast debt burdens, and the disastrous effects of global trade and structural adjustment packages (Taylor and Mackenzie 1992). This situation militates against any significant socioeconomic intervention on the part of national governments.

data.Article Title: Spatiotemporal Relationship Between Tsunami Inundation and Evacuation Behavior
data.Author Keywords: coastal hazards; evacuation; empirical study; spatial disparity; tsunami; Japan
data.Keywords Plus: SENDAI PLAIN; DISASTER; HAZARD; JAPAN; ISHINOMAKI; VULNERABILITY; EARTHQUAKE; SIMULATION; CITY
data.text: This study advances understanding of nature-society interactions by examining the spatiotemporal coupling of tsunami hazards and human responses. Using video footage of the 2011 Tohoku tsunami recorded in a rural coastal plain in Japan enabled analysis of inundation patterns and evacuation responses under different lead times. The results showed that the tsunami inundation progressed 912 m over 9 minutes and 30 seconds within the video-recorded area located approximately 2 km inland from the coast. Multiple regression and geographically weighted regression analyses revealed that inundation patterns were predominantly controlled by coastal proximity and surface roughness, while road and waterway configurations locally modified flow velocities through acceleration and deceleration effects. Evacuation analysis identified distinct response patterns associated with different temporal zones of tsunami inundation. Residents tended to evacuate more rapidly in areas inundated within 2 minutes of the tsunami's arrival, especially older adults. In contrast, evacuees in areas with extended lead times exhibited higher rates of delayed evacuation. These findings emphasize that evacuation behavior is determined by the timing of tsunami arrival and the spatial location of evacuees. Understanding these spatiotemporal relationships is essential for developing place-based evacuation strategies.

data.text: Climate-induced displacement is attracting increasing media, state, and scholarly attention, albeit often in a way that situates migration as either an example of climate adaptation or a failure thereof. Whether depicted as success or failure, both framings can invisibilize the preexisting socioenvironmental processes that render climate-induced migrations necessary-or, conversely, that can inhibit them entirely. Perspectives on displacement and environmental migration from within political ecology and human geography offer an alternative register, looking beyond unidirectional socioeconomic or environmental drivers to document how uneven development reproduces displacements relationally and historically. Drawing on these theorizations, as well as empirical research from agrarian Southeast Asia, this article develops the notion of cumulative socionatural displacements as one approach for conceptualizing socioecologically driven displacement in a world already on the move. We demonstrate this approach through an analysis of displacement in Southeast Asia that begins by tracing the evolving state, market, and agroecological relations that have made mobility integral to agrarian viability while setting the stage for more intense climate impacts. In doing so, we also center the long-term (nonclimatic) environmental changes that are often sidelined in both anthropocentric debates on rural displacements and climate doomsday scenarios. We argue that examining climate-induced migration as just one facet of cumulative socionatural displacements is necessary for overcoming the ontological and political impasses engendered by prevailing narratives that collapse climate migration into convenient but misleading binaries.

Conceptualizing Displacement and Transformation

Popular imaginaries of climate displacement, although long contested within work on environmental migration and displacement (Piguet 2013), remain durable in state, institutional, media, and even some academic accounts, including determinist strands of environmental science (e.g., Myers 2002; but see discussion in Agustoni and Maretti 2019). One highly cited World Bank report predicted that climate change will ' force ' more than 143 million people to relocate internally from South Asia, subSaharan Africa, and Latin America (Rigaud et al. 2018, xiv), and the Institute for Economics and Peace (2020, 4) suggested that extreme ecological shocks could displace up to 1.2 billion people globally by 2050.

It is important to differentiate such predictions from more nuanced theoretical engagements with climate displacement, including that of Miller (2019), who defined climate displacement as ' distress or involuntary migration, both internal and crossborder, as well as involuntary resettlement ' (112). Miller ' s engagement with the involuntary dimensions of displacement raises important questions of procedural and distributional justice vis- a-vis relocation schemes. At the same time, however, such nuance is often lost when media representations and state discourses engage the figure of the ' climate refugee ' in ways that play into racialized neo-Malthusian imaginaries 1 and exclusionary national security agendas (see critique by Baldwin 2013).

C limate change is unequivocally shifting the way people live and get by. Agrarian Southeast Asia is no exception and might be particularly susceptible to climate change given high dependence on rain-fed agriculture, accelerating agribusiness investments in land and preexisting social vulnerabilities. This implies that displacement can no longer be theorized without reference to climate change. Simultaneously, the dominant representations of climate displacement can leave much to be desired, particularly in agrarian landscapes where preexisting mobilities are often assumed away or taken as evidence of an already-arrived-at conclusion.

As recent work within human geography and political ecology notes, for instance, mobility and displacement have often been taken as one and the same, with out-migration alternatively read as either climate adaptation or a failure thereof (see, e.g., Middleton, Elmhirst, and Chantavanich 2018).

Critical work on environmental migration and climate disasters likewise illustrates the problematic persistence of ' catastrophist ' and ' resilientist ' binaries (Agustoni and Maretti 2019). As Gray et al. (2014) noted, however, some environmental displacement work nonetheless emphasizes displacement as involuntary permanent relocation or as a full and final exit from prior livelihood strategies. Important to our arguments here, such framings can invisibilize the preexisting socioenvironmental processes that render climate-induced migrations necessary or, conversely, that might inhibit them entirely. They are also at odds with understandings of migration to and from agrarian regions, which generally comprises only one dimension of intentionally multilocal and hybridized livelihood strategies (Kelley et al. 2020).

ROBERT B. KENT

ABSTRACT. The Shining Path insurgency began in Peru in 1980. The strategy emphasized rural revolution, establishment of liberated zones, and encirclement of cities. The counterinsurgent campaign in 1983 prevented the creation of a permanent territorial base in the departments of Ayacucho and Apurimac but led to expansion of insurgent operations northward in the central Andes. In the mid-1980s the insurgents advanced into the rain-forest region of the upper Huallaga Valley and onto the altiplano in the southern Andes. Lima and its surrounding shantytowns were included in insurgent activities by the late 1980s. The insurgents displayed an uncanny ability to maintain their struggle over a vast area and in different natural and social environments.

THE REGIONAL CORE

During the late 1970s the Shining Path left the university in Ayacucho and relocated to relatively inaccessible areas of the countryside, where it created "popular schools," worked closely with peasants, and began forcibly to disperse the representatives of the state, local capitalists, and large landowners (Gorriti Ellenbogen 1990, 86). Several provinces in northern Ayacucho and the province of Andahuaylas in neighboring Apurimac formed the principal territorial focus of these activities (Fig. 1).

Securely established in these areas, the Shining Path initiated its armed conflict in Ayacucho in 1980. It followed a Maoist model that called for liberation of the countryside, an end to market-oriented agricultural production, and disarticulation of the capitalistic marketing system. Theoretically those policies would eventually cut off the supply of basic food commodities to cities, increase urban social disorder, and allow the Shining Path to encircle the principal urban areas, culminating in the downfall of the Peruvian state.

data.text: Spatial accessibility measures are an important policy tool for managing healthcare provision and reducing health inequality. The two-step floating catchment area technique, in common with many alternative methodologies, requires that demand-side population be estimated using spatial interpolation techniques. This article studies the implications of adopting differing spatial representations of population on healthcare accessibility modeling outcomes. Results indicate that a dasymetric model yields lower accessibility scores than a standard pro rata model. More important, the difference is spatially disproportionate, suggesting that the degree of disadvantage experienced in rural areas may be greater than has previously been recognized.

Our approach uses an adaptation of the twostep floating catchment area method, and investigates the influence of three alternative spatial representation models of the population:

  1. Population is modeled by a single representative point in the census tabulation zone (we use the population-weighted centroid supplied by the Office for National Statistics [ONS]).
  2. Population is evenly distributed within the census tabulation zone.
  3. Populationisdasymetrically distributed within the census tabulation zone.

Method1isthesameasthatused,forexample, by Wang and Luo (2005) and Christie and Fone (2003). Method2 is essentially the pro rata method, often referred to as ''areal weighting'' in the areal interpolation literature, and it may offer moreaccurateestimates than Method 1 provided uniform distribution is a valid assumption. In a dense urban environment this may be plausible, but it is much less safe in a rural setting where population is almost certainly concentrated into small settlements separated by tracts of unoccupied land. Method 3 offers the prospect of a more realistic representational model, particularly in rural and urban-fringe situations, and requires some further explanation.

data.Article Title: Institutions, Extreme Weather, and Urbanization in the Greater Mekong Region
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: extreme weather; Greater Mekong Region; urbanization; urban land expansion
data.Keywords Plus: CLIMATE-CHANGE IMPACTS; TROPICAL CYCLONES; TEMPERATURE; RAINFALL; PRECIPITATION; VULNERABILITY; ADAPTATION; MIGRATION; DROUGHT; HEALTH
data.text: Climate change threatens many developing countries with more frequent and intense extreme weather events. Researchers, however, have not comprehensively examined how extreme weather influences urbanization and sustainable development. Based on the spatial estimates of precipitation, tropical cyclones, and temperature for the period of 2000 to 2010, we establish an eleven-year climatological record and calculate anomalies at the county and district level in the Greater Mekong Region (GMR). Combining this with urbanization data from the World Bank, we relate weather patterns to growth rates in urban population and urban land use and find that the above-average rainfall in the wet season along with more frequent cold waves and tropical cyclones tend to retard urban development. In contrast, crop failures caused by increasingly severe droughts during the dry season and heat waves accelerate rural-urban migration and the agglomeration of urban poverty. By identifying institutionally varying effects, we further find that nonsocialist countries have additional sensitivity to most weather extremes than more centralized socialist countries, which have stronger ability to mobilize resources for disaster management and relief. Our study contributes to the understanding of effects of weather shocks on socioeconomic outcomes in societies rapidly integrating with the global economy.

Study Area and Time Period

According to the United Nations, the AsiaPacific region is the world ' s most natural disasterprone region, with more than 41.2 percent of people living in poor conditions in 2013. Over the past decade, this region has seen a more than threefold increase in the number of deaths due to disasters (Kuntiyawichai et al. 2015). Composed of Yunnan, Guangxi, Cambodia, Lao PDR, Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam, the GMR has the highest exposure to weather extremes in the Asia-Pacific region (Jongman, Ward, and Aerts 2012). The GMR is hugely vulnerable to weather shocks due to its unique geographical and socioeconomic circumstances. First, a large proportion of GMR ' s population lives in low-elevation coastal zones that are particularly at risk from climate change and weather-related hazards, including sea level rise, storm surges, and typhoons. Half to two thirds of the cities in the GMR are exposed to floods and TCs (United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs Population Division 2013). Second, the GMR consists of developing countries, which account for most global deaths from weather-related disasters and are more vulnerable to climate change than developed nations (IPCC 2014b). In 2010, the GMR had more than 300 million inhabitants and 2,471 county-level (the fourth-level administrative division of China) or district-level (the third-level administrative division of Myanmar, Lao PDR, Vietnam, Thailand, and Cambodia) subareas, which are the 2,471 observation units in our

Data Sources and Variables

To examine how urbanization and urban expansion are affected by weather extremes, we rely on three types of data -urbanization, climatology, and local geographical and socioeconomic data. The dependent variables are the urban population change rate and the built-up area change rate in percentage, capturing urbanization and the urban expansion process between 2000 and 2010 in the GMR (Table 1). The data on urban population and the built-up areas are provided by the World Bank East Asia and Pacific Urban Flagship Study (PUMA; Mertes et al. 2015). To identify the extreme weather events and their impact on urbanization, multiple data sets of precipitation, TCs, and temperature from January 2000 to December 2010 are incorporated to construct an eleven-year climatological record for each county and district. Moreover, to control local climate, geographical, and socioeconomic differences, several groups of control variables such as baseline climate variables and local accessibility are also considered in this study.

Precipitation Anomalies. The precipitation anomaly is one of the direct indexes of the deficit or surplus of rainfall, which measure the difference between the observational data and the long-term climatological mean. In this study, the frequencies of monthly precipitation anomalies with values greater than 60 mm ( PM60 ) or less than -60mm ( NM60 ) are calculated to capture the precipitation extremes for each county or district (Manton et al. 2001). Introduction

Department of Geography and Regional Studies, University of Miami † School of Public Administration, National Center for Integrated Coastal Research, University of Central Florida ‡ Department of Geography, University of Utah

U rbanization and climate change have been identified as the two most significant trends to shape development and sustainability in the Global South in the decades ahead (Satterthwaite 2007; Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change [IPCC] 2014a). Cities in developing countries have been serving as engines of economic growth and centers of institutional change (UN Habitat 2007; Wei 2012). At the same time, climate change, especially more frequent and intense extreme weather events, could exacerbate resource scarcity and put vulnerable communities at risk (IPCC 2014a). Less developed regions, such as the Greater Mekong Region (GMR), have experienced a large and growing number of extreme weatherrelated deaths and economic losses (United Nations 2011).

The GMR is geographically composed of Yunnan and Guangxi in China, Cambodia, Lao People ' s Democratic Republic (PDR), Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam (Asian Development Bank [ADB] 2011). Since the 1990s, the GMR has recorded dramatic urban growth both in population and territory. From 2000 to 2010, the total urban population of this region increased from 38.5 million to 61.7 million, and the total built-up area expanded from 14,312 km 2 to 17,428 km 2 (World Bank 2015). The GMR is vulnerable to weather shocks and related hazards, such as increased rainfall in the wet season, decreased rainfall in the dry season, and intensified flooding and droughts (International Centre for Environmental Management 2010; IPCC 2014b). Therefore, as one of the most vulnerable regions to climate change, the GMR ' s urbanization and its response to extreme weather deserve further investigation (Krongkaew 2004; Francisco 2008; Jongman, Ward, and Aerts 2012).

A rich body of literature, mainly by ecologists and climatologists, has explored the associations between urbanization and extreme weather since the 2000s (Kishtawal et al. 2010; Brody et al. 2014), mainly the influence of urban development and other human activities on the frequency and magnitude of extreme weather and related hazards. Only a few qualitative studies point out that extreme weather events might undermine ongoing urbanization, and empirical studies focusing on the response of urbanization to weather shocks remain very limited (Hallegatte, Henriet, and Corfee-Morlot 2011; IPCC 2014a, 2014b). Given the massive population at high risk of extreme weather, as well as its ongoing institutional restructuring (Krongkaew 2004), a quantitative study of the GMR will improve our understanding of how extreme weather events affect socioeconomic outcomes, which is critical to regional development and sustainability in the Global South (Parnell and Walawege 2011; Harden 2012; Whitehead 2013).

Literature Review

There is general agreement that changes in the frequency and magnitude of extreme weather have profound impacts on human migration and urbanization (Kunkel, Pielke, and Changnon 1999; Hunter 2005; Warner 2010; Black et al. 2011; Gray and Mueller 2012; IPCC 2014a). The data on weather extremes have been compartmentalized into two groups: one based on climate statistics including extreme precipitation and temperatures and the other one referring to droughts, floods, or hurricanes that do not necessarily occur every year at a given location (Easterling et al. 2000). Given the climate and hazards characteristics of the GMR, we focus on three groups of weather extremes -extreme precipitation, hurricanes, and temperature extremes -and examine how they influence urbanization through hazards such as floods, droughts, and heat waves (Francisco 2008; Jongman, Ward, and Aerts 2012; IPCC 2014b).

Extreme Precipitation and Urbanization

Extreme precipitation refers to a significant change (increase or decrease) in monthly or seasonal precipitation. Extreme precipitation has been widely linked to severe hazards that have considerable effects on urbanization. Anomalously positive (above-average) rainfall is closely related to flooding, which leads to loss of life and property, as well as damage to public infrastructure and businesses in urban areas (Huong and Pathirana 2013). These losses can significantly affect regional and national economies, as well as urban development, which further leads to urban -urban or urban -rural migration from flood-prone cities to safe areas (Ingirige and Wedawatta 2011; Jha, Bloch, and Lamond 2012). Earlier studies agree that flooding in a rural area is likely to increase human mobility and trigger rural -urban migration, which increases urbanization rates and agglomeration of urban poverty (Hunter 2005). Recent studies, however, have found a contradictory result. Some qualitative research has pointed out that flood-displaced people tend to return as soon as possible to reconstruct their homes and livelihoods (Piguet 2008; Tacoli 2009).

data.Keywords Plus: REGIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; GUANGDONG-PROVINCE; POSTREFORM CHINA; ZHUJIANG DELTA; STATE POLICY; URBANIZATION; INVESTMENT; INEQUALITY; MIGRATION; GEOGRAPHY
data.text: Much of the development literature and the theory of urban transition have been based on an arbitrary division of production space into city and country side. Despite growing recognition of the need for an integrated approach to urban-rural relations, controversial issues related to the definition and measurement, of the phenomenon remain unresolved. This case study of spatial transformation in China's Pearl River Delta analyzes with greater precision the geographic extent and functional attributes of a zone of urban-rural interaction located outside and between major metropolitan centers. This zone has been the spatial focus of industrial and commercial development, although most of its population remains officially classified as agricultural. The peri-urban zone was initially left behind by the central cities in terms of its contribution to the regional economy After a decade of postreform development, this zone has moved ahead of the central cities and become the region; main destination for in-migrants and foreign investment. The growth of the zone of urban-rural interaction outside the central cities has absorbed a significant amount of the increased urban population, but it has not brought about a reduction of regional economic inequality because of the persistence of a backward economy in the periphery Theoretical questions are raised concerning the validity of several fundamental assumptions underlying the conventional model of urban transition.

Data and Methodology

Clearly, the PRD has undergone a remarkable process of accelerated economic growth and regional development. It is acknowledged that dramatic economic and spatial development in the PRD may not be typical of the general situation of the country. However, a detailed study of spatial transformation of a region that has moved 'one step ahead' of the nation may still shed important light on what may occur in other Chinese regions that have just started to experience a similar practice of economic reforms and opening up.

Data for this study were gathered through documentary research and field investigations conducted in China between 1980 and 1997. Updated information was obtained from the recent publication of national and provincial statistical yearbooks (CSSB 1996; GPSB 1996). Systematic and comparable data for quantitative analyses focus on the period of 1980 to 1990. There are two major reasons for using the 1980s data. First, choosing the 1980s as the period of study allows the utilization of economic data that are measured at the constant 1980 prices without the distortion of inflation. Second, in 1991 the provincial authorities of Guangdong conducted a comprehensive survey of county-level economic performance in the 1980s. This survey has resulted in a comprehensive data set at the county-level and on an annual basis for the years 1980-1990 (GPSB 1991). Because of the constant administrative changes that took place after 1990, the data set of the 1

Study Site

The Pearl River Delta (PRD; Fig. 1) 2 selected in this study represents a natural 'laboratory' suitable for empirical analyses to answer the questions raised above. Located on the southern coast of China's mainland, the PRD is one of the most populous and rapidly urbanizing regions in the country. A subtropical climate, fertile alluvial soils, and a water system good for year-round irrigation and transportation have made the PRD one of the largest rice bowls in China, supporting a large and dense population for centuries. The existence of large

metropolitan centers nearby, including Hong Kong and Guangzhou (the primate city of Guangdong Province), has created great market demand for the production of various farm commodities and led to the development of an agricultural system in which paddy rice cultivation and cash crops are intensely mixed. Over the years, the continued growth of farm commodities has given rise to thriving trade and manufacturing, based primarily on local agricultural produce. In turn, this has paved the way for cities and towns to flourish across the region. By the end of the nineteenth century, the PRD was already one of the most commercialized and urbanized economic regions in China, second only to the lower Yangtze (Skinner 1977, 211-249). Research Scope

This study investigates the development of a spatial form of urban-rural interaction in China's Pearl River Delta. Specifically, it seeks answers for three interconnected questions: 1) Does the kind of zone of intense urban-rural interaction postulated in the Ginsburg-McGee model exist in the Chinese context, and if so can it be identified and delineated? 2) How special is this zone when compared with other spatial entities such as the central cities and the countryside, and what are its functional attributes in terms of economic production, population, and land use? 3) What is the regional effect of the emergence of this zone, and what are the implications of its growth for economic and social development at the broader regional level?

Introduction

tudies of urbanization and national development have traditionally been based on an unambiguous distinction of city and countryside. Most research has tended to treat urban and rural development as separate issues, with little consideration of the linkages and interaction between the two components (Roberts 1978; Gilbert and Gugler 1982; Harris 1982). In recent years, however, a growing number of scholars have become increasingly critical about the adequacy of the arbitrary urban/rural dichotomy (Unwin 1989; Friedmann 1996; Douglass 1998; T acoli 1998). For instance, studies of urbanization in many developing countries have revealed a distinct phenomenon of urban-rural interaction 1 that can often be found in the areas surrounding and between major metropolitan centers (Ginsburg, Koppel, and McGee 1991; McGee 1991; Potter and Unwin 1995). These regions do not fit neatly into the conventional category of 'urban' or 'rural' settlements, but they demonstrate features of both types. While the significance of urban-rural interaction in developing counS

Theoretical Context

Despite its definitional difficulty, urban-rural interaction is generally understood as a process of linkages and exchange between the two loci of change in a broader context of social formation (Harvey 1985, 14-15; Unwin 1989, 12). It may take the form of the flow of people, commodities, capital, information, and other social transactions (T acoli 1998, 147; also Preston 1975; Gould 1982; Potter and Unwin 1995). It can also manifest itself in the new form of spatial complexes in which urban and rural or industrial and agricultural activities are intensely mixed or 'interlocked' (Ginsburg 1990, 31; McGee 1991, 7; Zhou 1991, 89). This study focuses on the spatial manifestation of urbanrural interaction with special reference to the development of what has been known as zones of 'urban-rural integration' ( chengxiang yitihua ) in the Chinese context.

This study investigates the development of a spatial form of urban-rural interaction in China's Pearl River Delta. The Telengana Context

Research was conducted among fifteen villages of the Western Medak district of the Telengana region, with two villages being the focal point of the ethnographic research. Food sovereignty interventions have been actively promoted by a nongovernmental organization (NGO), Rural Development Initiatives (RDI), in seventy-five villages in the area since the early 1990s. This research used a political ecology approach that combined a place-based study of local actors contextualized with a historical analysis of the capitalist transition of agriculture and a multiscalar treatment of food sovereignty. Methods included focus group discussions, surveys, semistructured interviews, life histories, informal discussions, and participant observation.

Secondary data in the form of land records, crop histories, and local news articles were also used.

The Telengana region (see Figure 1) forms part of a contiguous semi-arid belt and is considered 'backward' in terms of its human development (Nagaraj 2008). The region is characterized by rain-fed agriculture, poor soils, drought, and cultural and economic marginalization. Since India adopted neoliberal economic policies, already vulnerable farming systems have given way to widespread agrarian distress in the form of farmer suicides (Nagaraj 2008).

Elizabeth Louis

Texas A&M University

This article critically examines the role of food sovereignty interventions in the mitigation of the impacts of neoliberal economic policies on poor farmers in the Telengana region of India. Findings based on eighteen months of ethnographic research in the Telengana region reveal that small and poor farmers face socioeconomic and cultural constraints to the adoption of food sovereignty practices and ideals. Food sovereignty prescriptions based on localized, sustainable, and subsistence agriculture paradoxically constrained farmers' chances of maintaining viable rural livelihoods in a harsh economic climate. Based on these findings, I argue that contrary to assertions by advocates that food sovereignty is a precondition to genuine food security, farmers must first have food and livelihood security to exercise true food sovereignty that allows them more control over their livelihoods. Key Words: food sovereignty, food security, rural livelihoods.

Drawing the Lines: Food Security and Food Sovereignty

The ideological basis of food sovereignty implies control and autonomy over the food system, something that is not addressed by food security paradigms. The term attained global significance after V´ ıa Campesina, a transnational peasant coalition, deployed food sovereignty to oppose the General Agreement on Trade and Tariffs (GATT) as compromising the rights of nations to produce their basic foods and being inimical to the interests of peasant farmers (Edelman 2014). Since then, food sovereignty has been widely adopted, and its definition expanded, reflecting its growing appeal as a discursive weapon to protect the interests not only of small food producers but increasingly of consumers and states (Wittman, Desmarais, and Wiebe 2010).

data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: developmental paradox; existential exclusion; indigenous livelihoods; ontological marginalization; vegetal geography
data.Keywords Plus: TRIBAL POPULATION; COLONIALITY; HEALTH; SPACES; INDIA
data.text: In the ever-expanding era of urbanization where the dominance of the urban human increasingly defines global society, marginalized subaltern groups in remote rural spaces remain stark reminders of systemic inequities. Nowhere is this more evident than in India, a rising superpower whose rapid growth paradoxically coexists with deep-rooted societal divides. Within its vegetal geographies, such as the tea plantations of the Global South, landscapes of cultivation are not merely sites of production; they are living terrains where plants, labor, and social hierarchies intertwine, reinforcing the very inequities that urban progress claims to transcend. This study explores the ontological marginalization within the tea plantationscape of the Dooars region in India. Ontological marginalization is conceptualized as the systematic exclusion of marginalized ways of being, rooted in colonial histories and perpetuated by modern socioeconomic systems. The findings reveal a paradox of livelihood duality. On one hand, subsistence practices rooted in collective labor, seasonal variability in livelihoods, and reciprocal exchange continue to sustain households. On the other, these practices are increasingly enmeshed in exploitative wage economies that define the vegetal geography of tea gardens. In this landscape, the very plants that anchor livelihoods also structure social relations, tying human survival to cycles of cultivation that reproduce dependency and marginality. The research reveals how historical disruptions, contemporary structural inequalities, and gendered dimensions of exclusion have perpetuated intergenerational poverty and systemic vulnerabilities. It argues that addressing ontological marginalization demands rejecting colonial development logics and embracing justice-based frameworks that value diverse ways of being, knowing, and surviving.

Case Study, Methods, and Settings

This study is based on a cross-sectional, ethnographic investigation conducted over fifteen months, employing a mixed-methods approach at the household level. The site, also the primary field location for my doctoral research, enabled sustained engagement with the Oraon community and deeper contextual understanding. Data collection (July 2022 -September 2023) combined semistructured interviews, participant observations, case histories, and social mapping. Using purposive sampling, the Draft Electoral Roll of 2020 identified areas of high Oraon concentration in Jalpaiguri district, with Mal subdivision selected for its spatial variation and demographic density.

Mal subdivision, located in the Dooars region at the foothills of the Sikkim Himalayas, includes three community development blocks (Mal, Matiali, and Nagrakata), further divided into twenty-two Gram Panchayats (Figure 1). This population-based observational study employed both ethnographic observations and a systematic ' door to-door ' household survey, using a predesigned interview schedule. Random sampling selected 200 households per block (total 600 households; 2,909 individuals), with 487 male- and 113 female-headed households. The sample was designed using Daniel ' s (1999) formula for infinite populations, ensuring statistical robustness. Introduction

T he concept of ontological marginalization, where certain lives are rendered existentially subordinate and excluded from legitimate political and human recognition, finds its most influential articulation within biopolitical thought, which locates governance as inherently producing zones of neglect and exclusion. Foucault ' s Society Must Be Defended lecture in 1976 instituted the ' shift ' from sovereign power to biopower: a form of governance that distinguishes between lives worth fostering and those that may be left to die, excluding certain groups at the level of their very being (Foucault 2003). This racialized administration of life constructs a ' biopolitical hierarchy ' in which marginalized populations, such as Indigenous and tribal communities, are governed as risks and anomalies rather than full political subjects. For Foucault, such marginalization occurs when groups are defined as naturally dangerous, inferior, or internal enemies, rendered less fully human within societal logics (Foucault 2003; Murray 2003; C. Taylor 2011). Extending this, Agamben (1998) theorized homo sacer as ' bare life, ' stripped of political value yet subject to sovereign force, crystallizing the condition of ontological marginalization. Whereas Foucault emphasized historical shifts in power regimes, Agamben universalized the logic of exception, producing a more metaphysical and juridical theory of exclusion. In the same milieu, Hardt and Negri (2000) argued that under late capitalism, life itself becomes the site of production and control, with the multitude simultaneously exploited and rendered ontologically malleable; their focus on collective resistance underscores the abstraction and disposability of subaltern life in a globalized order. Esposito ([2002] 2011), through his theory of Immunitas , reframed marginalization as a protective mechanism of the political community, negating ' othered ' life to preserve social coherence and enforcing exclusion through purification. Building on such critical engagements with the politics of life, Lemke (2011) provided the first systematic overview of biopolitics, offering a framework to understand how political power targets ' life itself ' as its explicit concern. Influenced by Foucault, Lemke examined how, in the modern era, politics increasingly aligns itself with biological laws, giving rise to forms of governance that regulate ' bare life ' and construct ' biological citizenship. ' He critiqued and expanded on the work of later theorists such as Giorgio Agamben, Hardt, and Negri, situating biopolitical mechanisms within the context of neoliberalism and bioscience. This orientation, however, carries problematic historical resonances, including eugenics and racism, underscoring the ambivalent and often exclusionary nature of biopolitical governance.

Dualism in Geography of Backwardness: Equity or (In) Equality

When the government comes with promises of development, we are the ones who always lose our forests, land, and homes. Who is this development really for? (#R49, M, Grassmore TG)

The preceding quote captures the irony of pseudodevelopment, a phenomenon I observed during my doctoral field work in a rural tea garden in the Dooars region, at the foothills of the Darjeeling Himalaya. This apprehension, ' progress ' for some and ' disposability ' for others, emerged intensely through interviews and focus group discussions, which revealed among Oraon inhabitants a sense of exclusion not limited to poverty and neglect but extending to invisibility within developmental discourse: a basic absence from contexts defining modern progress (Paradies 2020). What surfaced was not only the irony of pseudo-development, where ' growth ' narratives mask deepening precarity, but also the existential ' weight of being ' relegated to the periphery of normative imaginaries of citizenship, value, and development.

Historical Foundations of Marginalization and Disruption of Traditional Equity Systems

Historically, Oraon social structures centered on collective labor and reciprocal exchange, fostering solidarity and equitable resource sharing. These systems were disrupted by colonial interventions and later neoliberal state policies, which formalized land ownership and replaced shared governance with private landholding (Majumder 2025a). Colonial land revenue systems (Guha 1968, 1980) prioritized extraction and surplus production, displacing the Oraon from ancestral lands and weakening mutual labor exchange, thereby introducing new stratifications. Land alienation became widespread, pushing many to forest fringes, a legacy that continues today, intersecting with postcolonial development agendas, industrial expansion, and displacement.

As one elder from Abhihill Tea Garden lamented:

The land that once sustained our ancestors now operates by others. Four generations ago, we were compelled to leave our ancestral homeland and were resettled here … laboring in the tea garden. We have spent our entire lives working relentlessly, hoping for a better livelihood, decent living conditions, and enough food for our families. Nothing has truly changed. (#R56, M, Abhihill TG)

data.text: How researchers describe groups living within or near the world's tropical rain forests has important implications for how and why these groups are targeted for assistance by conservation and development organizations. This article explores how data about market behavior can be used to assess one aspect of forest peoples' liveihoods: their dependence on forest resources as a source of market income. With the intent the importance of methodology, to how we describe forest peoples' livelihoods, I draw from a multiyear survey of market activity among the Tawahka-nested measures of the Tawahkas' engagement in forest-product sale. Results indicate of Honduras and distinguish dicate that whether or not the Tawahka-or any forest group-can be considered financially dependent on forest resources depends on the spatial and temporal scales at which data are aggregated. As a group, the Tawahka earned 18 percent of total market income from forest-product sale, but their group profile masked a high degree of heterogeneity at the village and household level. Similarly multiyear data indicated that while group-level generalizations adhere from year to year, they belie considerable change in households' market behavior across years. I discuss three ways in which the findings are relevant to the theory and practice of conservation and development in the humid tropics. I emphasize the importance of spatial scale in interventions, how market-oriented conservation schemes can benefit from a broader conceptualization of the economic context in which forest-product sale occurs, and how longitudinal analysis can reveal the dynamism of forest peoples' livelihoods.

Study Region

The Honduran Tawahka, who numbered about 1,000 at the time of the study, are a subgroup of Mayangna, or Sumu, of whom the majority live in Nicaragua. In Honduras, the Tawahka homeland is centered along the midchannel of the Patuca River. The area straddles three Honduran departamentos (political regions) and lies at the southwestern edge of what is known as the Mosquitia region (Figure 1). Here, the pine-covered coastal plain ( < 75 m) of the Mosquitia meets the Colón and Patuca ranges, which support broadleaf rain forests that include Honduras' most endangered biota (Cruz and Benitez 1994; Harcourt and Sayer 1996).

Most Tawahka live in one of five permanent communities (subsequently referred to in this article as Villages A-E) located along a 40-km stretch of river. Most communities have consolidated around a Catholic church and school, and most Tawahka children receive three years of basic education. Communities differ in size (in 1998, Village A had a population of 624; Village E, 64) and in the area of adjacent floodplain. Only Village A had a government-funded health clinic during the 1990s.

Below, I describe how the data were collected and organized.

Defining Terms

In this study, 'financial dependency' on forest resources at any analytical scale is defined as the sustained and near-exclusive use of forest resources as a source of market income. As discussed earlier, this narrow definition of forest dependency focuses only on the contribution of forest products to a group's ability to meet its market needs, and in no way addresses the myriad other ways in which peoples living in or near tropical rainforest derive benefits from their local environment. The following describes how I distinguish dependence from the three other nested measures of which it is composed.

First, for any scale of analysis, I define participants as those who sold forest products in a given time period. I distinguish levels of participation through draw , or the total income earned from the sector (measured here in Lps). As used here, 'draw' refers only to income flow and says nothing about the actual flow of resources from the forest, although elsewhere, forest-derived income has been used to proxy for the 'market consumption' of forest resources (see Godoy and Bawa 1993). Reliance , then, refers to the share of total market earnings derived from forest-product sale (measured as a percentage). I distinguish reliance as high, low, or moderate by stratifying the sample rather than by using an absolute measure (following Coomes and Burt 2000). data.Article Title: MIGRATION PATTERNS DURING A PERIOD OF POLITICAL AND ECONOMIC SHOCKS IN THE FORMER SOVIET-UNION - A CASE-STUDY OF YAROSLAVL-OBLAST
data.Author Keywords: MIGRATION; RUSSIA; USSR; ECONOMIC SHOCKS
data.Keywords Plus: UNITED-STATES; POPULATION; DYNAMICS
data.text: This paper examines migration in Russia during the period that preceded the breakup of the former Soviet Union (FSU) and during the current transition period. An unusually rich dataset is used to conceptualize the impact that the political and economic collapse of a world superpower has on a migration system. A regional case study of migration in Yaroslavl' Oblast from 1989 through 1992 is used to examine the relevance of expected outcomes given standard theories of migration, empirical regularities found in capitalist economies, and past trends in the FSU. The data clearly show a migration system undergoing political and economic shocks. A significant decline of the volume of flows and a relative increase in the importance of interrepublic movement indicate disruptions. Increased relative mobility for those in the later years of the working-age population and increased importance of urban-to-rural migration flows are also important changes evident in this migration system undergoing shock.

Data and Methods

Migration data for Phase I 1 come from the annual population register data collected in Yaroslavl' by the oblast government. Register data collected at the oblast level are probably of higher quality than those presented at the national level; by the time the national level receives the data, they have passed through several government offices, each having the potential to introduce error. Trained sociologists calculated this dataset by hand using the original registry forms. Although human error can occur in the absence of computerization in

Russia, the population accounting in this dataset is the best available to date.

Several major drawbacks, however, exist due to the nature of the registry system. First, inmigration data are more accurate than outmigration data. Individuals must register as they migrate into a place in order to receive social services, including housing, education, and public assistance, but no such incentives exist to register outmigration. Outmigration data are generally underestimated, but due to the absence of place-to-place migration data, we cannot estimate the level of undercounting. Within this particular dataset, however, we can measure 6% undercounting for intraoblast migration. Second, the urban accounting systems are more accurate than the rural ones. Rural inmigration and outmigration are likely undercounted. Third, there are two separate counts of intraoblast migrat

Yaroslavl' Case Study

The Russian and Soviet migration systems have undergone shocks in the past due to major violent events such as the I917 Russian Revolution, civil war, and World War 1 1 . Characteristics of the migration system persisted despite these events-the north-to-south and west-to-east flows and rural-to-urban flows.

The essential problem here is to conceptualize how the direction and composition of migration flows within the migration system(s) of Russia may change during the post-Soviet period-a time of instability, disintegration, and reintegration, not a wartime period. There are likely to be several overlapping yet distinct phases of migration. The reality of the situation suggests that although the phases may be distinct, no one phase will be evident in isolation in any one place or at any one point in time. Phase I, destabilization, describes the late 1970s and early 1980s when the reversal of the north-to-south net exchange occurred. Phase I foreshadows Phase 1 1 , disintegration, when the chaotic patterns occasioned by the current destabilization and politicaVeconomic shocks become evident. The initial period of destabilization ended in the late 1980s just as pereswoyka was ending. Phase I1 migration should be evident in the 1990s, with 1989 being a transition year when both Phase I and Phase I1 patterns co-existed.

Soviet and Russian Case

Questions relevant to the changing direction and composition of migration flows in the Soviet and Russian context during a shock period include: What happens to the direction and composition of migration flows when a socially, economically, and politically integrated multinational state with distinct ethnic homelands breaks apart? What happens when strong government control over social and economic processes begins to fade? When, if ever, do major systemic changes occur?

The answers to these questions lie, in part, within the context of the previous migration system, one that was not well-studied by Western social scientists. Many studies of migration in the FSU successfully predict the volume and direction of migration flows using standard economic models despite the contextual problems related to the noncapitalist setting (Rybakovskiy 1973; Zaytsev 1973; Lysenko 1977; Ball and Demko 1978; Fuchs and Demko 1978; Grandstaff 1980; Maksakova 1986; Mitchneck 1990, 1991). These studies note the improvement of material welfare and quality of life as determining factors in the decision to migrate and destination choice. Standard economic models produced highly accurate predictions of the volume and direction of the flows (Grandstaff 1980; Mitchneck 1990 and 1991). Introduction

oncern about potential climate change has C led to a number of studies addressing the possible impacts on agriculture (e.g., Santer 1985; Hodges et al. 1987; Smit et al. 1989; Cooter 1990; Curry et al. 1990; Rosenzweig 1990). Two themes emerge from these studies. First, global climate change could alter agricultural productivity, requiring adjustment of certain agricultural practices. Second, present strategies used to estimate climate impacts on agriculture have several shortcomings. Perhaps the most critical shortcoming involves accurate representation of climate change at a spatial scale where agricultural impacts are felt. Clearly, the impact of climate change over broad agricultural regions should result from the aggregated effects at local levels. Yet projecting climate change down to the local scale remains difficult. Many climate impact studies rely on general circulation model (GCM) output to provide initial estimates of climate change.

Review of Migration Trends

For Western social scientists conceptualizing migration patterns in Russia, standard tools such as Ravenstein's laws of migration, life-cycle theory, the Harris-Todaro model, public choice models, and many others may be useful. These models help us to predict migration patterns according to variables such as distance, gender, age, unemployment, and local government policy. The relevancy of these traditional models, however, to non-Western, developing countries has been questioned (Brown and Sanders 1981). Approaches that relate to both less developed and more developed contexts should be considered here due to the prevalence of multiple development contexts in Russia and the USSR.

data.Author Keywords: Nordic countries; European Union; electoral geography; urban-rural
data.text: In 1994, support for European Union (EU) membership was highly variable across Norway, Sweden, and Finland. The ''no'' vote was strongest in rural areas eligible for substantial EU subsidies. Moreover, the majority voted against EU membership in Norway. To explain these outcomes, this article focuses on the ways in which local and national differences mediated interpretations of the issues raised during the campaign. The analysis highlights Important forces shaping northern Europe today and their implications for the EU in the years ahead.

Mediating Factors at the National Level

Norway, Sweden, and Finland have distinctive political, economic, social, and cultural attributes and, for many, these influenced how the arguments surrounding EU membership were understood and interpreted. A brief examination of the situation of each of the Nordic countries that voted on EU membership can thus provide insight into the variable successes of the 'yes' and 'no' campaigns in northern Europe.

Mediating Factors at the Local Level

Beyond national differences among Finland, Sweden, and Norway, the remarkable continuity in the internal spatial character of the EU membership vote across all three countries requires explanation. For those living in the more densely populated areas of Norway, Sweden, and Finland, the arguments in favor of membership were apparently persuasive-persuasive enough even to overcome projections that EU membership would have negative economic consequences for the larger cities of Finland, Sweden, and Norway. These arguments were clearly less effective in the rural periphery, even when combined with projections showing the rural periphery benefiting from EU subsidies. The reasons behind this outcome can be discerned from the preceding discussion. The urban areas of the Nordic countries are dominated by those who define their interests more in national terms and who therefore were more easily persuaded by the macroeconomic and political influence arguments of the 'yes' campaign. By contrast, those living in more remote rural areas were more likely to be swayed by the prospect of diminished local control and the restructuring of the rural sector.

data.Article Title: From the Right to Energy to the Right to the Countryside and Back Again: Contextualizing Rural Energy Transitions
data.Author Keywords: land use; populism; poverty; rural areas; sustainability transitions
data.Keywords Plus: FUEL POVERTY; POPULISM; POLITICS; AREAS; UK
data.text: Rural areas as well as their interlinkages with urban agglomerations have gained increasing attention as the main sites where the current energy transformation toward the use of renewable energy is taking place. Due to this, contestations over transitions and emancipatory efforts to transform energy infrastructures cannot be detached from the structural conditions of rural areas and their entanglements with other spatial scales. In this sense, sustainable energy transitions reflect various differences between as well as within rural areas. Consequently, rural energy transitions are embedded in broader processes of rural change. This contribution to the Focus section illustrates interconnections between energy transitions and rural change as they relate to issues of land-use change in rural areas, rural poverty, and marginalization, along with rural populism. In doing so, we argue that energy transition plays an important role for all these issues of rural development and advocate for a systematic integration of the transformation of energy systems and rural change. We, thereby, believe that contextualizing rural energy transitions can contribute to the realization of a right to the countryside and of just and sustainable rural futures within the energy sector and beyond.

Introduction

C urrent transformations of energy infrastructures shape the development of cities and regions. Rural areas, however, have been particularly exposed to various effects of climate change but also transformed by responses to these threats, including the implementation of adaptation and mitigation measures such as the development of wind farms, solar parks, and biogas facilities. Rural areas have reemerged as locations where current energy transitions toward the use of renewable energy resources are being materialized (Naumann and Rudolph 2020). Rural areas have already been affected and transformed by the extraction of energy resources and the building of infrastructure for the large-scale production of electricity and heat, but the decentralized and horizontal deployment of renewable energy requires larger surface areas due a to a lower power density (Huber and McCarthy 2017). The expansion of renewable energies additionally incorporates areas in the energy system that had previously been less affected by energy infrastructures. Current energy transitions have the potential to reshape regions or result in the abandonment of spaces that have been integrated into fossil energy systems. This will produce both new energy landscapes and postcarbon landscapes in rural areas (e.g., Lennon and Scott 2017; Batel 2020; Pasqualetti and Smardon 2025). Therefore, the peculiarities and implications of rural energy transitions deserve attention from research and practice. The example of energy, however,

illustrates that rural areas are not separate, isolated entities but have complex and uneven relations with urban agglomerations (e.g., Regier, Berka, and Hoicka 2025), for example, as ' energy peripheries ' (Golubchikov and O ' Sullivan 2020), as parts of ' peripheralization ' (Langguth 2025) or ' urban -rural exploitation ' (Kelly-Reif and Wing 2016). Furthermore, Woods ' s (2007) notion of the ' global countryside ' reminds us how rural places are intertwined with global flows of capital, resources, people, and information.

In turn, energy transitions have become formative elements of ' planetary rural geographies ' and how they are contoured (Wang, Maye, and Woods 2025a, 2025b). Planetary rural geographies have been proposed as a research agenda to incorporate rural areas as spaces of crisis, conflict, and hope (Wang, Maye, and Woods 2025a).

Rural Energy Transitions and Rural Change

Different modes of energy provision have historically influenced rural areas and have entailed specific challenges, while also presenting opportunities for rural development. From a geographical perspective, the transition from a system based on fossil fuels toward a system predominantly based on decentral, flexible, low-carbon, and renewable energy consists of more than just substituting fuels. It involves structural changes to the energy supply, distribution, and consumption of energy, as well as a reconfiguration of related spatial patterns of economic and social activities (Bridge et al. 2013). In what follows, however, we use the term energy transitions to merely focus on transformations on the side of energy supply and its energetic sources.

data.Article Title: SPATIAL ACCESSIBILITY TO HEALTH-CARE FACILITIES IN SUHUM DISTRICT, GHANA
data.Author Keywords: GHANA; GEOGRAPHICAL ACCESSIBILITY; LOCATION-ALLOCATION MODELS; RURAL HEALTH; THIRD-WORLD
data.Keywords Plus: LOCATION-ALLOCATION MODELS; GEOGRAPHICAL ACCESSIBILITY; COUNTRIES
data.text: To improve geographical accessibility to health facilities in rural Ghana, it has been recommended that additional health facilities be built. Resource constraints make this recommendation infeasible. Using location-allocation models, this paper demonstrates that in the Suhum District of Ghana substantial improvements in accessibility can be achieved with better locational choices and without additional facilities. Also, additional facilities will produce little improvement in accessibility if location is not explicitly considered. The paper demonstrates the utility of location-allocation models for improving accessibility to services in the Third World.

Studv Area

The Suhum District is in the Eastern Region of Ghana (Fig. 1). It is one of 10 pioneering districts which the government of Ghana selected to implement the PHC policy in the country. Consequently, it is the focus of ongoing research into the planning and delivery of health services in Ghana. In fact, at the time of fieldwork for this research, the district was involved in a World Health Organization assisted project to delimit the catchment areas o f health facilities and identify gaps in service delivery.

According to the latest available (1 984) census, Suhum has a population of 146,100 and encompasses about 877.5 sq km (District Health Management Team 1987). The district is located on the edge of Ghana's forest belt. The district capital, Suhum, has a population of 19,298 and is 60 km from Accra, the national

Figure 1: Ghana and location of Suhum District.

capital. Suhum has several central place functions, including education, administration, commerce, and health. Besides Suhum, only Nankese has a population exceeding 3,000 people (3,414), and just 14 communities exceed 1,000. The remainder of the population is located predominantly in small rural farming villages (Fig. 2). Because of this skewed population distribution, Suhum is the hub of most activities in the district.

The district has 30 government health facilities altogether: the C-level facility at Suhum, six B-level facilities, and

Data Requirements and Modelling Approach

Essential data for this study included population and locational information for each community. Population data were obtained from the 1984 population census. Because Ghana does not have a digital spatial database, locations were digitized as x and y coordinates from the Ghana 1:50,000 map series obtained from the Ghana Geologic Survey in Accra. There were no major problems with the maps, but the population data of some smaller communities had been aggregated with larger centers close by. Another minor problem was communities with different locations but simi- lar names. These were carefully organized to avoid assigning the wrong population figure to any location. A simple distance generating algorithm was used to generate Euclidean distances between locations.

The analysis involves 150 population centers in the Suhum district as demand points and the population at each center as the proxy for demand. Euclidean distances are used because walking is the main mode o f travel in Suhum district. This avoids the problem of seasonal inaccessibility along different types of roads. The Tietz and Bart (1968) heuristic algorithm was used. The modelling approach treats the three levels of service independently and locates an optimal system of 30 facilities in keeping with the successively inclusive nature of the system. Seven of these will provide B-level services, and one of these seven will provide C-level

pMedian Accessibility to Higher-Level Services

Next, the provision of higher-level services beginning with B-level is considered. Because it is successively inclusive, seven of the 30 facilities in the actual system provide B-level services. In order to confomi to this hierarchical structure, the optimal model must select seven facilities from the 30 providing A-level services to maximize proximity to users. The results are presented in Table 2. Hodgson (1 984) demonstrated that such a bottom-up approach can result in suboptimal higher-order facilities. This effect is evaluated by selecting seven facilities freely from the open system of 1.50 demand points. This system, however, differs from the bottom-up solution by less than 1% (Table 2). The optimal p=7 system would provide an AWD of 3.28 compared to 3.7.5 in the actual system. Introduction

eveloping countries face the problem of D improving their health care delivery systems but lack the necessary resources to do this. Health facilities are often geographically inaccessible to the majority of the rural population (Freund 1986; Lasker 1981; McEvers 1980; Stock 1985). Women and children, in particular, experience difficulties in reaching a source of care (Phillips 1990), but the explosion of health care costs makes it increasingly difficult to improve geographical accessibility to services. Attempts to extend care are frequently hampered by financial and human resource shortages and other barriers (Phillips 1990).

The Geography of Health Services in Ghana

Historically, the Ghana Ministry of Health has grappled with an 'unacceptable disparity between service coverage and quality in urban areas compared with rural areas' (Adjei et al. 1984). In 1972,149 of 298 government doctors worked in the Accra-Tema metropolitan area which contained about 8% of the country's population (Sharpston 1972). In 1978, an estimated 70% of the population were unable to use the official health system (Ministry of Health 1978) because of prohibitive distances to rural facilities.

The dilemma of the Ghana Ministry of Health has been how to provide an efficient and equitable system of service throughout the country with a highly constrained budget. To accomplish this, Ghana adopted a Primary Health Care (PHC) policy in 1978 with a stated goal to 'maximize the total health of the Ghanaian people' (Mmistry of Health 1978,9). Details of Ghana's PHC are presented in Morrow (1983). In brief, the system is based on a three-level hierarchical structure (Ministry of Health 1978) of A-level, B-level, and C-level facilities. Each A-level facility is usually staffed with a minimally trained health worker.

Studv Area

The Suhum District is in the Eastern Region of Ghana (Fig. 1). It is one of 10 pioneering districts which the government of Ghana selected to implement the PHC policy in the country. Consequently, it is the focus of ongoing research into the planning and delivery of health services in Ghana. In fact, at the time of fieldwork for this research, the district was involved in a World Health Organization assisted project to delimit the catchment areas o f health facilities and identify gaps in service delivery.

According to the latest available (1 984) census, Suhum has a population of 146,100 and encompasses about 877.5 sq km (District Health Management Team 1987). A THEORY OF ECONOMIC TRANSITION

The successful evolution and development of greenhouse horticulture in Narpes illustrate a process that has been occurring in Finland and some other areas of Europe. Two excellent examples from other communes in western Finland are fur farming, centered on Jakobstad, and Konni clock manufacturing, in Ilmajoki. Each of these industries represents the adjustment of a local area to declining agricultural resources and increasing population, essentially the same conditions that once prevailed in Narpes.

An inductive theory explains the occurrence in rural areas of highly specialized industrial communities formed by similar small-scale enterprises, originally with quite low technological levels (Palomaki 1983). Thus far, empirical results have come from Finland and from central Europe. The point of departure is an older agricultural area, where all available agricultural resources have been used, so that expansion in any traditional way is no longer possible (Fig. 4). The economy is so one-dimensional that virtually no other ways of livelihood exist. Transportation is slow and expensive. No possibilities for commuting to adjacent, more developed areas exist because the process of urbanization there is still in an initial and rudimentary phase. Therefore, livelihood necessarily remains centered on the local area.
