data.text: Land change in the Amazon is driven by numerous factors including fiscal incentives, infrastructure, transportation costs, migration, and household decision making. Largely missing from the story to date, however, is the role of contentious social processes, including contention over land resources. By employing a case study of land conflict over a largeholding in southeastern Para, Brazil, and a regional-scale statistical model, we describe contentious land change (C-LC) in an area with a long history of antagonism between largeholders and the rural poor. We fuse the conceptual frameworks of political ecology with the methodological approaches of land change science to show that deforestation in the area of study is enhanced due to the interaction of diverse and adversarial agents rather than the independent actions of isolated land managers deforesting according to the dictates of microeconomic optimization. C-LC is a process of global reach and must therefore be added to the topical range of land change science. A combination of the explanatory richness of political ecology with the methodological rigor of land change science greatly enhances our understanding of land change processes.

Data Description and Regression Analytics

Thecase study of Bala do Sul ranch and the schematic representations shown in Figures 3 and 4 suggest that contention accelerates LC beyond what would be experienced due to agronomic demands for forest clearance. To assess this claim beyond the suggestive details of the case study, we turn to regression analysis and inference, modeling deforestation as a function of contention in addition to other explanatory variables often used in LC analysis, such as distance to markets, soil quality, and so on. Our analysis starts with broad descriptive statistics considering the link between LC and the experience of contention on individual properties. We then move to regression-based assessments of LC occurring in the Brazil nut polygon over the study period from 1984 to 2003. This involves analysis of (1) total LC under successive regimes of DALR participant and owner occupation and (2) preemptive deforestation on the part of owners. This final analysis is undertaken given postexpropriation outcomes have been observed before on satellite images, but owner impacts on land in advance of conflict have not, despite speculations that they might deforest to avoid DALR targeting (Simmons et al. 2007; Aldrich 2009).

Data Sources. The analysis is developed for individual properties in the Brazil nut polygon using a variety of sources. Here, we consider satellite images, a cadastral coverage of properties, and regional newspapers, given these provide the basic information on LC and contention u

Case Study of Bala do Sul Ranch 3

The case study focuses on a 9,700-hectare property referred to as Fazenda (Ranch) Bala do Sul. The details of conflict were extracted from an archive of more than 3,000 newspaper articles from two regional newspapers and supplemented with key informant interviews with ranchers who were willing to speak about the conflict. The case study is based on this property for three reasons. First, Bala do Sul serves as an emblematic test of the dedication of DALR SMOs, the clarity of laws regarding property expropriation in the social interest, and the resolve of largeholders intent on keeping what they say is theirs. Second, its majority owner, 'Jo˜ ao Machado,' is known through the region for investing heavily in his ranching operations and has always been vocal in his hostility toward DALR and the MST in particular (E. Santos 2004). Finally, the Machado clan dominated Brazil nut production and distribution in Par´ a during the first half of the twentieth century, an economic power they translated into local political control (Emmi 1999; Almeida 2006). The Machado power base began to erode with the arrival of southern capitalists who came with the opening of the Belem-Bras´ ılia highway (BR-010) and with the discovery of gold and vast deposits of iron in the Caraj´ as region just to the south of Marab´ a. Nevertheless, the Machados remain a force to be reckoned with and a target of choice for SMOs intent on toppling the still very real political power of largeholders (E. Santos 2004)

The Schematic Representation and Inference

The case study of the Bala do Sul ranch suggests a sequencing of alternating control over land and land use, situated within a process of contention between adversarial agents possessing contradictory objectives. We now proceed to a schematic portrayal of this contentious process and its LC implications to bridge the gap between case study and statistical description. We first consider the contentious process itself, both its social dynamics and implications for changes in land cover and land use, and then move on to a regression analysis of C-LC in the arc of deforestation.

Land Scarcity and Contentious Politics in Southeastern Par´ a

In southeastern Par´ a, and throughout Amazˆ onia more generally, largeholders have enjoyed the support of state and federal governments in gaining access to land at the expense of smallholders and landless rural workers. This has created land scarcity in the midst of plenty, concentrating land in the hands of a relatively small group of individuals who have not been shy about defending what they claim to be theirs. Amazonian land scarcity, a social construct, resulted from a series of enclosures that effectively excluded prior claimants from properties they long occupied (Peluso and Watts 2001; Simmons et al. 2007). Of particular note were legislative actions in the early twentieth century taken by the State of Par´ a, which allowed for the leasing of public lands. These leases permitted wealthy landowners to take possession of large stands of Brazil nut in the southeastern part of the state that had long been common property resources (Ianni 1979; Schmink and Wood1992).Asaconsequence, independent Brazil nut collectors were dispossessed and transformed into debt peons subsisting on informal holdings, the aforementioned posseiros. Those who benefited from the bounty of the state recomposed themselves as an oligarchy of the privileged few (Ianni 1979; Emmi 1999).

Introduction

∗ Department of Earth and Environmental Systems, Indiana State University † Department of Geography, Michigan State University, East Lansing ‡ Department of Geography, Kansas State University § Department of Sociology, University of Florida

S ince the opening of Amazˆ onia in the 1960s, human populations have grown precipitously, and a great deal of forest has been transformed into pastures and crops (R. Santos 1980; R. Walker et al.

2008). Estimates as of 2007 indicate that some 637,189 km 2 of standing forest has been removed, 17 percent of the basin's original cover (Fearnside 2001; Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais [National Institute for Space Research] 2005). Rapid loss of Amazonian forest has spawned multilateral investigations such as the Large-Scale Biosphere-Atmosphere (LBA) experiment in Amazˆ onia, which has greatly advanced our understanding of the region's environment (Avissar et al. 2002; Keller et al. 2004; Batistella et al. 2007). Although such integrative studies have contributed significantly to our knowledge of change in the region, important questions remain, particularly about the human drivers responsible for this massive environmental transformation. This article contributes to our understanding by addressing on-the-ground social interactions expediting forest losses that are of concern to both the scientific community and general public.

Research has identified a number of factors affecting forest loss in Amazˆ onia, with special attention on fiscal incentives, inadequate land titling, infrastructure, transportation costs, migration, and household-level processes. These factors, certainly important, leave the story only partly told, and recent research has drawn attention to the role of contentious social processes, associated with agrarian reform, in influencing land cover change (Fearnside 2001; Simmons et al. 2007; Aldrich 2009). Earlier work of a political economic orientation describes the impact of capitalist penetra- tion on the forests of Amazˆ onia, whereby a capitalist complex of social, institutional, and economic relations replaced the autarkic economies of Amazˆ onia with modern modes of production, bringing the primitive north into an orbit of exploitive exchange relations, and decimating the environment by transforming the sustainable agriculture of smallholder subsistence into empty pastures (Monbeig 1957; Velho 1972; Martins 1975; Ianni 1979; Mahar 1979, 1989; Foweraker 1981; Moran 1983; Wood 1983; Sawyer 1984; Schmink and Wood 1984, 1992; Hecht and Cockburn 1990; Cleary 1993; Branford and Rocha 2002).

Figure 1. Southeastern Par´ a and the Brazil nut polygon within the Amazon's arc of deforestation. (Color figure available online.)

The Social Context

The foundation for environmental change and social conflict in the arc of deforestation was laid long before the military regime took power and initiated its development programs in 1964. People have long oc- cupied southeastern Par´ a, including both indigenous groups and postconquest residents who came in search of livelihood from the earliest days of the colony, with gold discoveries on the Tocantins River and agricultural frontiers advancing from Goi´ as and Bahia. Significant populations did not grow until the first rubber boom, with migrations from the northeast spurred on by frequent and devastating drought (Ianni 1979; Jad˜ ao 1984; Dean 1987; Almeida 2006). When the rubber boom went bust, the poor of southeastern Par´ a switched to Brazil nut extraction, which flourished for several decades just after Malaysian rubber production destroyed the Amazonian extractive economy with low prices.

Implications for the Region's Forest

In addition to enabling the transformation of the Luta Posseiro into DALR, the return of democracy to Brazil also coincided with a period of rapid forest loss in southeastern Par´ a (Aldrich 2009). By no means do we wish to suggest that democracy is somehow implicated in Amazonian forest loss or that LC in southeastern Par´ a-and Amazˆ onia more widely-is solely attributable to DALR and its hard-worn partisans. Current basin-scale analyses point to the considerable role played by largeholders in pan-Amazonian LC processes (Alves 2002; R. Walker, DeFries et al. 2009), and southeastern Par´ a is no exception. Indeed, the region's ranchers took advantage of capital subsidies and tax exemptions in their efforts to convert the forests of the region into agriculture and extractive land uses (e.g., Hecht 1985). It is estimated that land reform in general accounted for 30 percent of the basin's deforestation between 1964 and 1997 (Alston, Libecap, and Mueller 2000, 5). Although the Brazilian government formally prohibits the formation of land reform settlements in forested areas, this is where much of it occurs (Fearnside 2001; Simmons et al. 2007; Caldas 2008).

data.text: With climate extreme events increasing in frequency and intensity in Malawi, the future of local food production faces serious threats, necessitating renewed efforts to build the adaptive capabilities of the majority poor smallholder farmers. In this context, seed security is critical to improving rural livelihoods and agrobiodiversity; however, knowledge of its role in climate change resilience is sparse. Drawing insights from vulnerability and resilience literature, this paper examines the role of seed security in enhancing climate change resilience in northern Malawi. Using a cross-sectional survey of 1,090 smallholder farmers and applying logistic regression analysis, the study found that households that are seed-secure were significantly more likely to report stronger resilience to climate change than those that were not seed-secure, even after controlling for theoretically relevant variables (OR = 1.89; p < .01). Other noteworthy predictors of climate change resilience included level of education, wealth, agroecological practice, and seed sources. Based on the findings, we advocate for promoting seed security as part of broader localized and place-specific action plans to foster resilience to climate change in agricultural regions.

STUDY AREA

The Mzimba District is in northern Malawi, with a total land size of 10 , 430 km 2 , making it the largest district in the country. With approximately 940 , 184 people representing 13 percent of the nation's population, Mzimba is one of the least populated districts in northern Malawi (Malawi Statistical Office 2019 ). The region is characterized by subtropical climatic conditions and an unimodal rainfall pattern with total annual rainfall ranging between 600 -1100 mm/year and lasting about six months or 195 days (Bezner Kerr 2014 ; Snapp and others 2019 ). Like the rest of the country, HIV/AIDS has been a significant problem facing the region. Despite the recent progress made, it is estimated that 10 . 6 per 100 adults aged 15 -64 live with HIV/AIDS, adversely impacting household food production (Niehof and Rugalema 2019 ; Mandiwa and others 2021 ). Mzimba district is a patriarchal society with clearly defined gender roles. The gendered nature of the district, like other regions, manifests in their farming practices. Men primarily produce cash crops like tobacco and maize, while women cultivate vegetables and other common crops like sorghum, pumpkin, and cassava. As a result, men primarily concentrate on cash crops while women manage the food crop seeds when it comes to seed management and saving.

DATA COLLECTION

This paper draws data from the FARMS 4 Biodiversity 1 cross-sectional survey conducted in Mzimba District from July to August 2019 . A multiple-staged technique was employed to select smallholder farmers ( n = 1090 ). Purposive sampling was used to select 30 village areas 2 in the Mzimba district for this study (Figure 1 ). The village areas were selected based on a gradient of seminatural habitats within a 1 km radius surrounding the study site. The rationale was to keep the sample locations about 2 km apart to prevent spatial autocorrelation. We then employed systematic sampling to select households. Specifically, each fifth house was sampled from where the research team entered the village. The questions primarily focused on household seed availability, access, utilization and varietal suitability, and climate change. Other thematic areas include household demographic characteristics, socioeconomic conditions, gender relations, dietary diversity, health conditions, adaptive capacity, and on-farm activities. Western University, Canada's nonmedical research ethics board, provided ethical clearance for this study.

ABSTRACT. With climate extreme events increasing in frequency and intensity in Malawi, the future of local food production faces serious threats, necessitating renewed efforts to build the adaptive capabilities of the majority poor smallholder farmers. In this context, seed security is critical to improving rural livelihoods and agrobiodiversity; however, knowledge of its role in climate change resilience is sparse. Drawing insights from vulnerability and resilience literature, this paper examines the role of seed security in enhancing climate change resilience in northern Malawi. Using a cross-sectional survey of 1 , 090 smallholder farmers and applying logistic regression analysis, the study found that households that are seed-secure were significantly more likely to report stronger resilience to climate change than those that were not seed-secure, even after controlling for theoretically relevant variables (OR = 1 . 89 ; p < . 01 ).

CHANGING GEOGRAPHIES OF THE SEED LANDSCAPE IN AFRICA: A NEED FOR SEED SOVEREIGNTY

For centuries, smallholder farmers' seed culture has thrived through informal networks and sharing practices deeply embedded in the informal seed system. Drawing from long-standing knowledge, farmers engage in the production, selection, and preservation of seeds, fostering a culture of sharing through barter, gifting, or local market transactions (Nabuuma and others 2022 ). This seed culture has demonstrated resilience in the face of challenges, ensuring a diverse range of seeds are exchanged and cultivated. A notable attribute of the informal seed system lies in its facilitation of easy seed diffusion, adaptation to local environmental conditions, and the preservation of greater genetic diversity (Westengen and others 2023 ). These qualities are increasingly recognized as essential for building resilient food systems, particularly in the context of climate change challenges.

data.text: Traditional approaches to studying human-environment interactions often ignore individual-level information, do not account for complexities, or fail to integrate cross-scale or cross-discipline data and methods, thus, in many situations, resulting in a great loss in predictive or explanatory power. This article reports on the development, implementation, validation, and results of an agent-based spatial model that addresses such issues. Using data from Wolong Nature Reserve for giant pandas (China), the model simulates the impact of the growing rural population on the forests and panda habitat. The households in Wolong follow a traditional rural lifestyle, in which fuelwood consumption has been shown to cause panda habitat degradation. By tracking the life history of individual persons and the dynamics of households, this model equips household agents with knowledge'' about themselves, other agents, and the environment and allows individual agents to interact with each other and the environment through their activities in accordance with a set of artificial-intelligence rules. The households and environment coevolve over time and space, resulting in macroscopic human and habitat dynamics. The results from the model may have value for understanding the roles of socioeconomic and demographic factors, for identifying particular areas of special concern, and for conservation policy making. In addition to the specific results of the study, the general approach described here may provide researchers with a useful general framework to capture complex human-environment interactions, to incorporate individual-level information, and to help integrate multidisciplinary research efforts, theories, data, and methods across varying spatial and temporal scales.

Methodology: Integration, Complexity, and Coupling of ABM and GIS

The IMSHED developed for this research has utilized data and models across scales, disciplines, and time periods. Data integration included working with data at different scales (e.g., individual-level data such as age vs. population data such as mortality rate), from different disciplines (e.g., ecological data such as forest regeneration vs. sociological data such as leave-home intention), and with varying degrees of uncertainty (e.g., accurate human individual demographic data vs. forest

volume data with a wider range of uncertainty). Far more so than data, however, the combination of methods and models from different disciplines reflects the breadth of the human-environment modeling challenges. For instance, IMSHED employs a fuelwood demand model (An et al. 2001) and an econometric model for electricity demand (An et al. 2002) to compute fuelwood demand on a household basis (see the section ''Demographic Submodel''). By integrating methods and empirical results concerning young adults' propensity to leave their parental homes and form their own households, IMSHED is able to project household dynamics and link them to panda habitat loss. In addition, ecological uncertainties or variability (e.g., variations in forest volume and regrowth rates) are taken into consideration through assigning varying values to the attributes of the forest pixel objects, which demonstrate the utility of object-oriented programming (OOP) for capturing environmental variability.

Introduction

Department of Fisheries and Wildlife, Michigan State University *Department of Geography, Michigan State University

***Department of Fisheries and Wildlife and Center for Systems Integration and Sustainability, Michigan State University

C omplex human-environment interactions have been increasingly attracting the attention of researchers with different backgrounds and research purposes. On the one hand, characterizing the environment and the complex role that human actions play within it is challenging. This is partially due to the inherent complexity of the processes. The accumulated impact of individual decisions made by dozens, hundreds, or millions of people is the immediate cause of human-induced environmental change. On the other hand, these individual actions are shaped by the particular social, political, economic, and environmental frameworks within which they occur. These frameworks change through time as conditions change. Furthermore, the imprint of these activities varies throughout space and across different spatial scales.

The science of complexity has provided key theoretical contributions and techniques for environmental modelers wrestling with these challenges (Flake 1998). It is concerned with the manner in which fundamental processes can lead to emergent phenomena or behaviors in complex adaptive systems (CAS), focusing on many kinds of complexities such as hierarchical structures, feedback, self-organization, scaling, and time lags (Malanson 1999). Levin et al. (1997) provide a broad overview of approaches to considering complexity in ecosystem modeling. They describe several advantages:

  •  Incorporation of substantial local and individual characteristics
  •  Recognition of the stochastic nature of complex systems
  •  Explicit characterization of the impact activities at one scale have on patterns at another

However, the challenge is also a technical or implementational one. How can researchers integrate data and models to deal with these complex processes? Since relatively few scholars have written on the links between rural livelihoods and value chains in the Philippines, this review also includes secondary material written by consultants, nongovernmental organizations, and the Philippine media. Combining sources has led to interesting insights into the four products under study. The value chains of bananas, coconut oil, tuna, and seaweed were chosen because they are, on the one hand, export champions (Figure 4 ), but on the other hand, characterised by upstream poverty and rural hardships. As many households live in coastal areas and are dependent on marine resources, it was thought to be important to choose two land-based and two marinebased products. The secondary material included in this article mostly covers one of the following aspects: value-chain structure and economics, environmental pressures, the prospects of upgrading, rural livelihoods, or the overfishing problem in the case of tuna (and, indirectly, seaweed).

ABSTRACT. The insertion of Philippine agriculture and fisheries into global value chains has not contributed significantly to rural poverty reduction, in contrast to several other Southeast Asian countries. While there are pockets of downstream export successes, upstream actors face persistent precarious conditions. This comparative investigation of the relationships between value chains and rural development fills a gap in the literature on the Philippines. An analysis of four important products affecting at least 3 million households illustrates the need to focus more on upstream value-chain governance and pro-poor rural development interventions. This article shows that the integration of livelihoods and value-chain analyses has the advantage of fleshing out upstream challenges that are relevant for agri/aquabusiness performance, socio-spatial policies, and refinements of rural development theories. It is unlikely that horizontal coordination/social capital as well as associated upgrading efforts will be effective without a stronger emphasis on vertical coordination and human-capital formation.

for exports; by 2014 the gap had widened, with imports valued at US$ 9 . 6 billion and exports at US$ 6 . 5 billion (CountryStat 2016 ). The empirical analysis in this article focuses on two land-based products and two marine products -bananas, coconut oil, tuna, and seaweed/carrageenan -as the contribution of production and trade in these products to rural poverty reduction remains inadequate, although the Philippines excels at the global level in terms of exports and regarding bananas and carrageenan product reputation. 2 Three research questions are addressed:

  • 1 How are Philippine banana, coconut, and seaweed smallholders, and tuna fishers inserted in their respective value chains?
  • 2 To what extent do product and process-upgrading efforts benefit smallholders and fishers?
  • 3 How are livelihoods impacted by changing value-chain dynamics and what strategies do smallholders and fishers employ to improve living standards?

VALUE CHAINS AND RURAL DEVELOPMENT

One of the most commonly adopted approaches to unravelling the challenges and options facing smallholders is the sustainable livelihoods approach (SLA). This approach organizes the complex issues around poverty in terms of three factors: capital's pentagon (human, natural, financial, physical, and social), the vulnerability context, and the institutional and political economy (International Fund for Agricultural Development n.d.). These three factors culminate in livelihood strategies that, in turn, determine livelihood trajectories. Based on these trajectories, smallholders consider subsequent options, changes, and improvements with respect to the capitals pentagon (the dashed line in Figure 2 ). A major outcome of livelihood research in Southeast Asia has been the observation that farming families are increasingly relying on nonfarm income (Rigg and Vandergeest 2012 ).

data.text: This study aims to assess the determinants of using safety devices in Brazilian households, taking into account different urban-rural country contexts and income distribution. Probit models are estimated using microdata from the 2009 Brazilian National Household Sampling Survey. On average, less than half of the underprivileged population adopts safety devices, whereas almost double as many do so among the wealthy. Findings also indicate an inverse association between the level of urbanization and adoption of safety protective devices, especially of modern ones-a pattern mediated by individual levels of victimization and safety perceptions. For example, previous victimization by theft or robbery is more decisive for adopting safety protective devices among economically underprivileged households compared to wealthier ones. These results provide evidence of the perverse effects of unequal commodification of security across a country that penalizes, in particular, the rural poor.

Case Study and Methods

Brazil is a Global South country located in Latin America with twenty-six states and one federal district that comprises 5,570 municipalities with a total population of about 210 million. The geography of the study is illustrated in Figure 1. The country has one of the highest homicide rates in the world and, according to the Instituto de Pesquisa Econ ^ omica Aplicada e F  orum Brasileiro de Seguranc ¸a P  ublica (2019), its homicide rate in 2016 was around 30.3 per 100,000 population, a rate three times the world average, twice the average of countries in North America, and thirty times the average of countries in Europe. Crime is far from being homogenously distributed in the country, and its rural areas provide favorable conditions for different types of crime (Scorzafave, Justus, and Shikida 2015; Justus, Scorzafave, and Sant ' Anna 2016; Ceccato and Ceccato 2017). The country is also known for its high degree of socioeconomic inequalities (C  ardia and Schiffer 2002) that are bound to affect victimization, perceived safety, and, not least, one ' s capacity to adopt safety protection measures and safety devices.

Figure 1 The study area: Brazilian geography divided into states and municipalities.

Data and Sample

The individual data used in this study were obtained from the 2009 Brazilian National Household Sampling Survey and its special supplement on safety. All individual data were weighted using the sample expansion factor provided by the Brazilian Institute for Geography and Statistics. This database contains unidentified information from a large number of randomly surveyed individuals such that reliable estimates are obtainable for the entire Brazilian population. This database covers details regarding individual characteristics, family structure, household living conditions, income, and work. The 2009 database also includes victimization and public safety data.

Given that the safety devices addressed in this study are those employed to protect a household, the unit of analysis is the household. For this reason, the sample is restricted to the reference individuals who represent the households contained in the sample (including single-family households). This reduced the overall sample from 399,387 to 121,163 individuals who represent their households (i.e., 121,163 households). Note that despite the reduction of the number of individuals, the filtered sample remains representative of the entire population of Brazilian households for the year 2009.

Empirical Models

This study combines descriptive analysis with probabilistic regression -probit -to answer the research questions put forward. The probit model is deemed more appropriate (compared to the logit model) as suggested by Hahn and Soyer (2005), given that the sample size is relatively large and the variables are not extremely independent. The dependent variable of the probit models is a binary, which is 1 if individuals use safety devices (irrespective of type) to protect their households and 0 if otherwise. Introduction

F eeling safe is a basic human right -a right that in a country such as Brazil is threatened by high rates of crime and violence and chronic, deepening socioeconomic inequalities (Ribeiro and Cano 2016; Ceccato and Ceccato 2017; Instituto de Pesquisa Econ ^ omica Aplicada e F  orum Brasileiro de Seguranc ¸a P  ublica 2019). Ineffective, failing criminal justice and poor policing practices (Caldeira 2013; Cavalcanti 2017, 2020; Ceccato, Melo, and Kahn 2018; Oliveira 2018) are two further reasons that make Brazilians seek self-protection. Moreover, the adoption of generic social policies for crime control in Brazil compared to specific local crime prevention approaches adopted in the United States makes households resort to private safety measures (Beato and Silveira 2018). Those who can afford these measures resort to solutions provided by an ever-increasing private security industry that offers a combination of various traditional and technological safety devices ranging from padlocks to gates, alarms, closed-circuit television (CCTV) cameras, and light sensors (Oliveira 2018).

such a context of lack of access to safety devices, natural surveillance and community neighborhood watches are deemed crucial for crime prevention (Yarwood and Edwards 1995; Sutton and Wilson 2004; Messner et al. 2017; Louderback and Sen Roy 2018). Most studies on the use of safety devices focus on their effect in preventing crimes, whereas in this study we investigate why people use these devices in the first place.

As with any other product, safety protection devices have been reported to be unequally vastly consumed among the urban rich (Oliveira 2018); however, little is known about their adoption by different income groups in different geographical contexts, from megalopolises to remote rural areas. In This study investigates the determinants of adopting safety devices in Brazilian households, taking into account different urban -rural country contexts. The question posed in this study is this: What are the determinants of the adoption of safety protection devices in Brazilian households? In addition, we identify the differences in the effect of these determinants by income strata to better understand the motivations for the use of household safety devices. Safety protection devices include an array of private precaution technologies ranging from window bars, extra locks, and dogs to modern gadgets such as alarms, electric fences, light sensors, and CCTV. This study builds on the study by Oliveira (2018) that first estimated probit models to assess the adoption of private safety technologies using microdata from the 2009 Brazilian National Household Sampling Survey -a sample covering the entire country.

Why Do People Use Household Safety Devices?

There are several reasons why individuals decide to invest in safety protective devices. One of them can be the fear of being victimized, namely, fear of crime. Previous research has produced evidence of how fear of crime triggers the adoption of housing safety measures (da Costa and Ceccato 2015). Fear can be personal or related to the safety or well-being of others, such as fear for family members and friends, which is often referred to as altruistic fear (Heber 2009), or the fear of others (Sandercock 2000).

Another important reason is the actual perceived risk of victimization, because crime does not happen randomly (Weisburd 2015), and researchers have shown that it tends to be highly concentrated in space and time. Individuals opt to buy safety protection devices to reduce the risk of victimization of themselves, families, or properties. Another reason is the fact that certain crimes are difficult to solve, such as residential burglary (Coupe and Griffiths1996), which makes individuals decide to act before it occurs.

Extending this research, Argent, Smailes, and Griffin (2007) developed an amenity index for local areas of nonmetropolitan southeastern Australia. For a detailed discussion and rationale for the use of these indicators, see Argent, Smailes, and Griffin (2007). This set of physical and social environmental attributes was argued to capture the essence of rural amenity and overlaps strongly with the complex of attributes that also make areas attractive for natural-resource-dependent industries, including farming. Arguably, rural land markets in Australia are currently in a high state of flux, with a panoply of competing interests seeking to capitalize on both the traditional and a range of newly emergent values anchored in land. Amenity-led migration is, we argue, an important strand of this renewed interest in rural lands, albeit one that is highly spatially selective. Employing a predictive and synoptic model of migration attractiveness across southeastern and southwestern Australia, we test its associations with migration currents into and out of rural communities for the 1990s and 2000s. This article finds that communities with high relative accessibility-to metropolitan and urban centers and the coast-and an established or emerging tourism industry have been most likely to experience net migration gains. Yet amenity migration also intersects with more traditional rural land uses and, in particular, irrigated agriculture. Farming, and the biophysical environment and cultural landscape it both draws on and produces, is an important attractor of amenity migration. Key Words: Australia, counterurbanization, rural amenity, rural migration.

M uchoftherapidlyexpanding literature on rural amenity and amenity-led migration has reached a broad consensus on two important points. First, in high-amenity rural areas, largescale commercial agriculture's long-term future appears doomed, caught in a powerful pincer movement between, on one side, cashed-up ex-urban migrants bidding up the price of scenically attractive farmland and, on the other, local governments happy to accommodate this demand to generate lucrative income streams from local taxes, growing populations, and a range of development and regulatory levies, thereby guaranteeing their own long-term financial viability (Smith and Krannich 2000). The second point of broad agreement centers on which population subgroups make up these in-flows. Overwhelmingly, these are seen to be ex-urban wealthy and upper middle-class households, seeking to pursue comfortable lifestyles in idyllic landscapes, effectively gentrifying the countryside (Curry, Koczberski, and Selwood 2001; Larsen et al. 2007; Nelson and Nelson 2010; Gosnell and Abrams 2011). A third point gaining purchase in the international literature is, however, the recognition of the independent influence that a suite of biophysical, economic, and locational attributes of rural place is playing in drawing migrants into select locales (McGranahan 1999; Deller et al. 2001; Hunter, Boardman, and Saint Onge 2004; Argent, Smailes, and Griffin 2007).

Amenity-Led Migration into Rural Areas: A Review

Rural amenity is a quality relating to two aspects of a locale: (1) the relative attractiveness of the general environment in which it is set and (2) more specifically, the qualities or facilities of the locale itself. The first of these is a locational attribute, the latter a site attribute, and both are likely to influence where people choose to spend time (Argent, Smailes, and Griffin 2007). As a component of internal migration (i.e., permanent population movement within national boundaries), amenity-led migration to favored rural areas is frequently considered as a key subset of counterurbanization. In the Australian academic press and popular media, this conflation is achieved through the evocative labels of 'sea change' (for coastal counterurbanization flows) and 'tree change' (for more inland counterurbanization destinations; Burnley and Murphy 2004; Costello 2007). Together, these labels conjure up an implicit set of environmental, locational, eco- nomic, and sociocultural variables that act as vital pull factors for this migration current, regardless of its participants' origins (see Burnley and Murphy 2004; Hugo 2005; Walmsley et al. 2006).

Extending this research, Argent, Smailes, and Griffin (2007) developed an amenity index for local areas of nonmetropolitan southeastern Australia. For a detailed discussion and rationale for the use of these indicators, see Argent, Smailes, and Griffin (2007). This set of physical and social environmental attributes was argued to capture the essence of rural amenity and overlaps strongly with the complex of attributes that also make areas attractive for natural-resource-dependent industries, including farming. data.text: Most discussions about solar microgrids focus on sustainable energy and development goals and the technical aspects of electricity generation, storage, transmission, and distribution. Very few explicitly examine the ways in which their introduction upsets and reshapes entrenched practices of electoral politics and citizen claim-making around electricity access and development. In India, as in many parts of the world, electricity represents the most visible symbol of economic development and social well-being. Democratic politics in many developing countries are linked to demands for access to electricity. The meshing of electricity, development, and democratic politics in postindependence India has produced a politics of clientelism in which parties have sought to gain voter support with promises of cheap or free electricity. Although this electricity-centered clientelism has expanded supply, it has simultaneously contributed to skewed spatial access, unreliable supply, and high debt burdens for state-owned electricity distribution companies. This article examines histories of clientelism and the contradictions emerging from the introduction of private solar microgrids in rural areas of the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh. It shows that although solar microgrids avoid electricity-centered clientelism, significant numbers of poor rural households in their supply areas are both excluded by their user-pays approach and unable to demand fair access through political representatives. The study calls for alternative governance and support programs at local levels that ensure that private solar microgrids can deliver reliable electricity to poor households. Key Words: clientelism, electricity, India, populism, solar microgrids.

Method

Our study is based on qualitative research conducted by the first author in UP between 2014 and 2018 in four periods and over ten months of fieldwork. Semistructured and open interviews were conducted with eight managers from four microgrid providers and with twenty-six individuals involved in UP ' s power sector, including current and retired bureaucrats associated with the Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited (UPPCL) and Uttar Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission (UPERC), consumer representatives, and journalists. Interview information was validated by cross-referencing and coded for analysis. Repeat field visits were made during each fieldwork period to nine microgrid systems in the central districts of Unnao, Sitapur, Barabanki, and Gonda. Secondary material was analyzed, including newspaper reports, policy papers, and legislation.

Democracy, Development, and Electricity-Centered Clientelism

Modernization and development have always been materially and symbolically associated with states establishing large-scale road, electricity, clean water, sanitation, and housing infrastructure. Indeed, the development of infrastructure for the delivery of what are deemed to be essential services has been the object of state formation around the world (Meehan 2014). In many postcolonial countries, democratic politics has centered on mobilizing support by invoking visions of poverty alleviation and development to key electoral groups (Corbridge and Harriss 2000; Witsoe 2013). Political parties have sought to win elections by guaranteeing their voter base access to modern infrastructure and services in exchange for their votes. These dimensions of political practice often operate through populist appeals, where charismatic politicians build ' personal ' ties with their constituents by combining popular narratives of progress with the delivery of material benefits, often distributed on the basis of a shared social affiliation (Kitschelt and Wilkinson 2007; Scoones et al. 2018).

data.text: The concern with space and, more fundamentally, the formulation of a larger, guiding spatial theory, was central to achieving Nazi objectives during the Third Reich. We disclose critical elements of that theory, focusing on two contributions: the first by the jurist and international legal and political theorist Carl Schmitt (18881985) and the second by the geographer Walter Christaller (18931969). Applying the perverted biopolitical logic of National Socialism required the military accomplishment and bureaucratic management of two interrelated spatial processes: deterritorialization and reterritorialization. Deterritorialization involved moving non-Germanized Germans (mainly Jews and Slavs) off conquered Eastern lands to create an empty space that was then reterritorialized by the settlement of legitimate Germans (although often not German citizens). Although many German academics were involved in designing and implementing these spatial strategies, we single out two. Carl Schmitt provided a politico-judicial justification for reterritorialization involving the geographical expansion of the Third Reich: Gro ss raum (greater space). Conceived four months before Germany's Blitzkrieg invasion of Poland that triggered World War II, Gro ss raum provided the (literal) grounds for Nazi reterritorialization. Walter Christaller brought his peculiar spatial imaginary of formal geometry and place-based rural romanticism in planning the empty space of the East after non-Germanized inhabitants were removed. His central place theory re-created the Nazis' territorial conquests in the geographical likeness of the German homeland.

Theories of Space and Nazi Ideology: A Reactionary Modernist Geography

The Nazi project was necessarily a geographical project (Schl¨ ogel 2003, 27-34). It was about creating a new world in the image of the perverted logic of National Socialism, a logic that Herf (1984) dubbed, 'reactionary modernism.' Herf (1984, 1) wrote, 'reactionary modernism' attempted to affect a 'reconciliation . . . between the antimodernist, romantic, and irrationalist ideas present in German nationalism and the most obvious manifestation of means-end rationality, that is, modern technology.' 11 On the one hand, National Socialism embraced modernity and instrumental rationality; something found, for example, in the Nazi emphasis on engineering, eugenics, experimental physics, and applied mathematics. They were also exemplified in the Nazi technologies of governance around the economy, population, planning, and settlement (examples of the former are found in Renneberg and Walker [1994], and Sz¨ oll¨ osi-Janze [2001a, 2001b]; and of the latter in Fehl [1992]; R¨ ossler [1994]; Rollins [1995]; Kay [2006]). On the other hand, cheek-by-jowl was National Socialism's other embrace: a dark antimodernity, the anti-Enlightenment. Triumphed were tradition, a mythic past, irrational sentiment and emotion, mysticism, and a cultural essentialism that turned easily into dogma, prejudice, and much, much worse (Pringle 2006).

Reactionary modernism necessarily entered the geographical marrow of the Nazi regime. That geography was defined by two interrelated spatial processes: deterritor

Spatial Theory

If anyone in human geography is associated with spatial theory it is Christaller. He might have been the very first spatial theorist in human geography, at least for the modern period in which the discipline was institutionalized. Christaller was part of a long tradition of formal, rationalist German location theorists that dated back to von Th¨ unen's ([1826] 1966) Isolated State , and that included Weber ([1909] 1929), L¨ osch ([1940] 1954), and Pred¨ ohl (1928). But none of them was a geographer except for Christaller (1966), who completed his doctoral dissertation, Central Places in Southern Germany , at the Department of Geography, University of Erlangen, in 1932 (for a discussion of German location theory, see Blaug 1979; Ponsard 1983; Barnes 2003).

Right from the start of his dissertation, Christaller framed his work as modernist, scientific, and rational. He began 'not with descriptive statements' but 'with a general and purely deductive theory' (Christaller 1966, 4). His aim was to 'find a general explanation for the sizes, number, and distribution of towns' (Christaller 1966, 2) and which was to be formulated as ' special economic geographical laws ' (3). Special economic geographical laws were 'not so inexorable as natural laws' (3), but they were almost as good. Similar enough, at least, that Christaller (1966, 4) concluded, 'it does not seem senseless to search for such laws.' He did, and he thought he found them.

Introduction

† Cultural Geography Department, Wageningen University; and Department of Geography, Royal Holloway, University of London

A nglo-American human geography has been mainly silent about the constitution of the geographies of Hitler's empire. The relatively few although often excellent contributions to the topic have sparked only limited interest (Bassin 1987; Charlesworth 1992, 1994, 2003, 2004a, 2004b; Cole and Graham 1995; Clarke, Doel, and McDonough 1996; Doel and Clark 1998; Cole 2003, 2009; Elden 2003, 2006; Keil 2005; Charlesworth et al. 2006; Gregory 2009). 1 In contrast, in history, philosophy, sociology, and political theory, critical examination and debate about the Nazi project and its theories have been energetic and widespread (see, among many others, Herf 1984; Burleigh 1988, 2000; Bauman 1989; Agamben, 1998, 2005; Browning 2004). Not in AngloAmerican geography, however, where even the recent interest in genocide, and in the writings of Agamben and Schmitt ( Geografiska Annaler B 88(4), 2006; and Legg 2012), has done little to provoke disciplinary discussion about the spaces of Nazism. This article is an attempt at remediation, concerned with outlining some of the elements that made up Nazi spatial theory, by exploring the works of two Nazi academics who influenced directly and indirectly postwar human geography: the legal theorist Carl Schmitt and the geographer Walter Christaller. Of the two, Schmitt (1888-1985) is better known and over the last decade or so has received considerable attention across the range of human sciences, including geography. 2

As a youth, Schmitt was a brilliant law student, completing his second dissertation, the Habilitation , in 1916, just before enlisting in the German army to fight in World War I. 3 Postwar he taught at a variety of German universities, which culminated in his appointment as Professor of Law at the University of Berlin in 1933. On 1 May of that same year he joined the Nazi party. During the 1920s, Schmitt was a prolific writer, concerned with the constitutional legitimacy of the Weimar Republic (Kennedy 2004). Although even then, as Vinx (2010) said, 'Schmitt's declared aim [was] to defend the Weimar constitution . . . at times [it was] barely distinguishable from [his] call for constitutional revision towards a more authoritarian political framework.' With the end of Weimar, and the beginning of the Third Reich, Schmitt was appointed National Socialism's 'Crown Jurist.' Increasingly he sought both legally and politically to justify Fascism, the F¨ uhrer, and concomitant violent deeds, including political murder. 4 For our purposes, most germane was Schmitt's geographical imaginary, which entered into the larger Nazi discourse and was represented most readily by Großraum ('greater space'). 5 Großraum provided a spatial justification for the National Socialist state expansion, for Germany to dominate a larger geographical region, and for the Nazis to take over the world.

Theories of Space and Nazi Ideology: A Reactionary Modernist Geography

The Nazi project was necessarily a geographical project (Schl¨ ogel 2003, 27-34). It was about creating a new world in the image of the perverted logic of National Socialism, a logic that Herf (1984) dubbed, 'reactionary modernism.' Herf (1984, 1) wrote, 'reactionary modernism' attempted to affect a 'reconciliation . . . between the antimodernist, romantic, and irrationalist ideas present in German nationalism and the most obvious manifestation of means-end rationality, that is, modern technology.' 11 On the one hand, National Socialism embraced modernity and instrumental rationality; something found, for example, in the Nazi emphasis on engineering, eugenics, experimental physics, and applied mathematics. They were also exemplified in the Nazi technologies of governance around the economy, population, planning, and settlement (examples of the former are found in Renneberg and Walker [1994], and Sz¨ oll¨ osi-Janze [2001a, 2001b]; and of the latter in Fehl [1992]; R¨ ossler [1994]; Rollins [1995]; Kay [2006]). On the other hand, cheek-by-jowl was National Socialism's other embrace: a dark antimodernity, the anti-Enlightenment.

Carl Schmitt, the Making of a Nazi

Trained in law during the waning years of the Wilhelmine Empire, Carl Schmitt became a leading legal and constitutional scholar and a political theorist in the Weimar Republic (1919-1933). Initially a professor of constitutional law at Bonn, during the 1920s he published in rapid succession a series of volumes on Weimar's constitutional and political status (Schmitt 2004, 2005, 2008). That preoccupation ended abruptly in January 1933, with the appointment of Hitler as Chancellor. In March 1933, on a trip to Rome, Schmitt got the call. Johannes Popitz, freshly appointed Reich Commissar for the Prussian Ministry of Finance, asked Schmitt to serve as Prussian Councillor of State. Schmitt immediately accepted. At that same time, Schmitt was in communication with Martin Heidegger, who urged him to 'join the revolution' (M¨ uller 2003, 37). Quickly, then, Schmitt found himself at the center of Nazi power, in his case also enjoying the patronage of Hermann G¨ oring, deputy to Hitler from 1941 after Hess flew to Scotland. In May 1933 Schmitt joined the Nazi Party and in November was appointed President of the National Socialist Jurists Association.

data.text: Although India's cooperative dairying program is lauded as a model of successful rural development, lack of uniformity in replication of the program across rural India has raised questions about the meanings of success. Differences between dairy cooperatives become especially apparent when crossbred cows are considered, so that the promotion of crossbreds by dairy development agencies has not always resulted in their actual adoption by farmers. This article seeks to explain the mixed reception accorded to crossbred cows by focusing on the link between development and place. By discussing both official discourses and local perspectives, the article enables two kinds of understanding of dairy development. First, the rise and fall of support for crossbred cows within India's national plans suggest that contrasts between official policies and local practices of dairying need to be attentive to the dynamics of both discourses and places. Second, the comparison between two villagesone utilizing crossbred cows and the other water buffaloes as principal dairy animalsshows that evaluations of success or failure cannot be made simply on the basis of adoption or rejection of crossbred cows but requires engagement with place-specific agricultural economies and social relations. Given the liberalization of India's dairy sector, official discourses and material experiences of cooperative dairying become significant for ascertaining future possibilities for small-scale farming and equitable economic growth in rural India.

Case Studies

Local perspectives on dairy development were gathered through ethnographic fieldwork conducted in 2000 and 2001 in the village of Mahdol in the state of Gujarat and the village of Saundara in the state of Madhya Pradesh. 7 Fieldwork consisted of data collection using surveys administered to every household and interviews conducted with a cross section of village residents. Both surveys and interviews were undertaken with a research assistant who was a resident of the village. Because these data were collected while I resided in the village, interpretations have also been supplemented through participant observation. Mahdol and Saundara were chosen as field sites because they reflect the variations in outcomes of dairy development that this research seeks to explicate. Crossbred cows are the principal dairy animals in Mahdol, whereas water buffaloes play this role in Saundara, so that the two villages provide an important basis for understanding how different development histories and regional economies affect the adoption of new technologies.

Recent geographic understandings of place have moved from humanistic notions of place as attachment, to materialistic understandings of place as a specific node in the wider production of space (Duncan 2000). This section is based on surveys of every household in the two villages. In the case of Mahdol, surveys also included houses in agricultural fields that are classified as part of Mahdol. Table 1 provides an overall comparison of the two villages and indicates that the village of Mahdol differs substantially from the village of Saundara in terms of number of households and total amount of agricultural land. The more important difference, however, is in terms of how land is distributed between households: 62 percent of households own some land in Mahdol but only 35 percent of households own land in Saundara. Although India's cooperative dairying program is lauded as a model of successful rural development, lack of uniformity in replication of the program across rural India has raised questions about the meanings of success. Differences between dairy cooperatives become especially apparent when crossbred cows are considered, so that the promotion of crossbreds by dairy development agencies has not always resulted in their actual adoption by farmers. This article seeks to explain the mixed reception accorded to crossbred cows by focusing on the link between development and place. By discussing both official discourses and local perspectives, the article enables two kinds of understanding of dairy development. First, the rise and fall of support for crossbred cows within India's national plans suggest that contrasts between official policies and local practices of dairying need to be attentive to the dynamics of both discourses and places.

Politics of Development and Cultures of Cattle 1 in India

In studies of the political economy of India, there has been much debate regarding the extent to which agrarian class interests are expressed through the Indian state (Rudolph and Rudolph 1987; Varshney 1995; Bardhan 2003; Frankel 2005). In the 1960s, the period when rural cooperative dairying was officially established as the national program of dairy development in India, economic policies were geared not just toward productivity but also toward self-sufficiency and redistribution. Contradictions between the aims of productivity and redistribution, however, were apparent right from the beginning and became especially prominent in the context of the Green Revolution in agriculture. The focus on technology-intensive agriculture, dependent on high-yielding hybrid seeds, chemical fertilizers and pesticides, large-scale irrigation projects, and mechanization, has been viewed as a key to India becoming self-sufficient in food grains (Lipton and Longhurst 1989; Hazell and Ramasamy 1991), but it has also been criticized for producing and entrenching inequalities in rural land ownership (Byres 1981; Harriss 1982).

Crossbred Cows and National Discourses of Dairy Development

National dairy development in India is based on replication of cooperative dairying bodies established by farmers in the state of Gujarat (NDDB 1987; Kurien 1997a). In 1946, villages around Anand, a small town in central Gujarat, became the site of a struggle against the monopoly on milk procurement and marketing granted to Polson, a private dairy company. This struggle compelled the British colonial authorities to rescind the monopoly, and the farmers of Anand organized themselves into the Kheda District Cooperative Milk Producers' Union (KDCMPU), 3 currently more popularly known as Amul, the brand name of its products. As the KDCMPU grew in the villages surrounding Anand, farmers began resisting the hold of small-scale private traders in milk. Thus, cooperative dairying sought to reform existing structures of marketing to return profits to dairy farmers as opposed to milk traders and dairy companies.

data.text: Livestock-based livelihoods are currently being promoted by international development agencies as part of global efforts to combat poverty. India's dairy development program, organized around village cooperatives, has become an important model for such efforts. This article aims to identify household characteristics that influence membership in India's rural dairy cooperatives by comparing two villages representing different degrees of success. Utilizing logistic regression methods, data collected through a comprehensive survey of all households in the two villages are analyzed to examine (1) how variables describing animal ownership, agricultural attributes, and household labor availability contribute to explaining membership in the dairy cooperative; and (2) whether factors influencing membership differ across the two villages. Our results indicate that although agricultural property ownership influences cooperative membership in both villages, the kind of dairy animal used and labor utilized for dairying work also have a significant and context-specific effect on household participation. Key Words: agriculture, cooperatives, dairying, land, rural development.

Background and Study Areas

This article focuses on two village dairy cooperatives: one is located in Mahdol 1 village in the state of Gujarat and is associated with successful dairy development; the other is located in Saundara village in the state of Madhya Pradesh, representing a less successful implementation of the program (Figure 1). Although a number of studies on dairy development in India have focused on the scale of the village cooperative (Doornbos et al. 1990), these studies have not explicitly sought to produce a comparison across regional differences in the program.

India's dairy development program is popularly traced to a struggle launched in 1946 by farmers residing in villages around Anand, a small town in the state of Gujarat. The farmers were protesting the grant of monopoly milk procurement rights to Polson, a private dairy company, by the British colonial government and linked their struggle to the larger anticolonial movement and its leaders in Gujarat. Faced with this resistance, the British government rescinded the grant and the farmers won the right to organize milk marketing on their own terms. This led to the formation of the Kheda District Milk Producers Cooperative Union (KDMPCU), more popularly known as AMUL, the brand name of its dairy products. In 1965, rural cooperatives were elevated to the status of a national model for dairy development. The National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) was established in Anand and entrusted with the task of replicating Anand pattern dair

Data

The data used in this study were collected on the basis of surveys conducted between January 2001 and September 2001 in the villages of Mahdol and Saundara. These surveys incorporated all households in the village and consisted of a structured questionnaire that was filled out by a female research assistant from each of the two villages. The first author conducted preliminary field work from November 1999 to April 2000 to ensure that people had become familiar with the purpose of the research and were more likely to be forthcoming with information about their household. Initial guidance regarding the filling of the questionnaires was provided by the first author. The research assistants obtained information through discussions with, and in the presence of, both men and women in the household. Questions were asked in the local language and forms were completed in Hindi by each research assistant. Translation of responses into English and data entry were conducted by the first author. The research assistants were acquainted with all households in the village by virtue of being village residents, but also due to the fact that one of them had served as an elected village representative in a local administrative body and the other held the position of a health worker in the village dairy cooperative. Data collection methods and the information collected were also verified by the first author when the completed survey forms were retrieved, between August and September 2001.

Methodology and Results

To identify the factors affecting dairy participation in the two villages, logistic regression was used to analyze the dichotomous dependent variable: membership in the dairy cooperative. Logit models were estimated for the probability of being a member of the dairy cooperative, as a function of the explanatory variables describing various household characteristics presented earlier in Table 1. For each logit model, the natural logarithm of the odds that a household is a dairy cooperative member is assumed to be a linear function of relevant independent variables and the maximum likelihood method is used to estimate the model. To aid in interpreting the regression results, we also report the odds ratio or the exponent of the regression coefficient produced by each logistic model. This ratio can be interpreted as a multiplier of the odds of being a member of the dairy cooperative. When this odds ratio exceeds one, the likelihood of being a dairy cooperative member increases that many times for each unit of change in the independent variable in the model. On the other hand, odds ratios less than one imply that the likelihood of dairy cooperative membership decreases.

data.text: Neither poststructural nor neoliberal. interpretations of development capture the full extent and complexity of rural transformations in the Andes. Poststructural critiques tend to view development as a process of cultural destruction and homogenization, while neoliberal interpretations identify a different development failure that inheres in inefficient patterns of resource use, and the nonviability of large parts of the Andean peasantry. In each case, the state is seen as a problem: as an. agent of dominating modernization, or as a brake on market-led transformation. The paper reviews these positions in the light of the transformations in governance, livelihoods, and landscape that have occurred in the regions of Colta, Guamote, and Otavalo, all centers of indigenous Quichua populations in the Ecuadorian Andes. These transformations question the accuracy of arguments about cultural destruction or nonviability. Instead they suggest that people have built economically viable livelihood strategies that, while neither agricultural nor necessarily rural, allow people to sustain a link with rural places, and in rum allow the continued reproduction of these places as distinctively Quichua. The cases also point to the increased indigenous control of political, civil, and economic institutions and the important roles that development interventions, including those of the state, have played in fostering this control. In sum, this suggests the need for more nuanced interpretations of development that emphasize human agency and the room to maneuver that can exist within otherwise constraining institutions and structures. It also suggests the value of placing livelihood and the coproduction of place at the center of any interpretation of the precesses and effects of rural development.

Reflections on Methodology

To attempt a comparative reading of the articulations between development interventions and microregional political economy opens up a series of methodological questions. Such ethnographically informed comparisons across different sites 'may entail a novel kind of fieldwork. Rather than being situated in one, or perhaps two, communities for the entire period of research, the fieldworker must be mobile, covering a network of sites that encompasses a process, which is in fact the object of study' (Marcus and Fischer 1986: 94). This raises several interpretative issues, for while the analysis of the process itself might remain 'thick,' discussions of the particular place-based manifestations of that process are necessarily thinner. Such a research approach also raises logistical issues. Multilocale work necessarily involves extended field presence, which is only possible at certain stages of a career. In my own case, the most in-depth basis for this comparative analysis was laid in 19881989, during a fourteen-month study of the processes of agrarian change and development in-

tervention in Colta and Guamote. That research involved intensive involvement in four communities, and sustained contact with leaders and staff of five federations of indigenous communities and with staff of six separate state and nongovernmental development organizations. Ways Forward? Hybrid Livelihoods and Comparative Ethnographies

Neoliberal and poststructural positions are, in one sense, like oil and water: their political agendas, normative intents, and epistemological positions are quite different. Partly as a consequence, they emphasize different dimensions of rural livelihoods. Neoliberal takes on rural development in the Andes draw our attention to the very real challenges that Andean people confront in making a living and negotiating their relationships with a range of product, labor, and other markets. Meanwhile, poststructural positions focus our attention on the ways in which rural people make living meaningful and struggle politically for spaces of autonomy and self-realization-themes on which the viability discussion, and much other development research, are largely silent.

Yet while their normative intents make these approaches fundamentally incompatible, their substantive concerns surely represent different parts of a larger whole in which rural people are engaged all the time: the challenge of securing a viable way of guaranteeing the material basis of their livelihood and, at the same time, building something of their own. If, in practice , people pursue these concerns at the same time, then analytical approaches that pay attention primarily to one or other dimension of them are likely to work with oversimplified notions of grassroots economic and political action, and of grassroots notions of 'development' and betterment. Indeed, I argue that if o

Introduction

hether seen as 'pioneering,' 'biting,' or 'an opportunity lost,' (respectively, Peet and Watts 1996b: 17; Cooper and Packard 1997: 15; Lehmann 1997: 568) Arturo Escobar's work (1984, 1988, 1991, 1995) has stirred the worlds of critical geography and development studies. 1 Emblematic of a broader poststructural critique of development, Escobar's analysis falls within a long and distinguished tradition that sees little possibility of improvements in human well-being without radical political economic change. His work questions the possibility of building or even imagining alternatives from within the current languages and institutions of development. 2 Indeed, it suggests that these very institutions and languages are deeply implicated in processes of cultural destruction. W

Poststructural critiques are not alone in posing profound and critical questions about rural development and its official institutions. Neoliberal interpretations similarly see little cumulative benefit from state intervention in rural areas. In much of Latin America, such approaches increasingly argue that large parts of the peasantry (or campesinado ) are no longer 'viable' in the face of a globalizing market economy. Thus, while, in the poststructuralist critique, the state and development are viewed as the aggressive agents of modernization, according to neoliberal critiques, they have largely stood in the way of the transformative and modernizing potential of the market. This leads to recommendations for further liberalization of market-based resource allocation from the constraints placed on it by state and customary institutions. That such liberalization would fuel a redistribution of rural resources (especially land and water) to more competitive and larger economic agents, and a

concomitant movement of campesinos out of agriculture and rural areas, is deemed desirable on efficiency grounds.

While empirically and normatively dubious, such interpretations command far more political influence than do poststructural ones. This makes it that much more important to build a counternarrative that meets them on their own turf while questioning many of their suppositions on conceptual and empirical grounds. Yet in this sense, poststructural positions are troublesome. By finding so little that is recoverable within the practice of development, by failing to address in any detail the economic dimensions of alternatives, and above all, by not exploring the diversity of development processes and outcomes, they fail to develop the empirical bases of a possible counternarrative. Furthermore, when subjected to empirical interrogation, the categorical assertions of such positions appear overstated, in turn suggesting theoretical weaknesses. As a result, and however unintentionally, they cede ground to neoliberal interpretations and the types of programs that might derive from them.

Critiques of Development in the Andes

The analytical tools and normative concerns of poststructural and neoliberal critiques of development (critiques that Cooper and Packard [1997: 2-3] term, respectively, 'postmodernist' and 'ultramodernist') differ profoundly. At one level, these differences are part of a far longstanding split in development studies between critical Marxian and sociocultural interpretations, and more developmentalist approaches informed by neoclassical economics and rational choice theory. Neoliberal approaches aim to understand the means through which resources can be most efficiently allocated to maximize their economic productivity. In their purest sense, they therefore criticize interventions that support rural producers on criteria other than competitiveness as diversions from the normative goal of efficiency maximization. In this view, people are producers and consumers of value-a value assessed in monetary terms. Poststructural critiques begin from a profoundly different notion of value, and of valid knowledge.

Development as Knowledge-Power Regime: Poststructural Critiques

While not alone in pursuing a critique of development informed by Foucault in particular,

and post structural theory more generally, Escobar's has been the most sustained critical project (Escobar 1984, 1988, 1991, 1995; Watts and McCarthy 1997: 73). In essence, he claims that development represents a further elaboration of the Enlightenment project, in the process imposing Northern interests on those of the South (Escobar 1995: 55-101; Apffel-Marglin 1998: 29; cf. Frank 1969). 7 Thus, the idea of development allows for the notion that there are people and places that are underdeveloped, 'backward' and poor, and therefore in need of development. This labeling turns them into the targets of development programs that then intervene in order to promote a particular ethnocentric notion of what it is to be developed. These interventions aim to turn rural people into efficient producers, and if they do not make this transition, then they ought be encouraged to leave the countryside: 'produce or perish,' Escobar puts it (1995: 157).

Food Diaries

Although food diaries have long been used in health and nutrition studies, this research method is still new and largely underused within the discipline of geography (but see Legwegoh 2012; Riley and Legwegoh 2013; Legwegoh and Riley 2014). In health and nutrition studies, for each meal, respondents are commonly asked to check food items from a predetermined food list on a daily basis for a period of time. Based on the number of meals that included a speci fi c food item, consumption frequency can be calculated, which can then be imported into nutrition software to calculate the nutrition intake or relation with other variables can be measured (Passos et al. 2003). Although this method provides important data regarding food availability, it does not provide detailed data on food access.

Thus, whereas in health and nutrition studies, food diaries largely focus on nutrition, our approach explicitly aims to use food diaries to understand and analyze food access. Wrigley et al. (2002) and Wrigley, Warm, and Margetts (2003) were among the fi rst to use food diaries in food access research, yet these studies remain highly quantitative and supermarket centered. This article aims to make a contribution to current debates in the literature on food access by describing a mixed-methods approach to study the access to food in one rural community in Cuba. Each of the forty households in our study was asked to complete a detailed food diary in which they indicated what they ate and where they acquired each of the ingredients that they used for a full week. Although in Cuba the state plays a central role in organizing the distribution of food items, this method revealed a much more complex web of rural food access. By addressing alternative networks of food access and informal social relations, we aim to show how the use of food diaries, in combination with qualitative data from interviews and participant observation, can provide detailed insights in the complex processes and networks of food access. Key Words: Cuba, food access, food diaries, mixed methods.

Cuba's Cooperative Agricultural System

The food diary method we present here fi ts within a broader project investigating local food systems and food access in rural Cuba. Many researchers, policymakers, and environmental activists argue that locally embedded food systems increase access to food. Beginning from this point of view, our research aims to test this hypothesis in a country where food systems are locally embedded by both law and history and where access to food is supposed to be equal for all (Benjamin, Collins, and Scott 1986).

After the collapse of the Soviet Union, with which Cuba had maintained strong trade relations for nearly forty years, the island nation was forced to turn to its own agricultural reserves to feed its population. With the U.S. embargo, dif fi cult access to oil resources and machinery, depleted soils due to the legacy of a heavily industrialized export-oriented agricultural system, and an urbanizing population, this proved dif fi cult. High food prices on the global market and vast fallow lands mean that food security and agricultural productivity remain pertinent issues.

data.text: Deep mapping is a research method and working practice mainly developed by artists and scholars that promises to blur the boundaries between science and art as well as between experts and local populations. This article presents the methodological thoughts and results of a deep map project carried out in a rural municipality in the Alpine region of Valle d'Aosta, Italy. Following two years of preparation, in 2019 our research team, consisting of scientists and artists, took up residence in a house in the village for a week. Based on these deep mappers' experiences and the results of the residence, it is argued that deep map practices can benefit from being combined with a research residence in the area under investigation, as well as by using a dialogic research design to develop a clear ethical and methodological stance. The research experiences further suggest that the creation of multimedia products for deep map projects can help to animate local populations and initiate continuous dialogues between residents and deep mappers. Finally, critical moments of the investigation design are highlighted, and theoretical gaps are addressed with a view to improving the design of future deep map projects.
