S outhwestern Asia is particularly noteworthy as a heartland of early urbanized civilization. From the ancient Near East comes much of our understanding of the rise of the first cities and state-level governments, monumental architecture, formal religious institutions, writing, and mathematics. Despite the fact that the vast majority (80-90 percent) of preindustrialized populations, in the Near East and elsewhere, led agrarian lifestyles and lived in rural communities (Mann 1986), only minimal attention has been directed to detailed studies of rural communities within the fabric of urbanized societies (Eickel- mann 1989:55; Schwartz and Falconer 1994:1; Butzer 1996). The traditional analytical orientation toward early urbanism is 'from the top down,' captured most bluntly by Oswald Spengler's generalization that 'world history is the history of city people' (1923:106). A common working assumption of this perspective holds that relatively homogeneous farming communities in the countryside compliantly supplied tax revenues, conscripted labor, and surplus foodstuffs for more dynamic and centrally important cities inhabited by merchants, craftsmen, bureaucrats, and urban elites (e.g., Redman 1978:215-16).

As a result of this urban bias, we are equipped currently with only a rudimentary comprehension of village economies and their fundamental roles in the coalescence or collapse of early civilizations (Schwartz and Falconer 1994). Many early civilizations, like those of the southern Levant (i.e., the region of modern Israel, Palestine, and Jordan), reveal greater long-term continuity in rural settlement and land use than in urban development (Falconer 1994). In such contexts marked by dramatically discontinuous urbanism, villages may provide our best evidence of longtermeconomicorganization.In fact, geographical research has a strong tradition focused on rural agrarian systems within larger political economies (Bassett 1988; Zimmerer 1991, 1993). Agricultural systems incorporating both subsistence farming and surplus-oriented production have been documented in a number of comparable settings, most notably in the New W orld tropics (Whitmore and T urner 1992; Denevan 1996). Thus rural investigations of early civilization provide an avenue of inquiry that is both particularly appropriate for the ancient southern Levant and more widely applicable to a variety of geographic research settings in both the past and present.

data.text: Almost 5 billion people-two thirds of the global population-now go online. The Internet has changed how we work, learn, govern, and fall in love. Yet despite its digital turn, geography has failed to grapple with the patterns and significance of Internet connection for rural people and places, particularly in the Global South. This article brings together agrarian studies and digital geography to situate emergent online practices within longer trajectories of agrarian change. To do so, I advance the concept of the digital village, a networked social space in which online practices emerge from existing agrarian relations to reconfigure the strategies of economic survival, the landscapes of home, and the tactics of politics. Drawing on ethnographic research in Myanmar, I show how agrarian relations shape patterns of digital connection and how farmers, migrants, and grassroots activists incorporate Facebook into daily efforts to secure livelihoods, support communities, and mobilize in struggles over land. This analysis yields two key insights: first, digital geographies are embedded in rural relations; second, agrarian questions increasingly play out online.

Building a Networked Field Site

Digital ubiquity raises new moral and methodological questions for geography (Duggan 2017; Holton and Harmer 2019). Many of these concerns are shared by interdisciplinary Internet ethnographers such as Burrell (2009), who argued for thinking about the field site as a network of physical and virtual spaces, iteratively constructed by the researcher. In doing so, she builds on the now-classic notion that global flows demand multisited anthropological strategies (Marcus 1995; Ferguson and Gupta 2002), one that is also gathering force in critical agrarian studies (cf. Paprocki 2018). These traditions inform my own multisited digital ethnography, one grounded in rural landscapes and iteratively extended into virtual domains.

I did not set out to study the digital village. Rather, I was confronted with the entanglement of on- and offline worlds over the course of a research project on land politics and agrarian change during Myanmar ' s postauthoritarian transformation. This study built on my previous work in Myanmar since 2013 and included ethnographic participation and 150 interviews with farmers, officials, and activists conducted between January 2017 and December 2019. I centered my research in the Kalay Valley, a former frontier of smallholder agricultural expansion where religious and ethnic minority Chin people and members of Myanmar ' s dominant ethnic group, the Burman Buddhists, farm rice, peanuts, and sunflowers in adjacent villages. Like many settlements in this part of northwestern Myanmar, Benjamin ' s village had been founded just two generations earlier when Chin farmers abandoned their swidden plots and came down from the nearby hills to pursue a better life via sedentary agriculture. The region ' s historic and continuing reliance on farming is typical of Myanmar, where 70 percent of the population lives in rural areas (Department of Population 2015) and over half of the labor force is employed in agriculture (Central Statistical Organization 2020). I had come to interview Chin Christian rice farmers and their Burman Buddhist neighbors to understand how different ethnic groups experienced agrarian change and struggles for land during Myanmar ' s self-styled transition from dictatorship to democracy in the 2010s. Yet I increasingly found myself in conversation with their children: youth who saw no future in farming but aspired to get married and settle down in the village. They had little to say about land reform but were enthusiastic about the arrival of the Internet.

From Digital Divide to Digital Village

The growing field of digital geography explores how digital tools represent and remake sociospatial relations. Scholars highlight the increasing entanglement of digital connection with research across the discipline, calling geographers to investigate the ways in which digital technologies challenge and transform place-based identities and social relations (Ash, Kitchin, and Leszczynski 2018). This diverse body of research includes feminist studies of digital labor (Richardson 2018), political economy analyses of the geoweb (Leszczynski 2012), insights into the geopolitics of computing clouds (Amoore 2018), and a political ecology of Bitcoin (Lally, Kay, and Thatcher 2022). Although digital geographers take seriously the particular technological affordances of social media sites (boyd 2015), they insist that the Internet is not a disembodied entity but rather a spatial phenomenon, unfolding in relation to existing geographies (Kitchin and Dodge 2011; Graham, Zook, and Boulton 2013).

data.text: British colonial rule in Africa in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries straddled a contradiction between promoting radical social transformation and maintaining political order. This article explores the relationship between changing techniques of rule and the stability of rule; in particular, the proletarianization and dispossession of African populations and production of an extractive economy in colonial Zambia. The 1920s saw the transition from charter rule by the British South Africa Company to the Colonial Office and the end of widespread rural unrest. Using archival and secondary sources, two key interventions marked a new mode of governing and spatial reorganization of power are examined: indirect rule through Native authorities and the constitution of Native reserves. These interventions sought to rework the political landscape and align relations between men and things in ways that furthered the aims of both extractive capitalism and colonial rule. The consequences and limitations of these new forms of intervention are examined by bringing together Marxist ideas of dispossession and the contradictions of colonial rule and Foucault's work on governmental power. In the final sections, a wider set of relations and processes beyond the state that worked to produce economic forms of subjectivity are explored, before arguing that the hallmark of techniques of rule that became widespread in British colonial sub-Saharan Africa is that they stabilized dispossession and worked to resolve central contradictions of colonial rule.

Colonial Rule, Dispossession, and Governmentality

A key aim of colonial rule in Northern Rhodesia, and elsewhere on the continent, was the production of a steady stream of labor for European enterprise. In Northern Rhodesia this focused on labor for the mines. For the BSAC, as we shall see, it took the form of forced entry of people into capitalist wage relations through disrupting previous modes of production. This process is instantly recognizable to Marxist scholars as a relatively straightforward case of primitive accumulation or accumulation by dispossession (Harvey 2003; Glassman 2006). Capitalism requires for its functioning the creation of a working class, a proletariat (Marx

1990). This proletariat is initially produced through 'brute force,' which alienates producers from the means of production-dispossessing people of their land and other productive assets-and thus forcing them to sell their labor to survive (Marx 1990, 915). Perelman (2001) argued that this process has two blades: 'The first blade served to undermine the ability of the people to provide for themselves. The other blade was a system of stern measures required to keep people from finding alternative survival strategies outside of the system of waged labour' (7-8).

This article explores the relationship between changing techniques of rule and the stability of rule; in particular, the proletarianization and dispossession of African populations and production of an extractive economy in colonial Zambia. British South Africa Company Rule in Northern Rhodesia

As Northern Rhodesia entered the 1920s, after three decades of colonial rule, British supremacy was precarious. The approach of the BSAC, which had administered colonial rule under Royal Charter since 1890, had been unflinchingly extractive. Adopting a twopronged strategy to produce wage laborers, the company had imposed a hut tax across the territory and curtailed those economic activities that offered an alternative to Africans beyond wage labor (Hall 1965; Meebelo 1971). Africans, however, did not rush to take up wage labor in European enterprises, preferring instead to rely on their own farming and industry 9 to produce tax revenues, as well as widely resisting and evading the imposition of the hut tax. The BSAC's response was frequently a violent one, seizing assets and disrupting production in the hope of producing a flow of cheap labor that would enable settler enterprises to thrive (Macpherson 1981). The use of demonstrative forms of punishment such as hut burnings and punitive raids-often termed 'demonstrations' in official records-formed a central plank of the imposition of British rule.

GEOGRAPHY OF A PESTILENCE

Prickly pear is the common name for several species of the genus Opuntia (family Cactaceae) that are indigenous to the western hemisphere. All are hardy, drought-resistant, subtropical perennials comprising a profusion of fleshy, flattened, segmented stems studded with tufts of spines and covered with fine, nettlelike cilia. Some, like the common pest pear Opuntia inermis, which is native to the Greater Antilles and the coast of the Gulf of Mexico, and 0. stricta, which is from Chile, grow in massive thickets between onehalf and two and one-half meters high, but others, such as 0. streptacantha and 0. tomentosa, both native to central Mexico, are tree pears reaching heights of eight meters or more. Depending on the species, they may be propagated very rapidly by seeds or by broken stem segments, which are transported by animals, strong winds, and floodwaters. In their native environments, these cacti have rarely been accorded the status of agricultural pests; however, introduced into other parts of the world, notably Australia, Hawaii, India, Sri Lanka, Madagascar, and southern Africa, they have quickly gained notoriety as noxious weeds. In Australia, the prickly pear turned into a land-greedy menace that ruined many farmers and ranchers and threatened the rural economy of an entire continent.

ABSTRACT. Prickly pear cactus, introduced into eastern Australia by early settlers, became a major pest in the early twentieth century and caused abandonment of large tracts of rural land. Governmental strategies to halt the pest were ineffectual; some helped the cactus to spread. The discovery in the mid-1920s that the larvae of the Cactoblastis cactorum destroyed the pest was attributable more to luck than to cohesive policy.

THE campaign waged from 1880 to 1940 by Australian governmental officials, scientists, and private landowners against the spread of prickly pear cacti throughout Queensland and New South Wales has been called "one of the world's most spectacular achievements in the history of economic entomology" (Johnston and Lloyd 1982, 216). The sheer speed with which the prickly pear invaded farming and grazing lands, the huge area it devastated, and its seeming invulnerability to conventional means of eradication had indeed presented a fearsome challenge. Scientific experts of the early twentieth century were all but at a loss for a solution (Steele 1923, 6).

data.text: In tropical countries, urbanization and rural deagriculturalization are intimately linked processes. Growth of the construction industry, which draws labor and materials from rural and periurban areas, is a key component of rural-urban interactions. Using a case study from the Perote Valley, Mexico, this article analyzes how urbandriven concrete aggregate mining affects rural agricultural lands and livelihoods. Land-cover changes associated with aggregate surface mining were examined by comparing aerial photographs, satellite images, and Global Positioning System field maps of the valley. In addition, sixty-six formal household interviews were conducted in three agrarian communities. Results indicate that between 1995 and 2006, mine surface area quadrupled, from 181 to 706 hectares, and the spatial distribution of surface mines followed a predictable pattern of extraction, from most to least accessible. Numerous factors persuaded farmers to convert fields to mines, including increased prices for aggregates, consumerist desires for new homes, and declining returns to agriculture. Moreover, farmers believed they could or would recultivate mined land following extraction. Yet, in 2006, among the three agrarian communities, 202 (45 percent) of the 482 hectares of agricultural land extracted were not recultivated. Although deep mines were more likely to be abandoned, findings suggest that land revalorization occurred among farmers, with the scarcity value of nonrenewable aggregates gradually surpassing the land's agricultural value. In the long term, diminished agricultural potential resulting from widespread mine abandonment might drive farmers to migrate to cities for employment, creating a positive feedback between urban demand for construction aggregates and mining of agricultural fields.

Study Region: Perote Valley, Mexico

Research was conducted in the Perote Valley, Mexico, because aggregate surface extraction is a prevalent and expanding land-use activity (Figure 1; Fry 2008a, 2008b). Since the mid-1990s, demand for the lightweight aggregate tepetzil has motivated many farmers here to mine and extract this resource from below agricultural fields. After tepetzil is extracted, much of it is processed into lightweight concrete blocks by local block-making facilities known as bloqueras. Although tepetzil deposits are located throughout the Perote Valley, much of the mining activity is concentrated in three once predominantly agricultural ejido communities: Sierra de Agua, Los Molinos, and Cruz Blanca (Table 1).

Figure 1. (A) Photograph of an upslope recultivated tepetzil mine. Average tepetzil depth is 5.7 m and average mine depth 6.9 m. Photograph is toward the north with Los Humeros in the background. (B) Photograph of an active valley-bottom tepetzil mine that was later abandoned. Tepetzil is the bottom deposit. Average tepetzil depth is 8.2 m and average mine depth is 13.9 m. Photograph is toward the south. Cofre de Perote (4,282 m) is in the background. Photographs taken by the author in 2006. (Color figure available online.)

Data Sources

Spatial analysis of tepetzil surface mining and landuse change in the Perote Valley was conducted using four georeferenced orthophotographs (2 m resolution), three georeferenced IKONOS satellite images (4 m resolution with four spectral bands), and Global Positioning System (GPS) field mapping. Orthophotos were obtained for March and May 1995. IKONOS images were acquired for 14 April 2003, 13 July 2003, and 16 November 2004. GPS data were recorded from August to November 2006. Together, the IKONOS images cover an area of ∼ 228 km 2 and make up the entire study area. These images contain most known tepetzil mines in the region. They also encompass Sierra de Agua, Los Molinos, and Cruz Blanca ejidos.

The satellite images were orthorectified using a digital elevation model (DEM) produced from a 1:50,000 topographic map (INEGI 1995), which was manually digitized. The images are high resolution and photograph-comparable and have a positional accuracy of less than 15 m, with the 4-m resolution setting the limit of discernible features. The 1995 orthophotos include the entire study region and have a positional accuracy of ± 12.5 m with the 2-m resolution setting the limit of discernible features. Comparisons between the 1995 orthophotos, the 2003-2004 IKONOS images, and 2006 field mapping were made within ArcGIS 9: ArcMap 9.3 (ESRI 2008). Within the images, landcover types were classified based on field observations.

Field Mapping: Mine Distribution and Mine Characteristics

In 2006, 102 mined areas, approximately 99 percent of mined areas in the region, were identified and mapped. GPS was used to record point coordinates at corners and angles around mine perimeters. In addition, mine depth was measured at various points within each mine, but these were not recorded at regular intervals due to inconsistent accessibility. Overburden depth (i.e., depth from the surface to the top of the tepetzil deposit) and soil depth were also recorded. From these data, mean depth per mine as well as volume of material extracted, tepetzil volume, and overburden volume were calculated.

Land use within each mine was categorized as active, abandoned, postextraction agriculture, tree plantation, bloquera, or other. Each mine was also assigned an extraction date (i.e., year mine extraction began) using one of two methods. First, extraction dates were obtained by comparing the 2006 field mapping data with the 1995 orthophotos and 2003-2004 IKONOS images, which provided benchmarks. It is possible that some of the mined areas classified as 1995 and 2003-2004 were in fact mined prior to those years. Therefore, key informants, including front-end-loader operators, dumptruck drivers, and land owners also provided extraction dates.

Introduction

The richest crop for any field Is a crop of bricks for it to yield. The richest crop that it can grow, Is a crop of houses in a row.

T he process of urbanization is a leading cause of global environmental change (Kalnay and Cai 2003; Lambin, Geist, and Lepers 2003; Grimm et al. 2008), with the highest rates of urban growth occurring in tropical countries (United Nations Population Fund 2007). Here, rapid urbanization is observable in an expanding built environment (L´ opez et al. 2001; Liu et al. 2005; Seto and Fragkias 2005; Li, Chen, and Sun 2007; Grimm et al. 2008) characterized by horizontal growth of low-income, informal settlements around cities (World Bank 2001; United Nations Human Settlements Programme 2003; Davis 2006). As farmers migrate to work and live in these peripheral areas, an associated process of deagriculturalization (or deagrarianization) occurs in rural areas (Araghi 1995; Bryceson 1996; Lobao and Meyer 2001). One important aspect of the linkage between urbanization and agricultural change is the transfer of labor from rural farming to urban construction (Firman 1991; Ramsaran and Hosein 2006). Another less well understood component is the relationship between urban demand for construction materials and rural landscape transformation. This article uses empirical data to analyze the impacts of construction material extraction, a fast-growing but understudied land use, on rural livelihoods and landscapes in the tropics.

Aside from studies on urban fringe environments and urban encroachment, research on urbanization in the tropics has focused on rural land-use/land-cover changes resulting from two urban-related processes: outmigration and multilocalization. Some research shows that forests regenerate when farmers abandon agricultural plots and move to cities (i.e., forest transition theory; Grau et al. 2003; Wright and Muller-Landau 2006; Par´ es-Ramos, Gould, and Aide 2008). In other instances, abandoned fields are converted to less intensive land uses such as pasture (Harden 1996; Wiggins et al. 2002), tree-based systems (Browder and Pedlowski 2000; Rudel, Bates, and Machinguiashi 2002), or fallow (Wiegers et al. 1999). Studies also show that in lieu of abandonment, many rural households become multilocalized (or multisited) in an effort to diversify their livelihoods (Bryceson 1996; Zoomers and Kleinpenning 1996; Rigg 1998; Reardon, Berdegu´ e, and Escobar 2001). Multilocalized households depend on multiple income sources in addition to traditional agriculture, and their land-use strategies might reflect the inputs of remittance monies (McKay 2005) or the urbanite lifestyle demands of nonlocal members (Padoch et al. 2008). Urban demand for nonagricultural and nontimber resources, such as mined construction materials, is also recognized as a major driver of rural land-use change in the tropics (Lambin, Geist, and Lepers 2003; Grimm et al. 2008); however, to date, it has received relatively little attention (but see A. L.

The Urbanization Process and Agricultural Change

The agricultural and industrial revolutions serve to illustrate the circular relationship between urbanization and agricultural change. Soja (2010) believes that the formation of the earliest cities and the development of agriculture are examples of mutual causality: Agricultural surplus was both an instrumental component and an outcome of city formation. A similar argument is put forth for industrial-driven urbanization in the nineteenth century, which can be viewed as both cause and consequence of agricultural change in Europe and the United States (Soja 2010). In 1845, Engels (1958) described this process in England. To him, fundamental changes in agriculture resulted from rapid industrialization in growing cities, better farm implements, and progress in science. Today, this is referred to simply as the urbanization process . In this circular model, mechanization and crop innovations lead to increased agricultural productivity, which, in turn, releases rural labor to work in a growing urban manufacturing sector. Enhanced agricultural productivity also supplies more food to growing urban populations.

Rural-Urban Households and Land Use in the Tropics

Livelihood and household-based studies conducted in the tropics show that deagrarianization not only leads to the physical abandonment of rural spaces but also to the reorganization of rural household livelihoods (Zoomers and Kleinpenning 1996; Bryceson 1996; Reardon, Berdegu´ e, and Escobar 2001; Rigg 1998). Driven by rising production costs and diminished returns for their products, smallholder farmers often rely on nonfarm income sources for their livelihoods (Bryceson 1996; de Janvry and Sadoulet 2001; Reardon, Berdegu´ e, and Escobar 2001; Wilson and Rigg 2003;

Eakin 2005; Goldstein, Childs, and Wangdui 2008). Many nonfarm income opportunities are located in urbanizing areas, creating a blurred boundary between rural and urban livelihoods (Bryceson 1996). To Wilson and Rigg (2003), this blurred boundary is part of a broader social and cultural shift that might ultimately destabilize the social utility of traditional farming. Rigg (1998) argued that the urban lifestyle, better educational opportunities, and greater exposure to Western media and culture often contend with rural land-use decisions.

data.text: Climate change adaptation is a power-laden process that requires engagement and negotiation between people with diverse needs, interests, and levels of authority. Entrenched hierarchies in adaptation decision making influence what is considered legitimate policy and action, whose values are prioritized, and the interests of which actors are excluded. Through content and discourse analysis of interviews and focus group discussions with policymakers and decision makers across multiple spatial and jurisdictional levels, we illustrate how specific actors involved in adaptation efforts comprehend and engage with tensions, institutional politics, and community-level power dynamics, focusing on the experiences of rural farmers who are often sidelined in adaptation processes. We advance critical scholarship on the politics of adaptation and the politics of scale to demonstrate how power relations move within and across levels of decision making, by scrutinizing the discursive and material construction of scales and subjects. We argue that nuanced investigations of power and its (re)production across levels and scales are crucial to expose the underrepresentation of marginalized citizens in adaptation debates and to envision subversive political interventions toward climate justice. Key Words: agriculture, climate change adaptation, climate justice, decision making, Ghana.

Methods

Data for this study were collected between February 2018 and April 2019 during five months of field work over two seasons. The lead researcher, with assistance from a Ghanaian collaborator (third author), conducted individual interviews and focus group discussions (FGDs) with 122 participants involved in climate change adaptation policy and decision making across community, local government, regional, national, and international levels (Table 1).

During the first field work phase, community leaders and elders helped the research team to recruit farmers over the age of eighteen for participation in individual interviews (forty-one) and FGDs (sixtynine participants, nine groups). Their median age was forty-nine, much higher than in regional census data. This was due to many younger community members having migrated to urban centers in search of alternative employment. Discussions lasted for up to two hours and were conducted with assistance from the third author who is fluent in Akan.

Case Study Background and Context

In many ways, Ghana has led the way for political change in sub-Saharan Africa since independence in 1957 (Haynes 1993). Following the 1993 Local Governance Act, the country shifted to a decentralized system of administration, aiming to delegate more power to local authorities and engender more democratic policy and decision making. However, competing political agendas, institutional arrangements in disarray, and constraints on resources continue to hamper grassroots development initiatives (Fridy and Myers 2019). Moreover, climate change exerts additional pressure on authorities as most rural residents rely on agriculture now threatened by

increasing temperatures and rainfall variability, and more intense drought and flooding events (Abbam et al. 2018). Hence, the central government has amplified efforts to support the agricultural sector in adapting to these challenges.

For this study, the research team chose multiple spatial and jurisdictional levels of adaptive decision making to establish scope and collect data (Figure 1). In addition to community, local government, regional, and national levels, we also assess international influences on adaptation initiatives, for instance NGOs and donors. Although these levels may well be situated on a vertical hierarchical scale mirroring a top-down political structure, we approach them here as fluid entities that shift, intersect, and overlap with social and political mobilities. Introduction

‡ Department of Languages and General Studies, School of Arts and Social Sciences, University of Energy and Natural Resources, Ghana

H uman geographers and other social scientists have repeatedly demonstrated the disproportionate impacts of the climate crisis. Inequalities embedded in uneven power relations continue to mandate who is most at risk to climatic hazards and how (Thomas et al. 2019; Barnett 2020). Individual citizens, governing authorities, nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), and international agencies are at the frontlines of climate action as the need to adapt and build resilience is increasingly urgent for societies to avoid loss of lives and livelihoods. Adaptation is a dynamic process that requires agents to negotiate across needs, interests, and levels of authority (Eriksen, Nightingale, and Eakin 2015; Harris, Chu, and Ziervogel 2018; Leck and Simon 2018), with many seeking power over resources and climate-related agendas that are shaped by multiple spheres of influence. Entrenched politics and hierarchies delineate approaches to adaptation (Ziervogel 2019) and produce ' winners ' and ' losers ' with respect to who can adapt to

Literature Review

We begin with an overview of pertinent concepts and debates that foreground geographic perspectives on hierarchies and power, and their contributions to the scholarly field of climate change adaptation: (1) theorizations of scales and levels of adaptive decision making; (2) the politics of scale; (3) the politics of adaptation; and (4) power in multiand cross-level adaptive decision-making processes.

Scales and Levels of Adaptive Decision Making

Scholars across the natural and social sciences have fought fierce battles over the usage and meanings of the concepts of scales and levels (Neumann 2009), generically defined as spatial, temporal, and jurisdictional modes of operation (Gibson, Ostrom, and Ahn 2000; Cash et al. 2006). In human geography and political ecology, these two concepts have undergone profound theoretical transformations (Neumann 2009; Jones et al. 2017). Most notably, the fields have moved away from notions of levels and scales as predetermined, territorial, and natural entities (Bulkeley 2005) to a more nuanced understanding of their constructed, dynamic, and contested nature (Benson 2010; see next section). Central to this conceptualization is the notion of performativity, indicating the actors who exist within levels and scales as complicit in the complex interactions, perceptions, and subjectivities that uphold scalar boundaries (Glass and Rose-Redwood 2014).

data.text: This article presents a substantive analysis using the Great Britain Historical Geographical Information System (GIS), one of the earliest national historical GISs. It develops exploratory techniques to explore local patterns of demographic change and applies these to the study of infant mortality in England and Wales from 1851 to 1911. The techniques developed could be applied to a wide variety of fields where the aim is to explore long-term spatio-temporal change using data published for administrative units that are affected by boundary changes. The Victorian and Edwardian eras saw the origins of the sustained infant mortality decline that characterized the entire twentieth century. Although the period has been extensively studied for a century and more, our knowledge of this vital phase is still surprisingly limited. In particular, much of the research to date has focused on urban areas and has thus stressed urban explanations as to why infant mortality began to decline. Because this article uses a comprehensive GIS database, we are able to challenge some of the orthodoxies that have emerged. It reveals that patterns of infant mortality decline in different parts of the country were more complex than has previously been described. Far from the national rate being driven by changes in urban areas, the largest declines and earliest declines in infant mortality were found in rural parts of the southeast of England, as the rural periphery lagged far behind. Urban areas were slow to decline due to the specific conditions that existed in them in this period.

The Data and Their Limitations

The core of this study uses data for the six decades from 1851 to 1911 taken from the Registrar General's Decennial Supplements. These provide the total number of births and infant deaths in each registration district for each of the decades in which we are interested. The study starts in 1851 as there are no equivalent data before this date. It ends in 1911 because after this the data were published annually and with more spatial detail. This period will be the subject of a later study.

As described later, the data have been extensively studied; however, four problems can be identified that have, to date, undermined their use: the volume of data, their spatial and temporal complexity, the aggregate nature of the data, and a lack of explanatory variables available in consistent form. The volume of data no longer presents a significant challenge to modern computing power as six decades of infant mortality data at registration district level gives around 3,800 individual rates. It is worth remembering, however, that until the last decade or two the computing power to handle such a data set would have been beyond most researchers in the field.

Spatial and temporal complexity is a problem into which GIS allows us to make significant inroads. Subdividing England and Wales into 635 districts provides a wealth of information about the country's geography. The Great Britain Historical GIS (GBHGIS; Gregory et al. 2002; Gregory 2005) holds the boundaries of these units as they change

Exploring Change Using Areal Interpolation

In the preceding analysis, arbitrary divisions were imposed between urban and rural and core and periphery to show that the stories of infant mortality decline were more complex than a national aggregate pattern driven by the urban experience. In this section, district-level data are used to further explore these divisions. As described earlier in the article, boundary changes have seriously undermined the utility of zone-based statistics such as the ones used here, as they make it impossible to compare data from one decade directly with data from the next. GIS allows data to be interpolated from a variety of sets of administrative units onto a single set of target units. This is done using a process termed 'areal interpolation.' The GIS enables this through the use of an overlay operation that calculates the degree of intersection between a set of source units, say the 1861 districts, and a set of target units, such as those for 1911. In its simplest form, known as 'areal weighting,' data for a variable y whose values for a source unit ys are known can be estimated for the target units based on the assumption that the data are evenly distributed across the source units. Introduction

I n their conclusion to the Population History of England 1541-1871 , Wrigley and Schofield (1981, 482) state that:

[T]he functioning of the national aggregate will never be well understood unless analyses or relations that appear to characterize the national entity are paralleled by similar work on a local scale. Only in this way can those aspects of English demographic and economic history in which there was homogeneity of behaviour throughout the country be distinguished from those where the national aggregate reflects an average condition that may prove to have been true of few individual communities, and that may therefore tend to lead to misguided conclusions about the relations between demographic and economic behaviour in the past. (Reproduced by permission of Edward Arnold [Publishers] Ltd.)

In the quarter century since this was written, remarkably little progress has been made on studying the different local experiences that make up the national aggregate. For researchers studying England and Wales during the Victorian era and more recent times, a lack of data cannot be given as a reason for this. From the 1850s to the 1900s the General Register Office (GRO) published Decennial Supplements that gave the numbers of births and age-specific deaths in each of around 635 registration districts (Nissel 1987; Szreter 1991). These are thought to be broadly reliable (Teitelbaum 1973). These data have now been in existence for a century and more and contain a wealth of detail about the changing patterns of mortality at a local level. Although large amounts of research have been done using them, to date much of it has either focused on the national aggregate or on the particular experience of urban areas because the complexity of the data has undermined researchers' abilities to explore its full detail. This is a limitation that modern computing techniques, in particular those associated with geographical information systems (GIS), have gone some way to easing.

To understand how the national aggregate functions weneedtounderstandchangeoverbothtimeandspace. As Massey (1999, 2005) argues, time is important because it provides us with the story of how a place developed. Without space, however, we only have one story, such as Wrigley and Schofield's national aggregate that potentially only represents the experiences of a few communities. Space is thus important because it provides us with different places. Studying these in ways that stress the differences between them allows us to tell the different stories that make up the national aggregate. Bringing space and time together, therefore, allows us to stress the diversity of experiences and avoid reaching misguided or oversimplistic conclusions.

The Data and Their Limitations

The core of this study uses data for the six decades from 1851 to 1911 taken from the Registrar General's Decennial Supplements. These provide the total number of births and infant deaths in each registration district for each of the decades in which we are interested. The study starts in 1851 as there are no equivalent data before this date. It ends in 1911 because after this the data were published annually and with more spatial detail. This period will be the subject of a later study.

As described later, the data have been extensively studied; however, four problems can be identified that have, to date, undermined their use: the volume of data, their spatial and temporal complexity, the aggregate nature of the data, and a lack of explanatory variables available in consistent form. The volume of data no longer presents a significant challenge to modern computing power as six decades of infant mortality data at registration district level gives around 3,800 individual rates. It is worth remembering, however, that until the last decade or two the computing power to handle such a data set would have been beyond most researchers in the field.

Stories of Infant Mortality Decline: Orthodoxies and Challenges

In spite of the availability of data, our knowledge of the patterns and causes of infant mortality decline have remained controversial to the extent that even the timing of the start of the decline remains unresolved. Contemporary observers were particularly concerned by high rates of mortality in the urban centers that were growing rapidly as a result of the industrial revolution. Not unnaturally, they focused on these areas and their problems and introduced public health measures in an attempt to solve them. Thus the 'urban story' developed that explained the national aggregate by relating it to urban problems and the responses to them; rural areas were largely ignored.

data.text: Maroon communities, or communities of descendants of fugitives from slavery, have been long-lasting examples of social movements pursuing political goals through the production and mobilization of space. They have been largely forgotten in academic analyses, however, which, in Latin America, are primarily focused on peasants and indigenous movements. Therefore, drawing on socioterritorial movements readings and maroon studies, this article analyzes how maroon-descendant communities have produced territory in both urban and rural spaces-including areas of forced displacement-locally and transnationally, to survive hegemonies deeply rooted in the legacy of slavery and to achieve political aims. These communities unsettle binary categories of rural and urban socioterritorial movements and monolithic visions of antistate struggle. This transterritorial, rural-urban appropriation of spaces resisting different powers follows the past logic of marronage to achieve freedom and security, re-creating in present times the political vision of historical maroon leaders regarding the construction of a grand Palenque in the Spanish-speaking Caribbean.

Through the Lens of Socioterritorial Movements

The analysis of new social movements in Latin America is characterized by the diversity of its subjects, from barrios to blocos (Black carnival clubs) to more politicized and traditionally organized groups (Friedmann 1989; Davis 1999; Choup 2008; Chesters 2012; Wabgou et al. 2012; Dixon 2014; Zibechi 2014; Gahman, Penados, and Greenidge 2020). Literature in this field has progressively shone more light on how these groups have found innovative ways to mobilize radically (Stahler-Sholk, Vanden, and Becker 2014). These involve challenging both neoliberal and progressive governments and resisting all types of subordination without aspiring to take state power (Stahler-Sholk, Vanden, and Becker 2014; Incl  an 2018).

With a vision of territory as a hierarchical and violent overlapping between the state and subaltern spaces (Halvorsen 2018), the concept of the socioterritorial movement first appeared in the work of geographers Manc ¸ano Fernandes (2000) and Martin (2001) on the Movimento dos Trabalhadores SemTerra (MST; Martin and Manc ¸ano Fernandes 2004). The MST is the most significant landless peasant social movement in Brazil (Hoddy and Ensor 2018). For Manc ¸ano Fernandes and Martin, every social movement produces physical and symbolic spaces. Socioterritorial movements, however, have the political goal of occupying space in a class struggle against globalization, neoliberalism, and homogenizing forms of the use of land and natural resources (Manc ¸ano Fernandes 2000). Introduction

T he reading of socioterritorial movements constitutes an emerging southern approach to understanding geographies of social change that examines how campesino (small-scale farmers) and indigenous groups in Latin America produce space to achieve their political goals (Manc ¸ano Fernandes 2005; Halvorsen, Fernandes, and Torres 2019; L  opez 2019). These studies emphasize actors who mobilize counterhegemonic or subaltern territories that resist capitalism and the state (Manc ¸ano Fernandes 2005, 2009, 2010; Bryan 2012; Zibechi 2012; Haesbaert 2013; Lopes de Souza 2015; Courtheyn 2018). Socioterritorial movements cannot be understood without the idea of counterhegemonic territories and vice versa. This article shows that the relationship between these two concepts cannot be fully captured without an analysis of race.

There are multiple definitions of race in scholarship produced in the Global North and from a geographical perspective (Nash 2003; P. L. Price 2010). Wade ' s (2008b) definition for the case of Latin American countries is useful because it highlights elements recurring in this article. He conceptualized race as a social construction that produces mixedness as well as discrimination and violence against indigenous and Black identities. In Latino societies, Whiteness and mixedness are associated with high status and development. These societies are invested in the

European aspects of their origins to the exclusion of indigenous and African characteristics. Thus, explicit proximity to Europeanness (not just Whiteness) in terms of ancestry and culture is a crucial aspect of defining race in Latin America, including Blackness.

By leaving race outside the study of socioterritorial movements there is a risk of reproducing academically the colonial discourse of subaltern denial and embodying new forms of cultural violence against Afro-Latin American groups (Galtung 1996; Quijano 2000). There is a general understanding that counterhegemonic territories have been initiated by campesino and indigenous movements, who have inspired new social movements in Latin America (Zibechi, cited in Streule and Schwarz 2019). For example, following the economic crisis that affected Argentina in the 2000s, organized unemployed workers have replicated campesino and indigenous peoples ' strategies of space making as a form of struggle (Mason-Deese, Habermehl, and Clare 2019).

data.text: Previous literature has not yet reached a conclusion on the relationship between innovation and income inequality; thus, this study examines this relationship across Chinese city regions from 2004 to 2012. A nonlinear relationship between innovation and income inequality is observed, and this result is robust to different measures of income inequality, threshold effect models, and subsample analysis and is also supported by a disaggregate analysis based on individual incomes. These findings suggest directions for public policy. To moderate income inequality attributed to innovation, policy should facilitate the income spillover to less skilled laborers by improving human capital and maximizing the employment compensation effect through reducing discrimination against the less skilled, particularly less skilled rural migrants.

Under the jurisdiction of the twentyseven provinces, there were 285 city regions at the prefecture level and above in 2012. Each city region administers a central city, a few county-level cities, and counties. Our study sample consists of those city regions and four province-status super city regions.

Introduction

I n recent decades, innovation has been recognized as a vital driver of economic growth and change (Pianta and Tancioni 2008). It leads to the emergence of new products, increased productivity, and development of new economic sectors. At the same time, innovation can also affect income distribution. Florida (2007) found that cities with higher innovation levels face greater income inequality in the United States because innovation increases the income of highly skilled laborers, but the effect does not ' trickle down ' to their less skilled counterparts. The advanced technology deriving from innovative activities inevitably increases the demand for highskilled laborers and their income and further encourages highly skilled laborers to migrate to other regions that have more job opportunities; this migration consequently increases income inequality in their home regions (Florida 2005, 2007). In many circumstances, less skilled laborers confront lower income and frequent unemployment. Similar conclusions are drawn by several empirical studies, which find innovation to be positively associated with income inequality (Faggio, Salvanes, and Van-Reenen 2010; Weiss and Garloff 2011; Breau, Kogler, and Bolton 2014). Other studies, however, suggest that innovation has a moderating effect on income inequality. According to this view, highly skilled laborers are found to help less skilled laborers develop and apply their innovative capabilities. Over time, less skilled but talented laborers evolve into highly skilled laborers (Florida 2005; Donegan and Lowe 2008). Moreover, innovation development spurs demand across the economy, not just in high-technology, skill-intensive sectors (Lusch and Nambisan 2015). Empirical studies also confirm the inequality-reducing effect of innovation (Antonelli and Gehringer 2013; Hopkin, Lapuente, and Moller 2014), and some research clearly indicates that innovation is the solution to income inequality (Maliszewski 2003; Peck 2005; McCann 2007; Donegan and Lowe 2008).

data.text: Changes in the nature of capitalist production over the past thirty years have allowed regions to assert a greater political and economic presence in the new global marketplace. Galicia, a Spanish region located in the northwestern corner of the Iberian Peninsula, was once Spain's lowest economic performer. Galicia's late move from a rural agrarian to an industrialized and technology-based economy has been accompanied by urban growth and drastic changes in land use over the past three decades. These changes have brought cultural consequences to the region, including prominent language shift from the regional language of Galician to the prestigious majority language of Castilian. To help analyze these themes, this article looks at the aims and application of both the European Union (EU) regional development and cultural policies and uses remote sensing tools to track the land-use change of urban centers and agricultural land over a thirty-year period in Galicia, along with historical and current analysis of Galicia's economy and sociolinguistic geographies. Results show that a policy mismatch exists between EU regional economic and cultural policies, wherein the former inadvertently damages the latter.

Urbanization and a Shifting Galician Economy

Restructuring of the Galician economy and the decline of agricultural production have affected the regional landscape in an abandonment of farms and an expansion of urban space. Data provided by the Ministry of Rural Affairs in 2008 revealed more than 100,000 family farms in Galicia averaging under 10 ha that had been divided through a split inheritance system (Constenla Bergueiro 2008). This system divides land by the number of children in a family, resulting in smaller and smaller plots over the generations. Galicia also has an elderly population and a decreasing population rate. These factors have pushed residents, especially young workers, out of the countryside and into cities.

Analysis of remotely sensed images showing landuse change over time allows a comparison of land use from as far back as the 1960s. These images can be analyzed for urban growth (Wilson et al. 2003) and rural land-use change (Muller and Zeller 2002; Weng 2002). To analyze land-use change alongside language shift, I have created two land-use change maps, which illustrate themes of urbanization and rural land use in Galicia over a thirty-year period.

Images of Galicia from April 1984 and April 2014 were collected from U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Earth Explorer. The year 1984 was selected as the start date to gather data before Galician industrialization and EU inclusion. In the 1980s, over half of the Galician population lived in village settlements of less than 5,000 people (Ferr  as Sexto 1996

Usage of Galician and Castilian

Speakership of Galician and Castilian in Galicia is roughly split in half, between those who always or mostly use Galician and those who always or mostly use Castilian, based on the latest published language survey results from the Galician Statistical Institute (Instituto Galego de Estatistica [IGE] 2013). As a co-official language, Galician is used in all government institutions and is taught in public schools across the region. Although it has undergone a variety of changes in the past decades, it is generally mandated that Galician be used to teach half of a pupil ' s classroom hours, although language of choice is often dependent on preferences of students in each locale (Hannum 2019). It is also important to note that Galician and Castilian are related, which aids in the learning and comprehension of Galician. Although high speakership levels of both languages persist, these figures also indicate the frequency of code switching (switching languages) in the region, because about half indicate the use of both languages yet favor one or the other. Looking at speakership by age begins to reveal the overall trend in Galicia. Younger people tend to speak Castilian more frequently than Galician, and elderly people speak Galician more frequently than Castilian (IGE 2013). This indicates that Galician speakers are dwindling, and Castilian speakers will become the dominant group in the coming years.

Introduction

C hanges in the nature of capitalist production over the past thirty years have sped the convergence of states and regions to a more equitable plane of economic competition (Paasi 2013). Devolution in many parts of the world has allowed substate territories to develop unique economic plans and more readily join the global economy. The same economic logic that once labeled developed and undeveloped states is now applied to substate regions. Local autonomy makes capital generation less dependent on location or natural resources in regions that might once have been overlooked in developed countries (Amin 2002). This economic advancement has cultural implications, however, especially for peripheral regions that have evolved in relative isolation. Within the European Union (EU), a Europe of regions rhetoric has been pressed, resulting in policies aimed at advancing regional economies to that of the EU average, simultaneously protecting regional heritage and cultural diversity.

Since the 1970s, the EU has made regional cohesion a priority, dedicating roughly one third of its budget to regional development. A large set of studies have analyzed the economic efficacy of these policies, resulting in mixed outcomes (Dall ' Erba and Fang 2017). Recent studies have pointed to a need for geographically tailored policy, which focuses on place-based initiatives considering regional characteristics to maximize economic convergence (Iammarino, Rodr  ı guez-Pose, and Storper 2018; Bourdin 2019). What has been overlooked in this expanding body of literature are the possible cultural implications of an economically converging and cohesive EU. The policies encouraged in the Europe of regions strategy present an unplanned tension between economic development and minority cultural protection. This article investigates the dual efficacy of regional convergence and diversity and cultural protection goals in the case of Galicia, Spain. This article aims at highlighting the inadvertent policy mismatch of regional development and cultural protection within the EU.

Situating Regional Economy and Regional Identity in Europe

Due to the restructuring of state coalitions into suprastate entities, regions are allowed more inclusion for competition with other regions and states, instead of being held to consensual management within the state system (Murphy 1999; Keating and Loughlin 2013). In Europe, regions can jump over the central state government by appealing straight to the EU Assembly of European Regions to lobby for regional needs and interests (Cappelen 1993; Bachtler, Mendez, and Wishlade 2016). Many peripheral regions of Europe have been experiencing economic convergence since the reform of structural funding and regional development funding implementation (Cappelen et al. 2003; Esposti and Bussoletti 2008; Keating and Loughlin 2013).

Spanish Political Economy

The Spanish constitution of 1978 established regions as autonomous communities within the unified political entity of Spain. Each region has been granted different levels of self-rule, the most independent of them being the three historical nationalities of Catalonia, the Basque Country, and Galicia (Seixas 2003). Governmental functions are assumed by either the central government or the autonomous communities or shared between the two as laid out in Article 5 of the constitution (Senado de Espa ~ na 2019). From 1980 to 2008, Spain experienced steady GDP growth and life expectancy increase overall. Inflation-adjusted GDP per capita in Spain in 1980 was $16,000, and the average Spaniard lived to seventy-six years of age. By 2008, GDP per capita had grown to $34,284 and average life expectancy had increased to eighty-one years (Gapminder World 2015). Spain was improving along most indicators of human development and growing financially as well. Wealth distribution over this time period was unequal within Spain, however, as a few regions tended to skew the average upward.

data.text: In his seminal work on cartography, Brian Harley develops insights and raises questions about the power of maps. This article takes up these insights and questions through an anti-essentialist reading of Foucault's later thinking merged with concepts from grounded theory. The research examines the interrelated economic, strategic, legal, and technical aspects of mapping activities that use and create cadastral (property) maps. Using multiple scales, I analyze cadastral mapping activities through decomposition into interactions, boundary objects, and contextual factors to establish how empowerment and limitation take place. The examples come from fieldwork in Poland that explores cadastral mapping discrepancies. Following the demise of socialist forms of government and property in 1989, studies from the 1990s found differences (by area) between officially mapped ownership and actual property usage of up to 40 percent in rural areas. Although most Polish cadastral maps from rural areas were then, and still are, officially accepted as accurate, many remain functionally unusable. Further, the high level of discrepancies failed, and still fails, to systematically disrupt cadastral mapping, farming, and other economic activities. Considering this background, the article explores the processes of making property rights and the limits of state-centric constructions of territory. Reflecting the increased use of geographic information systems in cadastral mapping and the controls of Common Agricultural Policy disbursements, the article also analyzes different meanings of accuracy and the limits of cadastral mapping's calculative power.

Research Project Design and Methods

This article covers a portion of results from a research project using a comparative approach on data collected over three years for longitudinal comparisons centered on cadastral mapping, boundary objects, and interactions. Three counties ( powiaty ), each located in a different historical partition of Poland, and distinguished by socioeconomic conditions and characteristics, were selected with the assistance of Polish geographers. The counties were chosen to maximize the historical, economic, and cultural diversity found in Poland within a small number of sites. After a preliminary visit to each county, I chose three villages in each county representative of the local diversity of agricultural activities and the different trajectories of transition since 1989. Ten interviews with randomly chosen rural residents were conducted yearly in each village. The nine village mayors of all communes ( W´ ojt ) were also interviewed yearly, along with the three directors of the county surveying offices, and staff from regional offices of the agricultural agency responsible for restructuring, modernizing, and administrating direct payments: the Agency for Restructuration and Modernization of Agriculture (ARMA). Finally, at the national level, interviews were held with Poland's chief surveyor and the head of the section of ARMA responsible for the Land Parcel Information System (LPIS) for auditing agricultural direct payment applications. Decomposition of Cadastral Mapping Activities: Some Methodological Notes

Key to studying the multidimensional interactions of cadastral mapping is the decomposition of mapping activities into interactions and boundary objects, which, analyzed in a particular context, facilitate understanding of the processes of empowerment and limitation. The study of cadastral mapping activities draws on several methodological precautions related to the study of power that Foucault noted in his lectures from 1976, concerning what he called the archaeological method . Most relevant here is the warning 'to understand power by looking at its extremities where its exercise became less and less juridicial' (Foucault 1997, 28). The limits of the cadastral mapping power originate with the fracturing of the cadastre's static representation because of ever-changing land usage and the delays in updating the cadastre to reflect these changes. No cadastral map is a stable reference to all physical or legal locations at all times, but it provides the formal and legal record of activities that have been administratively recorded.

Studying Power in Activities

The inversion of analysis of mapping power from the map itself to its use draws considerably from Foucault's engagements, particularly his later work (Elden 2007b) and his lectures on power. It also takes up concepts from infrastructure studies and grounded theory, especially the emphasis on the duality of interactions and boundary objects. Beyond dialectical processes of mapping, the concept of strategic logic, introduced by Foucault, provides the conceptual apparatus for the explanation of apparent inconsistencies and contradictions in cadastral mapping activities and helps ensure that the decomposition of infrastructure interactions and the elements of thematic domains reveal the empowerment and limitations that come through cadastral mapping.

Analysis of Cadastral Mapping

The theoretical framework for a consideration of property rights issues and the creation of calculable territory through the lens of mapping activities is the foundation for the analysis of these activities as interactions, boundary objects (e.g., parcels, surveys), and contextual factors (Figure 2). Power will be viewed as the capacity for these and contingent activities. Focusing on mapping activities means conceptualizing maps as artifacts that enforce their vision through inscription (Akrich 1992). Users often define quite different roles and complex relations to mapping, but ones that break the hierarchical institution's system for assigning and determining power. The privileging of sight in maps (Blomley 2003) reflects mapping's importance as the only means of seeing for those who cannot know the complex roles and relations it depicts firsthand. There are also changes, erasures, errors, and multiple cadastral maps to account for in cadastral mapping, however. Cadastral maps hold significance to empower and limit through relationships that meld multiple memories and infrastructures (Bowker 2006) into boundary objects that can facilitate coordination and overcome resistance. Each contention in cadastral mapping enacts struggles over property rights, conflicts involving administrative cadastral mapping activities, and state attempts to make territory calculable and legible.

Introduction

C onsiderations of the power of maps, beginning with Harley's (1989) seminal contributions to cartography and geography, have become a touchstone in cartography, critical geographic information systems (GIS), cadastral studies, political economy, and other subfields of geography. Geographers and cartographers also widely acknowledge that maps do not represent place as static mirrors of the world (Rorty 1981; Gelernter 1991) but, rather, provide selective constructions of dynamic activities and changes that exercise power through their visual representations, with explicit and implicit semiotic references permeating each cartographic text (Pickles 1991, 1997, 2004; Kwan 2007; Brown and Knopp 2008; Crampton 2010; Ettlinger 2011). As Harley and others acknowledge, map power is quite complex. The rich body of work that follows Harley's deconstructionist approach to mapping offers significant insights into the role of maps in state government (Ettlinger 2011), which more recently has been referred to as the state-led construction of calculable territory (Crampton and Krygier 2005; Crampton 2010; Rose-Redwood 2012). Government maps are regularly created, replaced, archived, and ignored. It follows that a map empowers in many ways when in use. What about the power of the forgotten, but still valid, map in an archive, the administrative map shown only once to a prominent international visitor, the map forgotten under the seat, the 'official' map of such dubious accuracy that it becomes irrelevant in praxis, or maps in conflict?

This article takes up these questions by engaging Harley's rejoinder that one considers how the numerous and vast mapping activities of the state enable and limit or, in other words, how activities of mapping manifest power. The power of mapping activities is sustained in the many interactions that enable and limit other activities. This article focuses on examples from cadastral mapping and its role in delineating property rights (Blomley 1998) as connected to the modern state's construction of calculable territory (Elden 2007a; Hannah 2009). The state maps, but it certainly relies on multiple mapping activities, which are widely known to be in disagreement with other government mapping activities or simply out of date. The accuracy of territorial inscriptions can be limited and even ambiguous, reflecting an incalculable territory, but still facilitate state control through the significance of mapping in administrative activities.

Studying Power in Activities

The inversion of analysis of mapping power from the map itself to its use draws considerably from Foucault's engagements, particularly his later work (Elden 2007b) and his lectures on power. It also takes up concepts from infrastructure studies and grounded theory, especially the emphasis on the duality of interactions and boundary objects. Beyond dialectical processes of mapping, the concept of strategic logic, introduced by Foucault, provides the conceptual apparatus for the explanation of apparent inconsistencies and contradictions in cadastral mapping activities and helps ensure that the decomposition of infrastructure interactions and the elements of thematic domains reveal the empowerment and limitations that come through cadastral mapping.

Key Concepts in Review

Following a recent emphasis on studying power arising in relations, this research takes up the challenge in Harley's insights (Harley and Laxton 2001) that the geographical consideration of maps requires a deeper engagement with the activities of creating and using these maps.

In other words, the theoretical framework for the study of mapping activities accounts for how they both empower and limit these activities as well as others. Material collected from actual activities explains processes of empowerment and limitation. A rich body of geographic literature drawing on Foucault's work analyzes historical and current uses of cadastral maps and their centrality as attempts at assuring the means of control (Biggs 1999; Withers 1999; Hannah 2000; Pickles 2004). The wide-ranging use of Foucault's work reflects his frequent admonition that others work freely with his insights.

data.text: This article aims to explore the role of home-based production networks within the industrialization process of rural areas in developing countries and its impact on the labor involved. Based on the structures of the Balinese clothing industry, the article explores the organization of production, provision of production and working capital, and composition and origin of labor. This article shows that home-based batik and embroidery clothing production in Bali is one of very few sources of income beyond agricultural work for immobile, rural labor. However, these production networks within the Balinese clothing industry are defined by weak labor relations vis-a-vis the clothing firm's exceptionally strong position.

Rural Home Production in Bali: The Batik and Embroidery Industry

The focus of Balinese clothing firms on the manufacture of two product groups, batik and embroidered garments, is largely the result of the demand for local souvenirs by the growing tourist population on this island. This development started in the 1970s, when beach market retailers started to sell batik sarongs and embroidered Kebaya (women's traditional blouses) to tourists visiting Bali. These items were initially collected by Balinese retailers first in Bali and then in East Java (Cole 1998, 262). Soon after, this domestic business generated multiplier effects, in which visitors to Bali started to purchase these items for resale in their home countries. Because of the market success of Balinese batik and embroidered summer wear in Australia, the United States, and Europe (Cole 1998, 265), these initially informal export businesses started to grow, and they experienced a rapid expansion during the 1980s. During this period, an increasing number of international buyers started business relations with Balinese clothing firms. At the same time, the number of people visiting Bali grew substantially (see Hassler 2005).

This growth of exports and increasing demand for souvenirs continued throughout the 1990s (Cole 1998, 270) and was reflected in the number of workers employed within the Balinese clothing industry. The Labor Composition of the Balinese Clothing Industry

The labor composition of the Balinese clothing industry is strongly localized because of the nature of the product and the organization of the production network. In contrast to the Javanese export clothing industry (Dicken and Hassler 2000; Hassler 2004b), there is no employment of foreigners, and even the involvement of workers from Java is small. Workers who are directly employed by Balinese clothing companies are usually involved in product development, marketing, quality control, and the production stages prior to, and after, sewing, while indirectly employed homeworkers are primarily in charge of sewing and the manual, labor-intensive production processes.

Fieldwork evidence suggests that employees in higher managerial functions such as accounting and sales belong to a well-established social network of neighbors and school friends. Trust is the main factor underlying this structure. Balinese company owners argue that close family members would expect too many privileges within the company. However, most clothing companies have a very flat hierarchical structure because of their size. Responsibilities are mainly concentrated with the company's owner. Introduction

C lothing manufacture has been a major facilitator in the industrialization of the Indonesian economy (Hill 1991, 1992, 1997; Pangestu 1997; Hassler 2004a). Throughout a general transition of the national economy, the overall share of agriculture declined within the gross national product, while manufacturing attained ever-increasing importance. Within this process, clothing production became the largest contributor to Indonesia's manufacturing sector (Aswicahyono 1997). As a result, Indonesia has established itself as the ninth largest clothing exporter within the global economy (WTO2002). The contribution of the national clothing sector to the Indonesian gross national product, however, is far from evenly distributed within the country. In fact, pronounced spatial disparities and concentration of economic activities are common phenomena in developing countries (e.g., see Xiaobin 1996; Lyons 1998; Zhao and T ong 2000; Rigg 2003). This is also the case in Indonesia, where Java has a clear primacy as a center for clothing production (BPS 2002) and is reflected in the spatial distribution of clothing firms on a subnational level.

data.text: Gardens have been an important site of environmental engagement in Australia since the British colonization. They are places where immigrant people and plants have carried on traditions from their homelands and have worked out an accommodation with new social and biophysical environments. We examined the backyard gardens of three contemporary migrant groups-Macedonian, Vietnamese, and British born-in suburban Australia and a group of first-generation Australians with both parents born overseas. In Macedonian backyards, emphasis was strong on the production of vegetables; in Vietnamese backyards, on herbs and fruit. British backyards were more diverse, some focusing on non-native ornamental flowers and others favoring native plants. The cohesiveness of the respective groups was partly an artifact of our sampling strategy. The Macedonian and Vietnamese migrants shared an affinity for productive, humanized landscapes that reflected their rural, subsistence backgrounds and crossed over into their attitudes toward the broader environment and national parks. The rural and village backgrounds help explain why intensive backyard food production has broken down among the next generation in (sub)urban Australia, becoming part of heritage rather than everyday practice.

data.text: During the last twenty-five years, housing policy in Sweden has radically changed. Once forming a pillar of the comprehensive welfare system, abbreviated the Swedish model, neoliberal housing politics have established market-governed housing provision with aminimum of state engagement. This shift has had consequences on the social geography of housing conditions. The research reported here analyzes social geographic change in Sweden's three largest cities-Stockholm, Gothenburg, and Malmo-between 1986 and 2001, relating observed patterns of gentrification and filtering to cycles of accumulation and to neoliberalization of housing policies. First, we outline the neoliberalization of Swedish housing policies. We then present an empirical analysis of gentrification and filtering in the three cities, spanning two boom periods (1986-1991, 1996-2001) and a bust period (1991-1996). The data reveal social geographic polarization manifested in the growth of supergentrification and low-income filtering. The analysis also introduces the concept of ordinary gentrification, supporting the move in gentrification research toward a broad generic conception of the process. Political reforms after 2001 are summarized and we argue that these underlie the continued increase in inequality and that the social geographic polarization mapped between 1986 and 2001 has probably intensified during this decade.

Research Method, Data, and Operationalizations

There have been few previous attempts to map gentrification over whole cities or city regions. The reason is simple: It is a tall order to secure data that can provide both theoretically adequate empirical measures and good spatial resolution over entire city regions and over a sufficient time period to capture the process. Early efforts either suffered from weak empirical operationalization, with empirical data weakly related to theoretical concepts (e.g., Ley 1986), or were rough around the edges given limitations in available data (Badcock 1989). More recent efforts by Wyly and Hammel (1998, 1999, 2000; Wyly 1999), Meligrana and Skaburskis (2005), and Podagrosi, Vojnovic, and Pigozzi (2011) display methodological progress toward adequate city-wide mapping, with finer operationalizations. Two problems common to empirical endeavors to map social geographic change are poor spatial resolution and difficulties separating change among the 'stayer' residents from change through migration. Previous efforts to map gentrification across whole cities have employed cross-sectional socio-economic data on administrative areas. These provide poor spatial resolution and are based on the assumption that upward socioeconomic change over a time interval indicates gentrification, which effectively disregards any socioeconomic change among the 'stayer' population.
