R apid urban change often leads to patterns of morphology, which are surprising in that they are unanticipated, often counter to what is expected. Regeneration and redistribution taking place in the industrial city, for example, have led to increasing specialization that manifests itself in phenomena as diverse as the ''edge city'' and patterns of segregation that form spontaneously among different population groups quite content to live side by side, notwithstanding mild preferences for adjacent locations. These patterns are often described as ''emergent,'' reflecting processes that act from the bottom up, producing growth and change that are organic and unplanned in their genesis. A particularly clear example is associated with the urbanization in some newly developed countries, particularly in East Asia. There, rural landscapes, usually within the hinterlands of large cities, are rapidly urbanizing, not through rural depopulation to the cities with their subsequent peripheral growth, but through a process of change in which a majority of the rural population are transforming their lifestyles and activities into urban pursuits in situ. In these situations, the long-standing migration of the population to large cities which has historically marked third-world urbanization is much less significant than the transformations that are taking place as the rural population becomes urban without substantial movement to the cities. This phenomenon is called ''desakota.''

Desakota is a pattern of settlement characterized by an intensive mixture of agricultural and nonagricultural activities that reveals itself as a close ''interlocking'' of villages and small towns (Lin 2001). These patterns are neither urban nor rural, but have demonstrated features of both. The term desakota was first used by McGee (1989, 1991), who identified these morphologies with the Bahasa Indonesian word ''desakota'' from the words for village ( desa ) and town ( kota ). He says ''These zones are characterized by high population densities, rapid growth of nonagricultural activities, labor mobility, occupational fluidity, and intense mixture of land with agriculture, cottage industries, industrial estates, suburban developments and other uses'' (McGee 1991, 16-17).

A Logic for Modeling Spontaneous Urban Change in China

Urban development everywhere is influenced by decision making at multiple levels and scales. But for desakota in China in general, and development in the Suzhou City region in particular over the period from 1990 to 2000, we simplify the chain of development decisions to two levels, local and global. The global level is reflected in aggregate social and economic factors that pertain to districts or townships within the region, and that are used to define instruments that steer development to favorable locations consistent with regional and national economic policy. The local level involves the decisions that households in rural villages and small towns make to realize local-scale economies through the transformation of their activities from rural to urban pursuits or to a mix of these. We call this ''two-front growth'' because it combines two different policymaking levels, both of which contribute to the simultaneous development of urban and rural areas by fusing ''cityleading-county'' initiatives in the cities with the ''household responsibility system'' that has been introduced in the countryside.

data.text: The Shimentai Nature Reserve in Yingde County, Guangdong Province, China, established recently in a subtropical upland forest area, has served for ages as an essential and customary source of livelihood for local people. Assessment of forest usage indicates heavy reliance by villagers on its diversified biotic resources. This forest dependence, associated with socioeconomic factors such as distance from village, ethnic origin, out-migration of rural youngsters, and a local tradition of conservation, is unlikely to decline in the near future. The reserve management recognizes the need to address the livelihood issues of local people and to win local support. A pragmatic adherence to provincial and higher-level policies that exclude forest-tapping activities could lead to more people-versus-park conflicts, which would dilute fundamental conservation objectives. A more enlightened and localized approach that nurtures a synergy between limited forest use and conservation while helping to develop new income sources could furnish workable alternatives.

In the past few decades, many developing countries have significantly expanded their PA systems (Ghimire 1994). For instance, between 1978 and 2000 China increased its nature reserves rapidly, from 34 to 1,227, incorporating almost 10 percent of its territory. The hasty designation of new PAS has created problems, notably the widespread escalation of peoplepark conflicts (Wells and Brandon 1992; Lewis 1996; Scott 1998; Liu and others 2001). The rising discords in developing countries are attributed largely to an anachronistic PA management myth that nature is separated from people and to the corollary that nature's integrity will be compromised if people are present (Wells and Brandon 1992; IUCN 1999). PA managers often had to confront the wrath of local residents whose livelihoods were intertwined with PA natural resources (Lewis 1996; Harkness 1998). Drowning in this sea of hostility, many PAS literally became 'paper parks' with degraded environmental quality. Richard Yarwood

University of Plymouth, UK

This article provides an overview of work that has examined the geographies of crime and policing in rural areas. Using policing in the United Kingdom as a jumping-off point, it outlines the significance of organized crime in rural places and argues that global, rather than community-based, perspectives are needed in its study and policing. It concludes by drawing attention to the value of Southern criminology in developing a research agenda to understand the geographies of rural policing. Key Words: crime, globalization, policing, rural, Southern criminology.

The rise in rural crime has come about due to two main factors. Social and economic change has seen the number of farms fall and close-knit communities collapse. Modern transport links now enable thieves to steal farm machinery and move it into mainland Europe in a matter of hours.

-NFU Mutual (2017), quoted in National Police Chief ' s Council (2018a, 3)

Rural Policing in the United Kingdom

Increasingly, rural policing in the United Kingdom is being driven by concern about thefts from agricultural premises (National Police Chief ' s Council 2018a). Surveys by The National Rural Crime Network (2018) have revealed that rural businesses have suffered high rates of victimization (Table 1) and, in 2019, the National Farmers ' Union (NFU) reported increases in thefts of agricultural vehicles (£9.3 million in insurance claims), quad bikes (£3.1 million), livestock (£3 million), and, specifically, Land Rover Defenders 2 (£2.1 million; National Farmers ' Union Mutual 2020; see Figure 1).

Although the quote acknowledges the connected, globalized nature of the countryside (Woods 2007), the study and policing of rural crime has remained rather insular by continuing to focus largely on ' the distinctive character of crime in rural and regional locales ' (Carrington, Hogg, and Sozzo 2016, 4) and the role of communities in policing them (Yarwood 2010; Ceccato 2015b). In turn, this can neglect some crimes, contribute to social exclusion, and support a view that communities are the cause and solution of rural problems (Desforges, Jones, and Woods 2005; Cheshire 2016).

The Global Countryside: From Places to Flows of Crime

Woods (2007) considered the globalized countryside to be ' knitted-together intersections of networks and flows that are never wholly fixed or contained at the local scale, and whose constant shape-shifting eludes a singular representation of place ' (499). Rural places are not easily identifiable, bounded communities; rather, they are constantly being ' thrown together ' by ' constellations of processes ' (Massey 2005, 141). Although geographers have taken up this call to understand rurality and globalization, their attention has mainly focused on legal activities (Carrington et al. 2018). Hall (2013) argued that ' discussions of contemporary processes such as globalization, regulation and economic liberalization which admit only licit actors offer both empirically and conceptually limited readings of those processes ' (380). He argued that a focus on organized crime groups not only reveals much about the spatiality and regulation of global crime but also sheds light on the processes, flows, and impacts of globalization. Three examples are outlined in the following sections (for full reviews, see Carrington, Hogg, and Sozzo 2016; Donnermeyer 2017).

data.text: The prevailing labor migration regime in Asia is underpinned by rotating-door principles of enforced transience, where low-wage migrant labor gains admission into host nation-states based on short-term, time-limited contracts and where family reunification and permanent settlement at destination are explicitly prohibited. In this context, we ask how migrant-sending families in Southeast Asian source countries-Indonesia and the Philippines-sustain family life in the long-term absence of one or both parents (often mothers). Through temporal concepts of rhythm, rupture, and reversal, we focus on how temporal modalities of care for left-behind children intersect with gendered power geometries in animating transnational family politics around care. First, by paying heed to the structuring effects of rhythm on social life, we show how routinized care rhythms built around mothers as caregivers have a normalizing and naturalizing effect on the conduct of social life and commonplace understanding of family well-being. Second, we explore the potential rupture to care rhythms triggered by the migration of mothers turned breadwinners and the extent to which gendered care regimes are either conserved, reconstituted, or disrupted in everyday patterns and practices of care. Third, we examine the circumstances under which gender role reversal becomes enduring, gains legitimacy among a range of poly care rhythms, or is quickly undone with the return migration of mothers in homecoming. The analysis is based primarily on research on Indonesian and Filipino rural households conducted in 2017 using paired life story interviews with children and their parental or nonparental adult caregivers.

Research Context and Methods

In response to the global -if gender-segmented -demand for waged domestic and care labor, developing countries in Southeast Asia have increasingly promoted overseas labor migration as a development strategy to address issues of poverty, domestic unemployment, and underemployment and to grow foreign exchange income through remittances (Asian Development Bank 2012). Women in the region move across transnational space -often as cheap and flexible labor with severely diminished rights -to plug growing care deficits (in terms of child care, elder care, and care for the sick) in globalizing cities and more developed economies.

As Southeast Asia ' s pioneer in producing global workers, the Philippines supplies ' workers of varying skill levels to over 100 countries ' (Asis, Scalabrini

Migration Center, PhilippineMigrants Rights Watch, and Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung 2005, 27). Making up 8 percent of the country ' s 100.98-million-strong population, the 7,979,716 Filipinos abroad in 2015 is a significant and reliable source of revenue (Department of Foreign Affairs 2015). Personal remittances accounted for 10.2 percent of the country ' s gross domestic product in 2018 (de Vera 2017). Among overseas Filipino workers, women migrants make up 55.8 percent of the total deployment (Philippine Statistics Authority 2017). Mazzucato and Schans (2011) were among the first scholars to argue that ' methodologically and theoretically, families are still predominantly conceived of as nuclear, living together, and bounded by the nation state. … Transnational families … have been treated as a temporary phenomenon, with family reunification in the host society the preferred outcome for all family members ' (704; see also Mazzucato and Dito 2018). With the increasing ubiquity of the ' permanently temporary ' migrant in regimes of unflexible noncitizenship in Asia, attention to family morphologies that bear the marks of the seemingly transgressive forces of increased migrations and mobilities has become more urgent. In response, scholars have focused primarily on how transnational families are lived in terms of spatial (dis)connectivities, as witnessed in the burgeoning literature on the complex role of information and communication technologies in negotiating intimacies and other kinds of relationships across transnational space (Peng and Wong 2013).

data.text: The role of extraregional linkages established by e-commerce in stimulating industrial renewal has yet to be sufficiently explored. We propose a framework that specifies the renewal of product as improvement in quality and the increase in the types of products, and understands product renewal as conditioned by the strength of extraregional linkages and the local capacity. Drawing on the original survey data on 241 Taobao villages in Zhejiang Province, a multinomial logit model is used to explore the factors influencing product renewal. We find that the improvement to production processes and merchants' management capabilities significantly contributes to product renewal, whereas the development of logistic industries and the establishment of e-commerce associations accomplishes the opposite. The authors argue that more attention should be paid to improve institutionalization of the Taobao business model to support the upgrading and renewal of local industries, such as improving local government recognition of e-commerce and popularizing e-commerce associations to a wider area.

The survey was conducted in Zhejiang Province, where rural e-commerce activities are more active because of the demonstration effect of Alibaba and other e-commerce enterprises. According to the statistics of Ali Research, there were 506 Taobao villages in Zhejiang Province in 2016, on which we based our questionnaire survey. The data on Taobao villages used in this study were collected through a survey on sampled village officials (drawn from the village head, deputy head, secretary, deputy secretary, accountant, or other senior position) conducted by a professional survey company between December 2017 and February 2018. Village officials were interviewed face to face and completed a standard questionnaire of forty-one questions, including question on the impact of Taobao and the basic condition of the village, businesses, product, sales, and so forth. Introduction

R ecent scholarly work in economic geography has been preoccupied with the conditions that stimulate regional industrial change (Binz, Truffer, and Coenen 2016; Lee 2017; Zhu, Li, and He 2019). Aside from local conditions and processes emphasized in evolutionary economic geography (EEG), such as technological relatedness, branching processes, and combinatorial knowledge dynamics, there is increasing evidence that extraregional linkages also contribute to the renewal and restructuring of regional resource bases and the creation of new regional industrial paths (Andersson, Bjerke, and Karlsson 2013; Zhu, He, and Zhou 2017). Regions are able to supplement locally available resources and knowledge with bodies of knowledge, resources, and capabilities residing elsewhere through building pipelines with other regions, and for that purpose to stay dynamic and innovative (Bathelt, Malmberg, and Maskell 2004; Chen 2015; He, Yan, and Rigby 2018).

Extraregional linkages can be established in various forms, such as market linkages, formal networks, and informal linkages (Trippl, Grillitsch, and Isaksen 2018). The literature on trade networks suggests that the market linkage is a conduit for an inflow of new knowledge and information embodied in the goods from outside regions, which is conducive for processes pertaining to the improvement of existing product lines and renewal and upgrading of industrial sectors (Loof and Andersson 2010; Andersson, Bjerke, and Karlsson 2013). Over the past years, the twin forces of globalization and the information and communications technology revolution are combining to create e-commerce, which has changed traditional ways of business. E-commerce, the digital dimension of the platform economy, opens the configurations of the scope, scale, and density of economic interactions (Richardson 2015). Geographically, e-commerce allows firms to interact with and participate in different locations and networks, and knowledge exchange and interactive learning can occur effectively through e-commerce between spatially distant actors (Amin and Roberts 2008; Richardson 2015). In other words, e-commerce leads to greater information flows and wider market coverage while reducing the dependence of regions on existing resources. We therefore argue that ecommerce can be regarded as one specific means through which regions develop critical external linkages to absorb and transform outside resources and knowledge into a renewal process of local industries (Acquier, Daudigeos, and Pinkse 2017). The role of e-commerce in renewal of local industries is still a relatively unexplored area of research, however.

How E-commerce Stimulates Product Renewal

Literature on global production networks has demonstrated that local actors such as firms and institutions might be able to obtain relevant resources and knowledge complementary to local capabilities by networking with other actors involved in such an international division of labor system (Yeung 2009; Coe, Dicken, and Hess 2008). Yet, its conceptual and methodological approach still has some limitations. First, it is not applicable to rural areas with a low innovation capacity. There is a consensus that the resources available in rural areas are quite ubiquitous and uncompetitive, making it difficult for them to participate in a global production network (Galliano, Goncalves, and Triboulet 2019). Despite a growth in the literature emphasizing global -local relations, suitable ways to build extraregional linkages for rural areas and how they affect the renewal and upgrading of local industries has been little explored. Second, much of the existing literature on extraregional linkages focuses on foreign direct investment (FDI; Bathelt and Li 2014; Y. D. Wang et al. 2016) or foreign trade (Mao and He 2019b).

Strength of Extraregional Linkages

The extraregional linkages constructed by e-commerce connect actors inside and outside regions, and are essential to providing local merchants with the resources they need to pursue their product renewal (Trippl, Grillitsch, and Isaksen 2018). In Taobao villages, e-commerce stimulates local firms to produce and supply new products by delivering effective new demand information from the external market. Conventionally, the cost incurred in access of information is particularly high, especially in developing countries, which is a critical challenge for firms in these regions to find customers and raise their incomes (Tarafdar, Anekal, and Singh 2012). The most basic benefit of e-commerce, though, is access to a larger network of providers, consumers, or resources. In other words, e-commerce enables online merchants to expand local markets into national or even global markets by reducing information costs. As various scholars in this field have confirmed, larger markets increase the incentive to produce new ideas, and hence induce product innovations (Schmookler 1962; Rothwell et al. 1974).

data.text: U.S. federal government agencies play an important role in mitigating some risks posed to communities by natural hazard events, especially communities with high proportions of low-income or minority residents. Ongoing efforts of the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) to reduce the buildup of forest fuels on national forests, particularly in dry mixed-conifer forests of the U.S. West, are an example. Federal land management agencies must comply with the Executive Order on Environmental Justice (EJ Order, 59 Fed. Reg 7629, 1994), but there is scant documentation of whether these agencies have substantively complied with the EJ Order in implementing land management activities. There is also little quantitative environmental justice (EJ) research on dispersed rural populations, such as those often found adjacent to national forests. Our research addresses these gaps. We apply a novel mixed-methods approach, including quantitative pattern analysis and interviews with forest managers, to examine whether the benefits of wildfire risk reduction created on twelve national forests in four western U.S. states were equitably distributed among nearby populations. We found that EJ impacts might have occurred on all twelve forests, but they tended to be localized and context specific. We also learned from interviewees that EJ was not considered in decisions about where and how to conduct wildfire hazard reduction and that EJ populations rarely engaged in collaborative project planning apart from the formal tribal consultation process. Our research expands the range of quantitative geographical analysis of EJ issues and our methods could be adopted by land management agencies to achieve more equitable distribution of costs and benefits from their management activities.

Methods

Our research addresses limitations in existing EJ scholarship by applying novel spatial analysis

procedures we previously developed for population and resource management activity data and integrating them with qualitative analysis. A detailed pilot test of the spatial analysis procedures has been previously published (Adams and Charnley 2018). In this section, we summarize them and show how they are linked to a qualitative interview protocol designed to uncover national forest decision-making factors in the planning and implementation of HFR that are not readily quantifiable.

National Forest Sample

The USFS has identified an especially acute need for forest restoration in dry mixed-conifer forests it manages. Forest ecologists have generally classified the fire regime of dry mixed-conifer forests as one of frequent fire recurrence with a broad range of severity, measured in terms of tree mortality: predominantly low severity (Agee 1993), low to moderate severity (e.g., Allen et al. 2002), and mixed severity (e.g., Perry et al. 2011; Odion et al. 2014). There is considerable variability in historical fire recurrence intervals and typical patterns of burn severity within the broad category of dry mixed-conifer forests. This variability is a function of factors interacting at multiple scales, from the locally specific, such as topography and prevailing winds, to global climate change. Not all dry mixed-conifer forest landscapes have an equal need for restoration, but as a broad class of forest type compared with others across the Western United States, this type might be most in need of restoration related to managing future fire behavior (Agee and Skinner 2005; Larson and Churchill 2012).

To ensure that the management context for HFR was roughly comparable for all potential sample units, we identified all national forest units in the Western United States that have at least some area of dry mixed-conifer forest. Data

HFR data come from the Forest Activity Tracking System (FACTS) database, a clearinghouse for recording and accessing the accomplishments of all USFS program activities (USDAFS 2016). To minimize the potentially high variability in year-to-year HFR program accomplishments, we collected records for the period 1 January 2006 to 31 December 2015 for each forest unit. Older data were not reliable. FACTS data have many attributes, but most are qualitative. Acreage accomplished is the only quantitative field in our FACTS data set that was reliable for all twelve forests. We thus examined only total acres treated in the quantitative analysis, although we acknowledge that acreage treated might not always be linearly related to a reduction of wildfire risk. We used additional descriptive attributes, including the type of fuel reduction treatment, to inform our interviews. HFR data from FACTS exist in tabular as well as geospatial form; both have data quality issues that we address in detail in Adams and Charnley (2018). For this analysis, each HFR polygon was reduced to its centroid and then expanded to form an abstract circular feature exactly matching its acreage accomplished attribute. This generalization was necessary to deal with many records where the acreage of the digitized polygon differed radically from the acreage accomplished attribute. The national forest is the unit of analysis; HFR data are not pooled across forests.

data.text: Minority populations frequently face heightened vulnerabilities compared to other racial groups during disasters. This research investigates how the responses to disaster issues of minority populations vary across rural and urban areas. The study examines differences in disaster evacuation vulnerabilities among minority populations by analyzing their evacuation status and choices of evacuation destinations. The 2023 survey employed a two-target groups approach, sampling minorities of all ages in both urban (eighty people) and rural areas (eighty people), and collected a total of 160 responses from northwest Florida. Our study could be influenced by various disasters, but we assume that people respond based on their perceptions of hurricanes. The survey was conducted using Pollfish, an online tool specializing in mobile application surveys, based on diverse eligibility criteria. Twelve logistic regression models were developed, examining evacuation status and future evacuation destination as dependent variables, with independent variables spanning socioeconomic, health, and past consequences dimensions. The results show that 61.3 percent of urban minorities and 81.3 percent of rural minorities evacuated at least once in past disasters. The study identifies statistically significant variables, highlighting evacuation behavior differences between urban and rural minorities, with implications for emergency management to address marginalized populations' evacuation needs more effectively.

Study Area

This study was carried out in the Florida Panhandle, known for its significant concentration of minority populations, and recognized as one of the most disaster-prone regions in the United States. Florida is vulnerable to disaster due to its tropical climate, exposure to oceans from three sides, and low sealevel elevation (Ghorbanzadeh et al. 2021; Miller, Arias, and Alvarez 2021). After two consecutive hurricanes -Hermine (2016) and Irma (2017) -the Florida Panhandle ' s oceanfront counties faced near devastation from Hurricane Michael (2018), one of the four most powerful hurricanes in U.S. history (Senkbeil et al. 2020). Florida is also ranked as the tenth most racially diverse state and is also home to a significant minority population and a large number of undocumented immigrants (Pew Research Center 2019; U.S. Census Bureau 2020).

This research was conducted in the eighteen Panhandle counties of northwest Florida: Escambia, Santa Rosa, Okaloosa, Walton, Holmes, Washington, Bay, Jackson, Calhoun, Gulf, Gadsden, Liberty, Franklin, Leon, Wakulla, Jefferson, Taylor, and Madison. We categorized the region ' s constituent zip codes into urban and rural categories, following the classifications outlined by AbdelMagid et al. (2023). To ensure accurate representation of rural populations, Florida ' s rural zip codes were identified using the definition of rurality provided by the Florida Department of Transportation Office of Policy Planning. We developed a questionnaire related to disaster scenarios in Florida, covering different aspects of disaster and approved by the Institutional Review Board of Florida State University. For this survey, we created two audience groups in Pollfish. The first group includes individuals who are non-White (Black/African American, Hispanic, Latino, Arab, Asian, or multiracial), age eighteen and older, and living in urban zip codes. The second group has the same criteria, except that they reside in rural zip codes. Statistical Methods

This study explored the factors influencing evacuation behavior among urban and rural minorities while exploring the impact of multiple binary independent factors on our decision variable for both groups. Initially, we examined whether there is a relationship between evacuation status during past disasters and future evacuation destination choices for these groups. To achieve this, we employed a chi-square test to determine if the evacuation behavior of respondents is associated with their urban or rural status. The chi-square test checks the independence of categorical variables and assesses how well an observed distribution fits an expected distribution (Das et al. 2023).

Additionally, to understand the strength of the relationship between urban and rural minorities concerning their evacuation status and destination choices, we used the Phi ( u ) coefficient and Cram  er ' s V measures. The Phi coefficient is used for 2 -2 contingency tables, whereas Cram  er ' s V is used for larger contingency tables. Scores for both measures range from 0 to 1, where 0 indicates negligible association and 1 indicates a strong association (Das et al. 2023). These measures provide insight into the strength of the relationship between categorical variables, complementing the chi-square test, which only indicates the presence or absence of a significant association.

Md. Shaharier Alam a , Mark W. Horner a , and Eren Erman Ozguven b a Florida State University, USA; b Florida A&M University -Florida State University College of Engineering, USA

D isasters might not discriminate, but they can unveil preexisting inequalities within our society, highlighting how various demographic groups experience the same disaster in distinct ways (Van Willigen et al. 2002). Minority populations face elevated mortality rates and substantial obstacles due to underlying inequalities during disasters (Downey 2016; Sharpe and Wolkin 2022). Mortality rates during disasters in the United States were significantly higher for non-Hispanic Black individuals (1.87 times) and American Indian/Alaska Native individuals (7.34 times) compared to non-Hispanic White individuals, based on mortality data analysis from 1999 to 2018 (Sharpe and Wolkin 2022). Black/African American and Hispanic communities have experienced more adverse mental health outcomes during hurricane evacuations than their White counterparts (Messias and Lacy 2007; Davidson et al. 2013). The aftermath of hurricanes has been particularly devastating for low-income minority communities in places such as New Orleans, with greater damage, higher unemployment rates and, increased psychological distress compared with White communities (Elder et al. 2007; Messias, Barrington, and Lacy 2012; Lewis et al. 2019). Evacuation policies favoring private transportation have hindered African Americans ' ability to prepare and evacuate during storms, leading to disparities due to perceived vulnerability, financial constraints, neighborhood crime, and

Sometimes, undocumented immigrants face even greater barriers during emergencies, including language barriers, limited social networks for support, financial constraints, and fears of legal repercussions tied to their immigration status (Messias, Barrington, and Lacy 2012; Wilson and Tiefenbacher 2012).

The challenges faced by minority populations can differ in urban and rural settings, as both areas possess unique sets of advantages and disadvantages, rendering them both vulnerable and resilient in distinct ways (Carpender et al. 2006; Kapucu, Hawkins, and Rivera 2013; Cutter, Ash, and Emrich 2016). Rural communities are vulnerable to disasters due to their less diversified economy, geographic isolation, inadequate transport infrastructure, poverty, decreasing population, weaker planning, inequitable access to recovery resources and administrative capacity, and so on (Davies et al. 2009; Kapucu, Hawkins, and Rivera 2013; Horney et al. 2017).

Disaster and Vulnerability

Disaster is an evolving concept and mostly defined as social disruption resulting from the convergence of a hazardous event and the societal response or the absence thereof (Perry 2018). Hoffman and OliverSmith (2002) described disasters as the points where geophysical events intersect with vulnerable populations, arising from ongoing natural and social processes over time. The extent of the disaster is not only determined by the severity of the hazard but also by how well society manages and mitigates its impact (Kusenbach, Simms, and Tobin 2010; Kelman et al. 2016).

Understanding the vulnerability to natural disasters is complicated because of its conceptual complexity (Cutter 2003). Broadly, the vulnerability to natural hazards has been viewed from two major perspectives (Wang et al. 2022). The first group viewed disaster from the lens of structural or physical characteristics. Early research in the field of disasters viewed disasters as an outcome of geophysical processes and predominantly focused on the hazard ' s physical characteristics (Blaikie et al. 2004).

data.text: Wildfires create a risk to pedestrians traveling through rural areas, because they might not be aware of the presence of a wildfire or its direction and rate of spread until is too late to successfully evacuate. In wildland areas of southern San Diego County, immigrants crossing the U.S.-Mexico border and border security agents are particularly at risk to wildfires. The objective of this study is to develop a framework of analysis and associated tools for examining the combined behavior of wildfires and pedestrian mobility to assess the potential threat of fire to pedestrians in wildland areas. Outputs from a geographic information system (GIS) overlay model for determining potentially dangerous fire zones, the Wildland-Urban Interface Evacuation (WUIVAC) model, and a model of pedestrian mobility in wildland areas were combined to generate wildfire risk to pedestrian maps. The key technical contributions of the study are the development and testing of the pedestrian mobility model and the framework and logic for integrating the results of three GIS-based models. The applied geography contribution is the testing of two scenarios of high risk from wildfires to pedestrians within the U.S.-Mexico border zone of San Diego County, California. The study results show that the travel times calculated by the pedestrian mobility model appear to be realistic and are affected by the terrain and vegetation characteristics of a study site, whereas the evacuation trigger buffers (ETBs) from WUIVAC are mostly influenced by the wind speed and direction parameters of the FlamMap fire spread model. A moderate fire danger to pedestrians in the most remote wildland locations of the study area is determined. The scenario test results suggest that if a wildfire occurs within 2 km (extreme southwesterly winds) or 6 km (extreme northeasterly wind) of pedestrians in the worst case location within the San Diego border region they would likely not have a sufficient amount of time to reach a nearby safety zone.

Study Area

The study area for this research is defined as the wildland areas of the U.S.-Mexico border zone within San Diego County, California. It extends from the eastern urban edge of San Ysidro (located about 12.5 km west of the Pacific Ocean) 10 km to the San Diego County line in the east. The southern limit is the border and the northern limit is approximately 8 km north of the border, as shown in Figure 1.

The terrain consists of foothills, mountains, and valleys. The border study area is characterized by a Mediterranean-type climate with long, dry, hot summers and short, relatively wet, and cooler winters with average precipitation ranges between 250 and 500 mm (Pyne 1984; Zhou, Mahalingam, and Weise 2005). The predominant landscape type is chaparral shrublands, with patchy occurrences of grasslands and woodlands (Hanes 1971). In addition to vegetation, other land cover and land use types include rock outcrops, reservoirs, and rural residential. The study area has a constant flow of illegal crossers and presence of law enforcement officers within the border zone.

Methods

To accomplish the study objectives, three spatially explicit models were implemented individually, and their outputs were combined. The first phase involved the development of a GIS overlay model for locating the area within the border zone of San Diego County that had the highest wildland fire danger. Once this area was determined, the next step was to determine the specific locations where pedestrians associated with the two scenarios (i.e., illegal immigrant and law enforcement officer) would be in greatest danger. Based on these locations, the PMM was used to estimate pedestrian travel times to safety zones. These travel times were used in the WUIVAC model as critical thresholds relative to which evacuation trigger buffers were generated. Combining the results of the three models enabled creation of a map of wildfire risk to pedestrians that depicts the likelihood that a pedestrian could reach a safety zone before the flame front of a wildfire at a given location could reach the pedestrian. The entire processing flow is depicted in Figure 2.

Figure 1 Study site (small rectangle) determined from geographic information system overlay model as the zone presenting the greatest risk to pedestrians from wildfires within the San Diego-Mexico border zone study area.

Pedestrian Mobility Model

The PMM was developed to estimate pedestrian mobility rates for wildland areas. This model utilizes the Path Distance function in ArcGIS 9.2 (ESRI) GIS software to calculate the least accumulative cost between adjacent grid cells, while accounting for surface distance, and horizontal and vertical cost factors (Zhan, Menon, and Gao 1993), as shown in Figure 2. PMM employs five travel constraint variables (slope, aspect, roads, trails, and vegetation) for which travel rate percentages are calculated to adjust estimates of pedestrian evacuation timing. A 30-m raster was utilized for data input and modeling. In view of these criteria, the final result of the PMM is a raster data set where a pedestrian travel time is assigned to each pixel in the grid. Based on the predefined objective for this study, pixels of the same travel time were combined to form travel time horizons in fifteen-minute increments.

Slope and aspect inputs to the PMM were derived from a 30-m resolution digital elevation model (DEM) from the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (Farr et al. 2007). Slope values were grouped into five interval classes and aspect values were grouped into ten classes as shown in Table 1 for a northward-traveling pedestrian. A combinatorial AND function was used to combine the slope and aspect data into fifty unique terrain combinations.

data.text: Scholars have long documented widespread aging and depopulation of rural communities in the Great Plains. Paralleling these trends is the emergence, growth, and spatial dispersion of new and longtime non-white populations across the region. The dual processes of population loss in many counties combined with the growth of new, non-white population groups suggest that the ethnic structure of the population is changing. In this article we utilize choropleth maps, Hoover and Simpson indexes, and cluster analysis to assess whether the emergence and growth of ethnic minority groups in the Great Plains between 1970 and 2008 is a localized phenomenon or region-wide shift in the ethnic composition of the population. Results suggest that as depopulation is occurring in many counties of this region, the growth of non-white populations, both immigrant and native born, is changing or restructuring the ethnic composition of the Great Plains.

Data and Methods

Data for the following analyses come from the 1970, 1980, 1990, and 2000 U.S. Decennial Census, the 2008 Population Estimates Program, the 2002 Census of Agriculture (U.S. Department of Agriculture 2002), and the Regional Economic Information System for 1969, 1979, 1989, and 2000 (Bureau of Economic Analysis [BEA] 2002). We focus our analyses on five demographic groups (Latino, black, Asian, Native American, and white populations) within the Great Plains. Although numerous definitions of the Great Plains region exist, we utilize boundaries inclusive of the major regional delimitations (Adamchak et al. 1999; Archer and Lonsdale 2003; Wilson 2009). To evaluate the extent to which ethnic restructuring is occurring in this region, we employ choropleth maps, Hoover and Simpson indexes, and cluster analysis.

The Hoover Index measures the concentration of a population in the study area. First introduced by Hoover in 1941, it remains a viable tool for understanding trends in population concentration and deconcentration at multiple scales, including the county, state, and region (Long and Nucci 1997; Otterstrom and Shumway 2003). Index values range from 0 to 100-the higher the value, the more concentrated the population; the lower the value, the more dispersed the population; a value of 0 indicates a population that is equally distributed (Plane and Rogerson 1994). Laura Simmons

University of North Carolina at Charlotte

Scholars have long documented widespread aging and depopulation of rural communities in the Great Plains. Paralleling these trends is the emergence, growth, and spatial dispersion of new and longtime non-white populations across the region. The dual processes of population loss in many counties combined with the growth of new, non-white population groups suggest that the ethnic structure of the population is changing. In this article we utilize choropleth maps, Hoover and Simpson indexes, and cluster analysis to assess whether the emergence and growth of ethnic minority groups in the Great Plains between 1970 and 2008 is a localized phenomenon or region-wide shift in the ethnic composition of the population. Results suggest that as depopulation is occurring in many counties of this region, the growth of non-white populations, both immigrant and native born, is changing or restructuring the ethnic composition of the Great Plains. Key Words: ethnic restructuring, Great Plains, internal migration, rural population, settlement patterns.

Factors Influencing Changing Settlement Patterns

Since 1990, Asian and Latino populations, inclusive of immigrants and long-term residents, have grown rapidly and dispersed away from gateway cities to new destinations throughout the United States (Kandel and Cromartie 2004). The processes of globalization, regional economic restructuring within the United States, and changes in U.S. immigration policy have facilitated the recent redistribution of these populations to new locations and, in the Great Plains, the emergence of these groups is stemming population loss and creating a more ethnically diverse population.

Globalization

Globalization is a process by which regional and national economies and societies are increasingly integrated into the international economy through trade, transportation and communication technologies, capital flows, and migration. It 'include[s] fewer barriers and risks to trade and financial and investment capital flows and, thus, greater global economic integration, greater flexibility in labor markets, a compression of time and space' (Hytrek and Zentgraf 2008, 5). Integration occurs across various geographic scales, altering labor supply and demand, creating large and extensive international migration flows from the Global South to the Global North as well as between countries of the Global South (Castles and Miller 2009). Demand for low-skill, low-wage labor in the Global North coupled with population growth without sufficient corresponding economic growth in the Global South has created a surplus of workers, generating pressure for immigration to the Global North. Thus, through the process of globalization, labor demands and shortages create, through international migration, new populations within Global North countries.

data.text: The paper examines holy rural and urban are interpreted and applied to counties in eleven states in the western United States, After reviewing various conceptual approaches, we Nm to a three-parr analysis of county commissioners' perceptions and census data to identify characteristics associated with urban-ness and rurality The analysis involves comparing qualitative and quantitative survey and interview data, using a multiple regression analysis to correlate census variables with commissioners' perceptions of their home counties, and using cluster analysis techniques on census variables to identify patterns and unevenness in rurality and urbanness. Three characteristics mentioned by the widest range of commissioners and found to be statistically significant in the regression analysis were population concentration total population, and the agricultural land base. Population concentration, in particular, was identified most frequently by interviewees as the single most important variable in characterizing an urban county and had the most meaningful contribution to predicting commissioners' perceptions of their home counties in the regression analysis. The cluster analysis identified live county types: largest urban centers, growing regional hubs, high growth rural, dispersed rural, and stable rural agriculture. These county types were widely distributed, reflecting the spatial unevenness of macroscale processes operating across eleven western states.

Studying Western U.S. Counties and County Commissioners

As sites where tensions between local autonomy and state control are manifest, counties are places where the rural can be interpreted with respect to the urban. Counties subdivide states into separate areas of local government;

thus, each location within a state is situated within the jurisdiction of only one county. Counties contain the imprint of grassroots governance and community yet also extend the control of state governance (Grant and Nixon 1968; Murphy 1970).

There is no single county archetype. While common to all states, the county is not a standardized unit. Nationwide, counties range in area from 24 square miles to over 20,000 square miles, and in population size from less than 250 to over nine million. In the western U.S. counties are particularly disparate, including tightly-bounded, high population density city-counties, such as Denver, Colorado, as well as expansive counties with unevenly distributed populations, such as San Bernardino, California.

In the western United States there are, and always have been, many more counties without major cities than counties with major cities. Butler (1990) provides an indication of this by identifying four and one-half times as many nonmetropolitan counties as metropolitan counties in the western United States. Nevertheless, in recent decades the human population of the region has increased exponentially, becoming more concentrated in large and me

Relating Commissioners' Perceptions with Census Variables

We compared ratings of commissioners' home counties with census data using a standard multiple regression analysis (in SPSS 7.5). Our goal was to identify relationships between the commissioners' perceptions and more conventionally used quantitative measures of urbanness and rurality. Each commissioner's rating for his/her home county is the dependent variable and six variables derived from the U.S. Census and U.S. Census of Agriculture are independent variables. The variables were selected because quantitative measures of population and agricultural land base are generally used to characterize urbanness and rurality and, more particularly, these measures are frequently cited by commissioners in both survey and interview responses:

  • total estimated population (1995);
  • population density (total estimated population in 1995 divided by the county area);
  • population concentration (a computed variable that represents the relative amount of population dispersal or clustering within a county; population concentration for a

county such as San Francisco, CA, in which the entire population of the county was in a large city, is 100, whereas a county with no Census Designated Places [CDPs] with populations greater than 2,499, such as Granite, MT with no small, medium, or large cities, has a value of 1); 7

  • population growth or decline (1990 to 1995);
  • proportion of land in farms or the agricultural land base (1992);
  • change in agricultur

Patterns from a Cluster Analysis of Census Variables

The forces shaping the western U.S. are neither isolated nor specific to the region. Mediating the effects of larger events and structures, however, are interactions between the region's peoples and geographies that establish the contexts within which counties in the western U.S. operate. Shapira and Leigh-Preston (1984) describe these contexts in this manner:

In a physical sense, the sheer geographical size of the region, the scarcity of water, the ranges of climate and topography, and the possibilities for agricultural and mineral development have always influenced the character of development in the West. . . . The physical and natural resource characteristics of the West continue to provide the specific terrain within which contemporary changes interact, just as earlier historical and economic structures provide a context for current economic development. However, as the West has become fully integrated into the national and international economy, the leading factors now influencing patterns of economic change and development in the region are less intraregional or regional-specific and more related to a series of broader developments currently affecting the U.S. economy. Meanings of Rural and Urban

While rural and urban are frequently used loosely without reference to their context or meaning (c.f. Brown 1980; Bellamy et al. 1990; Gamradt and Avery 1992; Bradshaw 1993; Wojan and Pulver 1995), this practice should not be mistaken for conceptual simplicity or the widespread acceptance of standardized definitions. Many scholars in this country and abroad reject simple definitions and debate the conceptual significance and everyday meanings of these terms. Discussions by British, U.S., and Mexican academics, for example, underscore the complexity of social attachment to rurality and the character of change in places considered to be rural or urban. 2 One way to approach the meaning and significance of rurality and urbanness is to chart changes in academic discussions about these issues. Cloke and Thrift (1994) identify four phases in academic approaches to interpreting rurality. 3

As sites where tensions between local autonomy and state control are manifest, counties are places where the rural can be interpreted with respect to the urban. Counties subdivide states into separate areas of local government;

Commissioners' Perceptions of What is Urban and Rural

Throughout the interviews and surveys, commissioners use measures of population and the agricultural land base most frequently to distinguish rural from urban counties. Threequarters of the interviewees identify population concentration as a very important variable in characterizing urban counties. Approximately one-half of the interviewees rate total population, population growth, and recent decreases in agriculture as very important. Onethird of the interviewees rate the presence of industry as very important.

STUDY OBJECTIVES AND METHODS

This study explores the everyday lived experiences of this borderland through an examination of its historical geography, evolving economic functions, border crossings, land ownership, and residential population. It draws upon both quantitative analysis of public data sets, close personal observations dating back to 1991 , and interviews with key informants and local residents. Data sets include the American Community Survey, United States and Canadian censuses, border crossing data from the Department of Homeland Security, and the 2014 Whatcom County property tax parcel geodatabase. Since 1991 , I have periodically visited Point Roberts, Washington, first while living in Vancouver, Canada, and later while living in Point Roberts during the 2011 -2012 academic year. During 2011 -2012 , I lived with my family at latitude 48 . 9933 o North on Boundary Bay Road in Point Roberts, Washington, and conducted participant

observation by immersing myself in community life. Challenges of everyday life such as daily border crossings, connecting utilities, hiring contractors, shopping, and educating middle-school and high-school age children revealed a new face to everyday life in this borderland. Between 2011 and 2015 , interviews were conducted with key informants: local business owners; Whatcom County planning, zoning, and environmental services personnel; and local utility providers, to develop a more complete picture of service provision in the shadow of an international boundary. MARK BJELLAND

ABSTRACT. Point Roberts, Washington is a geographical anomaly that opens a window into the lived experience of borders. Created by the imposition of an antecedent geometric boundary on an undulating coastline, Point Roberts has transitioned from a resource extraction frontier to a summer tourist destination for Canadians to a transnational borderland that defies notions of the bounded state as the container for society. The community is defined by the international border, which both connects and isolates it. Point Roberts relies on a mixture of services from both countries and fills a unique transnational economic niche, reflecting the complementarity between rural and urban and the United States and Canada. Point Roberts is a hybrid borderland: a privileged exurb for U.S. citizens working in Vancouver, a U.S. service center for Canadians, and a seaside retirement community with pockets of isolation and neglect. Keywords: borders, political geography, Vancouver.

A BORDERED WORLD

Julian Minghi's seminal review asserted that political boundaries are 'the most palpable political geographic phenomena' and are central to the study of political geography ( 1963 , 407 ). After half a century of geopolitical change and the addition of numerous new borders, Alexander Diener and Joshua Hagen affirmed that borders remain 'the most obvious political geographic entity in the lives of human beings' ( 2010 , 1 ). The precisely surveyed and demarcated borders of the contemporary world are central features of geographic space, reflecting the ideals of the modernist territorial state (Diener and Hagen 2012 ; Murphy 2013 ).

MAKING SENSE OF EXCLAVES

Exclaves are, by definition, border regions characterized by an 'unusually high degree of cross-boundary circulatory pressure' (Minghi 1963 , 422 ). Exclaves are part of a broader class of territorial outliers that represent deviations from the compact, geographically contiguous form that is idealized for nation-states. They are almost always the product of contingent historic, even accidental, circumstances during the establishment of borders. Most exclaves are tiny and lack geopolitical significance, yet their persistence challenges those who predict the eventual disappearance of the nation-state (Ormae 1990 ; O'Brien 1992 ; Gu  ehenno 1995 ; Castells 1996 ). Exclaves are more than geographical oddities; they offer valuable insights into the contingent practices of statecraft and the social construction of borders (McConnell 2011 ).

data.text: White-tailed deer, Odocoileus virginianus, anthrax epizootics have been frequently documented in Texas over the last two decades. Once outbreaks begin, there is evidence for the potential role of hematophagous flies as vectors for the disease. Hypotheses on the role of biting flies in the transmission of anthrax date back more than a century. Both laboratory experiments and field studies have provided evidence of a biting fly transmission pathway. In particular, several studies have implicated biting flies during severe wildlife outbreaks in North America. Despite these implications, there is a lack of spatial analysis relating flies and anthrax. Here we report on the spatial patterns of anthrax in white-tailed deer on a well-studied ranch with a documented anthrax history. These patterns were evaluated against the spatiotemporal patterns of biting flies during the anthrax risk period. Unbaited fly traps were used to collect flies across the study ranch from June through August 2005. Kernel density analysis confirmed biting fly hotspots concentrated in the areas with highest densities of deer carcasses. The average nearest neighbor index confirmed that deer carcasses were spatially clustered and density estimates suggest that these are in proximity to areas supporting high fly populations. Dual kernel density analysis of carcasses and deer population identified a large dry riverine habitat as a high anthrax risk. Fly catch rates across the period identified a similar pattern to the anthrax risk surface. The high overlap between areas of sustained high fly catch rates and anthrax cases does suggest a relationship warranting future research.

Materials and Methods

This study employed anthrax surveillance data from a deer herd and biting fly collections that were conducted on a wildlife ranch located approximately 80 km north of Del Rio, Val Verde County, Texas (Figure 1). Ecologically the ranch is situated on the Edwards Plateau ecoregion based on the Level III classification scheme (Yanli et al. 2009). The ranch encompasses ∼ 7,406 ha and is managed exclusively for white-tailed deer and game birds. Well-documented anthrax outbreaks occurred on the ranch in recent years (see Table 1 and Figure 1), and active surveillance for dead deer was conducted by ranch staff and researchers annually during the anthrax season from 2001 to present. In Texas, the anthrax risk period is primarily from late spring thru early fall (mid-May-early October; Hugh-Jones and Blackburn 2009). To date, anthrax cases have only been found in the central and eastern areas of the ranch, despite ranch-wide surveillance. Our work in the larger area surrounding the ranch from 2002 to present identified this area as an enzootic zone with cases confirmed nearly every year on this and ranches across the zone (Figure 1). The exact boundary of the enzootic zone remains fuzzy at best. To define the boundary, we used the county boundaries of those counties with reported cases since 2000. To illustrate the fuzziness of the zone, we used a semitransparent boundary.

Hematophagous Fly Collecting

Weimplemented a spatially explicit sampling design to evaluate the spatial and temporal patterns of biting flies relative to known areas of deer anthrax on the ranch. Biting fly sampling was conducted over three periods between 5 June and 21 August 2005 using seven unbaited Nzi fly traps (www.nzitrap.com; Figure 2). The Nzi is a nylon and polyester net trap with countershaded blue and black panels designed to attract flies through black body attraction (Mihok 2002). The top of the trap is translucent net mesh that allows natural light in. Once a fly enters the trap, it flies upward to a small opening in the net and into a series of two-liter trap bottles, eventually ending up in a plastic catch bag (Figure 2 inset). Traps were set up for approximately twenty-four hours at each sampling site. Forty-two sampling sites were selected prior to the collection period to represent the geographic area and diversity of habitats across the ranch. Sites were placed in proximity to unpaved ranch roads to facilitate rotation from day to day by an all-terrain vehicle (ATV) across the relatively large ranch. The order of sites was randomly selected for the first setup period and then repeated throughout the sampling season to ensure the time periods and spatial locations were represented near equally. Anthrax Mapping

Deer carcass locations on the ranch were recorded with Global Positioning System (GPS) units and mapped from 2003 to 2010. Carcasses were located by ground searches. In addition to carcasses directly sighted, anthrax spotters relied heavily on turkey vultures, Cathartes aura , circling overhead to find carcasses. This proved to be a most effective method for searching out carcasses as reported elsewhere in the literature (Turnbull et al. 2010).

Introduction

∗ Spatial Epidemiology & Ecology Research Laboratory, Department of Geography, University of Florida † MRI Global

Department of Environmental Sciences, School of the Coast and Environment, Louisiana State University

A nthraxremainsaproblemforbothwildlifeand livestock in parts of North America. In particular, white-tailed deer , Odocoileus virginianus, epizootics have been frequently documented in Texas over the last decade (Hugh-Jones and De Vos 2002; Blackburn 2006; Hugh-Jones and Blackburn 2009). Recently, researchers suggested that anthrax is an underdiagnosed and underappreciated disease requiring greater attention (Fasanella et al. 2010), including the need for wildlife surveillance (Blackburn et al. 2007; Fasanella et al. 2007). Despite being a disease of antiquity, the ecology of Bacillus anthracis , the etiological agent of anthrax, is still relatively poorly understood (Smith et al. 2000; Hugh-Jones and Blackburn 2009). Bacillus anthracis is a spore-forming, soil-borne bacterium (Van Ness 1971; Smith et al. 2000). Most recently, Alexander et al. (2012) defined naturally occurring anthrax as an obligate spillover disease, with the pathogen linked directly to the environmental conditions associated with maintenance or persistence. The dominant transmission hypothesis is B. anthracis reproduces by infecting vertebrate hosts (primarily large vertebrate herbivores), through ingestion of spores during browsing or grazing, including exposure from soil ingestion (Smith et al. 2000; Turnbull et al. 2008). Spores then germinate in the host and replicate, eventually resulting in death of the host animal. When blood or body fluids containing bacilli are spilled into the environment or exposed to oxygen, the vegetative cells sporulate and eventually contaminate the soil. Evidence suggests that there might also be potential for spore maintenance in the rhizosphere of certain grasses (Saile and Koehler 2006), which might ultimately play a role in persistence while promoting infection of grazing herbivores. Inhalation of spores from the environment has limited evidence but cannot be ruled out (Turnbull et al. 2008). Once outbreaks begin, there is evidence for the potential role of both necrophagous (Blackburn et al. 2010) and biting insects, primarily hematophagous flies, as potential vectors for the disease (Gates, Elkin, and Dragon 1995). A series of studies confirmed the successful isolation and transmission of B. anthracis by biting flies under both field and laboratory conditions. Ganeva (2004) summarized a number of fly studies specific to anthrax and documented that at least twentyone species representing five genera from the Tabanidae family could mechanically transmit anthrax bacilli on body parts such as the legs and mouth parts.

data.text: This article draws from geographic engagements with theories of racialization and NIMBYism to explore connections between economic development and the relational construction of racial identities. I investigate the discourses of local white leadership surrounding two interconnected economic agendas crafted with the goal of remaking the central Oregon town of Madras into an upscale, white community, including (1) entrepreneurial prison development, and (2) an urban renewal project emphasizing high-income residential construction and the removal of blighted housing. Community leaders framed these developments as essential to changing perceptions of Madras based on its racial makeup and entrenched poverty. White officials promoted prison recruitment and upscale housing development through a normative racial framework that reaffirmed the privileged status of whites, stigmatized Latinos and Native Americans, and (re)produced unequal spaces. Through this empirical focus, I call attention to the centrality of race in economic practices, emphasizing how racialized privilege and marginalization are reproduced through development agendas that give shape to geographies of opportunity and (dis)advantage.

Race, Restructuring, and Crisis in Central Oregon

Positioned in close proximity to outdoor amenities and other booming recreational communities, Madras is located on the edge of gentrifying central Oregon, where in-migration and tourism have fueled rapid increases in land prices and real estate speculation (personal interview 2006). Agriculture and manufacturing, specifically wood processing, continue to make up an important part of the local economic base in Jefferson County, and key crops include wheat, garlic, potatoes, mint, alfalfa, and vegetable and flower seeds (City of Madras Urban Revitalization Action Plan [CMURAP] 2007). Madras's industrial base, however, is encounter- ing challenges as local crops and seed production face increased competition and traditional manufacturing industries withdraw their local investments. More recently, city and county leaders have aimed to develop Madras into the sort of recreational tourist destination that surrounding communities like Bend, Redmond, and Hood River have become over the past decade. This economic development goal seems to contradict Madras's prison recruitment agenda but, in fact, the correctional facility and local agendas to remake Madras into a recreation destination go together hand in glove.

Producing Race and Carceral Redevelopment

The dynamics of incarceration have remained underexplored in geography until relatively recently. This new research examines state power and incarceration (Martin and Mitchelson 2009; Martin 2012), the space of the prison and the ways in which incarceration is experienced (van Hoven and Sibley 2008; Moran 2011), as well as prison siting dynamics (Che 2005; Gilmore 2007; Glasmeier and Farrigan 2007; Bonds 2009). Carceral geographies have also been interrogated in relation to punitive neoliberal policies that have eroded social entitlements while simultaneously rolled-out probusiness agendas have further funneled investments away from the poor (Peck 2003; Gilmore 2007; Bonds 2009). This scholarship calls attention to the spatiality of incarceration to demonstrate how the prison is necessarily insular and outwardly dependent, requiring walls to demarcate and separate at the same time that it necessitates connections to places and peoples to perform its purpose.

data.text: Social scientists have studied rural settlements for the past sixty-plus years using data on population size and changes in retail service functions. Building on these interdisciplinary contributions, we explore new perspectives on rural settlements by creating a database of Google hyperlinks of communities and road networks in Appalachian Kentucky. When distinguishing features of the 396 communities and 338 roads in forty eastern Kentucky counties are mapped and analyzed, they reveal fresh insights into unevenness and diversity. Sharp differences exist between the northern and southern halves of the study area and places on and off major roads. The constructed database and methodology offer additional opportunities to study the spatial and temporal dynamics of rural settlements and networks in other regions.

Study Area, Methodology, and Databases

Study Area

The study area borders the Ohio River in the north, the West Virginia and Virginia state boundaries in the east, and the Tennessee border in the south. Most of the region is east of Interstate 75, which runs north -south (Figure 1). The counties, varying in size and shape, are defined by rivers and creeks, mountain ridges, and pioneer trails. The total number of roads in the forty counties on the Kentucky highway map (Drake 2018 -2019) is 338. They are federal highways, including interstates and parkways traversing a half-dozen counties, two-digit state highways, and three- and four-digit local roads. The threeand four-digit roads are less traveled. The official map does not show all county and local roads. The counties with the most numbered roads on the map are Pike (twenty-one), followed by Harlan, Laurel, and Letcher (twelve each), Knox and Perry (eleven each), and Morgan, Rowan, and Fleming (ten each). Counties with the fewest roads are Estill, Lawrence, Lee, McCreary, Martin, Nicholas, and Robertson (five each) and Owsley County (only three). If all local roads were included on the official map, it would be nearly impossible to read.

There are no large cities in the region, but Cincinnati, Ohio; Lexington, Kentucky; Knoxville, Tennessee; and Huntington, West Virginia are nearby. I-75 runs north -south and I-64 runs east -west. The largest communities are Winchester, Maysville, and London. Two parkways (Mountain Parkway and Hal Rogers Parkway) run east -west

Methodology

One basic objective is to measure and map distinctive features of places and networks in these counties in a cyberspace context to discern if there are any significant county differences between large and small places and roads traversing them.

Traditionally, scholars use U.S. census data on county populations, sizes of places within a county, and population changes. These data are less useful in learning about the economic, social, or political importance of a place or a road or network, and travel times between places in a county. A state highway map is useful in identifying the locations of places, the physical distances between them, and the names and numbers of major roads running through them. Google data, or hyperlinks, are useful in identifying the importance of a specific place, comparing places, and learning about the travel times between them. Digital information can be obtained about both major and minor roads and places within a county.

Databases

Google data are obtained by entering a key word or words in the search box at the top of the computer screen (accessed 20 -28 March 2022 and 18 May -3 June 2022). The number identifies the number of entries or hyperlinks in the database. For example, one can enter Morehead, Kentucky; the number of a highway, such as Interstate 64 in Montgomery County; or the number of a highway running through a county, such as Highway 9 in Mason County. Each hyperlink page briefly describes features about the individual entry, such as some historical background, the business climate, agricultural and industrial data, tourist and leisure activities, and major news stories. Entries are ranked by an industry formula. The hyperlinks for a specific place can be compared with other places in the same county or another county. The same procedure can be used for roads. Hyperlink data were gathered for each place and each road in each county. Also, one can enter two places into the Google search engine, such as the county seat and another place in the county (e.g., Pikeville; Pike County, Kentucky þ Stopover; Pike County, Kentucky). The number of hyperlinks for the pair of entries, the roads linking those places, the travel time between them, and a small horizontal map showing the places in the search bar and the road linking them are all displayed on the screen. Time -distance data were collected for all places in a county to its county seat.

Building on these interdisciplinary contributions, we explore new perspectives on rural settlements by creating a database of Google hyperlinks of communities and road networks in Appalachian Kentucky. When distinguishing features of the 396 communities and 338 roads in forty eastern Kentucky counties are mapped and analyzed, they reveal fresh insights into unevenness and diversity. The constructed database and methodology offer additional opportunities to study the spatial and temporal dynamics of rural settlements and networks in other regions. ARTICLE HISTORY

interstate highways, cultural heritage sites, or a major metropolitan area. Some distinct place features are associated with Appalachia, a region with distinctive physical features, but also economies and cultures different from surrounding areas. For many, Appalachia is associated with coal mining histories, Scots Irish traditions, scenic landscapes, rural depopulation, and deep poverty.

For some, the mental or cognitive map of Appalachia is a region of uniformity, but for others there are significant cultural and economic differences between what is considered Northern, Central, and Southern Appalachia. Both differences and similarities are evident when looking closely at population growth and decline, rural highways and interchanges, median age, income and education levels, urban and rural settlement patterns, major employment categories, religion preferences, voting patterns, and broadband access.

Literature Review

There is an extensive interdisciplinary literature on rural Appalachia that includes the pioneering geography volume by Raitz, Ulack, and Leinbach (1984), the maps and analysis by the Appalachian Regional Commission (2020), and the same by Pollard and Jacobson (2019b). A number of recognized writers have added to the knowledge base about places and place making in rural Kentucky. These include Berry (2010) and hooks (2008). Three familiar or overriding themes have been used by these and other scholars to explore rural areas. The first examines declining populations; changing economic functions; and church, hospital, and school closings in small towns and communities. These have been the focus of previous rural research by many rural sociologists, economists, and geographers in the past half-century. Examples are Chisholm (1962), Pacione (1984), Gilg (1985), Philo (1992), Cloke (1997), Hart (1975, 1998), and Woods (2005). The second group focuses on communities. These studies focus on specific communities in the region or a specific subregion (e.g., southeast Ohio and eastern Kentucky) as well as distinct features of towns and roads (Johnson 2006).

data.text: Prison expansion can be considered a geographical solution to deindustrialization and globalization. Postindustrial prison development to address declining productive industries in amenity-rich rural areas, however, can catalyze struggles over shifting rural land uses, ideals, and identities. Using participant observation, interviews, and texts, this article examines a prison siting in Appalachian Pennsylvania. The prison and the changes it might bring were strategically constructed by local politicians and then by citizen opponents and proponents of the prison. Alternative discourses that indicated differing levels of reliance on making a living from the local land, desires for working or amenity land uses, views toward minority newcomers associated with the prison, and legitimacy in land-use decision making played key roles in the prison debate. While prisons may seem a viable avenue for rural economic development, this article suggests that alternatives, such as indigenous, small-scale enterprises based on local resources and urban-rural coalitions, may provide more sustainable and equitable development for rural and urban areas impacted by economic restructuring.

Methods

My working and living as a researcher in postindustrial Forest County were closely tied to economic recovery efforts there. Although timber harvesting in the early 1990s on the Allegheny National Forest (ANF) was unhampered, one of Forest County's major employers, an Evenflo manufacturing plant, had recently closed. The U.S. Forest Service, with authority and funding from the 1990 Farm Bill, supported the economic recovery of forest-dependent areas such as Forest County. As part of that partnership, I worked with the ANF in 1994 on a tourism promotion agency regionalization study. I returned to the ANF region a few years later to work on Forest Serviceand Forest County Action Team-supported economic recovery studies regarding the feasibility of developing ecotourism and a hunting and fishing museum in Forest County. I was working on these studies, which addressed Forest County's deindustrialization-related crisis, as well as on my related research regarding how shifts from Fordist manufacturing, monopolistic regulation, resource extraction, and blue-collar recreation (i.e., hunting) toward post-Fordist fragmented regulation and amenitybased recreation affected forest use (Che 2000), when the Allegheny Defense Project (ADP) brought the first federal court challenge on the ANF . The lawsuit halted timber harvesting on over 5,000 acres of the ANF . A Prison in the Forest (County)

Isolated Forest County, located in Appalachian northwestern Pennsylvania (Figure 1), has been negatively affected by the shift to post-Fordism since 1980 and has lost its major manufacturing employers. The Marienville Glass Plant, which had been in operation for over sixty years until its 1982 closing, had employed 300 people ( Forest Press 1982). Its parent company, Glass Containers Corp., closed the Marienville plant, partly due to its distant location, which had higher transportation costs than other company holdings ( The Derrick 1982). Relatively high transportation and labor costs also led the county's remaining industrial employer, an Evenflo plastics plant, to shift its operations to Georgia. 2 Subsequently, Forest County had one of Pennsylvania's lowest median household incomes, its highest unemployment rate, and a small (approximately 5,000 individuals), aging, and declining population.

Given the loss of glass and plastics manufacturing jobs, Forest County was increasingly dependent on traditional forest-based industries such as timber, oil, gas, and recreation. These industries were primarily based in the ANF, which covers 42 percent of the county. Forestbased industries provided 51 percent of the county's total payroll and proprietor income (Forest County Action T eam 1994), a figure exceeding the Forest Service's 15 percent benchmark for forest dependency.
