BLACK PLACEMAKING AND SPATIALIZING CULTURE

If placemaking, in a more mainstream sense, has been conceptualized as people giving space meaning through processes like naming, territory claiming, and taking part in social relations (Lombard 2014 ), what makes black placemaking distinct? Written to provide a counterpoint to the overwhelmingly negative media representations of urban black life, Marcus Anthony Hunter, Mary Pattillo, Zandria F. Robinson, and Keeanga-Yamahtta Taylor foreground the playfulness and pleasure with which black Chicagoans reclaim space and transform it into place ( 2016 ). Their definition of black placemaking as 'the ways that … black Americans create sites of endurance, belonging, and resistance through social interaction' ( 2016 , 1 ) is highly resonant for the present analysis. Central to the framework of black placemaking is how African-Americans resist being cast as victims of history or of socioeconomic deprivation, but instead are 'subjects (who) fashion places by inscribing them with their own interpretations, meanings, and cultural significance' (Hunter and others 2016 , 4 ). Black placemaking occurs through social interactions that create loci of cultural durability through, for instance, community sports teams, protests against violence, and neighborhood reunions (Hunter and others 2016 ). BLACK PLACEMAKING AND SPATIALIZING CULTURE

If placemaking, in a more mainstream sense, has been conceptualized as people giving space meaning through processes like naming, territory claiming, and taking part in social relations (Lombard 2014 ), what makes black placemaking distinct? Written to provide a counterpoint to the overwhelmingly negative media representations of urban black life, Marcus Anthony Hunter, Mary Pattillo, Zandria F. Robinson, and Keeanga-Yamahtta Taylor foreground the playfulness and pleasure with which black Chicagoans reclaim space and transform it into place ( 2016 ). Their definition of black placemaking as 'the ways that … black Americans create sites of endurance, belonging, and resistance through social interaction' ( 2016 , 1 ) is highly resonant for the present analysis. Central to the framework of black placemaking is how African-Americans resist being cast as victims of history or of socioeconomic deprivation, but instead are 'subjects (who) fashion places by inscribing them with their own interpretations, meanings, and cultural significance' (Hunter and others 2016 , 4 ).

data.text: This work advances the critical urban studies literature on planetary urbanization by emphasizing the everyday struggles experienced by the people who live in and through planetary transformations. Specifically, we empirically investigated people in eastern Montana who experienced the intensive and extensive oil and gas production of the Bakken Boom via interview and survey data. In the process, we interrogated Lefebvre's notion of the blind field and conclude that what we call the Bakken blind field represents a deeply engrained habit of the mind that functions for the energy industry as a means of neutralizing the transformative potential that always lurks in response to persistent socioenvironmentally exploitative practices. We suggest that the degree of illumination that results from personal hardships can determine the degree to which local exploitation is rejected (or accepted) as a necessary result of living with oil and gas.

Case Study Context: The Bakken Region of Eastern Montana

According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (2019), in 2018 the United States consumed 7.5 billion barrels of petroleum products, or 20.5 million barrels per day. With this figure increasing, the estimated 7.4 billion barrels of recoverable oil that remain in the broader Bakken region will not be ignored for long. More broadly, the region ' s oil supply represents a source of surplus value for major national and global energy firms. As such, the surplus value produced by these extractive mining activities is, for the most part, siphoned away from the region and funneled through firms with operations that are national and even global in scope, with headquarters in major urban centers. The results might be visually subtle, but the effect is to stitch the region into the broader urban-industrial fabric of global capitalism more and more deeply.

Moreover, the approach to governing the oil and gas industry is a state-by-state affair that is especially susceptible to the neoliberal ' growth machines ' that characterize many urban governances in North America and beyond (Logan and Molotch 1987). State officials and legislative bodies are pressured to ' compete ' with surrounding states in terms of providing business-friendly environments. Known in Montana as the ' Oil and Gas Tax Holiday, ' the 1999 Montana legislature provided the industry with an incentive to operate in the state by lowering the rate of taxation on new wells during the first months of production. This

Qualitative Methods

We conducted a series of ' long interviews ' (McCracken 1988) that would allow us to identify and investigate the narratives at work among the people of the Bakken in eastern Montana. The interviews were designed to foster conversations during which the interviewees would be given ample opportunities to describe in their own words how it is to live with oil and gas development. As is customary in qualitative research, we viewed interviewees as differentially positioned subjects embedded within broader discursive constellations (Fairclough 2003) and set out to unearth the specific narratives that demonstrated how informants constructed order in their everyday lives.

Because we were specifically interested in how locals live with the environmental exploitations inherent to emergent urban-industrial realities, we decided to focus on landowners who had experienced an industrial spill on their land regardless of the type of spill (salt water, oil, or produced water). Questions were tailored toward exploring the landowners ' experiences with the industrial mishap, their attitudes toward the industry (and the state), and the coping logics that owners constructed to reconcile the stressors that resulted from these impacts. We also contacted at least one mayor or county commissioner from each county who had been actively engaged in a cleanup operation. The interviews were audiorecorded, transcribed, and then subjected to a systematic content analysis (Denzin and Lincoln 1994) in rela

Quantitative Methods

We designed a survey instrument that consisted of thirty-five questions (due to space limitations we cannot include the survey). Nineteen questions used a Likert scale (1 -5) to assess the degree to which respondents agreed or disagreed with statements about the impacts of the Bakken boom on the economy, community, health, and environment. We noted that many properties are defined as split estates, meaning that every landowner would not necessarily hold mineral rights and every mineral rights holder would not necessarily own land. As well, economic benefits to personal incomes might or might not be directly linked to production of the mineral estate. We chose to not attempt to unwind the quagmire of mineral estates and split estates as matters of personal or household incomes. Instead, the survey simply asked respondents to indicate their overall household income (defined as eight different ranges of income) and the degree to which people they know have benefited from the most recent boom.

Three questions asked about respondents ' experiences with and perceptions of accidents related to the oil and gas industry. Five questions were designed to assess respondents ' expectations of how oil and gas accidents should be dealt with by governmental entities. Eight demographic questions were asked at the end of the survey. We employed a research service company to provide us with a list of roughly 10,000 residential addresses in the six counties of Montana ' s Bakken. We then random

Phase 1: Qualitative Methods and Results

This study is part of a wider research project investigating the socioenvironmental impacts of oil and gas development in eastern Montana (also see McEvoy et al. 2017). We already knew several narratives operating in the local communities of this region, so we set out in 2015 to build on this understanding by exploring the details and functions of these narratives. We hoped to discover the degree to which these narratives were shaping how local residents framed the environmental exploitations and risks associated with oil and gas development and the extent to which these narratives constituted degrees of blindness or illumination.

Introduction

I n Montana, the Bakken oil and gas region includes six counties, totaling just over 11,000 square miles (Figure 1). There are only 40,000 households in this six-county region, which has historically been dominated by agriculture and small towns. Billings, a city of roughly 100,000 people, is 300 miles to the west. Minneapolis is 600 miles to the east. Yet, if recovered in their entirety, Bakken oil reserves could equate to over four years of national energy independence (approximately 32.36 billion barrels of consumer fuels; U.S. Geological Survey 2019). Eastern Montana is thus an important industrial hinterland where oil and gas development fuses the region with emergent processes of ' extended urbanization, ' illustrating the progressive transformation of spaces formerly identified as ' rural ' into industrial-productive landscapes that serve the ever-expanding global accumulation of capital and concentration of people and resources in ' urban regions ' (Brenner and Schmid 2015).

Eastern Montana has long been connected to the global urbanization process. Dating back to settlement by white Europeans in the late nineteenth century, the region served as an urban-underpinning space providing industrial agricultural production (livestock and food grains; Cronon 1992). Oil and gas development began in Montana in the 1920s, with eastern

Montana experiencing its first major boom from 1950 to 1965 (Hennip 1973), followed by another in the 1980s. The Bakken inaugurated its most recent boom in 2005, spurred by innovations in hydraulic fracturing technologies. The industry ' s environmental operating standards are much improved as compared to decades past, yet even a cursory review of the Montana Board of Oil and Gas Conservation (MBOGC) quarterly reports demonstrates that salt water, crude oil, and the newly introduced industrial fluids used in ' fracking ' processes are sometimes spilled (see Board of Oil and Gas Conservation 2019). Anecdotal and empirical evidence demonstrates that the boom and bust cycles typical of extractive resource economies in rural communities are problematic; yet, following McEvoy et al. (2017), local understandings of the benefits and drawbacks in the Bakken remain mostly shaped by established sociopolitical ideals (e.g., conservative populism and libertarianism), which minimize risk perceptions.

We argue that the post-2005 Bakken boom has more deeply morphed the region into an emergent form of extended urbanization, a landscape replete with the kind of creative destructive impacts reported in other similar contexts (Arboleda 2015, 2016), what we refer to as an extractive resource urban rurality . This study provides an empirical

Planetary Urbanization and the Blind Field

Planetary urbanization represents one of the most prominent research thrusts in critical urban theory today (Merrifield 2013, 2014a; Brenner 2014; Peake et al. 2018; D. Wilson and Jonas 2018). This emergent body of literature stakes the claim that capitalist urbanization has now progressed to the point where the entire planet is implicated and engulfed in its influence and is increasingly marked by a dual process whereby, as Merrifield (2014b) put it:

The urban unfolds into the countryside just as the countryside folds back into the city. … Absorbed and obliterated by vaster units, rural places have become an integral part of post-industrial production and financial speculation, swallowed up by an ' urban fabric ' continually extending its borders, ceaselessly corroding the residue of agrarian life, gobbling up everything and everywhere in order to increase surplus value and accumulate capital. (524 -25)

Uneven Planetary Urbanization

It should be stressed that this planetary urban fabric is not a uniform or homogenous landscape that literally spans the world. Rather, it is multidimensional and unfolds through variegated pathways of uneven spatial development. In addition to extended urbanization, Brenner and Schmid (2015) identified two other mutually constitutive moments or forms of this process: concentrated urbanization and differential urbanization. These moments are presented to overcome the linguistic roadblocks manifest within the long-standing urban -rural dichotomy, and are understood to be dialectically related and analytically distinguishable.

data.text: Sedona, Arizona, an amenity town that trades on intangible quality-of-life attributes like spectacular scenery, the arts, and its nonmetropolitan location, has a conflict between low-wage employment catering to its tourist sector and expensive housing for its affluent residents. Many of those who work in Sedona do not live in the community. This study, based on a survey of 286 employees. shows that workers who live in Sedona do not have incomes that are significantly higher than commuters from the outside, but they live in housing that is almost twice as expensive. Employees who live in Sedona pay dearly for housing in order to be near jobs, natural beauty, and the cultural ambience of an amenity town. Commuters, on the other hand, incur high travel costs but enjoy cheaper housing and the lifestyle of small towns and rural areas. The emergence of amenity environments and long-distance commuting in Sedona is symbolic of the increased differentiation of nonmetropolitan landscapes.

Geographic Setting

Set in spectacular redrock country of the Verde Valley in north central Arizona, Sedona's current commuting and housing situation is an outgrowth of its physical, regional, and historical geography (Fig. 1). The landscape in the vicinity of the city consists of eroded forms in Supai Sandstone deposited 290 million years ago (Elston 1984). Over time, erosion sculpted magnificent buttes, mesas, and canyons, and iron oxide stained these rocks a rusty red. This dramatic landscape has served as the backdrop for western movies, inspiration for local artists, and attraction for permanent migrants and tourists.

Sedona was first occupied in 1879 but officially founded in 1902 when T C. Schnebly requested that the first post office be named after his wife, Sedona. Like other communities in the Verde Valley, Sedona's early development was based on ranching and farming. In addition, Sedona served as a stopping-off point for people traveling between Jerome, a booming mining town, and Flagstaff, the regional service center. In the late 1930s wealthy people were attracted to the area's scenery and climate, and by the end of World War 11, amenity-based development began in earnest (Those Early Days 1968; Willard 1984).

Equally complex is the economic history of the Verde Valley, Sedona's current laborshed. Early development was based upon ranching and farming

Survey

As part of a larger effort to assess Sedona's economic development future, we conducted a survey of the community's work force in August, 1991. From a list of members of the Sedona Chamber of Commerce, we chose every third business for a total of 199 businesses and attempted to distribute employee questionnaires to each business. A contact person was advised to give a survey questionnaire to each employee who, in turn, was instructed to mail the completed survey form directly to us. We successfully distributed questionnaires to 64 businesses with 846 employees. This low distribution rate was due to several factors, including high business turnover, business relocation, businesses with no employees other than the owner, and owners refusing to participate. Of the 846 questionnaires distributed, 286 were completed and returned to us at

Arizona State University in Tempe, a response rate of 33.8%.

The questionnaire provided information on where Sedona employees live, a host of demographic and socioeconomic characteristics, commuting and employment patterns, the current housing situation, and how they rate Sedona vis-a-vis their present community on a series of place attributes. Paper outline — first 3 sections (click to expand)

Introduction

ike many amenity towns across the United L States, Sedona, Arizona, has experienced phenomenal increases in land and housing prices as affluent retirees, actors, artists, writers, and locationally flexible businesses have discovered the quality of life in this scenic, nonmetropolitan setting. In conjunction with its rarefied physical and cultural setting, there also has emerged a strong tourism sector which draws an estimated three million visitors annually and accounts for a large majority of the community's employment. An inherent conflict has arisen between the mix of employment which is heavily weighted in favor of low-wage retail and service sector jobs and skyrocketing housing prices driven up by scarce land, eager demand, and affluent inmigrants. Much of Sedona's housing stock is out-of-reach to many of its employees. For these individuals, Sedona is job-rich but housing-poor.

Background

Amenity Towns

The emergence of amenity towns like Sedona on the nonmetropolitan landscape has attracted considerable attention in recent years, especially because these places have been at

'The authors wish to thank John Stuart Hall and K. David Pijawka of the Arizona State University School of Public Affairs and the Sedona Academy for their financial and moral support of this research.

the forefront of the resurgence of nonmetropolitan growth and in-migration (Beale 1975; Fuguitt 1985; Elo and Beale 1988). Usually defined as places that emphasize scenery, recreational potential, quaintness, historical significance, and rural settlement, amenity towns attract retirees, recreationalists, and others who value these intangible qualities of life (Coppack 1985). The value of land in amenity places is both a function of its contribution to the productive process and of its ability to produce uplifting experiences and meet psychological needs (Coppack 1988).

Nonmetropolitan Commuting

The growing emphasis on amenities in nonmetropolitan areas is one component of the increased differentiation of rural landscapes. Associated with this differentiation is the emergence of long-distance commuting. A s small towns take on a variety of functions in addition to their traditional roles as agricultural service centers, they draw labor from nearby towns and the surrounding countryside. Evidence indicates that commuting (defined as persons who cross a county boundary in getting to work) is just as prevalent in nonmetropolitan areas as in MSAs (Metropolitan Statistical Areas) and dispersed urban regions in spite of the dearth of public transportation in rural areas and the lower incomes which make private automobile ownership difficult (Hansen 1976).

data.text: In the United States, rural areas are growing as new immigrant destinations (NIDs) where refugees and other precarious migrant families settle to work within agro-industries such as poultry processing. Often lacking resources and infrastructure geared toward refugee-migrants, we argue rural NIDs place greater demands, socially and economically, on youth in these families. Focusing on refugee-migrant youth aged 18-25 years, we explore the life-work (Mullings 2021) youth perform in their homes, workplaces and the community. We argue that their household and sibling care, waged work and translation and culture brokering make social and economic life possible for refugee-migrant families in rural areas, but it differentially impacts youth themselves based upon their gender, legal status, English language proficiency, birth order and their age upon arrival to the United States. Focusing on refugee-migrant youth in a small, rural NID illustrates their centrality as flexible life-workers, enabling a flexible agro-industrial labor force, contributing to the family wage and acting as agents of community integration.

(Ex)Urban Metabolism in the Piedmont Megapolitan Region

Ourinterest in the megapolitan political ecology of the Piedmont megapolitan region is coupled with a large biophysical research effort funded by the National Science Foundation at the Coweeta LTER, whose research and data since 1980 address a range of ecological variables in southern Appalachia. Our megapolitan political ecology approach is an effort to better integrate social and ecological research of the LTERProject, focusing on how exurbanization establishes regional patterns of urban metabolism (Gragson and Grove 2006). In southern Appalachia, Gragson and Bolstad (2006) tracked land use changes as seen through Coweeta LTER research. Much of this research shows increasing urbanization of these areas, especially in the last several decades, and forecasts significantly more urban growth until 2030 (e.g., Wear and Bolstad 1998). Other relevant Coweeta LTER research highlights the settlement patterns (Kirk, Bolstad, and Manson 2012), bird populations (Lumpkin, Pearson, and Turner 2012), water quality issues (Webster et al. 2012), and stream fish populations (M. C. Scott 2006) intimately related to exurbanization in southern Appalachia. The exurban-themed research at the Coweeta LTER complements other urban ecological research from the greater network. The Central Arizona Project and the Baltimore Ecosystem Study are two explicitly urban LTER sites studying urban ecology (e.g., Pickett and Cadenasso 2006; Childers et al. 2011).

Our methods in this empirical section are multi

Southern Appalachian Exurban Metabolism

Coweeta LTER research, as well as other nonCoweeta research on exurban ecologies, gives examples of how exurban metabolism alters the pathways, connections, abundance, proliferation, and degradation of physical, biological, and chemical components ranging in size from the molecular to species populations (e.g., Hansen et al. 2005). This research bolsters our claim for urban metabolism in megapolitan political ecology, showing how urbanization at a regional scale has significant implications for how that region changes flows of chemical, biological, and physical components.

First, some of the human-oriented research at Coweeta LTER emphasizes how exurbanization metabolizes capital and land in many southern Appalachian communities. Southern Appalachian exurbs attract mostly the upper middle class, a few commuters and families, and many retirees. As an example, Macon County, North Carolina, home to the Coweeta LTERmainresearch site, is undergoing many of these exurban changes. U.S. Census data show that over one third of the county's population is over the age of sixty; agricultural economic output has fallen to roughly 0.1 percent of the county's overall economy; and despite a natural population growth of negative 1.8 percent from 2000 to 2010, the county's overall population growth was a positive 13.8 percent (U.S. Census Bureau 2010). One forecast predicts that in Macon County, by 2030, 'approximately 75 percent of new buildings will be constructed at urban and suburban dens

Urban Climate Effects and the Ring of Asphalt

A third piece of Coweeta LTER research indicating the changes in Piedmont megapolitan metabolism is an emerging ring of asphalt initiating urban climatological changes, a useful corollary to Luke's (2003) discussion of global city formation. Cities themselves modify weather and climate at scales ranging from local to global. The most comprehensively studied effect of the built environment on climate is the urban heat island (UHI), defined generally as the increase in temperatures of urban areas relative to surrounding rural areas, with pronounced effects on nighttime temperatures, caused by the land use features of urban development. Some of the more common symptoms of the UHI affecting both humans and nonhumans are warmer air and higher tree canopy temperatures. Changes in air circulations induced by UHIs are driven by differential heat capacity and thermal inertia between rural and urban regions. UHI-related temperature gradients depend strongly on factors like developed to undeveloped land ratio, green-to-nongreen surface ratio, sky view factor, and more (see Oke 1987). A surplus of surface energy over urban regions can be traced to enhanced surface sensible heat flux, ground heat storage, anthropogenic heating, and reduced evapotranspirational cooling. For the Piedmont megapolitan region, the increased infrastructural growth of urbanization could mean an intensification in the UHI.

University of Georgia

Drawing on megapolitan geographies, urban political ecology, and urban metabolism as theoretical frameworks, this article theoretically and empirically explores megapolitan political ecology. First, we elucidate a theoretical framework in the context of southern Appalachia and, in particular, the Piedmont megapolitan region, suggesting that the megapolitan region is a useful scale through which to understand urban metabolic connections that constitute this rapidly urbanizing area. We also push the environmental history and geography literature of the U.S. South and southern Appalachia to consider the central role urban metabolic connections play in the region's pressing social and environmental crises. Second, we empirically illuminate these human and nonhuman urban metabolisms across the Piedmont megapolitan region using data from the Coweeta Long-Term Ecological Research (LTER) program, especially highlighting a growing 'ring of asphalt' that epitomizes several developing changes to patterns of metabolism.

Megapolitan Political Ecology: Metabolizing the Urban(izing) Region

Urban political ecology illustrates understanding urbanization as a sociospatial process 'predicated upon the circulation and metabolism of physical, chemical, and biological components' that 'are never socially or ecologically neutral' (Heynen, Kaika, and Swyngedouw 2006, 12). Where this scholarship elucidates the connections between urbanization of nature, socioenvironmental change, and uneven power relations, it has remained mostly focused on larger cities. Urban-hinterland connections are often mentioned, but the impacts of urban metabolism on regional communities are rarely articulated.

To address this issue, we first argue that the megapolitan region is a helpful scale for understanding the function and flows of urban metabolism. This regional scale is relevant for the emergence of global cities shaped by processes of urbanization, which extend into even the most rural areas. Although often overlooked in urban political ecology approaches, these rural places, intimately connected to urbanizing landscapes via socioecological processes, shape flows of global capital and continue to define notions of planetary urbanism (Lefebvre 2003; McCarthy 2008; Brenner and Schmid 2012).

Megapolitan Regions

Megalopolis originally described the densely populated conurbation of the northeastern United States, including the entire corridor from Washington, DC, to Boston (Gottman 1966). Although the included metropolises are distinct jurisdictional entities, their connections, agglomeration, and exurban expansion comprise a unique spatial formation. Most recently, megapolitan research has taken an applied turn through scholarly work in policy, planning, and urban studies (Lang and Dhavale 2005; Ross and Danner 2010). 2 Very little, if any, critical research exists on megapolitan regions.

We suggest using the megapolitan region as a way to examine broader scale urban development dynamics that have significant, although often underemphasized, impacts in historically rural areas. This spatial unit is useful because at its core, the notion of a megapolitan region captures the connections between multiple cities of varying sizes and their rural hinterlands.

<<A-HEAD>> DATA AND METHODS

The main sources for this analysis are aquaculture lease hearing transcripts. Maine's Department of Marine Resources (DMR) notifies the public of all lease applications, except 400-square-foot Limited Purpose leases, by posting notices in local newspapers, alerting harbormasters, and sending notices to parties they deem interested. If more than five persons express concern, DMR holds a public hearing. Of the 263 lease hearings transcripts DMR possesses, 90 had public hearings. DMR writes detailed hearing transcripts, ranging from 15--75 pages and often including verbatim dialogue. DMR keeps these for all active leases and for all leases terminated in the past three years. Existing transcripts cover lease hearings between 1981 and 2015. All hearing documents were scanned into pdf files, and analyzed using NVivo11. The author and two assistants coded transcripts for types of concerns expressed. Using inductive coding, we quantified the

This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.

number of times each specific type of concern was raised in a hearing, which could happen multiple times at a hearing if multiple persons expressed the same concern. One person expressing the same concern multiple times was counted as one concern. Most members of the public testifying at lease hearings were coastal landowners, and transcripts provide an extensive record of their concerns with aquaculture.

<<A-HEAD>> STUDY SITE

Maine is an ideal study site because it consistently ranks in the top five U.S. states in saltwater aquaculture production (USDA 2014), and it is the most rural U.S. state (USCB 2016). Maine also has a long history of postproductive change. Agricultural land use peaked in the mid-1800s, and as the natural resource economy declined, Maine experienced gradual population loss from 1910--1960, but population rebounded after 1960. Explanations for the rebound include cheap land, proximity to the northeastern U.S. metropolitan region, the interstate highways, the back-to-the-land movement, and environmental amenities (Reilly and Renski 2008). Between 1960--2000, 95 percent of Maine's population growth took place in rural areas, and the state went from 50 percent to 60 percent rural. Rural growth was not due to agricultural revival; Maine's farm population dropped 75 percent (Sherwood and Mageean 2004). Out-migration continues from Maine four northern and eastern counties today. Lack of jobs drives youth outmigration all across the state; in-migrants are older and coming for environmental amenities. In 1960, Maine's average age was twenty-nine, which ranked slightly below the U.S. average, whereas in 2015 Maine was the oldest state with an average age of slightly more than forty-four years (USCB 2016). In-migration to rural areas is slowing, though, as most of coastal and rural Maine is projected to begin shrinking soon, and urban areas are now growing faster (Rector 2015).

<<A-HEAD>> AQUACULTURE CONFLICTS AND THE POSTPRODUCTIVE TRANSITION

Literature on aquaculture conflicts stresses tradeoffs coastal residents see between economic opportunities and environmental quality (Freeman and others 2012). Many places feature these jobs-versus-environment debates, especially locations with finfish---as opposed to shellfish and marine vegetable---aquaculture, which is seen as more environmentally damaging because of disease transmittal to wild fish, water-quality impacts, and the quantity of food needed to produce farmed fish. There are also conflicts between fishermen and aquaculture farmers because of concern over privatization and enclosure by large firms limiting access to fishing grounds (Walters 2007; Wiber and

To build on these studies, this paper turns to literature on the rural postproductive transition.

data.text: Geographic studies of refugee issues have emerged as salient topics of inquiry in the past decade. This spatial analysis of the migration experiences and heterolocal settlement patterns of refugees in an increasingly diverse part of the Pacific Northwest focuses on a place that the Atlantic Monthly recently called the last Caucasian bastion in the United States. Perceived as a region better known for its dense forests, progressive environmental policies, and rural ambience, the Portland metropolitan area and its hinterland in the Willamette Valley now resonate with ethnic and racial diversity. This article analyzes the spatial patterns and related networks of the three largest refugee groups in the region. Findings indicate that an overlapping and interrelated set of political, social, cultural, and economic networks are the most important factors in determining refugee residential patterns.

Methodologically, this project builds on the work of Bailey et al. (2002), Lawson (1999, 2000), Li (1998), and other geographers who have sounded the ''multi-method call'' for integrating quantitative and qualitative approaches in migration studies during the past decade. 2 The first step in this analysis was defining the groups to be studied in an area with relatively large numbers of refugees from many parts of the world. T o provide a significant number for analysis, the largest groups in the study area were selected-refugees from two nation states in the former USSRandrefugeesfromVietnam. The first group consists primarily of Russians and Ukrainians, white Protestants, who first began to leave their homeland after the breakup of the former USSR in the early 1990s and continue to arrive in large numbers today. In contrast, the next largest group in the study area, refugees from Vietnam, who are Asian and Catholic or Buddhist, first arrived more than two decades ago during and after the war in Vietnam, with newer arrivals coming in ever-larger numbers from other places in the United States during the past two decades.

There are three sociospatial reasons for selecting these particular groups. First, they provide examples of refugees with different racial and religious identities who also have differing settlement histories. Introduction

W ith more than fifty million refugees living in various parts of the world today, perhaps no moment in history has been this critical for examining the geography of refugee settlement and survival. In response to this world crisis, studies of issues surrounding the lives and landscapes of new refugees have become increasingly salient topics of research for geographers and other scholars, policy makers, and social service providers (see, e.g., Boswell and Curtis 1984; Black 1991, 1994, 2002, 2003; Boswell 1993; Hardwick 1993, 2002, 2003; W. Wood1994; Miyares 1996, 1998; Chimni 1998; Nicholson and T womey 1999; Hyndman 2000; Brun 2001). T o date, the majority of work by geographers has focused on refugee flows and destinations located outside the United States. A few notable exceptions to this include Desbarats's (1985) early work with Thai refugees in Los Angeles, Boswell and Curtis (1984) and McHugh, Miyares, and Skop (1997) work on Cubans, and J. Wood's (1997) and others' analyses of Vietnamese settlement patterns and evolving landscapes in U.S. cities and suburbs.

Goals and Research Questions

Despite recent criticism that population and ethnic geographers remain too focused on spatial patterns and too little concerned with broader social theories, settlement geography still matters. Local tensions and subsequent political decisions affecting the lives of foreign-born residents of particular places, in fact, are often a response to residential concentration. Understanding their residential patterns requires that we seek answers to related questions about migration paths, time of arrival, cultural and economic niches, racialization, and the impact of whiteness in receiving societies, as well as the potential subordination by majority residents.

data.text: Ranchettes are low-density, rural parcels typically from thirty-five to seventy acres that have proliferated across the Rocky Mountain West. They consume large amounts of land and increase fragmentation, leading to potentially negative impacts on the ecology and cultural identity of local places. Although many anecdotal accounts decry the rise in ranchettes, few studies measure their prevalence or spatial patterns. We use archival and contemporary land ownership data to measure ranchette development in La Plata County, Colorado, an amenity-rich county popular for recreation, retirement, and ranchettes. Results show continual yet slowing growth across the decades with patterns of growth spreading in a contagious effect around initial nodes of development.
data.method_section_html:
Auto-extracted method sections (click to expand)

Case Study: La Plata County

La Plata County, Colorado, population 51,334 in 2010 (U.S. Census Bureau 2011), has experienced steep growth and in-migration during the past few decades. It is home to the city of Durango, an ex-smelter town now replete with a quaint downtown entertainment district, a small college, and the Durango-Silverton tourist steam train. The Animas River runs through town, luring whitewater rafters and fly fishermen, and nearby is a ski resort, a smaller ski hill for locals, hot springs, and Mesa Verde National Park. The county also contains parts of the San Juan and La Plata Mountains (among the most scenic and wild in all of Colorado), the San Juan National Forest, and the Weminuche Wilderness Area (the largest in Colorado). Extensive tribal lands of the Ute Mountain and Southern Utes also contribute to a rural feel with wide open space. Just over 59 percent of the total county land area is federal, state, or local public land (Colorado State University 2010). In short, it has most everything New West settlers look for and has been gentrified and developed at a rapid rate since the 1980s, particularly with parcels of three acres and above (Wright 1993). 2 The county estimates that 22 percent of its housing units are seasonally occupied second homes (La Plata County 2011). As large ranches subdivide, the number of agricultural parcels has risen sharply in the past decade, particularly in the ten- to fifty-acre size range (Figure 4) but in both larger and smaller sizes as well.

Ranchettes are low-density, rural parcels typically from thirty-five to seventy acres that have proliferated across the Rocky Mountain West. They consume large amounts of land and increase fragmentation, leading to potentially negative impacts on the ecology and cultural identity of local places. Although many anecdotal accounts decry the rise in ranchettes, few studies measure their prevalence or spatial patterns. We use archival and contemporary land ownership data to measure ranchette development in La Plata County, Colorado, an amenity-rich county popular for recreation, retirement, and ranchettes. Results show continual yet slowing growth across the decades with patterns of growth spreading in a contagious effect around initial nodes of development. Key Words: exurbia, land use, natural amenities, New West, ranchettes.

小型牧场是低密度的，通常包括三十五到七十亩的农村地块，它们正在跨洛基山以西的地方 增生。它们消耗大量的土地并使碎片地块增加，导致对局部地方的生态和文化认同的潜在的 负面影响。虽然许多个案研究报告批评小型牧场的崛起，很少有研究测量其普遍性或空间格 局。我们使用档案和当代的土地所有权数据来检测小型牧场在科罗拉多州拉普拉塔河县的发 展，该县是一个市容丰富的，以休闲娱乐，退休，和小型牧场流行而闻名的县。结果表明， 在过去几十年，小型牧场有一个持续但是放缓的增长，在发展的初始节点周围呈传染性效应 的蔓延式增长模式。关键词：远郊，土地利用，自然设施，新西部，小型牧场。

Ranchettes and Rural Development in the Rocky Mountain West

After a century of rural to urban migration, a major settlement trend in the United States in the latter part of the twentieth century was unprecedented migration from the city to the country, or counterurbanization ( Johnson and Beale 1995; Manson and Groop 2000). Between 1990 and 2000, exurban populations grew more than twice as fast as nearby metropolitan areas (Berube et al. 2006). This trend was driven in part by growing affluence and structural changes to a postindustrial economy, increasingly footloose industries and occupations, and active retirement lifestyles but also by attraction to natural beauty and outdoor recreational opportunities and amenity-induced migration (Smutny 2002). From the 1960s to the 1990s, counties across the United States with national parks and federally designated wilderness areas grew as much as three times faster than all others (Rudzitis 1996). The U.S. Department of Agriculture developed a Natural Amenity Scale that standardizes the sum of natural amenities in regions across the United States (McGranahan 1999).

Agricultural Land Change in Colorado

In Colorado, thirty-five acres is the lower limit for parcels that are exempt from county subdivision regulations, so we use this as the lower limit of our ranchette definition. We define the upper limit of ranchettes as twice that size, parcels of 69.9 acres or less, so that one ranchette parcel cannot subdivide into two new ranchettes. These parameters apply for Colorado only; other states have statutes that can cause this definition to vary. We recognize that much low-density, exurban development takes place on parcels smaller than thirty-five acres, but we limit our analysis to ranchettes only, not all of exurbia.

data.text: Affection for agrarian livelihoods and rural and small-town environments has long been held by residents in many of the world's more developed countries. Although the rural proportion of the U.S. population has shrunk to a minority over the last century, fondness for rurality continues to manifest itself in a number of ways. Attachment to the rural ideal or rural idyll can be considered as attachment to the idea of a type of place, rather than specific place attachment. Based on literature, field observation, computer searches, and data from the U.S. Census of Agriculture, connections to idea(l)s of rurality apparent in popular culture are identified and illustrated. These include rural and agricultural tourism, small-scale farming and large-lot rural subdivisions, urban agriculture, farmers' markets and community-supported agriculture, creation of housing developments around farm activities, and rural-named housing and business developments. Idealized relationships with rurality call upon health and wellbeing, connecting to nature, aesthetics, privacy, and respect and nostalgia for rural livelihoods.

PURPOSE AND METHODS

This paper updates consideration of the 'rural idyll'/idealization in the United States; frames consideration not as specific place attachment, but as the very seldom considered idea of attachment to type of place; and connects type-ofplace rurality attachment to potential reaction to place homogenization and to social memory. It illustrates forms of virtual rurality that appear in the United States, updating some of the work done by Michael Bunce ( 1994 ) in the United Kingdom and North America and similar to Michael Woods' ( 2011 ) U.K. discussion. 'Virtual rurality' described here includes imagined and created expressions of rural areas and small towns with early to mid-twentieth century characteristics. Forms of rural/semirural living that bear some resemblance to traditional agriculture and rural life but that are unlikely to by themselves fully support a family today are included. Landscape changes creating virtual rurality may be facilitated by attachment to a type of place in social imagination -rather than the more commonly addressed attachments to specific places/locations, virtual rurality is associated with generalized type-of-place attachments and nonlocation-specific attempts at place-making based on rural idea(l)s.

Introduction

T he developed (particularly Anglophone) world has long held an emotional attachment for agrarian livelihoods, rural landscapes, and small-town environments, although the proportion of nonurban populations in these countries has shrunk to a minority. In spite of conditions that have led to most Americans having only 'superficial' exposure to rurality (Lichter and Brown 2011 , 566 ), attachment to what is imagined as rural continues. Relationships with rurality, and especially imagined or virtual rurality (Cloke 2006 , 22 ; Woods 2011 , 9 ), manifests itself in a number of ways. These range from miniaturization of farming as hobby farms and urban agriculture to symbolic references to bucolic settings in the names of housing subdivisions.

THE RURAL IDYLL AND PLACE ATTACHMENT

Geographers and others often consider place attachment, but generally with the idea of attachment to a specific place (Relph 1976 ; Tuan 1977 ; Manzo and Devine-Wright 2014 ; Cresswell 2015 ). Although rarely addressed in geography, psychologists Leila Scanell and Robert Gifford noted that people also can have attachments to 'generic' places ( 2014 , 27 ). data.text: Current discussions of energy policy seldom acknowledge the problem of energy poverty, a situation in which a household cannot afford to adequately heat or cool the home. In this article, we examine the concept of energy poverty and describe some of its contours in a rural part of North Carolina. Energy poverty, we suggest, is best viewed as a geographical assemblage of networked materialities and socioeconomic relations. To illustrate this approach, we focus on the geographical patterns of three key determinants of energy poverty in eastern North Carolina: the socioeconomic characteristics of rural households, the networked infrastructures of energy provision, and the material conditions of the home. Throughout, we highlight the lived effects of energy poverty, drawing on transcripts from interviews conducted with recipients of weatherization assistance in the region. The challenges of the energy poor, we suggest, deserve greater attention in public policy and as part of a broader understanding of welfare and care.
data.method_section_html:
Auto-extracted method sections (click to expand)

Energy as an Assemblage

On the surface, energy poverty is a straightforward relationship between household income and the cost of energy. In Boardman's (1991) often-used formulation, a household spending more than 10 percent of household income on energy bills should be defined as energy poor. It should be clear, however, that this financial equation is not simply a matter of incomes and energy prices but is mediated by a variety of factors and relationships, including the provision of energy to the home, the home's energy efficiency, and the unique requirements for an individual to be comfortable in his or her home. Boardman (1991) and Healy (2004) have examined some of these aspects of energy poverty in the European context, with a particular focus on the links between energy poverty and household risk factors. Both authors have produced empirically rich studies detailing the prevalence of energy poverty using large-scale census and survey data. Building from the work of Healy and Boardman, Buzar (2007a, 2007b) examines energy poverty at a finer scale in the former socialist countries of Central and Eastern Europe. Buzar (2007b) advocated a 'relational approach' to the study of energy poverty, one that combines an understanding of postsocialist energy policy and housing infrastructures with an appreciation for the lived experiences of the energy poor.

Although we are broadly supportive of this kind of approach, we wish to suggest that new avenues of inquiry can be opened up through an engagement

Energy Poverty in Eastern North Carolina

Our particular investigation is focused on three counties in eastern North Carolina (Figure 1). The area is typical of lagging rural regions throughout the U.S. South (Table 1) and is characterized by relatively high rates of poverty and unemployment, a declining economic base, low levels of educational attainment, and endemic health problems (North Carolina Rural Economic Development Center n.d.). It is this kind of socioeconomic landscape that presents a high risk for energy poverty (Colton and Leviton 1991; U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 2005).

In the United States, two federal programs have been established to assist those in energy poverty. The first is the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), which provides income subsidies to lowincome households, most often in the winter when heating bills are the highest. The second is the Weatherization Assistance Program (WAP), which updates and renovates houses occupied by low-income residents in an attempt to increase their energy efficiency. Weatherization improvements typically include adding or improving insulation and repairing nonfunctioning heating and cooling equipment. These improvements usually result in lower bills and safer indoor conditions for recipients. Since the program's inception, more than 6.2 million homes in the United States have been weatherized by the WAP (National Association for Community Service Providers 2009).

In North Carolina, the WAP is administered by the state's Dep

The Variable Landscape of Energy Provision

The landscape of eastern North Carolina is crisscrossed by a dense web of networked energy infrastructures. The ability of any particular household to effectively access these networks, however, is conditioned by a number of factors that vary geographically. Although such constraints are experienced by all energy users, they pose particular challenges for low-income residents. The primary heating sources used in the study area are electricity, liquid propane gas (LPG), and natural gas. These forms of energy have distinctive properties and vary in their ability to be efficiently converted from raw fuel to heat. Natural gas and LPG are much more efficient than electricity as a source of heat and, all things being equal, would be a more cost-effective method of space heating. All things are not equal, however, as the networks of energy provision can vary significantly by both cost and availability.

Figure 2 shows the percentage of residences using natural gas, electricity, and LPG, respectively, as their primary heating fuel. The experience of energy poverty emerges not only from the geographically uneven character of energy networks but also the ways in which those networks intersect with the materiality of the home. For the energy poor, a decline in the home's thermal efficiency brings on new challenges in the form of higher energy bills and indoor conditions that can at times become dangerous to the occupant.

The connection of the home to networked infrastructure beginning in the early twentieth century remade the house into a new space, a symbol of progressive society. Life was made easier by a range of electric appliances and the home more comfortable through the climate control enabled by air conditioners and furnaces. Introduction

∗ Department of Geography, University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill † Department of Geography, East Carolina University

C ontemporary discussions about energy policy in the United States have tended to focus on the need to transition from our current fossil fuel regime to one in which renewable energy sources play a much larger role. Amid the debates about energy security, climate change, and a new green economy, however, it is easy to overlook the fact that millions of Americans currently lack access to reliable, affordable energy regardless of source. In this contribution, we highlight some of the dimensions of this uneven landscape of energy consumption by examining the concept of energy poverty and tracing some of its contours in a rural part of North Carolina.

We use the term energy poverty to describe a situation in which a household cannot afford to maintain the home's indoor temperature at a level that allows for a comfortable or healthy lifestyle, a condition also known as fuel poverty . Our aim in what follows is twofold: First, we wish to put forward a view of energy poverty as a particular kind of techno-social assemblage, made up of an array of networked actors and materialities. A focus on the networked nature of energy poverty, we suggest, can help to highlight its historical foundations and multidimensional character. Our second aim is to offer a glimpse of the lived realities of energy poverty. To do so, we draw on results from a research project centered around in-depth interviews with households receiving weatherization assistance in eastern North Carolina. By giving voice to those coping with energy poverty, we hope to shed some light on a phenomenon that is seldom given a prominent role in contemporary policy debates and also to suggest some of the ways that the challenge of energy poverty might be viewed in the context of an expanded conceptualization of welfare and care.

Energy as an Assemblage

On the surface, energy poverty is a straightforward relationship between household income and the cost of energy. In Boardman's (1991) often-used formulation, a household spending more than 10 percent of household income on energy bills should be defined as energy poor. It should be clear, however, that this financial equation is not simply a matter of incomes and energy prices but is mediated by a variety of factors and relationships, including the provision of energy to the home, the home's energy efficiency, and the unique requirements for an individual to be comfortable in his or her home. Boardman (1991) and Healy (2004) have examined some of these aspects of energy poverty in the European context, with a particular focus on the links between energy poverty and household risk factors. Both authors have produced empirically rich studies detailing the prevalence of energy poverty using large-scale census and survey data. Building from the work of Healy and Boardman, Buzar (2007a, 2007b) examines energy poverty at a finer scale in the former socialist countries of Central and Eastern Europe.

Networked Infrastructures

The networked infrastructures of energy and other substances have been the focus of considerable recent discussion. This research has highlighted a number of ways in which networked infrastructures and their associated technological systems work to shape landscapes and spaces (Zimmerer 2011). First, infrastructures are important sites for mediating the relationships between, and thus producing particular understandings of, nature (on the one hand) and social or domestic space (on the other). This has been described as a metabolism , through which the flows of natural substances such as water, energy, or waste are isolated and channeled toward, or away from, the socially produced spaces of the city and home (Gandy 2004; Swyngedouw 2006).

data.text: As examinations of the rural-urban interface move beyond a focus on the rural or urban fringe as a location and move toward examining the patterns and processes that both divide and link rural and urban places, a broader (re)conceptualization of the rural-urban interface becomes increasingly important. Thus far the question of boundaries and interfaces between so-called urban and rural locales has mostly revolved around where and when such boundaries occur (including significant coverage of the differences and conflicts between urban vs. rural people), rather than asking what physical or social functions are being served by the rural-urban interface itself. In response, I (re)frame the rural-urban interface not only as a boundary between two distinct spaces but also as a conduit, a place of exchange, and a flux point between them. Using a particular case of contested ecologies in the exurban Sierra Nevada foothills of California, I (re)conceptualize the rural-urban interface as meaning, model, and metaphor (MMM), situating contrasting people and places in an ongoing negotiation of place and environmental meaning along the (ex)urbanizing edge. Although the differences between rural and urban are increasingly unclear, the division continues to be compelling from environmental and sociopolitical standpoints. I argue that (perceived) boundaries are instrumental in understanding physical-material change and for mitigating social conflicts occurring across them. As such, attention to the patterns, processes, and flows that connect or separate rural and urban areas is critical to forging effective and long-lasting solutions to contemporary social, economic, and environmental problems.

data.text: Results from an online survey of the mobility of people who grew up in Nebraska indicate that rural stayers, defined as those Nebraskans who have had some experience living in communities with fewer than 2,500 residents, express stronger place-based attachments than others. Key components of this attachment include general contentment living in Nebraska, connection to family, a desire to raise children in Nebraska, appreciation for the state's culture and hospitality, and for some, a fondness for the state's natural environments. The research draws on quantitative evidence and the personal stories shared by survey respondents. The findings from the Nebraska Roots Migration Survey are provocative in their suggestion that those who grow up in America's rural areas may develop a different set of values and social and place-based attachments than their urban peers.

METHODS

The Nebraska Roots Migration Survey builds upon an online residential decision-making survey that was first developed in 2014 (Morse 2015 ). The Vermont Roots Migration Survey was distributed on the social media networks of five individuals of differing ages who had attended a public high school while residing in Vermont. The aim of that survey, and the aim of the Nebraska Roots Migration Survey, was to ask people who had spent at least some portion of their adolescence in a specific state to explain in their own words why they chose to stay in, leave, or return to their home state. In addition to collecting narratives, the surveys gathered demographic data and offered a multiple-choice based list of factors for staying, leaving, or returning. For example, those people who identified as 'stayers' were provided a list of reasons for staying that included choices such as 'my work is in the state,' 'I would like to leave but I have not had the opportunity,' 'I appreciate the state's landscape (natural environments),' and 'I have stayed in the state to live near family.' A write-in box for 'other' was offered. Respondents were free to select as many factors that fit their experience as they liked.

The unexpectedly high response rate to the 2014 Vermont survey3 , 692 fully complete responses in a three week period (see Morse 2015 ; Morse and Mudgett 2018 )-indicated t

DEFINITIONS

The United States Census Bureau does not specifically define 'rural'; instead a rural place is defined as an absence of the urban (United States Census Bureau 2020 ). 'Rural' encompasses all population, housing, and territory not included in an urban area that is defined as a having at least 2 , 500 people (United States Census Bureau 2020 ). Census categories do not always adequately describe the lived experience of a place. As Michael Woods ( 2011 ) has explained, rural is an elusive concept; around the world, demographers, geographers, and government leaders struggle to develop definitions of rurality that are both uniform and conform to personal experience of living in a place. Rural is relative. For the person living on a farm many miles from a town of 10 , 000 , that town may feel urban, and to the urbanite, a trip to the suburbs may feel like a trip to the countryside. How rurality is experienced as an identity, a place, and a representation also varies person to person and culturally (Halfacree 2006 ). For the purposes of clarity, we adopt the U.S. Census definition of rural in this analysis.

In our analysis, survey respondents from towns of 2 , 500 or more people are classified as urban while those from towns of under 2 , 500 are classified as rural. Introduction

N ebraska occupies an empty space in the American geographical imagination. The entire Great Plains region may appear as 'placeless' or even a 'nonplace' to those who fly over or drive through it as quickly as possible to get from one coast to another (Cresswell 2015 ). Yet, research with people who have grown up and live in Nebraska now suggests that its rural communities are rich with social interaction and places to which residents are deeply attached. It is a place that many people have been happy to make their home. Drawing on results from an online survey of the mobility of people who grew up in Nebraska, this paper asserts that those who have chosen to remain in the state and who have experienced living in or around rural towns, defined as communities of under 2 , 500 people, are even more content to stay in Nebraska than those from urban communities. The findings from the Nebraska Roots Migration Survey are provocative in their suggestion that those who grow up in America's rural areas may develop a different set of values and social and placebased attachments than urban residents.

IMMOBILITY IN MIGRATION RESEARCH

Research on residential mobility has often focused on why people leave a place, rather than why they choose to stay. This is especially true regarding migration research on the Great Plains, where rural depopulation and the region have been seemingly synonymous with each other since the early twentieth century (Loveridge, Yi, and Bokemeier 2009 ; Gilbreath 2012 ; Jacquet, Guthrie, and

2

Jackson 2016 ). Subsequently, there is little literature on 'stayers,' the people who have chosen to stay in this rural landscape.

PLACE ATTACHMENT IN RURAL-MIGRATION RESEARCH

Nearly a half-century ago, Yi-Fu Tuan asserted that 'Place is a center of meaning constructed by experience' ( 1975 , 15 ). He argued that we know places, especially places like the home and neighborhood, through our experiential and sensory engagement with them, and such engagement produces meaning in people's daily lives. Tuan grappled with definitions of 'rootedness' and 'sense of place,' suggesting that rootedness describes those who have remained in place and lack an ability to reflect on their place, whereas those of a certain mobility status can develop a broader sense of place ( 1980 ). In recent years, geographers have focused on the embodied dimension of place, and even mobile experiences of place, in a variety of settings and modes (see Cresswell 2015 , for a review). Given the decades-long history of investigations into the meaning of place, it is surprising that the role of place-based experience and emotional attachment to particular geographies has not been a central concern in migration studies.

data.text: Current scholarship on poverty in the U. S. borderlands argues that limited low-income housing and unenforced land development regulations cause poor domestic water access in south Texas's predominantly Mexican-American rural and periurban low-income communities (colonias). In this article, I argue that water politics, not only poverty or failed public policy, determined the trajectory of inadequate water access. Drawing from legislative archives, legal documents, and court records, I examine two companion legal cases (Jimenez v. Hidalgo WCID 2 et al. [1971] and Fonseca v. Hidalgo WCID 2 et al. [1971]) that challenged the ability of farmer-controlled water control and improvement districts (WCIDs) to dominate regional water governance by excluding colonias from district territory. This territorial exclusion denied colonias residents the right to vote for WCID board candidates and, thus, denied residents the political standing to change the district's operation from irrigation to domestic water supply. Drawing on current scholarship in critical legal geography, the article details how emerging legal discourses rescripted narratives about colonias residents' access to water through debates over the political territoriality of the WCIDs. Moreover, the legal process shifted the terms of debate from voting rights to historical precedent, the market, policy failure, and prospective water rights. The final legal ruling against colonias residents foreclosed any standing they had in regional water governance and shunted them into their current position of passive consumers of dysfunctional public services with limited ability to change their relationship to regional water management institutions.

Critical Legal Geography

Law inscribes spatial practices and orders the material landscape. It designates identities and establishes institutions of social and political life, creating bounded domains of social interaction. The law codifies what can be done where and by whom. Critical legal geography examines how law enables human territoriality through discourse and practice (Blomley 1994; Chouinard 1994; Delaney 1998; Forest 2000; Blomley, Delaney, and Ford 2001; Holder and Harrison 2003; von Benda-Beckmann, von Benda-Beckmann, and Griffiths 2009). Legal constructions of social interaction claim significant scholarly attention because, as Delaney, Ford, and Blomley (2001, xix) wrote, 'social space represents a materialization of power, and much of law consists in highly significant and specialized descriptions and prescriptions of the same power.' Allied with a larger critical project in human geography (Blomley 2007, 2008b; Schlottmann 2008; Olson and Sayer 2009), scholars in legal geography examine discourse in legal practices to move beyond the ideology of legalism, which depoliticizes space and legitimizes actions of powerful actors (Delaney 1998, 19).

One perspective in legal geography is law-in-space, or the legalities of space whereby scholars examine the 'situated legal practices . . . [that] contribute to the shaping and reshaping of the spatialities of social life' (Delaney 2003a, 68). Groundbreaking work in legal geography demonstrates that space and legal territory reinforce racial hie

Introduction

P oet Gloria Anzald´ ua described her home on the U.S.-Mexico border, the Lower Rio Grande Valley, as a place 'where the third world grates against the first and bleeds' (Anzald´ ua 1987, 25). She famously described this hemorrhage as a 'border culture.' Many have pointed to colonias as an example of this rupture. Colonias are predominantly low-income, Mexican-American rural and periurban subdivisions characterized by irregular housing and poor water and sanitation infrastructure. Despite two decades of infrastructure investment and new land development regulations, colonias have expanded rapidly. Approximately 238,000 people live in at least 1,350 colonias, with 119,000 people facing unknown deficiencies in water or sanitation in south Texas (Parcher and Humberson 2007, 2009). Colonias reflect trenchant problems that originate in the region's uneven development, and their persistence naturalizes poor water and sanitation as a cultural or historical condition of the border.

Critical legal geography opens a new perspective on the struggle for domestic water in the Lower Rio Grande Valley. Discourses are important to understand the allocation, restriction, and use of natural resources (Bridge and McManus 2000), but some discourses are more powerful than others. The law inscribes and codifies human-nature boundaries (Delaney 2003b) and translates these meanings into material outcomes because it has the explicit backing of the state. The legal process demarcates the boundaries of water politics because the law determines who holds legitimate power to organize, distribute, and manage a region's physical water resources. In the United States, water's territoriality is increasingly important as water governance devolves to local special districts or what some have called 'shadow governments' (Mullin 2009). Therefore, attention to the legal discourses, which demarcated social and political control over the Rio Grande water, provides a framework to examine how competing narratives of water access are constructed and contested in relation to the territoriality of the farmer-controlled water districts.

Critical Legal Geography

Law inscribes spatial practices and orders the material landscape. It designates identities and establishes institutions of social and political life, creating bounded domains of social interaction. The law codifies what can be done where and by whom. Critical legal geography examines how law enables human territoriality through discourse and practice (Blomley 1994; Chouinard 1994; Delaney 1998; Forest 2000; Blomley, Delaney, and Ford 2001; Holder and Harrison 2003; von Benda-Beckmann, von Benda-Beckmann, and Griffiths 2009). Legal constructions of social interaction claim significant scholarly attention because, as Delaney, Ford, and Blomley (2001, xix) wrote, 'social space represents a materialization of power, and much of law consists in highly significant and specialized descriptions and prescriptions of the same power.' Allied with a larger critical project in human geography (Blomley 2007, 2008b; Schlottmann 2008; Olson and Sayer 2009), scholars in legal geography examine discourse in legal practices to move beyond the ideology of legalism, which depoliticizes space and legitimizes actions of powerful actors (Delaney 1998, 19).

Colonias and Water Access in South Texas

Water and poverty are intimately linked in the historical geography of the Lower Rio Grande Valley. Poverty in the region is experienced and defined by poor access to water and inadequate sanitation. In the early twentieth century, newly arrived Midwestern farmers organized WCIDs to convey water from the Rio Grande to citrus and vegetable fields. The farming elites manipulated local politics and society along ethnic lines for decades (Anders 1982; Carroll 2003). Irrigated agriculture was predicated on cheap water, controlled by farmers on WCID boards of directors, and cheap Mexican labor controlled by poll taxes, Jim Crow segregation, substandard schools, and the Texas Rangers (Warburton, Wood, and Crane 1943; Stillwell 1947; Montejano 1987; Tiefenbacher 2001; Barrera 2004; Brannstrom and Neuman 2009).

data.text: This article examines the geographic distribution of Optional Practical Training (OPT) employment by international student graduates of Missouri's colleges and universities between 2007 and 2017. OPT is a temporary employment program that international students are eligible to apply for after graduating with a degree from a college or university in the United States. It offers twelve months of employment authorization, and students can work anywhere in the United States provided the work is related to their degree. OPT has seen remarkable growth over the past two decades, but employment has mainly concentrated in major urban centers. Based on more than 24,000 OPT employment addresses of Missouri graduates, this research shows that nearly 97 percent of Missouri's OPT took place in metropolitan areas, most of which was out of state. Within Missouri, OPT employment was regional, with Missouri's OPT students more likely to cross the country to work than to cross the state. Most local OPT work in college towns was located on campuses, rather than in the surrounding community. Indeed, the data show how Missouri's smaller cities, towns, and rural areas-and their local economies-have all but missed out on the benefits of homegrown OPT employment.

Auto-extracted method sections (click to expand)

Data and Methods

A Freedom of Information Act request was submitted to ICE, a division of the DHS, for all practical training authorization data covering all F-1 international students who had studied in SEVP-certified institutions within the state of Missouri from 2004 through 2018 (ICE 2018).

All data received from ICE arrived preanonymized so that no personal information could be identified. The data were then filtered by postcompletion OPT only. The data included address information for students ' graduating institutions and places of employment. Only those observations with both employer information and a full address were included in our analysis. Fields that contained unknown, ASE (actively seeking employment), not currently employed, or N/A were designated as having no employer information and were not used in the analysis. Next, because the addresses were all self-reported, the data contained many spelling variations, which required extensive cleaning to standardize city names. Data Issues and Limitations

OPT data collected by the federal government provide some of the most detailed and immediate snapshots of postgraduation migration and employment available. Caveats are warranted, however. The data here -and, indeed, in all OPT studies -are to varying degrees incomplete. At best, they are an approximation. In this section we address some of the potential issues and limitations.

After finding a job on OPT, students are required to report their employment information, including employer name and address, either to their schools, who input the information into SEVIS, or, since March 2018, through an online self-reporting portal (U.S. DHS 2018).

Matt Foulkes

University of Missouri, USA

This article examines the geographic distribution of Optional Practical Training (OPT) employment by international student graduates of Missouri ' s colleges and universities between 2007 and 2017. OPT is a temporary employment program that international students are eligible to apply for after graduating with a degree from a college or university in the United States. It offers twelve months of employment authorization, and students can work anywhere in the United States provided the work is related to their degree. OPT has seen remarkable growth over the past two decades, but employment has mainly concentrated in major urban centers. Based on more than 24,000 OPT employment addresses of Missouri graduates, this research shows that nearly 97 percent of Missouri ' s OPT took place in metropolitan areas, most of which was out of state. Within Missouri, OPT employment was regional, with Missouri ' s OPT students more likely to cross the country to work than to cross the state. Most local OPT work in college towns was located on campuses, rather than in the surrounding community.

Overview of Optional Practical Training 1

Most international students studying in the United States enter the country on an F-1 visa, which is considered a ' nonimmigrant ' visa in that lawful status within the United States is for a limited amount of time and it confers no path to permanent residency (U.S. Department of State, Bureau of Consular Affairs n.d.). 2 Nor is it categorized along with employment visas like H-1B. Rather, an F-1 visa is a student visa wherein individuals are admitted to the United States for the ' duration of status '-that is, as long as students are fulfilling the terms of their academic program they are considered to be in ' valid status ' and thus lawfully allowed to remain in the United States. While in school, F-1 students stay ' in status ' by enrolling in the required number of credit hours. After the completion of their program, and if they apply and are approved for OPT, they stay ' in status ' by being employed (U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Service [USCIS] 2020).

Data and Methods

A Freedom of Information Act request was submitted to ICE, a division of the DHS, for all practical training authorization data covering all F-1 international students who had studied in SEVP-certified institutions within the state of Missouri from 2004 through 2018 (ICE 2018).

All data received from ICE arrived preanonymized so that no personal information could be identified. The data were then filtered by postcompletion OPT only. The data included address information for students ' graduating institutions and places of employment. Only those observations with both employer information and a full address were included in our analysis. Fields that contained unknown, ASE (actively seeking employment), not currently employed, or N/A were designated as having no employer information and were not used in the analysis. Next, because the addresses were all self-reported, the data contained many spelling variations, which required extensive cleaning to standardize city names. The finished product was then geocoded to obtain corresponding decimal degree coordinates based on employer ' city name ' and ' state ' fields.

data.text: This article looks at the changing nature of property access regimes in northeastern Maine. The state's unique open lands tradition has come under threat as a result of the large-scale restructuring of the timber industry from vertically integrated forest products companies toward individual and institutional investor-owners. Using a large conservation project in the town of Grand Lake Stream as a case study, I argue that new investor-owners have been able to generate profits by enclosing long-standing common access regimes and commanding monopoly rent payments. After reviewing literatures on rent, enclosure, and the commodification of nature, I examine two prominent examples of this process of rent extraction through the enclosure of common access regimes: lease lots and working forest conservation easements. The article concludes arguing for regulatory intervention, as well as the need for more concrete case studies on the impacts of financial investment on the biophysical environment.
