Paper outline — first 3 sections (click to expand)

Introduction

This regional case study uses nonconventional data to document shifting migration systems across New England and impacts on real estate markets since the arrival of COVID-19. Understanding how this unique event affected migration and housing markets is important for several reasons. First, migration between urban and rural regions has been volatile since the 1970s, responding to different shocks and technological change, and this article contributes to well-established themes examining urban-to-rural migration. Second, similar migration-inducing crises (health, climatic, economic) will undoubtedly emerge in the future, so gauging how such events affect migration is important for future preparation and response. Finally, the empirical analysis uses nonconventional data to examine pandemic-induced migration shifts, highlighting the possibilities big data hold for asking new geographic questions.

The remainder of this article contains four sections. A literature review examines how the pandemic could transform urban -rural migration systems documenting ebbs and flows of urban -rural migration over five decades, discussing how exogenous shocks alter migration systems, and highlighting ways heightened rural in-migration can affected real estate activity. We then describe the unique data used in the analysis. The results section presents temporal and spatial changes in settlement systems and real estate markets emerging during the pandemic. We conclude with key insights and identify important unanswered questions.

Literature Review

Temporal Dynamics in Rural -Urban Migration Systems

Migration between urban and rural regions across the United States has long interested geographers, and for two centuries, rural -urban migration has been most common. Today, the United States is nearly 80 percent urban, whereas in 1930, it was evenly split between urban and rural (P. B. Nelson 2021). Despite the prevalence of rural-to-urban migration, these flows have reversed at times over the last fifty years, and certain rural areas today enjoy counterstreams of urban in-migrants. In the 1970s, demographers noticed extensive rural population growth, coining the decade a ' rural renaissance ' (Beale 1976, 1977). This renaissance was driven by a confluence of factors including the Arab oil embargo, regional economic restructuring, and residential preferences (Frey and Johnson 1998). The renaissance waned in the 1980s, yet growth returned during the 1990s ' rural rebound, ' closely tied to amenity destinations and technologies enabling remote work (Beyers and Lindahl 1996; McGranahan 1999; Beyers and Nelson 2000).

Migration Response to External Shocks

Demographic history shows that various shocks have influenced migration over time. Migration is an economic bellwether, as households often move when economic conditions change, and large shocks to local, regional, and global economies can induce migration. Well-known regional restructuring in the United States shifted investment and employment from the Rustbelt to the Sunbelt in the latter half of the twentieth century. These geographic shifts coincided with expanding service sector employment and declining manufacturing. Migration systems changed accordingly with net migration from Rustbelt to Sunbelt of nearly 4 million in the 1970s (Bluestone and Harrison 1982). Economically induced migration has been particularly acute for certain cities. Detroit ' s population peaked in 1950 at 1.85 million, yet by 2010, it was barely 700,000, a 62 percent decline (McDonald 2014). Buffalo, Cleveland, and Gary have also seen population decline driven by out-migration (Cowell 2013; Hackworth 2015; Schindler 2016). Population shifts play out unevenly in specific neighborhoods.

data.text: Potential death from traffic collisions is a common hazard faced by nearly everyone. This analysis uses geographical approaches to examine fatal collision risk in the state of Indiana from 2003 to 2011. The state averaged 757 fatal collisions annually. About 60 percent occurred in urban or suburban areas. Risk was highest in low-density exurban and rural areas and on highways, county roads, and interstates. County sheriffs and state police were more likely to face fatal collisions than municipal police. Significant black spots existed around the Illinois and Kentucky state lines. Fatal collisions were less clustered than nonfatal collisions. Fatal collisions exhibited positive spatial autocorrelation but the global Moran's I for counties was close to random. Approximately 10 percent of ninety-two counties had significant local spatial autocorrelation in fatal collision rates. Police and emergency response resource distributions should be considered in light of fatal collision black spots in the state.

Measurement and Method

Exploring the geography of fatalities is challenging because collisions are comparatively rare and, given that a crash occurs, fatal collisions are a low-frequency event. In a broad geography, the chances of any selected space hosting a traffic collision thin substantially. To partially address the 'rarity' problem, this analysis uses a nine-year aggregation of fatal collisions. The fatal collision rate is operationalized as the percentage of all collisions resulting in at least one fatality. Given a collision occurs in an area, what is the probability it resulted in at least one fatality?

Operationalizing the places of collision incidence is also challenging. There are different ways of defining spatial areas in which crashes occur. One is the point-level location of fatal collisions. The second is aggregation of collision points distributed among different areas or categories (e.g., county, road type, locality). Once we aggregate point locations, identifying the scale of the bounded geographies involved becomes an issue because it invokes the modifiable area unit problem (MAUP). Different levels of spatial aggregation produce different findings (Thomas 1996; Lassarre and Thomas 2005). MAUP's impact is lessened by using the smallest possible areal units and different scales of spatial aggregation (Paez and Scott 2004). Therefore, three spatial units of analysis are used herein. data.text: Colorado's 1992 vote on Amendment Two was the first meaningful, broad-based test of attitudes on gay rights within the United States. Analysis of voting results distinguishes places of tolerance from places of rejection. Social differences separating these places reflect typical contrasts between ''traditionalists'' and ''modernizers'' found in cultural conflicts at the national level. Places showing support for gay rights are recreational-based mountain communities, urban areas, and university communities. Those showing opposition are rural, agriculturally based communities. Suburban areas produced a more ambivalent vote.

Auto-extracted method sections (click to expand)

Methodology

Voting data are available in aggregate form only, which sets limits on their use. Because of ecological problems, they are considered weak indicators of the dynamics of individual decision making. However, vote counts do effectively summarize the trend of decisions made at each place reported and allow the identification of spatial patterns in voting outcomes. These patterns, in turn, generally correlate well with important social characteristics of the places involved, identifying real associations and a meaningful geography.

Voting results are reported at two levels, for entire counties and for precincts within counties. Both scales were used in exploring the links between place character and voting. The first encompasses the entire state, comparing outcomes among all Colorado counties; the second considers a more local scale, looking at differences among census tracts within two selected counties. Because of their size, counties are weak representatives of the social spaces within which most persons experience their lives, while census tracts are closer in scale to such spaces. Data are readily available for counties, yet quite costly to organize at the tract level. It was felt that selective analysis at both scales, with a comparison of results, would be a reasonable compromise given these constraints.

Richard K. Ormrod and David B. Cole

University of Northern Colorado

Colorado's 1992 vote on Amendment Two was the first meaningful, broad-based test of attitudes on gay rights within the United States. Analysis of voting results distinguishes places of tolerance from places of rejection. Social differences separating these places reflect typical contrasts between 'traditionalists' and 'modernizers' found in cultural conflicts at the national level. Places showing support for gay rights are recreational-based mountain communities, urban areas, and university communities. Those showing opposition are rural, agriculturally hascd communities. Suburban areas produced a more ambivalent vote. Key Words: gay rights, votes, social spaces, Colorado.

Social and Political Context

The gay and lesbian rights movement is a welldeveloped, mature political movement that has made important gains at local, national, and international scales (Nava and Dawidoff 1994; Cruikshank 1992; Adam 1987). It is also a part of a larger set of 'new' social-political movements pursuing either more complete civil rights for specific constituencies or fundamental changes in traditional social arrangements or practices (Aronowitz 1992, 11; Cruikshank 1992, 118; Epstein 1991, 46). These include the civil rights, antiwar, antinuclear, women's liberation, ecological, and consumer movements, among others.

data.text: The rural U.S. West is increasingly valued for its unique natural beauty, tourism potential, and the outdoor recreational activities it provides rather than for its grazing potential, lumber mills, or extraction of valuable minerals. With this transition in mind, we examine demographic changes in the region within the context of selective migration. We build on research conducted in the late 1990s that studied the changing spatial patterns of migration and income migration within the rural Mountain West. We update the current economic and demographic structure of the region and then document how 1990s patterns have persisted through an analysis of population concentration and income migration using U.S. Census and Internal Revenue Service data. Positive net migration and income migration have focused on New West (high amenity) counties, whereas the Old West, comprised of government, mining and manufacturing, farming, and other (diversified) counties, has fallen farther behind in income migration. Consequently, selective migration to areas of natural beauty and recreation potential has increasingly transformed the rural New West into its own peculiar geography, distinct in demographics as well as environment from the Old West, revealing a growing spatial inequality between these two areas, especially in income and housing.

Methods

With all the research that has sought to describe and analyze the reasons behind population changes in the rural West, scholars still struggle to agree on the exact areas that are part of the New West (Robbins et al. 2009). In this article we chose to reevaluate the same New West counties designated by Shumway and Otterstrom (2001) for consistency.

Thus, we separated counties in the Mountain West states (Arizona, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming) into the same five groups according to their economic structure: (1) government; (2) high amenity (New West); (3) mining and manufacturing; (4) farming and ranching; and (5) diversified or ' other ' (counties without a single dominant economic sector; see Figure 1). We used k -means cluster analysis of data from rural counties related to county typology codes and natural amenity index data developed by the Economic Research Service of the U.S. Department of Agriculture as well recreation-based economies designations developed by Beale and Johnson (1998) to classify high-amenity counties and the other types of counties. We also included the same counties as the previous study, even those that have since been classified as urban by the census. 1

Population Concentration

In the years since the previous research (Shumway and Otterstrom 2001), we still expect population growth to be increasingly spatially concentrated in high-amenity areas. One way to demonstrate this is by calculating a Hoover index, which measures spatial focus over time (Long and Nucci 1997; Otterstrom and Shumway 2003). 2 The principal use of the index is to identify whether population trends exhibit tendencies toward more uniform distributions, or whether they serve to focus population in a more concentrated pattern (Plane and Rogerson 1994).

Income Migration

After establishing the continued population growth of high-amenity counties in the Mountain West, we now turn to income movements associated with population change. Our findings support the view that not only people, but money is continuing to flow to New West counties, although there is some indication of growth in the diversified counties.

The rural U.S. West is increasingly valued for its unique natural beauty, tourism potential, and the outdoor recreational activities it provides rather than for its grazing potential, lumber mills, or extraction of valuable minerals. With this transition in mind, we examine demographic changes in the region within the context of selective migration. We build on research conducted in the late 1990s that studied the changing spatial patterns of migration and income migration within the rural Mountain West. We update the current economic and demographic structure of the region and then document how 1990s patterns have persisted through an analysis of population concentration and income migration using U.S. Census and Internal Revenue Service data. Positive net migration and income migration have focused on New West (high amenity) counties, whereas the Old West, comprised of government, mining and manufacturing, farming, and other (diversified) counties, has fallen farther behind in income migration.

Amenities, Migration, and the New West

Factors influencing migration in the United States have changed in their order of importance due to increases in overall wealth. Based on the demographic transition model, Zelinsky (1971) developed the concept of the mobility transition to explain how and why amenities became such a driving force of migration in the post -World War II United States. The basic concept is that as countries (regions) developed, the magnitude, type, and direction of migration would change from rural-to-urban to a more mixed pattern that included urban-tourban and urban-to-rural movements. The idea has its roots in Engle ' s Law that demonstrated as household income increased, a smaller proportion of income was spent on basic necessities. As applied to migration, Engle ' s Law suggests that as a society increases in income and wealth, people ' s choices concerning where to live also expand.

data.text: Property development in exurban areas has the capacity to undermine the amenity values that undergird that development. Predicated on that contradiction, this research seeks to explain the emergence of local, informal, planning-based regulations in the traditionally antiregulatory context of rural Montana. Adopting both the insights of institutional common property theory and those of critical materialist analysis of economic growth, the work reconciles accounts of development as inherently ecologically self-destructive with those stressing creative development and adoption of rules for collective self-governance. Using a detailed case analysis of a Montana county undergoing rapid growth, it examines what drives localized land use regulation, what controls are enacted, and whether such controls are resisted or facilitated by development capital. Findings suggest that informal regulations seek to control externalities of development on valuable amenity commons and that they are adopted with the acceptance, if not encouragement, of the development community. These fragile instruments are vulnerable to opposition, however, highlighting problems of more general relevance: Growth depends on a deregulated development regime, which produces externalities that undermine the valorization of property. Localized regulatory planning regimes are therefore both a solution to contradictions inherent in growth and a potential source of future planning problems.

Study Area and Methods

To address this question, we examined the planning process in Park County, located in southwestern Montana (Figure 1A), a site chosen specifically because it is emblematic of fast-growing areas demonstrating resistance to regulatory control. The difficulties planners face in adopting growth restrictions in Park County are exemplified by the failed effort to adopt a county-wide growth policy. In late 2004, the county convened a meeting to adopt a nonbinding growth policy, as mandated by state law. Here, the overflowing crowd forced the event to be moved to the county fairgrounds (Tschida 2008), where a chaotic twelve-hour event unfolded, in front of a screaming and yelling crowd (Nolt 2008). Vociferously opposing the entirely nonbinding plan as an assault on property rights, the crowd eventually brought the proceedings to a halt, and the commissioners ultimately gave up. Susan Gilbertz

Montana State University-Billings

Property development in exurban areas has the capacity to undermine the amenity values that undergird that development. Predicated on that contradiction, this research seeks to explain the emergence of local, informal, planning-based regulations in the traditionally antiregulatory context of rural Montana. Adopting both the insights of institutional common property theory and those of critical materialist analysis of economic growth, the work reconciles accounts of development as inherently ecologically self-destructive with those stressing creative development and adoption of rules for collective self-governance. Using a detailed case analysis of a Montana county undergoing rapid growth, it examines what drives localized land use regulation, what controls are enacted, and whether such controls are resisted or facilitated by development capital. Findings suggest that informal regulations seek to control externalities of development on valuable amenity commons and that they are adopted with the acceptance, if not encouragement, of the development community.

Institutions and Political Economy

A century of research on institutions and economics has come to emphasize the ongoing possibility of collective self-regulation (Commons 1934). Beginning from the acknowledgment that where the extraction or use of a resource can externally impact its availability or value for another user, research has outlined both the tremendous challenges in controlling externalities and the diversity of creative arrangements that do so (Ostrom 2005).

The challenges emerge first from designing a system of rules that can direct use sustainably. Where ecological systems are complex (e.g., in a fishery), simply organizing and setting appropriate limits presents difficulties. On top of this, however, come the far more daunting problems of encouraging users to control their practices within those limits and enforcing these arrangements where formal police powers might not exist and users must govern one another. The so-called prisoner's dilemma, where cooperation benefits all but the incentive to 'free ride' is high, causes observers to predict cooperation to be the exception rather than the rule (see Poundstone 1992 for a history of the concept).

The Problem of Planning in the 'New West'

Such questions are especially pressing in the Western United States, where some forms of regulation might be truncated as others flourish. Here, population migration poses serious challenges to existing institutions and the rapid arrival of new types of migrants, often desiring amenity housing and lifestyles in largely rural and historically agrarian areas, creates a concomitant explosion of real estate development activities where few were present before (Johnson and Beale 1994; Beale and Fuguitt 1995; Shumway and Davis 1996; Nelson 1997; Cromartie and Wardwell 1999; Beyers and Nelson 2000; Vias and Carruthers 2005). Balancing growth with the maintenance of traditional production systems and the visually open landscapes associated with them occupies the attention of older residents, newcomers, and the planning communities that must adjudicate multiple interests, aesthetics, land and water demands, and economic priorities (Sheridan 2001; Walker and Fortmann 2003; Brehm, Eisenhauer, and Krannich 2004; Ghose 2004; Gosnell and Travis 2005; Haggerty and Travis 2006; Gosnell, Haggerty, and Byorth 2007).

data.text: This article develops the concept of signaling hinterlands to explain how digital social networks extend and shift the interconnections between a metropolis and its hinterlands. The relationship between metropolis and hinterlands-the multiple, overlapping, networked geographies on which cities rely-is a long-standing area of geographical inquiry. This dynamic reflects networks of densely and more sparsely populated places connected by asymmetric relations, thus far primarily envisioned as physical goods-related production activities. How do these relationships change in a geographical political economy centered around digital technologies? We argue that digital technologies expand the productive capacity of the hinterlands, reshaping the dynamics between places within and beyond the metropolis. With digital social networks and digital platforms, places can gain value through their potential to signal and amass social, cultural, and economic capital. Signaling hinterlands reflect the simultaneously cultural, symbolic, technological, political, and economic relations involved in networking places under digital capitalism. We leverage Google Maps visitor posts to document the interconnections between the San Francisco Bay Area metropolis and Calla Lily Valley, a rural locale that we argue has become a digitally induced hinterland. Mapping postings from users who recorded visits to Calla Lily Valley, we examine how digital traces re-create and alter the asymmetric relations between rural and urban, metropolis and hinterlands in the digital economy.

Calla Lily Valley as a Signaling Hinterland

The greater Monterey Peninsula encompasses an exurban and rural area on the central California coast roughly 120 miles south of San Francisco, making the region an easy weekend trip from the heart of Silicon Valley. The region has long been a tourist destination famous for the golf courses of Pebble Beach, the Monterey Bay Aquarium, the picturesque beaches and towns including Carmelby-the-Sea, and the iconic Highway 1 road trip along the Big Sur coastline, one of the most famous highway stretches in the world. Given its famous and legible imagery, and its proximity to the Bay Area, the region has experienced significant changes alongside tech industry growth, inspiring new attention. These dynamics have not just fed activity into long-standing, prominent attractions like the aquarium. Rather, the area ' s visibility on digital social media platforms and the search for new places to ' discover ' appears to have changed both how people recreate and where they visit, creating new linkages between the metropolis and regional locales.

In this article, we examine this dynamic by focusing on Calla Lily Valley, located along the Big Sur coast, a remote, ninety-mile coastline beginning just south of Carmel-by-the-Sea. Calla Lily Valley refers to a small canyon along Garrapata Beach where calla lilies bloom in the spring, fed by a creek that runs to the Pacific Ocean (see Figure 1). Introduction

Department of Public Policy and Administration, Rutgers University -Camden, USA † Department of Geography, Dartmouth College, USA

T his article develops the concept of signaling hinterlands to explain how digital social networks extend and shift the interconnections between a metropolis and its hinterlands. The relationship between metropolis and hinterlands -the multiple, overlapping, networked geographies on which cities rely -is a long-standing area of geographical inquiry. Hinterlands are areas outside the metropolis connected by asymmetric relations to the metropolis, reflecting networks between densely and more sparsely populated places. Thus far, the literature characterizes the activities underlying the metropolis -hinterlands dynamic primarily around physical goods, in terms of production activities (e.g., agriculture, mining) and waste acceptance. How do these relationships change in a geographical political economy centered around digital technologies, where material goods represent only part of the productive capacity of hinterlands areas?

We argue that digital technologies expand the productive mechanisms underlying the hinterlands relationship beyond physical goods, reshaping the networks between places within and beyond the metropolis both in terms of which geographies have value as hinterlands, as well as what resources they offer. With digital social networks and platforms such as Instagram, Yelp, and Google Maps, places gain value through their potential to signal and amass social, cultural, and economic capital under digital capitalism. This dynamic enables a set of activities -and a corresponding set of hinterlands -where production extends beyond physical goods. Signaling hinterlands help elucidate the simultaneously cultural, symbolic, technological, political, and economic relations involved in networking places through digital platforms. We leverage an original social media data set to document the interconnections between the San Francisco Bay Area metropolis and Calla Lily Valley, located on the California central coast. We argue that Calla Lily Valley has become a hinterland enabled by digital technologies. Mapping the relationship between Calla Lily Valley and the Bay Area, we show how digital traces re-create and alter the asymmetric relations between rural and urban, metropolis and hinterlands in the digital economy.

Platforms and the Digital Growth Machine

Digital capitalism has produced important sociospatial shifts that have transformed cities and solidified the digital technology industry ' s economic influence (Sadowski 2020). Acting in coordinated ways to form what we have termed the ' digital growth machine ' (Rosen and Alvarez Le  on 2022), urban and digital technology sector actors leverage urban and digital capital accumulation possibilities to create new profit opportunities through four interrelated pathways. First, building on long-standing urban growth dynamics, the digital growth machine supports land development and technology sector industrial attraction to pursue urban growth and exchange values. Second, it creates mechanisms for increasing and extracting exchange values beyond traditional land development and intensification. Third, it enables intermediation and new markets. Fourth, the digital growth machine develops new urban digital renderings, such as the interactive maps on Yelp, NextDoor, and Google Maps, which shape land and asset-related value and perceptions of place.

Hinterlands as Operational Landscapes of the Digital Growth Machine

Prior research conceptualizes the relationship between the metropolis and the nonmetropolitan places on which it depends as its ' hinterlands, ' which Brenner and Katsikis (2020) defined as ' the variegated non-city spaces that are swept into the maelstrom of urbanisation, whether as supply zones, impact zones, sacrifice zones, logistics corridors or otherwise ' (24). Framed as hinterlands, nonmetropolitan areas can serve as landscapes for extraction to support urban functions. In this way, the metropolis and its hinterlands are linked through spatial networks across which capital, goods, resources, and people flow. As metropolitan regions have grown in size and complexity, so, too, have their hinterlands (Cronon 1991; Aguilar, Ward, and Smith 2003; Billen, Garnier, and Barles 2012; Brenner and Katsikis 2020).

data.text: Recent geographical scholarship on the politics of calculation has led to a reevaluation of the role of statistics, census-taking, and mapping as calculative techniques that have been of primary importance to the rise of the modern territorial state. The current study contributes to this literature by examining how the political technologies of street addressing have been employed to reconfigure the territory of the United States as a calculable space of security. Drawing on extensive archival research and thirty semistructured, in-depth interviews, this study provides a genealogy of calculable space, focusing particularly on the extension of city-style street addressing systems into rural communities to aid emergency management, homeland security, and various other governmental measures as part of the general process that Foucault (2007) has referred to as the urbanization of the territory. As a case study, I consider the campaign to readdress rural areas in West Virginia to illustrate the social and political processes at work in remaking the territory into a space of calculation by encoding the landscape with a spatial regime of inscriptions. The results presented here show how 911 addressing systems have been central to the reorganization of political space at a time when the apparatuses of security are being enhanced by the apparent marvels of geospatial technology. To the extent that such technologies are themselves implicated in reshaping the very spaces that they are designed to represent, this study calls our attention to the pervasive role that spatial calculation plays in the production of a geo-coded world.

Methods

Before delving into the historical material presented in the next section, a brief discussion of methods is in order. The research presented here on the spatial history of street addressing in the United States is the result of both extensive archival work over the past decade and the analysis of thirty semistructured, in-depth interviews that I conducted in 2008 with street addressing coordinators, GIS specialists, emergency response managers, county commissioners, postal officials, planners, private contractors, and local residents. In the selection of interview participants, I adopted a purposeful sampling strategy (Patton 2002), whereby individuals who were professionally involved in street addressing programs as well as those who had been directly affected by such programs were contacted as potential interviewees. All interview participants agreed to allow their real names to be used in the presentation of results during the consent process.

After receiving ethics approval to conduct research with human subjects from the Institutional Review Board at Texas A&M University in April 2008, and funding to support the project from the Library of Congress, I sent a preliminary e-mail query to the National Emergency Number Association (NENA), because this organization has played an integral role in developing standards for designing street addressing systems to aid emergency response management in the United States (e.g., Lucy 1995). Introduction

Calculation is therefore key to the constitution of the modern state . . . Since the seventeenth century, the predominant ontological understanding of the world has been its calculability.

-Stuart Elden, 'Missing the Point: Globalization, Deterritorialization and the Space of the World' (2005, 15-16)

Figure 1. Scenes from the so-called 'July riot' of 1998 in State College, Pennsylvania. Source: Blair and Cole (1998). (Color figure available online.)

After several hours, local police in riot gear created a barricade and used tear gas, pepper spray, and nightsticks to disperse the crowd, arresting a total of twenty people, over half of whom were students at Pennsylvania State University, for disorderly conduct and failure to disperse on lawful order (Blair and Cole 1998; Parfitt 1998a). In the days that followed, community leaders, police, university administrators, students, and local residents debated the ultimate causes of the 'riot' and how to prevent such events from reoccurring in the future (Parfitt 1998b). The most common explanation was the irresponsible abuse of alcohol, although a strong case can also be made that lax police enforcement, the annual July arts festival, and antistudent zoning ordinances contributed to the events that unfolded (Alt 1998). What interests me here, however, is not so much what caused this particular riot but rather how the subsequent response by local authorities, which I discuss below, powerfully illustrates the extent to which the calculative rationalities of 'number' have become entrenched in the workings of modern government.

Space, Politics, Calculation

The interrelations of space, politics, and calculation have become a major focus of critical geographic inquiry as an increasing number of geographers have sought to trace the historical emergence of various calculative techniques as part of a critical spatial history of modern technologies of power (Braun 2000; Hannah 2000, 2009; Duncan 2002; Blomley 2003; Elden 2005, 2006, 2007; Legg 2005, 2006, 2007; Crampton and Elden 2006; Rose-Redwood 2006, 2008a; Dillon 2007; Huxley 2006, 2007, 2008; Rose-Redwood, Alderman, and Azaryahu 2010; Crampton 2011; Ettlinger 2011). Crampton and Elden (2006), for instance, pointed out that whereas much is known about the history of quantification as a method of geographical analysis, far less research has explored how numerical calculation itself has historically reshaped political practices and the geographies of everyday life. This distinction between quantitative methods in geography and the geographies of calculation is significant, because it draws attention to the way in which calculative rationalities have been used to refashion the world in their own image.

Sovereignty, Discipline, Security

In his lecture course, Security, Territory, Population, Foucault (2007) distinguished three mechanisms of power-sovereignty, discipline, and security-and he suggested that each is associated with different calculative techniques of spatial organization. In schematic terms, Foucault (2007, 11) began with a preliminary assessment by proposing that 'sovereignty is exercised within the borders of a territory, discipline is exercised on the bodies of individuals, and security is exercised over the whole population.' He quickly cautioned, however, that such a characterization of the spatial strategies of power is too simplistic, as the management of spatial 'multiplicities' is central to all three mechanisms of power under consideration. Nevertheless, the question of space is taken up in different ways within each dominant regime of power, and Foucault therefore devoted much of his attention to examining precisely these differences.

data.text: Declining populations, aging inhabitants and infrastructure, limited economic opportunities, and under-or unappreciated natural environments characterize a number of rural communities in the western United States. Faced with the challenges of providing for their residents, some of these communities have chosen to permit undesirable land-use activities, including the disposal of hazardous or nuclear waste. Central to the development of such sites is how a place is perceived and portrayed. Our purpose in this article is to examine how a dominant perception and portrayal of one such place-Tooele County, Utah-was created and used to facilitate the development of hazardous-waste-disposal sites. We use the geographical concept of place to illustrate how meanings and values are attached to a region in order to justify its becoming what it is and how such views persist.

CONCEPTUALIZING PLACE AND PLACE PERCEPTION

Geographers have developed a number of concepts to help understand human modification of the earth's surface, including the idea of 'place.' Robert Sack defined place as the milieu in which humans transform the earth into the home of humankind (1999). The juxtaposition of the physical environment, social relationships, and place perception create milieus in which what Sack calls 'projects' happen. Projects are what we as humans do-everything from teaching students, to incarcerating criminals, to creating industrial wastes that are toxic. In order for such a project to occur, a place must be created: Every activity has to happen somewhere, and every project we undertake either creates a new place as a requirement for its fulfillment or appropriates another place that was designed for another project. Projects often occur in multiple places that must be linked by communication, transportation, and socioeconomic networks. Thus the geography of our world results from the fact that our lives and our projects require a geographical structure of specific places and associated networks of flows that must be maintained-at least until they are no longer useful-in order for the original projects to succeed.

ABSTRACT. Declining populations, aging inhabitants and infrastructure, limited economic opportunities, and under- or unappreciated natural environments characterize a number of rural communities in the western United States. Faced with the challenges of providing for their residents, some of these communities have chosen to permit undesirable land-use activities, including the disposal of hazardous or nuclear waste. Central to the development of such sites is how a place is perceived and portrayed. Our purpose in this article is to examine how a dominant perception and portrayal of one such place-Tooele County, Utah-was created and used to facilitate the development of hazardous-waste-disposal sites. We use the geographical concept of 'place' to illustrate how meanings and values are attached to a region in order to justify its becoming what it is and how such views persist. Keywords: hazardous waste, NIMBY, perception, place, Tooele Counw, Utah.

CONCEPTUALIZING PLACE AND PLACE PERCEPTION

Geographers have developed a number of concepts to help understand human modification of the earth's surface, including the idea of 'place.' Robert Sack defined place as the milieu in which humans transform the earth into the home of humankind (1999). The juxtaposition of the physical environment, social relationships, and place perception create milieus in which what Sack calls 'projects' happen. Projects are what we as humans do-everything from teaching students, to incarcerating criminals, to creating industrial wastes that are toxic. In order for such a project to occur, a place must be created: Every activity has to happen somewhere, and every project we undertake either creates a new place as a requirement for its fulfillment or appropriates another place that was designed for another project. Projects often occur in multiple places that must be linked by communication, transportation, and socioeconomic networks.

THE FORGOTTEN AND MARGINALIZED RURAL WEST

Most of the recent focus in the rural western United States has been on areas where economic growth is occurring-the 'New West.' Steven Deller and his coauthors demonstrated that economic growth in the rural West is concentrated in highamenity areas (2oo1), whereas stagnant economic growth characterizes most lowamenity areas. This can lead to the perception that low-amenity areas with stagnant economies are good locales for activities that other places are unwilling to accept: waste deposits, prisons, material testing and disposing of toxic material, and industrial-scale livestock production. Whereas more affluent communities may resist and more powerful communities may retard such activities, struggling communities will often compete with each other for the right to host such waste flows, arguing that any economic development is better than none.

POPULATION

The issue of definition is crucial in determining the current population of American Indians. Clearly, the number of individuals who are of Native American ancestry has been repeatedly underenumerated in the federal censuses of population. When the census first began to compile figures for American Indians, the tallies were much lower than even the lowest estimates for pre-Columbian times and reached a low of 250,000 in 1890 (Thornton 1987). From 1890 to 1950 Native American population growth was slow. The pattern in part resulted from the 1924 Indian Citizenship Act, which extended rights of United States citizenship to all Native Americans and which thus led to more accurate enumeration of all Indians, because both reservation and nonreservation residents were counted. The 1950 census reported a Native American population of nearly 380,000. In each of the six decades from 1900 to 1950, the number of Native Americans increased by slightly more than 7 percent.

The greatest population increase occurred in 1960 after the Bureau of the Census adopted self-identification: Native American population rose to almost two million in 1990, a 455 percent increase in forty years. Significantly, the growth rate for each census after 1960 exceeded that for both the African-American and non-Hispanic white majority of the United States. Between 1980 and 1990 the Native Ame

GEOGRAPHICAL DISTRIBUTION

One unique aspect of the geography of Native Americans that emerges from their long interaction with other Americans is the reservation system. The reservations are composed of four classes of recognized lands: reservations and trust lands, tribal jurisdictional statistical areas (TJSAs), tribal designated statistical areas (TDSAs), and Alaskan national village statistical areas (ANVSAs). Each class has specific characteristics relative to its independence from federal intervention. Reservations and trust lands were generally established by treaty, statute, or executive or court order (U.S. Department of Commerce 1980). There are 310 reservations in the United States, of which 298 are federal reservations and 12 are state

reservations. Approximately 22 percent of the Native Americans defined by the 1990 census, a total of 437,431 individuals, resided on reservations or trust lands. TJSAs refer to portions of Oklahoma that were allotted to individual tribal members or to trust lands there that have been designated by tribal officials as areas of tribal jurisdiction for their Native American residents. The 17 TJSAs contained approximately 10 percent of the Native American population. TDSAs are identical to TJSAs but are located outside Oklahoma. The 19 TDSAs accounted for 3 percent of the Native American population. The ANVSAs are home to 2.5 pe

MIGRATION PATTERNS

Movement of Native Americans from rural or reservation locations to metropolitan or other urban locales represents an important change in their geographical distribution. Examination of the regional variation resulting from this migration is made at two scales: nine census divisions, and the states as regions. To measure migration we define a migrant as a person whose residence at either scale differed in 1990 from that in 1985. Like most Americans, Native Americans tend to move short distances (Long 1988). Approximately 51 percent of Native Americans changed residence between 1985 and 1990, but 42 percent of that number moved locally, within the same county or metropolitan statistical area (MSA); 35 percent crossed county or MSA boundaries but stayed in the same state; only 23 percent emigrated to another state. Of interstate migrants, only 13 percent moved to a different census division. With one-quarter of the total migrant Native American population moving between state or census divisions, the level of migration was still relatively high.

REGIONAL FLOWS

The twenty largest migration flows between census divisions illustrate the effectiveness of migration (Fig. 3). Effectiveness is a measure of the net migration relative to the gross migration between two areas. The level of effectiveness is derived by dividing the net migration between two regions by the gross migration flow between them, which yields a percentage ranging from zero, when the numbers of migrants are equal, to 100, when movement is in one direction only (Plane 1984). At the census-division level, the most obvious movement was from the West South Central division, which had net flows to every other census division. Two other census divisions, the Pacific and the West North Central, had strong net outflows, but both had one or more net in-migration flows.

The effectiveness of migration between census divisions, in contrast to simple total net migration, demonstrates the linkages between census divisions. New England, for example, received major net inflows from the West South Central division, the Mid Atlantic division, and the Pacific division. Concurrently, it had large outflows to the Mountain division and the East North Central, West North Central, and South Atlantic divisions. This article intends to address questions associated with whether patterns of population growth and income migration are associated with new and old West economies. Defining the New West

In this case, we defined the rural West as those counties in the U.S. Mountain Census Division designated as rural (nonmetropolitan) as of 1993 based on the rural/urban codes developed by Butler and Beale (1994). Using these codes, we selected a total of 246 rural counties. Once counties were designated as rural, we used the Economic Research Service (ERS) county typology codes as a framework for examining county level economic structure (Cook 1994). These codes include six mutually exclusive economic types-farming, mining, manufacturing, government, services, and nonspecialized-as well as a number of overlapping policy types, including a retirement designation. We also used the ERS's natural amenity index, which includes factors measuring aspects of climate, topography, and water (McGranahan 1999). We also added a set of measures developed by Beale and Johnson (1998) to determine recreationbased economies.

Using continuous versions of the typology variables along with the natural amenities index and the recreation measures as our clustering criteria, we performed a cluster analysis using SPSS k-means clustering procedure. After creating the clusters, we compared and contrasted them along demographic and locational dimensions. Each cluster is labeled by its dominant economic characteristics. J. Matthew Shumway and Samuel M. Otterstrom

One of the most recognizable and important changes occurring in the West is rapid population growth. This article intends to address questions associated with whether patterns of population growth and income migration are associated with 'new' and 'old' West economies. Rural restructuring in the U.S. has created a group of counties with service-based economies. In the Mountain West, a number of counties with service-based economies are located in areas with high levels of environmental or natural amenities, creating what has been termed the 'New West.' Migration to the rural parts of the Mountain West, and the income transfers associated with migration, are increasingly concentrated within these New West counties. Rapid population growth, the changing characteristics of in-migrants, and their spatial concentration in New West counties provide a basis for conflicts over what the rural West is becoming. Key Words: environmental amenities, income migration, New West.

Rural Restructuring and the Environmental Model of Development

According to Galston and Baehler (1995), during the 1980s and into the 1990s, increased international competition in both natural resource commodities and manufactured goods lowered the real prices of natural resources, decreased the importance of primary goods within the national economy, and decreased the amount and/or limited the spread of ruralbased manufacturing in the U.S. Such restructuring has affected types of employment opportunities for rural residents. Brown and Deavers (1988) and Summers, Horton, and Gringeri (1990) document a decline in employment in extractive industries producing primary goods in rural areas, some highly selective growth in manufacturing, and enormous growth in services. McGranahan and colleagues (1986) categorize most of this growth in service sector employment as 'household-oriented' services, including health care, education, retail trade, personal services, entertainment, and recreation.

Population and Income Concentration in the Rural West

If, as has been argued, the new rural economy of the Mountain West follows the environmental model of development, population growth

in rural counties should be concentrating in those counties with growing amenity economies, rather than those in traditional Old West, extractive-based economies. Before this comparison can be made, the New West must first be identified. In order to determine this we used a data-clustering technique to show which counties are closely related to each other in terms of their economic and other geographic characteristics.

data.text: To date, only a handful of studies have empirically investigated the relationship between school locations and their constituencies-i.e., the accessibility of schools. This article makes a contribution by presenting an in-depth case study of school accessibility in three counties in West Virginia. The study utilizes an extensive dataset of distances between students and eighty-four elementary school locations. The study examines whether or not the distribution of travel cost between resident locations (blocks) and schools is equitable on the basis of the density of resident populations and the socioeconomic status (SES) of resident populations. The article also carries the analysis one step further, investigating the effect of access on student achievement. The findings for the first hypothesis indicated that spatial inequities in access to school were substantial and varied by county and school zone. In terms of the relationship between SES and access to schools, results were inconclusive and could be described in the familiar unpatterned inequality paradigm supported by a great deal of accessibility research. The analysis involving student achievement showed that distance to school had a significant and inversely related effect on third-grade test scores. The article concludes by arguing that these exploratory initial findings should be expanded upon in future geography-based studies. First, the finding that significant clusters of poor accessibility indeed exist should be investigated vis-a-vis the implicit assumption in school consolidation planning that school catchment areas conform to some kind of higher rational principle. Second, the findings point to a need for more research regarding the import of socioeconomic status in school accessibility. Finally, the results indicate that access is negatively associated with achievement, but that relationship needs to be scrutinized in greater detail.

Berkeley County is located at the eastern end of the state, within commuting distance (80 miles) of Washington, DC. The county remains rural, but is one of the most affluent counties in West Virginia. Conversely, Jackson County is located at the western

Statistical Methods

Familiar methods are used to analyze the accessibility patterns. For the first hypothesis, I use zero-order correla- tions to measure the strength of linear association between the population density variable (population under eighteen per unit of area) and access (per block). This is extended using an analysis of inequality in access values, weighted by population under eighteen, for each district as a whole. For the second hypothesis, I use a two-sample Wilcoxon rank-sum test (Mann-Whitney two-sample statistic) to test the hypothesis that access and SES are from populations with the same distribution. Finally, after an investigation of spatial effects in the data, I use linear regression analysis (ordinary least squares) to estimate the strength of travel cost (i.e., access) and other variables as predictors of student achievement.

This study examines whether or not the distribution of travel cost between resident locations (blocks) and schools is equitable on the basis of (1) the density of resident populations and (2) the socioeconomic status of resident populations. A third issue carries the analysis one step further to investigate the effect of access on student achievement. These three associated hypotheses are discussed below.

  1. Equality of School Access. There are many reasons why schools are located where they are, and why zone boundaries are drawn as they are. The investigation of access equality asks the question: do school locations and catchment boundaries make geographic sense? In other words, are school locations and the boundaries that define their constituencies drawn in such a way that travel distances are minimized? A working hypothesis is that, within a given school zone, access to school is related to the density of school population (i.e., population under eighteen per areal unit). Hypothetically, access should be directly proportional to population density: blocks with a lower density of school-age population should have lower access, and blocks with a higher density of school-age population should have higher access. Introduction

To date, only a handful of studies have empirically investigated the relationship between school locations and their constituencies-i.e., the accessibility of schools. This article makes a contribution by presenting an in-depth case study of school accessibility in three counties in West Virginia. The study utilizes an extensive dataset of distances between students and eighty-four elementary school locations. The study examines whether or not the distribution of travel cost between resident locations (blocks) and schools is equitable on the basis of the density of resident populations and the socioeconomic status (SES) of resident populations. The article also carries the analysis one step further, investigating the effect of access on student achievement.

The findings for the first hypothesis indicated that spatial inequities in access to school were substantial and varied by county and school zone. In terms of the relationship between SES and access to schools, results were inconclusive and could be described in the familiar 'unpatterned inequality' paradigm supported by a great deal of accessibility research. The analysis involving student achievement showed that distance to school had a significant and inversely related effect on third-grade test scores.

The article concludes by arguing that these exploratory initial findings should be expanded upon in future geography-based studies. First, the finding that significant clusters of poor accessibility indeed exist should be investigated vis-à-vis the implicit assumption in school consolidation planning that school catchment areas conform to some kind of higher rational principle. Second, the findings point to a need for more research regarding the import of socioeconomic status in school accessibility. Finally, the results indicate that access is negatively associated with achievement, but that relationship needs to be scrutinized in greater detail. Key Words: accessibility, community, rural, schools.

Consolidation: Bigger Schools and Longer Bus Rides

School consolidation is usually an unwelcome but persistent phenomenon in rural areas. West Virginia, one of the most rural states in the U.S., has been particularly hard hit by consolidation: between 1987 and 1994, 26 percent of West Virginia schools were closed (Howley 1996). The immediate impacts of this include longer distances between home and school, longer bus rides, bigger schools, and separation of school and community- outcomes that are largely unsought by rural families. Although some recent studies have documented the negative effects of long bus rides, research on busing in general has been virtually nonexistent since the early 1970s, and no one knows what the magnitude of the current problem is (Zars 1998). What is known is that, in most rural states, transportation costs now far exceed other expenditures, such as the cost of feeding school children (Rural Challenge Policy Program 1999b).

Legal Challenges

One of the most important legal battles over consolidation and increased distance between home and school surfaced in West Virginia a few years ago. In 1997, the West Virginia Fourth District Court ruled in favor of parents attempting to block the consolidation of two rural high schools. The case involved the merger of Circleville High School, a school listed on the National Register of Historic Places consisting of 130 students in grades 7-12, and Franklin High School, a school of 500, also spanning grades 7-12, about seventeen miles from Circleville.

The fundamental problem with the consolidation plan lay in the decrease in access to the school for Circleville students. The heart of the issue, parents argued, was that students from Circleville would have to spend sixty to one hundred more minutes on the bus after consolidation, and three-fourths of the students would have to be on the bus more than one and a half hours each day. Some students would have to be on the bus as much as two and a half hours each day, beginning at 6:30 a.m. (Rural Challenge Policy Program 1999a).

data.text: A deficiency common to both the historical debates over loss of agricultural land and the current discussions of urbanization and sprawl is a limited understanding of landuse dynamics beyond the urban fringe. Data aggregated at the county level poorly capture the fine-grained pattern of land-use change beyond the dynamic urban-rural interface. Furthermore, current urban-based definitions are poorly suited to delineate these areas, and low-density, exurban land use is difficult to measure using existing land-cover databases. Urbanization and the conversion of once-agricultural or other natural resource lands to other uses has traditionally been tracked using urban areas, as delimited in the U.S. Census. Urban densities are typically defined as areas with more than 1,0000 people per square mile, or 1.6 people per acre (U.S. Census Bureau 2000). Assuming an average of 2.5 people per housing unit, this translates to roughly 0.7 units per acre, or approximately 1 unit per 1.6 acres. The analytical units used in the census, however, both overbound and underbound areas with urban densities. About one-third of urban areas in 1990 comprised lower-than-urban housing density, thanks to overbounding. But, then, one-third of locations that had urban-level housing densities failed to be included in urban areas as a result of underbounding, which, if counted, would have constituted another 18 million acres of urban area. An increase over time of the average number of acres required per housing unit in exurban and higher-density locations occurred in roughly one-third of U.S. Counties from 1960 to 1990 and persisted from 1990 to 2000. In 2000 roughly 38 million acres were settled at urban densities, and nearly ten times that much land was settled at rates from low, exurban density (as low as one house per 40 acres) to higher rates (LIP to one per to acres). This represents a continuing encroachment on land previously given over to other uses-habitat or agriculture. Practitioners of natural resource management need to recognize the ubiquity of exurban development and better incorporate the fine-scale patterns of land use beyond the urban fringe.

ABSTRACT. A deficiency common to both the historical debates over loss of agricultural land and the current discussions of urbanization and sprawl is a limited understanding of landuse dynamics beyond the urban fringe. Data aggregated at the county level poorly capture the fine-grained pattern of land-use change beyond the dynamic urban-rural interface. Furthermore, current urban-based definitions are poorly suited to delineate these areas, and low-density, exurban land use is difficult to measure using existing land-cover databases. Urbanization and the conversion of once-agricultural or other natural resource lands to other uses has traditionally been tracked using urban areas, as delimited in the U.S. census. Urban densities are typically defined as areas with more than 1,ooo people per square mile, or 1.6 people per acre (U.S. Census Bureau 2000). Assuming an average of 2.5 people per housing unit, this translates to roughly 0.7 units per acre, or approximately i unit per 1.6 acres.

LAND DATABASES

Several commonly available databases are used to track the nation's agricultural and urban land base. The U.S. Census of Agriculture was established in 1840 to provide data on the nation's agricultural resources; data were collected on a decadal

basis before 1920 and on a quinquennial basis thereafter. "Land in Farms" is the primary statistic tallying the conversion of agricultural land, and a rapid decline in farmland acreage is commonly considered an indicator of urbanization. However, because the census only tracks existing farms in any given census and does not survey nonfarm property, details about what a farm was converted to are not collected and must be inferred. That is, only a ceiling can be placed on estimates of the amount of development using census of agriculture data.

data.text: In light of the grave challenges ahead under the Trump administration and the rise of right-wing populism in the West, it is critical that geographers across subdisciplines embrace activist and engaged scholarship. Opportunities for such engagement often emerge organically in our everyday lives at the intersection between personal interests, ethics and commitments, and nascent research agendas. In this article, I share two experiences with community-engaged and activist research: (1) establishing the Los Puentes Spanish-English dual-language immersion program in partnership with a low-income rural North Carolina public school system and (2) collaborating on the Building Austin, Building Injustice participatory action research project with a community-based workers center to document and lobby for improvements to construction workers' conditions in Austin, Texas. Through a situated and positioned personal account, I seek to not only provide two examples of activist research but also illustrate the diversity of encounters and how they can emerge in unlikely places and outside conventional activist arenas. In conclusion, I draw on lessons learned through these experiences to reflect on the various challenges and opportunities for activist scholarship within geography in the future.

Personal Encounters with Community Engaged and Activist Research

From early in my career I was committed to bridging gaps between on-the-ground praxis and academia I experienced on returning to graduate school after working with a rural development nongovernmental organization (NGO) in Peru for two years. I was an ambivalent academic, sharing the concerns expressed to me now by many of my graduate students: I feared that I would spend my career studying people, their suffering, and their problems without actually contributing toward improving circumstances. Initially I identi fi ed more as a community practitioner or applied scholar than an activist, but I came to learn that those labels, although unfair, for many connoted a noncritical, atheoretical, and top-down approach. This did not re fl ect my positionality or my commitment to conduct critical, policy-relevant, theoretically informed empirical research that would bene fi t vulnerable people. Encountering activist scholars and their work proved to be critical in my academic formation and in fi nding a middle space to occupy. Although still not free of anxiety, frustration, and ethical dilemmas surrounding my research, in activist and engaged scholarship I found a path to which to aspire. Throughout my career I was fortunate to have the opportunity to participate in various forms of activist and engaged work through research, teaching, fundraising, service, and volunteering. Often these opportunities emerged progressively at the intersection of personal interests and commitments and na

In light of the grave challenges ahead under the Trump administration and the rise of right-wing populism in the West, it is critical that geographers across subdisciplines embrace activist and engaged scholarship. Opportunities for such engagement often emerge organically in our everyday lives at the intersection between personal interests, ethics and commitments, and nascent research agendas. In this article, I share two experiences with community-engaged and activist research: (1) establishing the Los Puentes Spanish -English dual-language immersion program in partnership with a low-income rural North Carolina public school system and (2) collaborating on the Building Austin, Building Injustice participatory action research project with a community-based workers center to document and lobby for improvements to construction workers ' conditions in Austin, Texas. Through a situated and positioned personal account, I seek to not only provide two examples of activist research but also illustrate the diversity of encounters and how they can emerge in unlikely places and outside conventional ' activist ' arenas.

Personal Encounters with Community Engaged and Activist Research

From early in my career I was committed to bridging gaps between on-the-ground praxis and academia I experienced on returning to graduate school after working with a rural development nongovernmental organization (NGO) in Peru for two years. I was an ambivalent academic, sharing the concerns expressed to me now by many of my graduate students: I feared that I would spend my career studying people, their suffering, and their problems without actually contributing toward improving circumstances. Initially I identi fi ed more as a community practitioner or applied scholar than an activist, but I came to learn that those labels, although unfair, for many connoted a noncritical, atheoretical, and top-down approach. This did not re fl ect my positionality or my commitment to conduct critical, policy-relevant, theoretically informed empirical research that would bene fi t vulnerable people. Encountering activist scholars and their work proved to be critical in my academic formation and in fi nding a middle space to occupy. Although still not free of anxiety, frustration, and ethical dilemmas surrounding my research, in activist and engaged scholarship I found a path to which to aspire.

Student-Centered Methodology

Given the complex layers of factors that are interwoven across multiple socio-spatial spheres to influence student aspirations, we adopted a multimethod approach that included both qualitative interviews with students and parents and a quantitative survey of students. Interviews and surveys were conducted simultaneously in three rural eastern North Carolina counties selected because of their significant growth in Latino population over the past decade. The analysis we present in this article focuses heavily on the in-depth interviews with students, although we present a few selected survey results to support our discussion.

Based on a modified version of the instrument developed by Portes and Rumbaut (2001), we conducted a survey with high school students in one county school system. All eighty-one Latino students were invited to participate, with forty-four completing the survey after obtaining parental consent. The student sample included nineteen females and twenty-five males, of whom thirty-one were foreign-born and forty-two were of Mexican origin. The survey was designed to capture students' own ideas of their academic aspirations, as well as their perceptions of what shaped those aspirations. Questions addressed factors such as home life, school environment and activities, neighborhood characteristics, and access to higher education, among others.

Introduction

The following narratives of liminal citizenships illustrate how macroscale immigration policies impinge on the lives of undocumented students-shaping their hopes, dreams, fears, achievements, and aspirations. These narratives reveal agency-that is, how students play an active role in constructing new forms of citizenship to legitimate their rights to higher education through their achievement, hard work, drive, and desire to contribute to society. These stories also illustrate some of the ways in which legal status plays a role in immigrant reception, subjectivity, and identity formation. Given the space limitations, we present only three students' stories as a touchstone for analysis of the major themes that emerged across interviews, and we also incorporate excerpts from other informants' narratives. The stories and selected quotes are relatively representative of the experiences and sentiments shared by most students. The case of the college graduate is presented in greater depth, as he was able to share his postgraduate and subsequent employment experiences.

Ra´ ul came to the United States just two weeks before his tenth birthday. His parents had been in Florida working in a factory and then moved to rural North Carolina to work in tobacco processing. The following is part of his story, mostly in his own words.

The first thing I remember is being at a gas station and there was a huge American flag waving. I was pretty miserable at first. Kids can be pretty mean sometimes, especially not even knowing what they are saying, but knowing it's not kind. I think they had their own stereotypes and comments they would make, not so much intentional but just a reflection of what they grow up with. You are a product of your environment and surroundings . . . and we are in the South. After a while it wasn't so bad . . . you find the better crowd.

It wasn't actually until high school that I started thinking about things. I never thought about the technicalities; I just always knew I was going to go to college. It wasn't until junior year, laws started getting tougher and then it really hit me senior year because now it's time to start to apply and start thinking about funding . . . that's when everything started happening. It was really tough to face that.

For the longest time in high school I wasn't even comfortable with the fact that I was undocumented. Because somehow I did feel guilty . . . I had done something wrong . . . I felt that maybe they were right. I actually told one of my good friends and she laughed because she thought I was joking. So eventually I thought, 'Why even bother?' It was tough to sit there and smile and pretend you have all these options when you're really struggling to keep your head above water and find a rescue. Looking at schools . . . I didn't even indulge myself in those thoughts because it was just an exercise in imagination.

Despite various barriers facing undocumented students, most have high academic aspirations. Students construct new forms of citizenship, legitimating their claims to higher education access through their achievement. Their liminal status, however, contributes to the formation of conflicted, 'in-between' identities. Latino Students in the U.S. South

Since the 1990s, the southern United States has experienced a dramatic increase in its Latino population. In some North Carolina counties, the proportions of Latinos within student populations have reached as high as 25 percent (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction [NCDPI] 2010). This study focuses on rural eastern North Carolina, 2 which is one of the most economically disadvantaged areas of the state and the nation. Agriculture and concentrated animal feeding operations, primarily hogs and poultry, play a prominent role in the region's economy and in attracting Latino immigrant workers (Torres, Popke, and Hapke 2006).

Using the General Social Survey (GSS) data from 1972 to 2018, we explore this urban-rural schism in party preference by running several ordinary least squares models and specifications. Controlling for individuals' traits, we find that differences in the preference for governmental action to address social problems lie at the heart of this gender gap and are further explained by location. Urban women are far more likely than urban men to call for the government to solve problems of income inequality; rural women, like rural men, are much more likely to emphasize individual responsibility and self-sufficiency.

Hypotheses

The foregoing leads to two hypotheses -that the urban -rural schism in the gender gap is a product of the presence of an urban -rural happiness gradient or the greater compassion of urban women, when also controlling for the many other demographic factors posited in the literature to be related to the gender gap (age, marriage, race and ethnicity, income, education, etc.; Greene, Elder, and Saunders 2006). Fortuitously, by taking those factors into account, broader North -South, blue state -red state differences go away and thus do not feature in what follows.

Figure 3 Variations in General Social Survey responses to compassion questions, by gender.

The modeling strategy is as follows. We focus on differences in party preferences as the dependent variable and regress it on locational variables in two equations, male1 and female1, to verify the existence of the urban -rural gradient in the gender gap. We then control for demographic factors that influence party preference in models male2 and female2, per Greene, Elder, and Saunders (2006), to confirm that the gender gap still exists in the presence of these influences. The third pair of variables (male3 and female3) tests for the influence of variations in happiness, and the fourth pair (male4 and female4) tests for the effects of compassion. Details of the variables used follow. We also ran additional robustness tests and tested our models for interaction effects between the gender variable and the main inde

The Dependent Variable

The dependent variable was constructed from the GSS question:

Generally speaking, do you usually think of yourself as a Republican, Democrat, Independent, or what?

Democrat (ASK A) 2

Independent (ASK B) 3

Other (SPECIFY AND ASK B) 4

No Preference (ASK B) 8

A. Would you call yourself a strong (Republican/ Democrat) or not?

Strong 1

Not very strong 2

B. Do you think of yourself as closer to the Republican or Democratic Party?

Republican 3

Responses to this question enabled us to classify each GSS respondent into one of the following categories:

  1. Strong Democrat
  2. Other Democrat
  3. Independent-leaning Democrat
  4. Centrist independent
  5. Independent-leaning Republican
  6. Other Republican
  7. Strong Republican

For the years 1972 to 2018, the GSS yielded 64,814 individual observations (28,614 men and 36,200 women). Although the dependent variable is ordinal, several recent studies have shown ordered logit and ordinary least squares (OLS) to be comparable (Ferreri-Carbonell and Frijters 2004; Van Praag, Van Praag, and Ferrer-i-Carbonell 2004; Blanchflower and Oswald 2011); thus, to test our model we employed OLS. 6

Location

The first pair of models regress party preference on place of residence to confirm the presence of the gender gap using the GSS ' s classification of cities with greater than 250,000 population, cities with population between 50,000 and 250,000, and suburbs, with rural areas as the base case. The varying presence of the gender gap is assessed by comparing the coefficients associated with these variables in the two models.

Control Variables

The second pair of models controls for the GSS respondents ' social and demographic characteristics; that is, by the individual differences in party preference revealed by earlier researchers: income, highest year of school completed, marriage, race (black household), national origin (foreign born), and condition of health. Other candidate variables were omitted to avoid problems with multicollinearity. Information on each of these variables also came from the GSS. Income was specified by quintiles. By including these variables, we were able to control for connections between life course and party preferences that result from the interplay of aspirations and attainments. Early in life, women are more likely than men to fulfill their material and family life aspirations, but as they move into the retirement years this advantage is reversed. Men surviving to old age benefit disproportionally from the positive effect of retirement, whereas women suffer disproportionally from the adverse effects of widowhood (Easterlin 2003; Plagnol and Easterlin 2008). 7

Adam Okulicz-Kozaryn

During the Reagan Revolution, a significant gender gap emerged, accompanied by an urban -rural schism in party preference by gender, one manifestation of the nation ' s widening urban -rural divide. Using the General Social Survey (GSS) data from 1972 to 2018, we explore this urban -rural schism in party preference by running several ordinary least squares models and specifications. Controlling for individuals ' traits, we find that differences in the preference for governmental action to address social problems lie at the heart of this gender gap and are further explained by location. Urban women are far more likely than urban men to call for the government to solve problems of income inequality; rural women, like rural men, are much more likely to emphasize individual responsibility and self-sufficiency. Key Words: compassion, gender gap, political geography, social geography, urban -rural schism.

A Gap and a Schism

During the 1980s, the electorate moved toward the Republican Party, men more than women, as can be seen in Figure 1. The resulting cleavage, the ' gender gap ' (Wirls 1986, 316), was firmly established by the 1990s when a surge of voters self-identifying as independents stemmed further Republican gains. By then women had become ' the majority of the Democratic party by default and not by active realignment, ' even as their support for the Democrats sagged from preReagan levels (Wirls 1986, 327; also see Miller 1991).

Figure 1 Political affiliation by gender, 1972 -2018.

Figure 2 Party preference by location and gender, 1972 -2018.

Contrasting Explanations

As noted, there are both male- and female-centered explanations for the emergence of the gender gap but very little on its spatial variation, despite Kofman and Peake ' s (1990) call for a gendered approach to political questions in geography. Indeed, a web search located only four papers that specifically discuss the geography of the gender gap, although there is a literature on urban -rural and urban -suburban voting patterns in the United States. Each of these papers was concerned with the decline of the Old South. Norrander (1999) stated that the gender gap emerged because, during the Reagan realignment, both men and women in the South became more Republican, whereas in the North only men ' s party preferences shifted rightward; those of northern women remained the same.
