Data: The Michigan Agricultural Tourism Survey

Until recently, little systematic research had been done to evaluate the economic impact (income, wages, taxes) of the increasingly important agritourism businesses in Michigan. This is because, first, state government leaders are still not sure who should collect the data and promote agritourism. The traditional state tourism department, Travel Michigan, is just now considering how to promote these farm businesses, once considered as out of their area. The MDA has an Agricultural Development Division with five full-time employees, but no one is assigned solely to promoting agritourism, though some in the office feel more attention must be paid to agritourism development if and when the state budget crisis eases (Craig 2005). Second, given the great diversity in the types of operations, it is difficult to collect comparable data in a large enough sample to make statistically sound generalizations. Only with a significant sample size can any reliable generalizations be made regarding the economic importance of these operations.

After discussions with the heads of some growers groups who helped with recruiting, in 2003 members of the project team convened three Michigan agritourism focus groups in three parts of the state: in Kalamazoo (southwest Michigan), Ellsworth (northwest lower peninsula), and Flint (approximately 50 miles north of Detroit) with the eventual goal of implementing a systematic agritourism survey. Agricultural tourism incorporates visits to farms for the purposes of on-site retail purchases, enjoyment, and education. Long popular in the European Union (EU), agritourism is gaining popularity throughout the United States. Interest has grown as a result of stagnant grain prices, rising farm costs, and growing international competition. For rural areas seeking new economic options, the potential of these operations to generate new sources of income through sales and horizontal linkages to other tourism-based activities has sparked interest beyond the farm gate. The Challenge of the Global Marketplace

Agriculture has always been an uncertain business. Global trade patterns have changed dramatically in recent decades for all agricultural commodities, including corn, barley, sorghum, rice, wheat, soybeans, cotton, tobacco, fruits, vegetables, essential oils, and other specialty crops such as honey. Most experts include the following factors as root causes of the current reorganization of the global food, drug, and fiber system: (1) the inclusion of agricultural products in the 1994 World Trade Organization (WTO)agreementshas brought new producers such as Canada, Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, and even China into the global marketplace (Knox, Agnew, and McCarthy 2003); (2) livestock and avian diseases within the United States, and more importantly abroad, have slowed both meat/poultry exports and domestic meat consumption, reducing domestic and international grain demand; and (3) trade/consumer disagreements regarding the safety and environmental impacts of genetically modified (GM) grains, oil crops, tobacco, and cotton have lowered demand for some GM varieties of these products, while dampening overall demand for U.S.

Agritourism as a Response to Agricultural Restructuring

Declining exports and changes in rural land use are related to the growth potential for Michigan agritourism. Although agritourism has taken place in areas such as alpine Austria for nearly one-hundred years (Pevetz 1991), it has recently become a key strategy in the EU's 1992 and 1996 Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) to diversify agricultural economies impacted by cost-price squeezes and the technological treadmill (Busby and Rendle 2000; Nilsson 2002). Agritourism, which is supported by structural adjustment funding in the EU, fits into the multifunctional European model of agriculture. Agriculture is viewed as key to maintaining food production/security, rural landscapes, and environmental protection (Hollander 2003). In agrarian-touristic peripheries not suited for intensive agriculture, but where the primary, secondary, and tertiary sectors are coordinated and local specialties are produced for local consumption and export, tourism and related land uses can result in interregional transfer of external resources and endogenous development (Conrad 1990).

data.text: Family farms have long generated income from agricultural tourism including U-picks, wagon rides, corn mazes and petting zoos, but contemporary agricultural tourism reflects much greater sophistication in terms of product variety, services, activities, and marketing. In Michigan, farm operators have moved beyond classic products and activities and the traditional consumer base. New sources of revenue derive from classes on beer, cider, mead and wine making, yarn spinning, perfume/soap-making, farm markets, fishing, educational classes, school tours and hospitality including weddings and on-farm restaurants. This case study of Michigan agricultural tourism reports results from a systematic survey of 154 agritourism operations conducted throughout the state during summer and fall of 2013 with a focus on the economic benefits of the fast-changing sector. This study summarizes tax revenues, sales and employment trends for the farm operations participating in the survey but also quantitatively assesses the contribution of agricultural tourism to Michigan's economy through an extrapolation of the sample to estimate state-wide totals. Results from OLS multivariate regression analysis intended to identify relationships between employment, advertising and scale to gross sales per day are also reported. These analyses show the importance of agricultural tourism to rural and peri-urban places in Michigan and throughout the nation, while raising concerns about a growing division between large and small operators and what this growing gap may mean for the future of the sector.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION

This case study is based on a survey of agricultural-tourism operations in Michigan conducted from May to November of 2013 . The survey was preceded by qualitative research, consisting of a set of focus groups and a series of interviews, to help define the main issues as seen from the perspective of Michigan's agricultural-tourism farms. Coordinated by the Michigan Agritourism Association (MATA), three focus groups, each consisting of seven to ten specialty crop agricultural-tourism operators, were convened in Lansing, Traverse City, and Kalamazoo. In addition, site visits were made to sixteen operations around the state, resulting in longer, recorded depth interviews. The questionnaire was informed by results from the focus groups and interviews, combined with a review of current literature.

The six page survey had four sections: basic information on the firm (opening/closing dates, hours of operation, inventory of products sold, number of full-time and part time staff, and advertising costs and venues); Likert-type scale items on the benefits of respondent operations to customers; Likert-type scale items related to problems and benefits of direct on-farm sales; and perceived economic benefits of their agricultural-tourism operations to the state, the operators of the business, and employees (income, revenues, wages). AN EXPANDING DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL TOURISM

Identifying a sector-wide term that incorporates all activities and dimensions of agricultural tourism has proven quite difficult (Barbieri et al., 2015 ). This lack of agreement regarding the breadth and depth of agricultural tourism goes beyond the mere need for an appropriate consensus term. Rather, the different terms used in legally binding laws and regulations related to agricultural tourism are different for different states. Specifically, what farmers legally call the services provided by their operations may importantly include or exclude their

farms from 'Right to Farm' legislation, subsidized insurance programs, signage permits, entrepreneurship classes, extension support programs, association advertising, health department regulations, and even liability insurance programs (Bagi and Reader 2012 ; Barbieri 2013 ; Rogerson and Rogerson 2014 ; Barbieri et al., 2015 ; Knowd 2015 ). What to call these activities matters to consumers, but more importantly -in a legal sense -to farm operators and those that manage them.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION

This case study is based on a survey of agricultural-tourism operations in Michigan conducted from May to November of 2013 . The survey was preceded by qualitative research, consisting of a set of focus groups and a series of interviews, to help define the main issues as seen from the perspective of Michigan's agricultural-tourism farms. Coordinated by the Michigan Agritourism Association (MATA), three focus groups, each consisting of seven to ten specialty crop agricultural-tourism operators, were convened in Lansing, Traverse City, and Kalamazoo. In addition, site visits were made to sixteen operations around the state, resulting in longer, recorded depth interviews. The questionnaire was informed by results from the focus groups and interviews, combined with a review of current literature.

Introduction

S ince its inception (Luo and Wang 2003), the twostep floating catchment area (2SFCA) method has become a popular measure of spatial accessibility, particularly in its application to health care access (McGrail 2012). Spatial access emphasizes the importance of spatial separation between supply (i.e., facilities) and demand (i.e., population) and how they are connected in space (Joseph and Phillips 1984). The 2SFCA method captures two important aspects of spatial accessibility valued by people: proximity to service providers and availability of service while its scarcity matters. Many subsequent improvements to the original 2SFCA method have focused on different ways of conceptualizing the distance decay behavior and can be integrated into a generalized 2SFCA framework, where the distance decay function takes a continuous form, a discrete variable or a hybrid between them (Wang 2012). In essence, the method yields an accessibility score that is the ratio of supply and demand, each of which interacts with the other in distance decay. It measures the convenience of residents at a location reaching and obtaining a service that might be provided by multiple facilities.

From the preceding review, the 2SFCA is resident (or demand) oriented and assesses residents ' relative ease of getting a service from a residential location. By turning the regular 2SFCA upside down, this article proposes a method for examining an equally important property on the supply side. In other words, by switching the supply and demand terms in the formulation of 2SFCA, we have an inverted 2SFCA (i2SFCA) to measure, for lack of a better term, the ' crowdedness ' (or busyness, saturation, or stress level) for a service provided at a facility. To my knowledge, there has been no work reported in the literature on such an approach.

  1. Is there any theoretical foundation for this approach?
  2. What is the connection between the regular and inverted 2SFCA methods?
  3. Can we validate the method in an empirical setting?
  4. How can the method help us enhance our research and practice in real applications (e.g., health care)?

The remainder of the article attempts to answer these questions. The fi rst section review the regular 2SFCA and derive the i2SFCA method from a Huffbased model to solidify its theoretical foundation. The next section illustrates the implementation of i2SFCA in a case study of measuring crowdedness of hospitals in Florida. Based on the case study, the next section compares the results from 2SFCA and i2SFCA and examines the connection between them. After that, I provide some validation of the i2SFCA results and discuss possible follow-up applications. The article concludes with a brief summary.

data.text: The article begins with a historical account of Hudson's rural settlement theory and the various attempts to replicate Hudson's research. Harvey's exhortation by our theories you shall know us is discussed as a motivation for replication. Motivations not considered are the detection of fraud, mendacity, and incompetence, because these are the domain of reproducible research. Replication research in medicine, psychology, economics, and criminology is reviewed. The varying distinctions between replication and reproducible (R&R) research in each discipline are described. In each discipline the essential papers that have defined the replication crisis and the strategies that researchers have presented are discussed. These strategies include recommendations for systematic reviews and the standardization of research protocols, including the PRISMA and STROBE protocols that are now the accepted format for research in medicine. All four disciplines recommend the use of a formal meta-analysis following the systematic reviews of previous research contributions. There follows a brief discussion of a case study of a meta-analysis in geography that represents a model for others to follow and, second, the suggestion that geographically weighted regression analyses can be seen as a method for replicating the validity of a model across space. The article concludes with a review of the recently developed technology of computer and Jupyter Notebook as a way of facilitating research replication.

Methods for Replication in Geography

The preceding discussion has shown that a common response to replication in several of human geography ' s cognate disciplines has been to engage in systematic reviews accompanied by a meta-analysis of the similar studies. This is true of geography as well. Google Scholar searches of the terms metaanalysis , geography , and geographical do reveal numerous papers, but they tend to be primarily in the medical literature, looking at geographical aspects of diseases and medical conditions including, for example, obesity and cancers (see Clifford et al. 2005; Wang and Beydoun 2007). Khatami, Mountrakis, and Stehman (2016) and Grekousis (2019) both adopted the PRISMA protocol discussed earlier in their systematic reviews of the literature prior to their meta-analyses. It is disappointing that geography as a discipline does not have its own protocol for a systematic review. It is hoped that this will change.

Also prevalent are meta-analyses in the environmental and ecological literature. An early example of the latter is Bender, Contreras, and Fahrig ' s (1998) meticulously documented and well-cited meta-analysis of the patch size effect on habitat loss and population decline. Since that paper was published, there have been many developments in terms of methodologies and software for conducting meta-analyses.

Geographically Weighted Models: Testing Theories across Space

Geographically weighted models, regressions, and discriminant analysis are a particularly attractive and potentially highly visual way in which to test theories about relationships across space. GWR has been used widely since its introduction by Brunsdon and others in 1996. Geographically weighted models are ' replication machines ' : The same model with slightly varying data is replicated across a landscape of data points. It is therefore of great interest when the data change and the replication fails. Essentially, it shows how the estimates of the model ' s variable coefficients will change over space and that replication is not necessarily a problem but an opportunity for insights (similar to spatial autocorrelation; Goodchild 1986). There might indeed be a reason why the details of a model that works in one location will not be applicable in another area. The first country studied was Peru. Motivations: Testing Rural Settlement Theory

T he year 1969 was a watershed with respect to exploration; two men were the first to land on the moon. It was also a defining moment for some in geography. Harvey (1969) published Explanation in Geography , his paean to a scientific approach. Harvey was honored in 2012 by the University of Bristol with an honorary degree. The university orator, Larner (2012), described the immense impact made by Harvey ' s book, noting that it began by stating ' by our theories you shall know us. ' That is actually how Harvey ended the book, not how he began it (Harvey 1969, 486). In 1969 I started studying for a degree in geography at Cambridge University. Harvey ' s book was required reading. The same year, Hudson (1969) published his Theory of Rural Settlement and that, too, was required reading in a department that had five historical geographers, one of whom was Henry Clifford Darby, the head of the department. Hudson ' s theory adopted a scientific approach to the early colonial settlement of Iowa and used point pattern analysis to study how the spacing of settlements changed from a clustered to a more regular pattern as population density increased.

Replication in Geography  s Cognate Disciplines

In the leitmotif earlier, Tokarczuk (2018) was indeed channeling (irresistible pun intended) Heraclitus ' s warning, ' You cannot step twice into the same river. ' If the Greek philosopher is correct, is there ever any possibility of reproducing or replicating research in the discipline of academic geography, or is it a chimera, a wild goose chase, as Gould (1970) once famously argued with respect to statistical analysis in geography? With respect to the use of statistics in geography, technological advances to recognize and remove spatial autocorrelation prior to the application of statistical models and to apply, for example, geographically weighted models to highlight local variation have all helped to inspire a renaissance in the statistical analysis of geographical variation (see following discussion). Similarly, N € ust and Pebesma (2020) and Sui and Kedron (2020) both suggest, in part, technological solutions, including the use of computer notebook technology (see comments later relating to Jupyter Notebook), to assist reproducibility and replication (R&R) in current geographical research.

Replication in Medicine: Galvanizing Complacency

Medicine realized that it had a problem in reproducing and replicating results when Ioannidis (2005) published his iconoclastic paper declaring that the results of most medical research were false. To help mitigate the likelihood of publishing false results, Ioannidis and his colleagues implicitly endorsed a meta-analysis (Uitterlinden et al. 2006) and then subsequently published guidelines for systematic reviews and analyses in medical research. Three years later they published two widely cited articles on the PRISMA approach: Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analysis (Liberati et al. 2009; Moher et al. 2009). This, together with the STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) protocol (Von Elm et al. 2007), has since become the de facto standard for meta-analysis in medical and epidemiological research.

data.text: Most of the United States was surveyed before settlement with a rectangular survey system called the Public Land Survey (PLS). Surveyors mapped out square townships that were subdivided into one-square-mile sections that could in turn be further divided for sale or homesteading. The system began in northwest Ohio and spread westward through the Midwest and across the Great Plains. Farms took the form of these squares, roads ran along section lines, and county and other boundaries were aligned along them. The effects of the PLS in rural areas are well known; the rectangular survey produced a characteristic checkerboard pattern in agricultural areas and resulted in higher road densities in surveyed areas. The survey is often treated as homogenous, and a ubiquitous sign of federal authority inscribed on the land. This statement is not true in the Intermountain West; although the PLS was applied throughout this area, the extent of the PLS landscape in the interior West is small. There are several distinct types of gridded landscapes distinguished by the presence of agriculture and urbanization. The future spread of these landscapes is likely to be limited, although some will likely shift between types.

Methods and Data

This article agrees with Wyckoff ' s (2014) tenet that ' It is the predictable rectangularity of the sectionline roadscape that most clearly reveals the survey system in the rural West ' (248). Mapping section line roads provides an effective way of mapping the PLS landscape, but this is easier said than done.

Figure 3 Area surveyed according to Public Land Survey (PLS).

Section line roads are not a distinct or meaningful category of roads; the Federal Highway Administration ' s Highway Performance Monitoring System is the nation ' s database on highways, but it does not distinguish section line roads as it does for roads with different ownership, number of lanes, pavement type and condition, traffic, or level of access control (Federal Highway Administration 2019). Geographic information systems (GIS) street networks (whether TIGER or from other sources) include no attributes identifying roads along section lines.

There is no simple GIS methodology that can be used to identify section line roads. Like survey lines, streets in GIS are represented by lines with no dimension but length. There is no reason why these road lines would match up exactly with survey lines or boundaries, allowing them to be selected using a simple spatial overlay (Tresidder 2005). data.text: In the twenty-first century, there are three American Wests, which cut across cultural, political, physical, and economic boundaries. Parts of the West are booming, building homes, and adding population; others are legally off limits to such development; and much of the West has been bypassed by such development and growth. These are called here the Booming West, Protected West, and Bypassed West. Maps of climate, political boundaries, ethnic and racial identities, or presidential voting patterns do not match these three Wests. Each West has a different relationship to the others and might see them as threats or opportunities, and each West can be expected to grow in different areas at the expense of other Wests. The boundaries between the three Wests could be important locations; sharp transitions can exist between Wests, perhaps nowhere more so than where a fast growing metro area abuts a national park or forest boundary. Finally, the effects of climate change cut across the three Wests and have different implications for their future. Continued population growth will further emphasize the boundaries between each of the three Wests and raise the stakes for their control.

The Three Wests Defined

The Booming West is defined by growth, perhaps most commonly of population. Much of this has taken place in fast growing urban areas, and for that reason this region could be called the urban or metropolitan West. This is misleading, because many booming areas are too small or exist at too low a level of density to warrant the name urban. Sedona, Arizona, and Mammoth Lakes, California, are seasonal resorts and retirement destinations that might not meet traditional notions of urbanity but are very much part of the Booming West. Exurban or rural development in the form of ranchettes purchased by newcomers in states such as Colorado is another example; as with cities, the amenities that attracted people to these areas are threatened by their construction (Shumway and Otterstrom 2001; Harner and Benz 2013).

The Booming West is based not on the Old West extractive industries of the past but on an amenity-based or service economy. Scenery, outdoor recreation, and perceptions of a pleasant climate can attract residents and employers (Powers 1996). The Booming West therefore encompasses much of what has been defined as the New West, although defined based on the footprint of its growth rather than standard census or other boundaries.

Although many well-known places in this West have existed in some form since the 1700s or even earlier (Meinig 1998; Moehring 2004; Abbott 2008), the current Booming West is really a fairly recent phenomenon, taking root since the end of World War II

Mapping Out the Three Wests

The three Wests can be mapped to show their approximate locations. The Booming West is defined as including all urbanized clusters and areas according to the 2010 Census. These include census blocks added together to encompass settlements with at least 1,500 people outside group quarters (defined as facilities such as prisons, dormitories, or military housing). This definition allows for bodies of water or undeveloped land to allow for noncontiguous settlements and includes airports outside a populated area; city boundaries are not a part of the definition. There are 623 such places within the West.

The Protected West is defined as including national park units, national forests, military bases, Department of Energy land, wildlife refuges, the BLM ' s national monuments and ACECs, and wilderness areas administered by the National Park Service, National Forest Service, and BLM. Indian reservations, as well as state and local parks and private preserves, are also included. Boundaries for these came from the Protected Areas Database of the U.S. (PADUS; U.S. Geological Survey 2017). The Bypassed West is defined as everything not in the Booming or Protected Wests; this includes both private land outside the Booming West as well as BLM lands excluding wilderness or ACECs.

data.text: The COVID-19 pandemic has exacerbated many preexisting challenges facing rural communities and brought tensions in rural-urban relations closer to the surface. This article offers an explorative contribution to discussions in critical geography by comparing media narratives surrounding urban flight to rural places during the COVID-19 pandemic. Comparing field sites in rural Michigan (United States), Ontario (Canada), and the Atlantic bubble (Canada), we use an emerging theorization of the right to be rural to explore how urban flight and rural displacement are tied to concepts of community, identity, and safety. This approach is grounded in the political economy of rurality and emphasizes the power relations, inequalities, and historical contingencies that structure the experiences of full-time and part-time rural residents during the pandemic. Our exploratory discussion surfaces critical tensions in the geographically and socioeconomically uneven implications of the pandemic, including the anxious economic acquiescence experienced in many tourism-dependent rural regions and both the hard and soft ways in which rural regions responded to increased demands for access. We argue that the political economy of rural-urban relations is critical to understanding the social processes that will shape the right to be rural during and after COVID-19.

Introduction

School of Environmental Design & Rural Development, University of Guelph, Canada † Department of Media & Information, Michigan State University, USA ‡ Department of Sociology & Social Anthropology, Dalhousie University, Canada

A sthe novel coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic spread across North America in spring 2020, it simultaneously sharpened rural -urban divides and highlighted rural -urban linkages (cf. Weeden 2020b; Maclaren and Philip 2021). Governments across all jurisdictions wrestled with whether and how to require people to stay apart, or stay home, to keep everyone safe. Public health interventions involved limiting travel and movement at international, interregional, and interhousehold scales. North American jurisdictions used a blend of ' hard ' (i.e., punishable with a fine or arrest) and ' soft ' restrictions, the latter appealing to individual responsibility and relying on social pressure. Rural regions with low virus case counts early in the pandemic faced a rising tide of people with means looking to escape from urban ' hot spots ' (Petersen 2020). Although some local tourism initiatives tepidly welcomed the tide, encouraging ' staycations ' in nearby communities, many rural individuals and communities pleaded with people to stay home

(Petersen 2020). The dissonance between such conflicting responses produces poignant commentary about how economic class, geography, and rights frameworks have collided during the pandemic.

With little certainty about when and how abruptly the COVID-19 pandemic will end (even as effective vaccines spread across the Global West), it is important to examine its impact on rural -urban dynamics, as pandemic-driven waves of urban flight threaten to displace existing rural people and communities and redraw the map of where people live. We draw on the political economy of rurality to contribute to a growing body of critical conversations in geography about place, power, and policy in contemporary rural life -the intersection of which is increasingly framed as the ' right to be rural ' and constitutes the lens through which we explore media coverage of rural -urban dynamics during the pandemic (Foster 2018a, 2018b; Foster and Main 2020; Weeden 2020a, 2020b, 2020c; Foster and Jarman 2021). By examining key media narratives from our respective field sites in Michigan, Ontario, and Atlantic Canada (see Figures 1 and 2), we explore the power relations, inequalities, and historical contingencies that structure the experiences of both full-time and part-time rural residents during the pandemic. We argue that inherent tensions in accessing or acquiring a ' right to be rural ' are central to regional COVID-19 experiences, conflicts, and inequalities.

The Right to Be Rural?

French sociologist Henri Lefebvre ' s 1968 ' right to the city ' proposed the reclamation of urban life from capitalist, individual entitlements by putting community experiences at the heart of civic decision making (Lefebvre 1996; Harvey 2003, 2008). Civic movements around the globe subsequently picked up the ' right to the city ' as a resistance cry against gentrification, privatization, and the encroachment of neoliberal capitalism into civic life. Rural scholars (Barraclough 2013), including ourselves (Foster 2018a, 2018b; Foster and Main 2020; Weeden 2020a, 2020b, 2020c; Foster and Jarman 2021), have asked whether there is also a ' right to the rural. data.text: Northern Wisconsin's tourism economy has drawn the attention of scholars interested in the economic linkages that exist between it and sending areas in the urban and suburban Upper Midwest. Interrelationships between the two areas have left an indelible mark on the rural landscape through the presence of lakefront vacation homes owned by nonresidents. Where are these properties located, and where do the nonresident landowners call home? Geospatial data for 816,000 parcels, provided by the Wisconsin State Cartographer's Office, are utilized to reveal the extent and value of nonresident property in the Northwoods. Schumpeter's theory of Creative Destruction is used as a framework to explain the emergence of tourism-dependent communities in the region, and case studies reveal the impacts of nonresident property taxes on public school funding. These findings suggest that as population in the Northwoods declines in upcoming years, communities will increasingly rely on nonresident investment to sustain local institutions.

<<A-HEAD>> METHODS

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT Determining the extent of the study area required conversations about the boundaries of the Northwoods region, as it is considered as much a vernacular region as a formal region. An academically intuitive definition would include the calculation of forest cover and population density, but it is common for people to use a highway intersection, river crossing, a vista of rolling hills covered in pine trees, or a roadside bait shop as cognitive indicators that they have arrived (Nelson 2017). For the purposes of this study, the Northwoods includes twenty-one counties in the northern third of the state (Figure 1). Most of this vast, 21,000 square mile (13.44 million acre) region is covered with stands of mixed hardwood and softwood trees, concentrations of freshwater lakes attributed to the geologically recent Wisconsin glacial period, and pockets of agricultural land that remain from the cutover period of the nineteenth century. The western, southern, and eastern margins of the study area transition from heavily forested landcover commonplace in the interior to the agricultural landscape for which Wisconsin is recognized.

[Insert Figure 3, photo of Northland Pines High School, here]

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT To gauge the impact of second-home ownership in the areas throughout the Northwoods, a detailed analysis of parcel ownership was conducted for the each of the four school districts. Figures 3--6 identify the total number of parcels owned by locals, Wisconsin residents who are not local, Minnesota, Illinois, and 'Other' areas. These figures also show the value of the parcels owned by the same groups of parcel owners. Though the Hayward School District is the largest in total area (358,590 acres), Northland Pines, the third largest among the four at 141,864 acres, holds the highest total assessed private property value, at more than $3 billion. Hayward comes in at a close second with $2.7 billion. The wealth of both districts is tied more to second homeowners than either Hurley or Grantsburg. Both Hayward and Northland Pines are owned by only 44 percent and 42 percent local residents, respectfully, while Hurley is nearly owned by 50 percent locals and Grantsburg by 66 percent of the local population. The resulting land values in each of the school districts is also reflected by total tax revenues.

The primary residences of parcel landowners in these school districts differs greatly between them. In all cases, the largest ownership of parcels is among local residents, followed by nonlocal Wisconsin residents, mainly from the Milwaukee and Madison metropolitan areas. Minnesota residents comprise the third highest number of landowners in the Grantsburg and Hayward school districts---not surprising given their proximity. Residents of Upper Michigan outnumber other out-of-state landowners in Hurley, and Illinois residents held the third highest number of parcels in the Northland Pines School District. Data derived from the WSCO indicate that the property controlled by nonlocal Wisconsin residents and out-of-state residents is assessed higher than the property of permanent residents, particularly in the Hayward and Northland Pines school districts.

data.text: Contrary to recent literature that portrays the High Plains as an over-exploited region of economic and demographic decline and as place that should be deprivatized, abandoned, and restored to a buffalo commons, this study suggests that the irrigated Ogallala region is not dying. It is experiencing, instead, a major redistribution of population into nucleated Ogallala oases sustained by the presence of ample groundwater for irrigation. Although more remote rural areas with irrigated agriculture are losing population, they endure nonetheless as important components of the cultural landscape in their role as hinterlands for the Ogallala oases. This paper examines the relationship between proximity to groundwater use and population change in the Ogallala aquifer region of Kansas during the 1980s. The analysis focuses on three levels; the county, incorporated and census designated places, and rural census county subdivisions. The association between proximity to groundwater and population change is statistically significant among counties, among places larger than 500 inhabitants, and among more densely-populated rural areas. Groundwater use is not associated, however, with population change in places with fewer than 500 people or in sparsely-populated rural census county subdivisions. These patterns of population change are not merely reflections of historical inertia. They are better explained by active responses to the advantages of agglomeration and access to ground-water than to the passive unfolding of past patterns of population redistribution. In this context, a triage-type development policy that favors Ogallala oases larger than 500 inhabitants seems a more appropriate response to regional problems than the alternatives of growth poles, service sharing strategies, outright abandonment, or laissez-faire.

Groundwater Use and Population Change

Multiple regression analyses of the association between groundwater use per unit area and the population change (in percent) between 1980 and 1990 in western Kansas are conducted at three different scales: county, place, and rural county subdivision. Standardized regression coefficients (Beta weights) are examined to measure the relative importance of the independent variables.

County Level

A comparison of the maps of county population change 1980-1990 (Figure 3) and groundwater use in 1990 (Figure 2) suggests a strong, positive association. An initial regression equation of eleven independent variables is reduced to six in order to eliminate problems of multicollinearity. These variables-size of the

largest place in 1980; groundwater use per square mile in 1990; per capita income in 1980; the percentage of farm employment in 1980; the percentage change in farm size between 1978 and 1987; and the percentage change in irrigated acres between 1978 and 1987-account for sixty-two percent of the variance in the population change between 1980 and 1990 (Table 1).

An examination of Beta weights reveals that population change is most closely associated with the size of the largest place in the county. Groundwater use per square mile in 1990, however, is the second most important factor and it contributes significantly to explanation of population change when controlling for the other independent variables. Importantly, the inclusion of reported groundwater use as an independent variable yields a higher level of explanation than has been the case for other studies that have used irrigated acreage as the indicator for water use.

The county-level analysis suggests a strong association between population growth and the size o f the place, and that association is confirmed upon examining the 91 incorporated or census-designated places in western Kansas between 1960 and 1990 (Figure 4 and Table 2). Surprisingly, only places with fewer than 500 inhabitants have collectively lost population since 1960. Places between 500 and 999 inhabitants experienced very close to zero growth, and places 1,000 or larger tended t o gain population. The population of the three largest cities, Dodge City, Garden City, and Liberal, increased by almost 58 percent and they accounted for much of the region's total growth. While small places have not fared well, larger towns in western Kansas defy the stereotypical regional image of decay and despair. Indeed, population growth in the three largest places is well above the national average. More generally, incorporated and census-designated places grew by about 21 percent between 1960 and 1990 while the remainder of the region declined by about 22 percent.

The impact of selective outmigration i s reflected by the median age of a place's inhabitants. In 1990, median age varies inversely with size of place; median age ranges from 39.6 years in the smallest places (less than 500 inhabitants) to only 28.5 years in the three largest cities.

Introduction

This, finally, is the punch line of our two hundred years on the Great Plains. We . . . harvest wave after wave of immigrants' dreams and send the wised-up dreamers on their way; plow the top soil until it blows to the ocean; ship out the wheat, ship out the cattle; dig up the earth itself and burn it in power plants and send the power down the line; dismiss the small farmers, empty the little towns; drill the oil and natural gas and pipe it away; dry up the rivers and springs, (and) deep drill for irrigation water as the aquifer retreats. (Ian Frazier 1989:209-210)

he public image of the High Plains has not fared well in recent years. The percepT tion that it is an exploited region in serious economic and demographic decline has led some to conclude that the problems in the region west of the 98th meridian and east of the Rocky Mountains are of such severity as to warrant deprivatization of the land and restoration of an ecologically safe 'buffalo commons' (Dallas and Aaronson 1990; Matthews 1990; Popper and Popper 1988; 1987). As Paul (1 992) has demonstrated, the reestablishment of the buffalo commons in portions of the southern Canadian prairies is already underway.

The symptoms of regional decline include, among others, low density, the demise of small towns, continuous declines in county populations since the turn of the century, lack of economic opportunity, selective outmigration of the young, an ever-increasing median age, and reductions in the number of small-scale farms and farm population (Burns 1982; Murdock et al. 1986). Like the inhabitants of Appalachia, High Plains residents are often portrayed a s dependent on agriculture and extractive industries, the fates of which are controlled by factors external to their region, and a s people who have little control over their region's destiny. In response to these 'problems,' various policies have been proposed. These range from deprivatization and abandonment to triage approaches that focus resources on needy communities that have a reasonable probability of long-term survival with assistance; from growth-pole strategies at a microscale to growth-pole approaches at the metropolitan scale; and from grass-roots self-help efforts to service sharing among communities (Daniels 1989; White 1992).

Contrary to these portrayals of the High Plains as a withered and exploited place, this study highlights the exceptions that disprove the contention that the High Plains is a 'failed region.' Throughout this alleged desert of despair are 'oases' of growth and economic viability-oases that depend upon their proximity to groundwater and the economic gains attributable to groundwater exploitation. These Ogallala oases are sustaining their populations and their economic well-being over the long term.

Western Kansas

Thirty-two counties in western Kansas constitute a subregion of the six-state, 184-county Ogallala region defined and delimited by the congressionally-mandated High Plains Study (High Plains Associates 1982) (Figure 1). In 1980, the western Kansas portion of the Ogallala aquifer contained more than 245 million acre-feet of drainable water (O'Connor and McClain 1982). Although at least a portion of each county in the study area overlies the Ogallala aquifer, the local availability of groundwater ranges from very abundant to none, often within the same county. Most of the water (over 90 percent) drawn from the Ogallala is used to irrigate crops (Kromm and White 1981). The role of groundwater has increased as the availability of surface water has declined. Since 1960, mean annual stream flow has decreased substantially partly due to a decline in base flow brought about by groundwater depletion and partly because of more efficient on-the-farm water conservation measures. Runoff to streams has declined by one-half in western Kansas since 1959 (Ratzlaff 1992).

Causes of Population Decline in the High Plains

The long-term decline of population in the High Plains has various causes, among which are: environmental degradation, technological change, economic development constraints, demographic structure, and external factors. Environmental conditions include droughts, floods, pestilence, as well as human activities that exceed the carrying capacity of the land. The impact of the dust-bowl era of the 1930s on the demise of the Plains is still used as an example to support the notion that the Plains i s unsuited for cultivation (Weber 1991 ; Popper and Popper 1988; 1987). A 1937 study commissioned by Congress concludes that "even the relatively small population of the Great Plains cannot be sustained adequately . . . [and that] the explanation lies as much in unwise land use as in climate and other natural conditions." In addition to concerns about over-cultivation, overstocking of range lands, and uncaring absentee owners, the report also mentions unbalanced withdrawal and depletion of groundwater supplies as a major problem for sustainability (U.S. House of Representatives 1937:39).

data.text: Deregulation introduced by the 1996 Telecommunications Act brought unprecedented change to broadcasting, including the consolidation of independent radio stations within mega-networks. Acting in response to decreasing diversity in station ownership, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) launched low-power FM (LPFM) radio in 2000. In the FCC's vision, thousands of community-based radio stations would serve local needs and increase diversity in programming and station ownership. However, despite its potential for serving urban minorities and improving connections between stations and local communities, fewer than 1,200 LPFM radio stations were established between February 2000 and July 2007. In this article we examine the distribution of LPFM stations, efforts by full-power broadcasters to limit LPFM expansion, and groups that have benefited most from the LPFM initiative. Our findings reveal that few LPFM stations have been established in densely populated urban areas that are subject to spectrum crowding. In lieu of helping inner-city minorities, the main beneficiaries of LPFM have been white Americans living in rural areas. Although civic and community organizations have been successful in establishing stations, the greatest number of LPFM stations are operated by religious organizations. This study can be viewed within a broader framework involving diverging interests of national corporations and small communities.

Methods and Findings

As noted by Lucas (2006), instead of thousands of new community-based licenses forecasted by the FCC, the LPFM initiative resulted in just 1,200. Geographic information system (GIS) software is used to evaluate the influence of full-power station crowding on LPFM stations. An FCC database containing the locations of 9,169 full-power FM stations is used to examine station density. After plotting each full-power station's antenna location using latitude and longitude coordinates, a circular buffer with a twenty-mile radius is created around each station. It should be noted that the twenty-mile radius introduces a slight bias into the results because radio signals travel farther over flat terrain or when taller antenna heights or higher power levels are used. However, the twenty-mile radius is determined to provide a representative area of reception for full-power stations. Subsequently, station competition is evaluated by identifying the number of full-power stations contained within each buffer. The number of other stations within each buffer ( N -1) ranges from zero in less populated areas with a single full-power station to more than forty in large metropolitan areas.

With 600 KHz between channels, the FM spectrum (88.1-108.1 MHz) can accommodate thirty-three full-power channels. Oklahoma State University

Deregulation introduced by the 1996 Telecommunications Act brought unprecedented change to broadcasting, including the consolidation of independent radio stations within mega-networks. Acting in response to decreasing diversity in station ownership, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) launched low-power FM (LPFM) radio in 2000. In the FCC's vision, thousands of community-based radio stations would serve local needs and increase diversity in programming and station ownership. However, despite its potential for serving urban minorities and improving connections between stations and local communities, fewer than 1,200 LPFM radio stations were established between February 2000 and July 2007. In this article we examine the distribution of LPFM stations, efforts by full-power broadcasters to limit LPFM expansion, and groups that have benefited most from the LPFM initiative. Our findings reveal that few LPFM stations have been established in densely populated urban areas that are subject to spectrum crowding. In lieu of helping inner-city minorities, the main beneficiaries of LPFM have been white Americans living in rural areas.

Background

The Radio and Geographic Research

Terrestrial radio has retained its influence over the last eighty years because of its ubiquity and low cost. An inexpensive radio receiver provides nearly anyone with access to news, music, and other entertainment. In terms of serving listeners, radio stations operate within fixed geographic regions controlled by transmitter power, antenna height, local terrain, and competition from other stations on the same frequency.

Geographic research examining radio is relatively limited in scope. A few studies have looked at the distribution of radio stations (Innis 1954, 1972; Bell 1965; Doucet 1983; Greve 1996; Dimmick and Wang 2005), decentralization associated with broadcasting (H¨ agerstrand 1986), ethnic programming (Carlson 1997; Garner 2006), and radio's role in the context of other communications systems (Abler 1974; Hillis 1998). Studies have also examined the impact of radio on the formation of cultural boundaries (Morley and Robbins 1995; Hangen 2002).

A Look Back at Radio in the United States

Bekken (2000) identifies three categories of radio broadcasting that have evolved within the United States: commercial, public (government sponsored), and community. During the early 1920s, most radio stations were operated by nonprofit entities such as religious organizations, labor unions, civic associations, and educational institutions. Financial support for commercial-free broadcasts came mostly from private donations or corporate sponsors (Mooney 2006). In 1923, 500 radio stations in the United States served approximately 1million listeners and by 1926 nearly two thirds of American households had at least one radio receiver (Liebowitz 2004). In terms of its spatial diffusion, radio grew unevenly across the United States, beginning in large cities with high-power 'clear channel' amplitude modulation (AM) station frequencies.

data.text: Travel accounts of the Reconstruction U.S. South (1865-1880) played a formative role in the process of determining where the region fit within the nation-state after the Civil War. Postbellum travel narratives by northern men and women, in particular, dealt with the South's contradictory placement as both an occupied territory of the North/nation and part of the national body itself through a discourse of imperialism that translated a North-South regional binary into a colonizer-colonized distinction and framed the South as an imperial holding of the U.S. This article uses postcolonial studies and postcolonial geographies of North America to examine three textual themes that sustained this imperial framing of the South within northern travel narratives: discourses of civilization, descriptions of nature, and discussions of whiteness. The first two themes bolstered northern travelers' positioning of the South as an imperial holding, although gender contoured how northern travelers participated in a civilizing mission directed toward newly emancipated African Americans and how easily these travelers assumed the role of imperial explorer in rural and marginal southern sites. By contrast, white rural poverty in the postbellum South, through its simultaneous racial similarity to and class difference from white northern travelers, problematized a clean separation of North from South and highlighted the imperfections and contradictions of the postbellum South as an imperial holding of the North/nation. This article argues for more critical attention to the production of southern difference in the mid-nineteenth century and the postbellum South's place in relation to future American imperial projects.

Postcolonial Studies and Postcolonial Geographies of North America

Postcolonial studies have had powerful impacts across the social sciences and humanities, even if ''the postcolonial has not lent itself to a consensual definition'' (Slater 1998, 652; Sidaway 2000). ''The postcolonial'' can signify both the time period and social conditions following decolonization (Spivak 1995) and a theoretical concept linked to postmodern and poststructural theory and issues of representation and knowledge production (Rattansi 1997; Slater 1998; Venn 1999; Sidaway 2000; Singh and Schmidt 2000). Across these definitions, ideas about ''the postcolonial'' coalesce around questions of power and subjectivity (Pieterse and Parekh 1995; Jacobs 1996; Loomba 1998) and critical attention to ''the mutually constitutive role played by colonizer and colonized, centre and periphery. . . in forming. . . the identities of both the dominant power and the subalterns'' (Memmi 1967/1991; Rattansi 1997, 481; Slater 1998). Postcolonial studies center on the production of difference through a colonizer-colonized binary (Stoler 1995; Stoler and Cooper 1997; Loomba 1998), whose always ambivalent construction marks the failure of complete colonial authority and enables moments of resistance (Bhabha 1986, 1990).

Within postcolonial studies, Edward Said's Orientalism (1978) has been a foundational text (Rattansi 1997; Loomba 1998). Said (1978, 2-3) argued that Orientalism comprises three interconnected facets: a ''European material civilization and culture''; ''a style of thought,'

Critical Engagements with Nineteenth-Century Travel Narratives

The threat of the return of the colonial through the South also haunted the 1860s and 1870s. As northern travel writers and journalists ventured through the postbellum South, their attempts to place the region somewhere within a national body were always fraught with difficulties. Despite these challenges (or perhaps because of them), post-Civil-War travel accounts formed an important aspect of the South's construction as both a place and an object of knowledge in the mid-nineteenth century and affected national policy and opinion in key ways in that time period (Harris 1967; Meinig 1998). In some cases, the travelers who penned these narratives were ''special correspondents employed by leading Northern journals to satisfy the public demand for news of the recently vanquished Confederacy'' (Harris 1967, 2). Their serialized accounts reached large audiences in major northeastern newspapers and periodicals and formed an important means through which northern readers learned of the South, its landscapes, and its peoples.

Postbellum travel narratives can be situated more broadly in the context of nineteenth-century travel writing, a genre that has received critical attention in recent years (Blunt and Rose 1994b; Robertson et al. 1994; Gregory 1995; Rojek and Urry 1997; Duncan and Gregory 1999b). Imperfectly Imperial: Northern Travel Writers in the Postbellum U.S. South, 1865-1880

Jamie Winders

Department of Geography, Syracuse University

Travel accounts of the Reconstruction U.S. South (1865-1880) played a formative role in the process of determining where the region fit within the nation-state after the Civil War. Postbellum travel narratives by northern men and women, in particular, dealt with the South's contradictory placement as both an occupied territory of the North/nation and part of the national body itself through a discourse of imperialism that translated a North-South regional binary into a colonizer-colonized distinction and framed the South as an imperial holding of the U.S. This article uses postcolonial studies and postcolonial geographies of North America to examine three textual themes that sustained this imperial framing of the South within northern travel narratives: discourses of civilization, descriptions of nature, and discussions of whiteness.

Historical Analyses of the South

Although little consensus exists on what the South is or what it constitutes as an object of analysis, the idea that the South is different both from and within the nation-state has provided a powerful construct across southern history and studies. Considered by many scholars to be ''the most distinctive region in the nation'' (Woodward 1968; Degler 1987, 5; Grantham 1994/ 2001), the South has stood as the ''other'' defined in opposition to the North/nation (Woodward 1971; Koeniger 1988; Radford 1992; Carlton 1995; Cobb 2000). Although scholars have shifted from straightforward reiterations of southern distinctiveness to analyses of ''how race, class, gender, etc. [have] shaped individual and group identities in the South'' (Cobb 2000, 23), the final prepositional phrase in this clause, ''in the South,'' remains. That the South is some thing or some where in which identities can be shaped and which itself can impact national history is assumed, leaving the region's epistemological status unexamined. Whether writers pen southern encomiums or expose ´s, the region retains an ontological security grounded in its history and demarcated by the Mason-Dixon line. 2

Postcolonial Studies and Postcolonial Geographies of North America

Postcolonial studies have had powerful impacts across the social sciences and humanities, even if ''the postcolonial has not lent itself to a consensual definition'' (Slater 1998, 652; Sidaway 2000). ''The postcolonial'' can signify both the time period and social conditions following decolonization (Spivak 1995) and a theoretical concept linked to postmodern and poststructural theory and issues of representation and knowledge production (Rattansi 1997; Slater 1998; Venn 1999; Sidaway 2000; Singh and Schmidt 2000). Across these definitions, ideas about ''the postcolonial'' coalesce around questions of power and subjectivity (Pieterse and Parekh 1995; Jacobs 1996; Loomba 1998) and critical attention to ''the mutually constitutive role played by colonizer and colonized, centre and periphery. . . in forming. . . the identities of both the dominant power and the subalterns'' (Memmi 1967/1991; Rattansi 1997, 481; Slater 1998).

data.text: Future climate change impacts on humans will be determined by the convergence of evolving physical climate and socioeconomic systems. Rural areas of the northeastern United States have experienced increased temperature and precipitation extremes, especially over the past three decades, and face unique challenges due to their physical isolation, natural-resource-dependent economies, and high poverty rates. To explore the impacts of future extreme events on vulnerable, rural populations in the Northeast, we analyzed future (2046-2075) annual maximum daily maximum temperature, annual minimum daily minimum temperature, annual maximum daily precipitation, and annual minimum two-week summer precipitation for two greenhouse gas emissions scenarios using four global climate models and gridded temperature and precipitation observations. We then combined those projections with estimates of county-level population and relative income for 2060 to calculate changes in extreme person-events compared to a historical period (1976-2005), with a focus on Northeast counties that are rural (less than 250,000 people) and vulnerable (in the bottom income quartile). For all counties and lowest income quartile counties in the rural Northeast, extreme heat person-events increase nineteen-fold and twenty-nine fold, respectively, under the high greenhouse gas emissions scenario, far exceeding the decrease in extreme cold person-events. The number of extreme precipitation and drought person-events does not significantly change across the rural Northeast. For the high greenhouse gas emissions scenario, counties in the bottom two income quartiles experience the 1976-2005 once-per-year daily heat event twenty-three times per year by 2046-2075; the lower greenhouse gas emissions scenario reduces the incidence to eleven times per year.

Gridded observations were developed by Livneh et al. (2013), hereafter LI2013, for the contiguous United States based on the methods of Maurer et al. (2002). Maurer et al. (2002) has been widely used in water and energy budget studies as well as climate change assessments (Wood et al. 2004; Westerling et al. 2006; Hayhoe et al. 2007; Elsner et al. 2014). LI2013 is derived from daily temperature and precipitation observations from approximately 20,000 National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Cooperative Observer (COOP) stations gridded to a spatial resolution of 1/16  (  7km). Available daily meteorological data include maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation, as well as wind from reanalysis, covering the time period 1915 to 2011 (Livneh et al. 2013). Additional details of LI2013 can be found in Livneh et al. (2013).

Projections of maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation were derived from four realizations of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 multimodel ensemble (CMIP5; Taylor, Stouffer, and Meehl 2012). CMIP5 is the basis for IPCC AR5 (IPCC 2013), heavily informs the U.S. Third National Climate Assessment (NCA; Walsh et al. 2014), and has been extensively evaluated and used for climate change research. Extreme Metrics

We use four extreme climate metrics to assess the impacts of climate change on rural Northeast populations: number of days above the annual (once-per-year) maximum daily maximum temperature (Txax), number of days below the annual minimum daily minimum temperature (Tnan), number of days above the annual maximum daily precipitation (Pax), and number of days below the annual twoweek summer (May -August) precipitation minimum (SPan). There are a variety of extreme event metrics that have been used globally and for the United States (e.g., Frich et al. 2002; Horton et al. 2015; Schoof and Robeson 2016). We choose these metrics based on three criteria. First, metrics must have potential societal impacts for the Northeast. Second, metrics must be event based, such that the number of events multiplied by population yields a meaningful quantity. Third, metrics must be calculated using anomalies to prevent underlying climate from dominating results. For example, days with Tx over a fixed threshold would be concentrated in the southern part of the domain. Using anomalies is also intuitive from an impacts perspective, as areas with higher temperatures or more precipitation over the historical period would have some adaptive capacity (e.g., community accessible air conditioning, flood prevention infrastructure). data.text: This article presents new quantitative results on the distribution of residential green space for people with disabilities in the United States, building on and bridging scholarly research in two distinct domains: one involving approaches that quantify disparities in green space access among racialized minorities and socioeconomically disadvantaged groups, and the other using qualitative methods that demonstrate that most green spaces remain inaccessible and unwelcoming to disabled visitors. Using generalized additive models (GAMs) that controlled for demographic factors and climatological characteristics, we find that residential areas with more green space generally have a higher proportion of disabled residents. The statistical results run counter to expectations from the literature, thus complicating the prevailing narrative and indicating a need for mixed-methods research to examine multiple dimensions of access and environmental justice. Using cluster analysis to assess spatial trends, we detect residential clusters of high disability and low green space and find that they are located in predominantly non-White, urban, and more socioeconomically disadvantaged neighborhoods compared to clusters of high disability and high green space. Cluster analysis results suggest that there are inequities in green space access at the intersection of disability, race, and class, as well as across the urban-rural continuum.

Study Area

The study area is the continental United States, which comprises forty-eight conterminous states and the District of Columbia. We omitted Alaska, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico because our cluster analysis methods rely on polygon contiguity and these areas are not contiguous to the continental United States.

The United States is a large region with diverse demographics and green space availability. Nearly 20 percent of the population has a disability (U.S. Census Bureau Public Information Office 2016), which is a higher prevalence than the global estimate of 15 percent (Kostanjsek et al. 2013). Green space provision is spatially heterogeneous, with more coverage in rural areas compared to urban ones (Wen et al. 2013). At the same time, green space availability has been trending downward nationally with rising urbanization (Nowak and Greenfield 2018). As green space coverage declines, it becomes increasingly urgent to quantify disparities in green space distribution and to identify localities with a critical lack of green space.

Data

Our data set is at the scale of census tracts and includes data collected during the year 2010 or close to it. Census tracts are common proxies for neighborhoods and are widely used to represent residential neighborhood characteristics, including green space coverage (Wen et al. 2013). We used the TIGER/Line shapefile for the tract boundaries (U.S. Census Bureau 2012).

Demographic data were downloaded from the National Historical Geographic Information System, which came from the U.S. Census Bureau ' s 2010 decennial census and the 2008 -2012 American Community Survey (ACS; Manson et al. 2019). We obtained data on disability, age, sex, household income, educational attainment, race and ethnicity, and employment. The Census Bureau defines disability as the presence or absence of limitations related to vision, hearing, cognitive, ambulatory, independent living, and self-care capacity. One caveat is that disabled, low-income, and racialized individuals are ' hard-to-count ' (Lee et al. n.d.), rendering disability more visible among White, wealthier populations.

To distinguish census tracts across the urban -rural continuum, we used 2010 Rural-Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) codes from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (2020). We categorized census tracts as metropolitan, micropolitan, or rural. These categories are determined by levels of urbanization, population density, and daily commuting patterns.

Methods

Data Processing: NDVI and Tree Canopy. There were two stages of data processing for NDVI and tree canopy. First, we used zonal statistics from the exactextractr package in R version 4.0.2 (Baston 2021; R Core Team 2021) to calculate mean NDVI (250 m) and mean percentage tree canopy (30 m) for each census tract. The exactextractr package allows cells to be partially covered by zones and weighs cell values by the covered area fraction, unlike most other implementations of zonal statistics that only consider each raster cell to be either completely within or outside of overlaid polygon zones. The result is more accurate summaries, particularly for small tracts where a large proportion of cells overlaid by the tract are ones that intersect tract boundaries. To our knowledge, this is also a higher performance implementation than other R methods and makes computations for the entire conterminous United States more tractable.

Then, with the outputs, we calculated the empirical cumulative distribution function (ECDF) of tracts within each climate class for mean NDVI and mean percentage tree canopy. In doing so, we rescaled their values to range from zero to one relative to their climate. This allows green space values to be comparable between climates. For example, the Southeast where it is more temperate is much greener than the Southwest where it is more arid; thus, the Southeast ' s green space will be higher on average than that in the Southwest. Introduction

† Department of Environmental Medicine & Public Health, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, USA

T o date, widespread interest in green spaces and their health benefits has generated two distinctive areas of geographic research (Foley 2018). One line of research uses spatial analysis to quantify disparities in access to green spaces among different populations and estimate their associations with health outcomes (Foley 2018; Labib, Lindley, and Huck 2020). This scholarship reflects increasing attention to inequities in environmental benefits in the environmental justice literature since the late 1970s, a shift from environmental justice ' s historical focus on environmental harms amid marginalized populations (Byrne 2017). A substantive body of environmental justice research focuses on distributive justice of urban green spaces -the notion that there should be equal allocation of green space regardless of social axes of difference (Byrne 2017). In practice, distributive justice examines whether different populations have equivalent levels of access in terms of green space number or size, proximity, or green space per capita (Byrne 2017). Scholars have found unequal distributions of urban green space in the United States, with racialized minorities and socioeconomically disadvantaged neighborhoods having significantly worse access to green space than predominantly White and wealthy neighborhoods (Heynen, Perkins, and Roy 2006; Dai 2011; Duncan et al. 2013). Other studies find that although disadvantaged groups live closer to parks compared to privileged groups, they tend to have access to smaller, lower quality parks (Rigolon 2016; Williams et al. 2020). From this evidence, it is clear that environmental injustice and racism figure into the inequitable allocation of green space and that marginalized communities are deprived of the restorative benefits of such spaces.

What Counts as Green Space (Access)?

Green spaces are natural environs that include trees, grass, parks, forests, natural reserves, greenways, and community gardens. A customary approach to quantifying green space is using a vegetation index or a land-use database (James et al. 2015). Vegetation indexes are developed using satellite imagery that captures light reflected by green plants and thus characterizes a terrain ' s greenness. Of these indexes, the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) is the most used in epidemiological studies (James et al. 2015). Land-use databases classify land into categories based on their primary use. Categories relevant to green spaces include tree canopy, forests, and open space. Yet another approach is to measure the distribution of parks or open spaces and people ' s proximity to them. In our study, we use and compare data from a vegetation index and a land-use database. We considered using park data, but in our review of national data sets, we found that they have limited coverage of local parks.

Disability and Inaccessible Green Spaces

In 1990, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) was signed into law, prohibiting discrimination against disabled individuals in the United States. Although this generated guidelines for making parks and playgrounds more accessible and inclusive (e.g., via the 2000 ADA Accessibility Guidelines for Play Areas and the 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design), many recreational spaces continue to be inaccessible, thus restricting disabled people ' s access to these spaces and their participation in recreational activities (Younker 2010; Rimmer et al. 2017; Calder, Sole, and Mulligan 2018). Furthermore, these guidelines only include accommodations for a narrow range of disabilities (e.g., wheelchair users), overlooking access issues for individuals with other disabilities (e.g., hearing impairment, visual impairment, cognitive disability). To design green spaces that are truly inclusive, access issues must be considered for all people with diverse disabilities.

data.text: The effects of heat waves on traffic collisions require investigation to improve traffic safety during extreme heat events. A time-stratified case-crossover design was used to examine associations between heat waves and traffic collisions in Alabama between May and September from 2009 to 2018. We derived a heat wave index, defined as the daily mean temperature greater than the 95th percentile for two or more consecutive days, by meteorological data from Phase 2 of the North American Land Data Assimilation System. We obtained traffic collision records from the Alabama Department of Transportation. A nonsignificant and negative association between traffic collisions and heat waves was noted, with a 1.4 percent decrease (95 percent confidence interval [CI] [-3.1 percent, 0.4 percent]) in traffic collisions on heat wave days compared to non-heat wave days. Similar results were found when the analysis was stratified by driver-related factors (i.e., gender, age, race, employment status, and driver residence distances), vehicle-related factors (i.e., vehicle usage), and collision-related factors (i.e., rural or urban roads, speed limits, and intersections). A significant and positive association was observed on heat wave days without precipitation, however (23.5 percent increase; 95 percent CI [7.3 percent, 42.3 percent]). In conclusion, traffic collisions were not associated with heat waves in many collision-related conditions in Alabama.

Study Design and Statistical Analysis

A time-stratified case-crossover design, which is suitable for assessing short-term exposure with acute outcomes, was applied in this study to examine the association between heat waves and road traffic collisions (Crouse et al. 2012; Liu et al. 2017; Wu, Zaitchik, and Gohlke 2018; Zhan et al. 2020). This study design was proposed by Maclure (1991) and frequently used in environmental health studies (Basu, Dominici, and Samet 2005; Janes, Sheppard, and Lumley 2005a, 2005b; Crouse et al. 2012; Tong, Wang, and Guo 2012). In case-crossover designs, each collision-involved driver serves as his or her own control; therefore, known and unknown timeinvariant confounders, such as demographic factors (e.g., age, gender, and socioeconomic status), individual characteristics (e.g., lifestyle and physiological status), seasonality, and overlap bias, are inherently adjusted by study design. In other words, the casecrossover design emulates a retrospective nonrandomized crossover study. In this design, each case event (a traffic collision) is matched with a counterfactual control exposure period. In the time-stratified sampling design, all days that are on the same days of the week and within the same month as the case days were selected as control periods. For example, days of the week within calendar months could define strata so that the exposure for a case occurring on Monday, 6 July 2015, would be compared with exposure occurring on all other Mondays in July (i.e., 13, 20, and 27 July

Traffic Collision Records

We obtained the records ( N ¼ 493,829) of drivers involved in road traffic collisions in Alabama for the warm months (May -September) of 2009 through 2018 from ALDOT. Each record included the driver ' s demographic information (gender, age group, race, and employment status), collision date, road functional class, collision location (with the latitudinal and longitudinal information), self-reported vehicle usage, and collision-related factors (i.e., rural or urban roads, whether occurred at the intersection, and speed limits) reported by the police. We selected records with valid latitudinal and longitudinal information (492,500 records, approximately 99.7 percent of total records) for analysis.

Heat Wave Indexes

Heat waves are measured using different approaches without a widely accepted definition (Smith, Zaitchik, and Gohlke 2013). In this study, heat waves were defined as the daily mean temperature above the 95th percentile for two or more consecutive days (i.e., HI95th) because researchers have found this relatively simple metric to be predictive of adverse health outcomes (Anderson and Bell 2011; Kent et al. 2014). We used three other daily mean temperature -based heat wave indexes (HIs), which involved using 90th, 98th, and 99th percentile thresholds (i.e., HI90th, HI98th, and HI99th), to confirm our results made by HI95th (Supplemental Table S.1). In the first step, all historical daily temperatures in the warm seasons (1 May -30 September) from 2009 to 2018 at the same grid cell were ranked to calculate its percentile threshold for that specific grid cell. Then, we marked a heat wave day (taking HI95th as the example) for the grid cell if its daily mean temperature on that day was higher than the 95th historical daily mean temperature at the same grid cell for two or more consecutive days. We mapped the 95th percentile threshold grids ( N ¼ 915) in Figure 1. Introduction

C limate change is recognized as a contributing factor to increasingly frequent, intense, and prolonged extreme heat events (Meehl and Tebaldi 2004). Compared to other regions of the United States, the Southeast experienced the most widespread increase in heat wave days from 1979 to 2011 (Smith, Zaitchik, and Gohlke 2013). In Alabama, each ZIP code had an average of approximately 125 heat wave days (defined as one day or more with a maximum daily heat index of > 80  F), which accounts for 82 percent of the 153 days from May to September (Kent et al. 2014).

Extreme heat events are considered significant contributing factors to the increased frequency and severity of road collisions (Qiu and Nixon 2008). Approximately 24 percent of road traffic collisions in the United States every year are related to adverse weather conditions (Goodwin 2003). Moreover, extreme heat events are likely to coincide with other adverse weather conditions, such as precipitation, intense solar radiation, and high humidity, posing an increased threat to traffic safety. For example, a sharp temperature rise likely affects atmospheric water storage and thus the magnitude, frequency, and intensity of rainfall (Shahid and Minhans 2016). Temperature changes can also affect humidity; high humidity can cloud windows and windscreens and reduce visibility (Al-Harbi, Yassin, and Shams 2012). In addition, human work capacity declines in high-temperature environments (Kjellstrom et al. 2009; Basaga ~ na et al. 2015), which can increase accident risks (Rowlinson and Jia 2015) and cause heat-related illnesses (e.g., heat exhaustion or stroke) under conditions of prolonged exposure (Arcury et al. 2015). Numerous studies have shown that driver performance declines in hot environments. People might become irritable and drowsy, tend to miss signals, drift out of their lane, and make large steering adjustments (Zhou et al. 2014; Basaga ~ na et al. 2015). High road surface temperatures could also cause vehicle breakdowns (e.g., flat tires) and make roads soften or buckle, which could lead to collisions (Vajda et al. 2014).

Using vehicle air conditioning is common when driving in a hot environment. Data on vehicle air conditioning use in Alabama during our study period are not available, even though previous research showed that vehicle air conditioning use was estimated at between 43 percent and 49 percent in the United States (Farrington and Rugh 2000).
